title: Cache Merging as a Convergent Replicated State for Multi-Agent Latent Reasoning
summary: Multi-agent latent reasoning composes agents' KV-caches into one context for a final agent. Prior work (Agent Primitives) does this by concatenating caches along the sequence axis with RoPE re-encoding, which we call BagMerge. BagMerge is non-commutative, and the best input ordering is unpredictable, shifting with the regime, the latent-step budget, and the model scale. We make this exchange a convergent replicated state. First, CanonicalMerge fixes the layout by content: ordering caches by mean K-norm at a middle layer renders the merged cache byte-identical under any input permutation, verified algorithmically (arity N<=5) and bit-for-bit on real Qwen3-1.7B and 4B state. Second, we separate the replicated state from decode-time layout: the state is a set of content-addressed latent fragments whose merge is set union, a state-based CvRDT (commutative, associative, idempotent, absorbing), and CanonicalMerge is its deterministic render. Because the render is byte-equivalent, every N=2 accuracy number carries over unchanged and re-delivered duplicates are absorbed rather than re-concatenated. On a partitioned-reasoning benchmark, CanonicalMerge matches the best BagMerge ordering in every regime-by-budget-by-ordering cell without knowing which order is best, trading a small, statistically insignificant accuracy margin for an unconditional structural guarantee. The behaviour transfers to real multi-document QA (HotpotQA), while the closest training-free output-fusion baseline (PackLLM) loses by 45 points at matched budget, placing cache-level merging in a regime distinct from output-level fusion. Finally, at k>2 the approach transports and colocates latent traces but does not by itself compose them, which we characterize to motivate future work.

AI.tldr: CanonicalMerge introduces a commutative, associative, idempotent, and absorbing merge operation for multi-agent KV-caches, making the merged state a convergent replicated data type (CvRDT). By ordering caches by mean K-norm at a middle layer, it achieves byte-identical renders regardless of input permutation, matching the best BagMerge ordering without needing to find it, and outperforms output-level fusion baselines like PackLLM by 45 points on HotpotQA.
AI.motivation: Prior multi-agent latent reasoning (Agent Primitives) uses BagMerge — concatenating KV-caches with RoPE re-encoding — which is non-commutative and has unpredictable optimal input ordering that shifts with regime, latent-step budget, and model scale. This creates a practical reliability problem: performance depends on an arbitrary input permutation. The authors seek to make the agent exchange operation a convergent replicated state that is independent of input ordering.
AI.method: The paper proposes two key ideas: (1) CanonicalMerge, which fixes cache layout by content — ordering caches by mean K-norm at a middle layer, yielding byte-identical merged caches under any input permutation (verified for arity N≤5 on Qwen3-1.7B and 4B). (2) Framing the replicated state as a set of content-addressed latent fragments whose merge is set union, forming a state-based CvRDT (commutative, associative, idempotent, absorbing). CanonicalMerge serves as the deterministic render of this state. Duplicate deliveries are absorbed rather than re-concatenated.
AI.result: On a partitioned-reasoning benchmark, CanonicalMerge matches the best BagMerge ordering across every regime-by-budget-by-ordering cell, with only a small, statistically insignificant accuracy margin traded for unconditional structural guarantees. On HotpotQA (multi-document QA), it outperforms the training-free output-fusion baseline PackLLM by 45 points at matched budget. For k>2 agents, the approach transports and colocates latent traces but does not by itself compose them.
AI.conclusion: CanonicalMerge provides a principled, permutation-invariant merge operation for multi-agent KV-caches, eliminating the ordering sensitivity of BagMerge while preserving accuracy. This places cache-level merging in a distinct and superior regime compared to output-level fusion. The k>2 limitation — where traces are colocated but not composed — is characterized as a direction for future work.

title: Simulation Based Reward Function Validation for Multi-Agent On Orbit Inspection
comment: 13 pages, 6 figures. This submission integrates a published correction made to the original manuscript. The DOIs for both the original manuscript as well as the correction are provided
summary: A proposed method for the control of groups of inspection spacecraft is Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL). While MARL has already been employed for this purpose in previous work, the reward functions used focus on reaching a finite set of predetermined inspection points around the target. In this work, we study and develop a generalized reward function for the MARL inspection task informed by the analysis of 3D reconstructions of inspected objects in orbit. Because the reward function is generalized such that any number of images at arbitrary locations may evaluated, we also allow trained agents to have complete control over when images are collected. With this approach, we gather insights into best practices for not only the specific MARL inspection task, but also gain key takeaways informative to the broader inspection task outside of a MARL context.

AI.tldr: A generalized reward function for MARL-based spacecraft inspection is developed using 3D reconstruction analysis, enabling agents to autonomously decide when to capture images from arbitrary locations, yielding insights applicable beyond MARL contexts.
AI.motivation: Previous MARL inspection approaches rely on reaching predetermined inspection points, limiting flexibility. A more generalized reward function is needed to evaluate arbitrary image collections and give agents full control over imaging decisions.
AI.method: The authors develop a generalized reward function for MARL inspection tasks informed by 3D reconstruction analysis of inspected orbital objects, allowing evaluation of any number of images at arbitrary locations, and enabling agents to autonomously control image acquisition timing.
AI.result: The approach yields insights into best practices for MARL inspection tasks and produces key takeaways that are informative to the broader spacecraft inspection problem outside of MARL-specific contexts.
AI.conclusion: A reconstruction-informed, generalized reward function enhances MARL-based inspection by removing the constraint of predetermined inspection points, and the findings generalize to non-MARL inspection scenarios.

title: Congestion-Based Slot Pricing in a Railway Auction Game
summary:
We present a multi-agent system for studying the allocation of discrete, congested resources among heterogeneous strategic agents, motivated by the problem of railway slot allocation under deregulation. Multiple operator-agents, differing in size and capacity, interact through a shared auction mechanism over repeated rounds under time-constrained decision-making. The mechanism combines a congestion-based base price that increases with aggregate demand with an asymmetric corrective adjustment that penalises the agent requesting the most slots and rewards the agent requesting the fewest, and is designed to mitigate strategic dominance by large agents while preserving transparency and congestion sensitivity. We formulate the interaction as a repeated game with incomplete information and implement the system as a real-time, web-based multi-agent environment in which human participants control individual agents and observe live marginal-cost and competitor feedback.
  We report exploratory observations from two structured sessions with domain experts acting as operator-agents. The congestion mechanism responds to aggregate demand as designed and the corrective incentives are actively triggered, but agents representing large operators persist with high-request strategies despite the penalty, suggesting that corrective pricing is necessary but not sufficient to neutralise strategic dominance in this multi-agent setting. A post-session debrief indicates that participants' decisions were driven by the assumed agent role rather than personal disposition, and provides qualitative support for strategic motives, such as preserving market presence and raising rivals' costs, operating alongside short-term profit maximisation. We discuss implications for multi-agent mechanism design under asymmetric budgets and outline directions for analytical validation and larger-scale multi-agent experiments.

AI.tldr: A multi-agent auction system for allocating congested resources (e.g., railway slots) reveals that corrective pricing mechanisms partially mitigate but do not fully neutralize strategic dominance by large operators, as agents prioritize market presence and raising rivals' costs over short-term profit.
AI.motivation: Deregulation of railway slot allocation introduces heterogeneous strategic agents (operators of varying size/capacity) competing for discrete congested resources. Standard auction mechanisms risk strategic dominance by large agents, motivating the design of transparent, congestion-sensitive mechanisms with corrective incentives to level the playing field.
AI.method: A repeated game with incomplete information is implemented as a real-time web-based multi-agent environment. The auction mechanism uses a congestion-based base price (increasing with aggregate demand) plus an asymmetric corrective adjustment that penalizes the highest-requesting agent and rewards the lowest-requesting agent. Two structured sessions were conducted with domain experts as human operator-agents, with live marginal-cost and competitor feedback.
AI.result: The congestion mechanism responds to aggregate demand as designed and corrective incentives are triggered. However, large operators persist with high-request strategies despite penalties. Post-session debriefs reveal decisions are driven by assumed agent roles rather than personal disposition, with qualitative evidence for strategic motives (market presence preservation, raising rivals' costs) alongside short-term profit maximization.
AI.conclusion: Corrective pricing is necessary but insufficient to neutralize strategic dominance in asymmetric multi-agent settings. Mechanism design must account for strategic motives beyond short-term profit maximization. Future work includes analytical validation and larger-scale multi-agent experiments.

title: STRUCTSURVEY: Structured Agentic Retrieval for Automated Survey Paper Generation
comment: 8 pages, 1 figure, appendices, SurgeLLM, RAG4Reports, ACL
summary: The rapid growth of scientific publications makes it increasingly difficult to track and synthesize research progress. While Large Language Models (LLMs) can support automated survey generation, existing methods retrieve unstructured data and require models to infer conceptual, methodological, and taxonomic relations from raw text at generation time. We introduce STRUCTSURVEY, a hierarchical multi-agent framework that shifts structural reasoning from generation to retrieval by dynamically constructing graph-based representations of entities, relations, and topical taxonomies. We evaluate STRUCTSURVEY on a new reference-grounded benchmark of ACL survey papers for reproducible long-form scientific summarization. Compared with embedding-only retrieval baselines, STRUCTSURVEY improves ROUGE-1 recall by +2.9 and ROUGE-2 recall by +1.0 on average, without reducing precision. It also improves LLM-as-a-Judge ratings for logical structure, depth, and synthesis, showing that explicit structural retrieval yields surveys closer to human-written organization and reasoning.

AI.tldr: STRUCTSURVEY is a multi-agent framework that builds graph-based representations during retrieval (rather than generation) to produce better-structured, more coherent scientific surveys, demonstrating improved ROUGE scores and human-like logical organization.
AI.motivation: The explosion of scientific publications makes manual survey writing infeasible. Existing LLM-based survey generation methods retrieve unstructured text and force models to infer conceptual, methodological, and taxonomic relations on-the-fly during generation, leading to poor structural coherence.
AI.method: A hierarchical multi-agent framework that constructs graph-based representations of entities, relations, and topical taxonomies during the retrieval phase (rather than at generation time), effectively shifting structural reasoning upstream. Evaluated on a new reference-grounded ACL benchmark for long-form scientific summarization.
AI.result: Compared to embedding-only retrieval baselines, STRUCTSURVEY improved ROUGE-1 recall by +2.9 and ROUGE-2 recall by +1.0 on average, without reducing precision. LLM-as-a-Judge evaluations also showed improvements in logical structure, depth, and synthesis quality.
AI.conclusion: Explicit structural retrieval — embodying entities, relations, and taxonomies in graph form — yields surveys that more closely match human-written organization and reasoning, outperforming generation-time inference approaches.

title: CausalSteward: An Agentic Divide-Conquer-Combine Copilot for Causal Discovery
summary: Learning causal models from high-dimensional data is a significant challenge, particularly in real-world settings where violations of core assumptions lead to causal identifiability issues. Although massive amounts of prior knowledge are available, and contain valuable causal information, effectively integrating this knowledge into the causal discovery process remains an open problem. We introduce CausalSTeward (CAST), a novel human-in-the-loop framework for interactively assembling large causal models. CausalSteward is a multi-agent collaborative system that tackles high-dimensional causality through a divide-and-conquer approach where large clusters of variables are iteratively partitioned and then separately analyzed. Our framework fuses prior knowledge with a data-driven approach by using tailored tools such as retrieval augmented generation and conditional independence tests. Finally, we use this work to examine the capabilities and limitations of causal reasoning in multi-agent frameworks, and how the human-in-the-loop can contribute to accurate and trustworthy results.

AI.tldr: CausalSTeward (CAST) is a human-in-the-loop, multi-agent framework that constructs large causal models from high-dimensional data by iteratively partitioning variable clusters and integrating prior knowledge with data-driven methods like retrieval augmented generation and conditional independence tests.
AI.motivation: Learning causal models from high-dimensional real-world data is challenging due to frequent violations of core causal assumptions, causing identifiability issues. Although abundant prior knowledge exists, effectively incorporating it into causal discovery remains an open problem.
AI.method: CAST employs a divide-and-conquer strategy where large variable clusters are iteratively partitioned and analyzed separately. It fuses prior knowledge with data-driven causal discovery through retrieval augmented generation and conditional independence tests, all within a multi-agent collaborative system augmented by human oversight.
AI.result: The paper examines the capabilities and limitations of causal reasoning within multi-agent frameworks and evaluates how human-in-the-loop interaction contributes to achieving accurate and trustworthy causal model assembly.
AI.conclusion: Human-in-the-loop multi-agent systems like CAST offer a promising direction for scalable, reliable causal discovery from high-dimensional data by synergistically combining prior knowledge, data-driven tests, and human oversight.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation to Support Railways Engineering Tasks: A Case Study
summary: The growing number and complexity of technical regulations represent an important challenge for all professionals in regulated industries. This paper describes a case study, from design to deployment, of building a Retrieval-Augmented Generation system for the consultation of complex technical regulations in the railway domain. Although developed for the railway sector, this testimony of an industrial experience is of particular value for technical domains where regulatory compliance and accurate information retrieval from complex documentation are essential requirements. It also constitutes a human-centered approach for implementing LLM-powered technical documentation consultation across various regulated industries, balancing technological capabilities with domain expertise.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an industrial case study on designing and deploying a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system for consulting complex technical railway regulations, offering a human-centered methodology applicable across regulated industries.
AI.motivation: The increasing volume and complexity of technical regulations pose a significant burden on professionals in regulated industries, necessitating efficient and accurate information retrieval solutions that balance AI capabilities with domain expertise.
AI.method: The authors describe a full lifecycle case study — from design through deployment — of building a RAG system tailored to the railway domain, employing a human-centered approach that integrates LLM-powered retrieval with domain-specific regulatory knowledge.
AI.result: The paper reports on the practical experience of implementing the RAG system in an industrial railway context, highlighting the system's effectiveness in navigating complex technical regulations and the importance of human-in-the-loop design.
AI.conclusion: A human-centered RAG approach proves valuable for technical documentation consultation in regulated industries. The railway-focused case study provides transferable insights for other domains where regulatory compliance and precise retrieval from complex documents are critical.

title: ExPerT: Personalizing LLM Responses to Users' Domain Expertise via Query-Wise Semantic and Keystroke Behavioral Cues
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used by end users, yet existing personalization methods relying on static profiles or text-only signals fail to capture query-specific expertise variation. We present ExPerT, a query-wise personalization framework that adapts LLM responses to users' query domain expertise by combining semantic and behavioral cues. ExPerT consists of two key components: (i) a semantic-behavioral expertise inference module that jointly interprets query text and keystroke dynamics via in-context LLM prompting, and (ii) an expertise-conditioned response generation that adapts the level of detail, terminology, and conceptual complexity. Our user study with 40 participants and 1270 queries demonstrated that ExPerT reduced expertise inference error by 65.7% compared to the strongest baseline (MAE = 0.398 vs. 1.162) and improved response satisfaction by 17.52% (from 3.71 to 4.36) on a 5-point Likert scale.

AI.tldr: ExPerT is a query-level personalization framework for LLMs that infers user expertise from both query semantics and keystroke dynamics, then adapts response complexity accordingly, significantly outperforming static-profile baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM personalization methods rely on static user profiles or text-only signals, failing to capture how a user's expertise varies across different query domains (e.g., a user may be an expert in physics but a novice in cooking).
AI.method: ExPerT uses two components: (1) a semantic-behavioral expertise inference module that combines query text analysis with keystroke dynamics (typing patterns) via in-context LLM prompting to estimate domain expertise per query; (2) an expertise-conditioned response generation module that adjusts detail level, terminology, and conceptual complexity to match the inferred expertise.
AI.result: In a user study with 40 participants and 1,270 queries, ExPerT reduced expertise inference error (MAE) by 65.7% compared to the best baseline (0.398 vs. 1.162) and improved user satisfaction by 17.52% on a 5-point Likert scale (from 3.71 to 4.36).
AI.conclusion: Integrating behavioral signals like keystroke dynamics with semantic analysis enables accurate, query-specific expertise inference, leading to significantly better personalized LLM responses than static-profile approaches.

title: Embedding Inference Attack
summary: Embedding models are essential components of modern Information Retrieval (IR) systems, yet they are typically hidden behind APIs. Recent works have shown that dense IR system can lead to security vulnerabilities such as embedding inversion attacks. However, such attacks usually require that the attacker knows the embedding model for the attack to be applicable. In this paper, we study IR systems under a black-box setting in which the adversary observes only the unordered set of retrieved documents, without ranking or similarity scores. We demonstrate that in such contexts, tailored queries allow an adversary to identify which embedding model is in use from a set of known model candidate, which we coin as an embedding inference attack (EIA). We also show that certain queries remain discriminative even when the system includes a reranker as a potential defense mechanism. We further validate our method on a real Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system, in which the tailored queries bypass the LLM's tendency to reject inputs it does not recognize as well-formed questions. Finally, we propose and evaluate other mitigation strategies such as similarity thresholds.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces an "embedding inference attack" (EIA) that enables an adversary to identify which embedding model is being used in a black-box IR system by observing only the unordered set of retrieved documents, without access to rankings or similarity scores. The attack remains effective even with reranking defenses and works against real RAG systems. Mitigation strategies like similarity thresholds are also explored.
AI.motivation: Prior embedding inversion attacks assume white-box access to the embedding model. In practice, embedding models are hidden behind APIs, creating a black-box scenario. The authors aim to investigate whether an adversary can infer the underlying embedding model from only the unordered set of retrieved documents, exposing a new privacy/security vulnerability in IR systems.
AI.method: The authors craft tailored, discriminative queries designed to produce distinct retrieval patterns across different candidate embedding models. By issuing these queries to a black-box IR system and observing only the unordered set of returned documents (no scores or rankings), the adversary matches the observed retrieval pattern against known model fingerprints. This is extended to evaluate robustness against reranking defenses, tested on a real RAG system where queries bypass the LLM's input validation, and further assessed against mitigation strategies such as similarity thresholds.
AI.result: Tailored queries successfully identify the embedding model from a candidate set under black-box conditions. The attack remains effective even when a reranker is deployed as a defense. On a real RAG system, the crafted queries circumvent the LLM's tendency to reject non-well-formed inputs. Similarity threshold mitigations are proposed and evaluated, though their effectiveness varies.
AI.conclusion: Black-box embedding inference attacks pose a realistic threat to production IR and RAG systems, as adversaries can fingerprint the underlying embedding model without privileged access. Current defenses like reranking are insufficient, and while mitigation strategies such as similarity thresholds help, the vulnerability highlights a need for stronger protections in deployed IR systems.

title: Benchmarking Code Improvement with Progressive, Adaptive, and Interactive Feedback
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are typically evaluated on code generation and program repair using binary functional correctness: a generated program or patch either passes or fails a test suite. This protocol is simple but coarse, as it ignores partial progress, feedback use, regressions, and the refinement trajectory through which models often improve code. We introduce PAIR-Bench, a progressive and adaptive benchmark for evaluating code improvement: transforming an incorrect or incomplete program into a more correct one through feedback-guided refinement. PAIR-Bench uses progressive hinting, a structured feedback protocol with two controls. Failure-region control determines what the feedback targets by grouping hidden failing tests into failure scenarios, while hint-depth control determines how much repair-relevant information is revealed, from coarse symptoms to implementation-level guidance. This design enables PAIR-Bench to measure whether a model repairs targeted failures, generalizes beyond the hint, preserves already-correct behavior, and how much assistance it requires. By evaluating repair trajectories progressive metrics rather than only final pass/fail outcomes, PAIR-Bench provides a finer-grained assessment of LLM code-improvement capability.

AI.tldr: PAIR-Bench is a new benchmark that evaluates LLMs on code improvement through progressive, feedback-guided refinement, using structured hinting with failure-region and hint-depth controls to measure repair trajectories rather than just binary pass/fail outcomes.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM evaluation protocols for code generation and program repair rely solely on binary functional correctness (pass/fail), which ignores partial progress, feedback utilization, regressions, and the iterative refinement trajectory. A finer-grained assessment framework is needed.
AI.method: PAIR-Bench introduces progressive hinting with two control dimensions: (1) failure-region control, which groups hidden failing tests into failure scenarios to target feedback; and (2) hint-depth control, which varies the granularity of repair-relevant information from coarse symptoms to implementation-level guidance. Evaluation uses progressive metrics that track repair trajectories, generalization beyond hints, preservation of correct behavior, and the level of assistance required.
AI.result: PAIR-Bench enables measurement of whether a model repairs targeted failures, generalizes beyond the hint, preserves already-correct behavior, and how much assistance it requires — providing finer-grained assessment than binary pass/fail outcomes.
AI.conclusion: PAIR-Bench offers a more nuanced, trajectory-aware evaluation framework for LLM code-improvement capability, capturing the refinement process rather than only the final outcome.

title: TokenScope: Token-Level Explainability and Interpretability for Code-Oriented Tasks in Large Language Models
summary: Understanding how Large Language Models (LLMs) make token-level decisions during code generation remains a major challenge for both researchers and practitioners. While recent tools provide insights into model internals or generation outcomes, they often lack decoding-time signals, fine-grained uncertainty measures, and interactive mechanisms for exploring alternative generation paths. We present TokenScope, an interactive interpretability and analysis tool for decoder-based LLMs that exposes token-level metrics, attention patterns, and structural information during generation. TokenScope supports interactive token replacement, counterfactual branching, and code-aware aggregation via abstract syntax trees. By unifying decoding-time signals with structural program analysis, TokenScope enables systematic investigation of LLM behaviour during code generation.

AI.tldr: TokenScope is an interactive interpretability tool for LLM-based code generation that provides token-level metrics, attention patterns, and decoding-time signals, enabling counterfactual branching and AST-based structural analysis.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM interpretability tools for code generation lack decoding-time signals, fine-grained uncertainty measures, and interactive mechanisms for exploring alternative generation paths, leaving a gap in understanding token-level model decisions.
AI.method: TokenScope exposes token-level metrics (uncertainty, probabilities), attention patterns, and structural information during decoding. It supports interactive token replacement, counterfactual branching (exploring alternative generation paths), and code-aware aggregation via abstract syntax trees (ASTs).
AI.result: The paper presents TokenScope as a tool; it unifies decoding-time signals with structural program analysis to enable systematic investigation of LLM behaviour during code generation. (Specific empirical results are not detailed in the abstract.)
AI.conclusion: By bridging decoding-time interpretability signals with structural code analysis, TokenScope enables researchers and practitioners to systematically investigate how LLMs make token-level decisions during code generation.

title: Multilayer Q-Matrix-Embedded Neural Network for Cognitive Diagnosis (M-QCDNet): Structure-Aware Deep Learning Architecture for Psychometric Interpretability
summary: The research proposes a multilayer Q-matrix-embedded neural network for cognitive diagnosis (M-QCDNet), which integrates the structural interpretability of cognitive diagnostic models (CDMs) with the deep learning neural network (NN). M-QCDNet structures the item-skill relationship using the Q-matrix as a structural prior, ensuring latent mastery profiles remain interpretable and consistent with cognitive theory, followed by the proposed loss function with an L2 penalty to penalize skills not aligned with the Q-matrix and to balance predictive performance and structural alignment. Corresponding evaluation matrices, the interpretable alignment-based metrics that quantify the degree to which predicted skill activations correspond to item-level skills, were further developed. M-QCDNet offers practical benefits for classroom practice, enabling early detection of learning difficulties and supporting mastery-based interventions. By embedding diagnostic validity into model design, M-QCDNet bridges psychometric transparency and neural flexibility, advancing interpretable, fair, and actionable AI for cognitive diagnostics.

AI.tldr: M-QCDNet is a neural cognitive diagnostic model that embeds the Q-matrix as a structural prior, ensuring interpretable mastery profiles aligned with cognitive theory, and introduces alignment-based evaluation metrics and an L2 penalty to balance predictive performance with structural fidelity.
AI.motivation: To bridge the gap between the structural interpretability of traditional cognitive diagnostic models (CDMs) and the flexibility of deep neural networks, addressing the need for AI-driven diagnostic tools that remain psychometrically transparent, fair, and actionable in educational settings.
AI.method: A multilayer neural network architecture that incorporates the Q-matrix (item-skill mapping) as an embedded structural prior; a novel loss function with an L2 penalty term that penalizes skill activations inconsistent with the Q-matrix; and newly proposed interpretable alignment-based evaluation metrics that quantify how well predicted skill activations correspond to item-level skills.
AI.result: M-QCDNet achieves a balance between predictive performance and structural alignment with the Q-matrix, yielding mastery profiles that remain interpretable and consistent with cognitive theory, while the proposed alignment-based metrics provide meaningful quantification of diagnostic validity.
AI.conclusion: By embedding diagnostic validity directly into model design, M-QCDNet successfully integrates psychometric transparency with neural network flexibility, advancing the development of interpretable, fair, and actionable AI systems for cognitive diagnosis in classroom practice.

title: PACE: A Neuro-Symbolic Framework for Plausible and Actionable Counterfactual Explanations
summary: Counterfactual explanations explain machine learning predictions by identifying minimal input changes that would alter a model's decision. Although many existing methods successfully generate prediction-changing alternatives, they often produce unrealistic or infeasible recommendations due to a lack of explicit mechanisms for incorporating domain knowledge and intervention constraints. Neuro-symbolic AI offers a promising direction by combining data-driven predictive models with symbolic reasoning capable of representing human-understandable rules and feasible actions. This paper presents PACE, a modular neuro-symbolic framework for generating feasibility-aware counterfactual explanations. The framework separates prediction and reasoning into two components: a neural predictive model for classification and a symbolic reasoning layer that enforces domain-specific constraints during counterfactual generation. By explicitly modeling feasible interventions, the framework produces explanations consistent with domain knowledge while remaining interpretable and actionable. The approach is model-agnostic and adaptable to domains requiring realistic decision support. A case study is conducted on the Adult Income dataset, combining a multilayer perceptron classifier with Answer Set Programming (ASP) rules encoding feasible modifications to education, occupation, and working hours while preserving immutable attributes. Results highlight the trade-off between counterfactual validity and plausibility and show that symbolic constraints yield explanations that better satisfy domain-specific feasibility requirements, illustrating the potential of neuro-symbolic methods for transparent, feasibility-aware counterfactual explanation in explainable AI.

AI.tldr: PACE is a modular neuro-symbolic framework that generates feasibility-aware counterfactual explanations by combining a neural classifier with Answer Set Programming (ASP) symbolic constraints, ensuring domain-consistent and actionable recommendations.
AI.motivation: Existing counterfactual explanation methods often produce unrealistic or infeasible recommendations because they lack explicit mechanisms for incorporating domain knowledge and intervention constraints. Neuro-symbolic AI offers a solution by uniting data-driven prediction with symbolic reasoning that enforces human-understandable rules and feasible actions.
AI.method: PACE separates the pipeline into two components: (1) a multilayer perceptron (MLP) classifier for the predictive task, and (2) a symbolic reasoning layer using Answer Set Programming (ASP) rules that encode domain-specific constraints — such as feasible modifications to education, occupation, and working hours while preserving immutable attributes like age or gender. This modular, model-agnostic design generates counterfactuals by searching for minimal changes that flip the prediction while satisfying ASP-encoded feasibility constraints.
AI.result: A case study on the Adult Income dataset demonstrates a clear trade-off between counterfactual validity (successfully flipping predictions) and plausibility (domain feasibility). The symbolic ASP constraints yield explanations that better satisfy domain-specific feasibility requirements compared to unconstrained generation.
AI.conclusion: Neuro-symbolic methods like PACE show strong potential for producing transparent, feasibility-aware counterfactual explanations, bridging the gap between accurate model predictions and actionable, domain-consistent decision support in explainable AI.

title: AgentsCAD: Automated Design for Manufacturing of FDM Parts via Multi-Agent LLM Reasoning and Geometric Feature Recognition
summary: Parts manufactured with Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM) often require Design for Additive Manufacturing (DFAM) modifications to ensure printability, structural integrity, and reduced post-processing. Current slicers identify defects such as steep overhangs but are unable to modify the underlying geometry. This work presents AgentsCAD, a multi-agent system that bridges raw boundary-representation (B-Rep) geometry and Large Language Model (LLM) reasoning to automate targeted DFM. The workflow begins by parsing a STEP file. The agentic system detects overhangs above a 45°threshold, constructs a face-adjacency topology graph, and optionally injects semantic feature labels from a GraphSAGE model trained on MFCAD++ (59,665 parts), before dispatching a Claude Sonnet design-reasoning agent that recommends reorientations, fillets, chamfers, and similar modifications. A GPT-4o vision-language verifier inspects rendered views to confirm geometric integrity. Outputs include a modified STEP file and a human-readable report. A test case on a birdhouse model demonstrates that the system correctly diagnoses overhangs, selects appropriate defect mitigation strategies, and proposes physically valid corrections, partially solving the geometry-to-language translation problem central to LLM-driven CAD modification.

AI.tldr: AgentsCAD is a multi-agent LLM system that automates DFAM modifications on B-Rep CAD geometries by detecting overhangs, reasoning about corrections, and verifying results using vision-language models.
AI.motivation: Current FDM slicers can detect defects like steep overhangs but cannot modify the underlying geometry. There is a gap between geometric analysis and automated design correction, requiring a system that bridges B-Rep geometry with LLM reasoning for targeted DFAM modifications.
AI.method: A multi-agent pipeline that parses STEP files, detects overhangs above 45° via face-adjacency topology graphs, optionally enriches geometry with GraphSAGE-learned semantic feature labels (trained on MFCAD++ with 59,665 parts), dispatches a Claude Sonnet agent for design reasoning (recommending reorientations, fillets, chamfers), and uses a GPT-4o vision-language verifier to confirm geometric integrity via rendered views.
AI.result: A birdhouse test case demonstrated the system correctly diagnoses overhangs, selects appropriate mitigation strategies, and proposes physically valid corrections, producing a modified STEP file and a human-readable report.
AI.conclusion: The system partially solves the geometry-to-language translation problem central to LLM-driven CAD modification, showing that agentic architectures can effectively bridge B-Rep geometry and LLM reasoning for automated DFAM.

title: Bi-NAS: Towards Effective and Personalized Explanation for Recommender Systems via Bi-Level Neural Architecture Search
summary: Recommender systems are vital in helping users navigate vast amounts of information, offering personalized suggestions and effective explanations for these recommendations. While previous efforts have attempted to provide such explanations, evaluating their effectiveness across various scenarios remains a challenge. Enhancing these explanations is essential for improving user engagement, trust, and decision-making. To facilitate effective explanations within the recommender system, we propose a Bi-level Neural Architecture Search (Bi-NAS) framework to optimize explanations. This approach simultaneously refines cross-attention mechanisms and feature interaction functions by exploring both intra-layer and inter-layer design spaces. Furthermore, we integrate Large Language Models (LLMs) to enhance explanation generation, leveraging zero-shot prompting to produce more effective and personalized justifications. By aligning user feature preferences with item quality scores, our approach ensures that explanations reflect both user intent and item attributes, improving transparency and reasoning depth. Extensive evaluations on four real-world datasets demonstrate that Bi-NAS not only boosts recommendation accuracy but also significantly improves the effectiveness of explanations for recommender systems, providing users with clear and reliable insights into the suggestions they receive.

AI.tldr: Bi-NAS, a Bi-level Neural Architecture Search framework, jointly optimizes cross-attention mechanisms and feature interaction functions for recommender systems, enhanced by LLM-generated explanations via zero-shot prompting, achieving both improved recommendation accuracy and explanation quality across four real-world datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing recommender systems struggle to provide effective, personalized explanations across diverse scenarios, and evaluating explanation quality remains challenging. Better explanations are critical for user engagement, trust, and decision-making, motivating the need for an optimized, automated approach.
AI.method: The Bi-NAS framework performs bi-level neural architecture search over both intra-layer and inter-layer design spaces to simultaneously optimize cross-attention mechanisms and feature interaction functions. It additionally integrates LLMs with zero-shot prompting to generate personalized explanations, aligning user feature preferences with item quality scores to ensure transparency and reasoning depth.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on four real-world datasets show that Bi-NAS improves both recommendation accuracy and explanation effectiveness, delivering clear, reliable, and interpretable insights to users.
AI.conclusion: The Bi-NAS framework successfully bridges the gap between recommendation performance and explanation quality by leveraging automated architecture search and LLM-based generation, offering a scalable solution for transparent and trustworthy recommender systems.

title: Mitigating Confirmation Bias through Hand-Drawing Videos
comment: Accepted to IEEE VIS 2026 Short Papers. 4 pages plus references
summary: Understanding data visualizations is essential for informed decision-making, yet interpretation is often shaped and even distorted by prior beliefs. We investigate whether an embodied pedagogical approach, in which viewers observe the dynamic hand-drawing of a visualization, can mitigate confirmation bias and improve interpretation accuracy. We conducted a study comparing static bar charts to videos in which charts are constructed through hand-drawing, across contexts that either align with or challenge participants' prior beliefs. The results indicate that hand-drawn videos helped participants accurately interpret data, even when the data conflicted with their prior beliefs. This approach also reduced belief-consistent errors and increased belief-overriding responses. These findings suggest that exposing the construction process of a visualization supports more accurate reasoning and mitigates the influence of confirmation bias. Consequently, this work introduces a promising design space for bias-mitigating data interfaces.

AI.tldr: Hand-drawn visualization videos reduce confirmation bias and improve data interpretation accuracy compared to static bar charts, especially when data conflicts with viewers' prior beliefs.
AI.motivation: Data visualizations are often misinterpreted due to confirmation bias — viewers' prior beliefs distort how they read charts. The authors investigate whether revealing the construction process of a visualization through hand-drawing can counteract this cognitive bias.
AI.method: A controlled study comparing two conditions: static bar charts versus videos of bar charts being constructed via hand-drawing. Stimuli were presented across contexts that either aligned with or contradicted participants' prior beliefs. Accuracy, belief-consistent errors, and belief-overriding responses were measured.
AI.result: Hand-drawn videos significantly improved interpretation accuracy when data conflicted with prior beliefs. This condition also reduced belief-consistent errors and increased belief-overriding responses, demonstrating a mitigation of confirmation bias.
AI.conclusion: Exposing the construction process of visualizations fosters more accurate reasoning and diminishes confirmation bias. The work opens a novel design space for bias-mitigating data interfaces rooted in embodied, process-oriented presentation.

title: Cognitive Firewall: A Proactive, Zero-Trust, Multi-Gate Framework for LLM Safety
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can be induced to produce harmful content through multi turn strategies in which no single user message appears clearly unsafe. Existing runtime safeguards commonly evaluate prompts or responses as isolated messages, which limits their ability to recover ac-cumulated intent, verify asserted authority, or detect harmful objectives decomposed across a dialogue. This paper presents the Cognitive Firewall, a proactive runtime oversight framework that interposes an independent oversight model between a user and a protected target mod l. The framework decomposes safety assessment into four categorical gates: an intent gate that identi-fies the operational objective of a request, a zero trust context gate that treats claimed roles and permissions as unverified evidence, a consistency gate that detects escalation and decomposition across turns, and an output risk gate that inspects candidate responses before release. Gate decisions are combined through escalation rather than score averaging, allowing any confident danger signal to block an interaction while preserving an auditable rationale. Experiments on four jailbreak benchmarks and a benign safety test set show that the Cognitive Firewall substantially reduces attack success across single turn, multi turn, authority based, and human crafted attacks. It lowers attack success to 2 percent or below on three attack sets and to 14 percent on the most difficult human crafted set, while maintaining an 8 percent over refusal rate. These results indicate that decomposed, conversation level oversight can improve proactive containment and auditability for LLM safety.

AI.tldr: The Cognitive Firewall is a runtime oversight framework that inserts an independent model between users and target LLMs, decomposing safety assessment into four categorical gates (intent, zero-trust context, consistency, output risk) that escalate confident danger signals to block harmful multi-turn interactions, reducing attack success rates to ≤2% on three benchmarks and 14% on the hardest set with an 8% over-refusal rate.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM safeguards evaluate prompts or responses as isolated messages, making them vulnerable to multi-turn jailbreak strategies where harmful intent is decomposed across turns with no single message appearing clearly unsafe. They cannot recover accumulated intent, verify asserted authority, or detect decomposed harmful objectives across a dialogue.
AI.method: The Cognitive Firewall interposes an independent oversight model between user and target LLM, decomposing safety into four categorical gates: (1) Intent Gate — identifies operational objectives; (2) Zero-Trust Context Gate — treats claimed roles/permissions as unverified evidence; (3) Consistency Gate — detects escalation and decomposition across turns; (4) Output Risk Gate — inspects candidate responses pre-release. Gate decisions are combined via escalation (not score averaging), so any confident danger signal blocks the interaction while preserving auditable rationale.
AI.result: The framework reduced attack success rate to ≤2% on three of four jailbreak benchmarks (single-turn, multi-turn, authority-based) and to 14% on the most difficult human-crafted attack set, with an 8% over-refusal rate on benign inputs.
AI.conclusion: Decomposed, conversation-level oversight via categorical gating with escalation logic improves proactive containment and auditability for LLM safety compared to isolated message-level evaluation.

title: A global predicted-fMRI drive signal from TRIBE does not predict YouTube replay heatmaps
comment: 7 pages, 1 figure. Code, video-ID manifest, and per-video results: https://github.com/mercurialsolo/tribe-replay-heatmaps
summary: Deep multimodal brain-encoding models now predict fMRI responses to naturalistic video with high accuracy. Whether their predicted neural signals also forecast behavioral engagement is unknown. We run TRIBE, the winning model of the 2025 Algonauts brain-encoding challenge (Llama-3.2 + V-JEPA2 + Wav2Vec-BERT), on 48 YouTube videos and reduce its predicted cortical response to a per-second engagement curve, the global field power. Correlated against each video's "most replayed" heatmap, a passively-collected proxy for which moments viewers return to, the curve shows no evidence of predicting re-watch behavior. The pooled position-controlled partial correlation is +0.058 (95% CI [-0.04, 0.15]; one-sample t(47)=1.21, p=0.23), indistinguishable from zero and not significantly above simple loudness and motion baselines (loudness +0.04, paired p=0.74). The raw correlation is also near zero; the moderate values reported for music videos reflect a genre-specific intro/onset-replay artifact rather than content prediction, and do not generalize. The null holds across six cortical-network readouts and under an autocorrelation-preserving permutation test. We release the code, the video-ID manifest, and an acquisition method that works despite YouTube's SABR-only streaming.

AI.tldr: A state-of-the-art brain-encoding model (TRIBE) predicts fMRI responses to videos but fails to forecast which moments viewers re-watch, with correlations indistinguishable from zero and not exceeding simple loudness/motion baselines.
AI.motivation: To test whether deep multimodal brain-encoding models that accurately predict fMRI responses to naturalistic video can also forecast behavioral engagement, specifically re-watch behavior as measured by YouTube's "most replayed" heatmaps.
AI.method: The authors applied TRIBE (Llama-3.2 + V-JEPA2 + Wav2Vec-BERT), the winning model of the 2025 Algonauts challenge, to 48 YouTube videos. They reduced predicted cortical responses to a per-second engagement curve via global field power and correlated these against "most replayed" heatmaps. Analyses included position-controlled partial correlations, comparisons against loudness and motion baselines, six cortical-network readouts, and an autocorrelation-preserving permutation test.
AI.result: The pooled position-controlled partial correlation was +0.058 (95% CI [-0.04, 0.15]; t(47)=1.21, p=0.23), indistinguishable from zero. This was not significantly above loudness (+0.04, paired p=0.74) or motion baselines. Previously reported moderate correlations for music videos were attributed to a genre-specific intro/onset-replay artifact rather than genuine content prediction. The null result held across all six cortical-network readouts and under permutation testing.
AI.conclusion: Brain-encoding models that excel at predicting neural responses do not automatically generalize to predicting naturalistic behavioral engagement. The apparent predictive success in music videos is an artifact, and the null is robust across multiple analysis approaches.

title: Safeguarding LLM Agents from Misalignment through Provenance Analysis
summary: As LLM agents gain increasing access to powerful tools, ensuring that their actions are aligned with the user's intent becomes critical. When an agent's proposed tool invocation deviates from the user's intent -- a phenomenon called misalignment -- it may lead to harmful consequences that are difficult to undo. Existing runtime guardrails rely on an LLM-as-a-judge paradigm that lacks a systematic framework for reasoning about alignment, often producing judgments that are inconsistent or difficult to audit. Motivated by provenance analysis, we propose a provenance-based conceptual framework that formalizes misalignment detection as determining whether a proposed tool call is supported by traceable evidence in the agent's context. Building on this framework, we propose ProvenanceGuard, a multi-stage pipeline that analyzes the agent's action for three types of misalignment before the selected tool is executed and only allows the action to take place when it is considered aligned with the user's input query. We evaluated our proposed approach on two different benchmarks, Agent-SafetyBench and WorkBench, across 10 backbone LLMs. Compared to the LLM-as-a-judge baseline, ProvenanceGuard reduces error rate on misaligned traces from 42.9% to 1.8% on Agent-SafetyBench and from 32.1% to 17.3% on WorkBench, while reducing intervention burden on task-successful traces from 30.5% to 12.8% and introducing no statistically significant increase in unnecessary interventions on aligned traces. These results demonstrate that structured, provenance-based reasoning provides an effective and practical foundation for safeguarding LLM agents from misalignment.

AI.tldr: ProvenanceGuard introduces a provenance-based framework for detecting misalignment in LLM agent tool calls, using a multi-stage pipeline that checks traceable evidence before execution. It reduces misalignment error rates dramatically (42.9%→1.8% on Agent-SafetyBench) compared to LLM-as-a-judge baselines, while also lowering unnecessary interventions on successful traces.
AI.motivation: As LLM agents gain access to powerful tools, misalignment—where a proposed tool invocation deviates from user intent—can cause harmful, irreversible consequences. Existing LLM-as-a-judge guardrails lack a systematic reasoning framework, producing inconsistent and hard-to-audit judgments. The authors are motivated by provenance analysis to create a principled, evidence-based approach to misalignment detection.
AI.method: The authors propose (1) a provenance-based conceptual framework that formalizes misalignment detection as determining whether a proposed tool call is supported by traceable evidence in the agent's context, and (2) ProvenanceGuard, a multi-stage pipeline that analyzes the agent's action for three types of misalignment before tool execution, blocking actions that lack provenance support relative to the user's query.
AI.result: Evaluated on Agent-SafetyBench and WorkBench across 10 backbone LLMs, ProvenanceGuard reduced misalignment error rates from 42.9% to 1.8% (Agent-SafetyBench) and 32.1% to 17.3% (WorkBench). Intervention burden on task-successful traces dropped from 30.5% to 12.8%, with no statistically significant increase in unnecessary interventions on aligned traces.
AI.conclusion: Structured, provenance-based reasoning provides an effective and practical foundation for safeguarding LLM agents against misalignment, outperforming LLM-as-a-judge approaches in both detection accuracy and reduced intervention burden.

title: I\textsuperscript{2}RiMA: Spectral Riemannian Representation with Temporal Attention for Mental Stress Detection based on EEG Signals
summary: Cross-subject EEG stress detection remains challenging because discriminative stress-related patterns are both subject-dependent and frequency-specific. Conventional Riemannian methods model spatial covariance mainly in the time domain, overlooking neural oscillations that are critical for high-level cognitive state decoding, while standard temporal tokenization often fragments inter-slice temporal coherence. To address these limitations, we propose \method{}, an Intra-Inter Riemannian Manifold Attention Network for EEG-based stress detection. \method{} constructs spatial covariance matrices independently at each frequency point and maps them to the SPD tangent space, preserving channel-wise geometry together with frequency-specific discriminative cues. It further introduces frequency cluster aggregation to select informative spectral components and reduce redundancy by forming compact, data-driven frequency clusters aligned with EEG rhythms. Finally, an intra-inter slice attention module adaptively integrates local slice-level spectral dynamics and global temporal context across EEG sequences. Experiments on three datasets show that \method{} consistently outperforms five state-of-the-art baselines, achieving up to 82.78\% balanced accuracy while remaining efficient with only 1.60M parameters and 31.95M FLOPs.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes I²RMA-Net, an attention network operating on Riemannian manifold representations of EEG for cross-subject stress detection. It constructs per-frequency spatial covariance matrices, maps them to tangent space, performs frequency cluster aggregation, and uses intra-inter slice attention to capture both local spectral dynamics and global temporal context.
AI.motivation: Cross-subject EEG stress detection is hindered by two key issues: (1) conventional Riemannian methods model spatial covariance only in the time domain, ignoring frequency-specific neural oscillations critical for cognitive state decoding; (2) standard temporal tokenization disrupts inter-slice temporal coherence. Both subject-dependent and frequency-specific patterns need to be jointly addressed.
AI.method: The proposed I²RMA-Net has three main components: (1) Per-frequency spatial covariance matrix construction mapped to the SPD tangent space, preserving channel geometry and frequency-specific cues; (2) Frequency cluster aggregation that groups informative spectral components into compact, data-driven clusters aligned with EEG rhythms to reduce redundancy; (3) An intra-inter slice attention module that adaptively integrates local slice-level spectral dynamics with global temporal context across EEG sequences.
AI.result: I²RMA-Net consistently outperforms five state-of-the-art baselines on three datasets, achieving up to 82.78% balanced accuracy, while maintaining efficiency with only 1.60M parameters and 31.95M FLOPs.
AI.conclusion: The method effectively addresses cross-subject EEG stress detection by jointly modeling spatial covariance in a frequency-aware manner on the Riemannian manifold and preserving temporal coherence via intra-inter slice attention, achieving strong performance with computational efficiency.

title: Auto-FL-Research: Agentic Search for Federated Learning Algorithms
summary: Federated learning (FL) research often depends on many small but consequential algorithmic choices: optimizer variants, server aggregation rules, local training schedules, normalization, regularization, and model architecture. These choices are expensive to explore manually and difficult to compare fairly when candidate changes can also alter the FL training or evaluation path. In this work, we present Auto-FL-Research (AFR), a constrained coding-agent workflow for FL algorithmic recipe search. Agents may propose and implement candidate training algorithms, including server aggregation rules, client update schedules, local objectives, and registered model variants, while task profiles fix the mutation surface, compute budget, communication contract, and final model evaluation. Each campaign records candidate scores, runtime, edited files, artifacts, and failure status. We evaluate AFR on five healthcare cross-silo FLamby tasks and on grouped-client profiles for the five fixed LEAF datasets plus the LEAF synthetic task. Five-seed repeat evaluations support gains on four FLamby tasks and five of six LEAF profiles, while also exposing seed-sensitive and search-selected failure cases. Same-budget controls show that several gains correspond to FL-recipe changes, whereas other improvements are recovered by fixed-surface scalar controls or fail under repeat or held-out evaluation. These mixed outcomes are part of the contribution: they show how agent-generated candidates can be separated into repeated FL mechanisms, fixed-surface tuning effects, and selected single-run artifacts.

AI.tldr: Auto-FL-Research (AFR) is a constrained coding-agent workflow that automates the search for algorithmic recipes in federated learning, evaluated on healthcare and LEAF benchmarks; results reveal that agent-generated improvements can be decomposed into repeatable FL mechanisms, scalar tuning effects, and irreproducible artifacts.
AI.motivation: FL research requires many interdependent algorithmic choices (optimizers, aggregation rules, local training schedules, normalization, regularization, architecture) that are expensive to explore manually and difficult to compare fairly when candidate changes alter training/evaluation paths. Automating this search is the core motivation.
AI.method: AFR is a constrained coding-agent workflow where agents propose and implement candidate FL training algorithms (server aggregation rules, client update schedules, local objectives, model variants) under task profiles that fix mutation surface, compute budget, communication contract, and evaluation. Each campaign records scores, runtime, edited files, artifacts, and failure status. The system is evaluated on five FLamby cross-silo healthcare tasks and six LEAF tasks (five fixed datasets plus synthetic) with grouped-client profiles, using five-seed repeat evaluations and same-budget controls.
AI.result: AFR achieved gains on four of five FLamby tasks and five of six LEAF profiles, but also exposed seed-sensitive and search-selected failure cases. Same-budget controls revealed that some gains stem from genuine FL-recipe changes, while others are attributable to fixed-surface scalar tuning or fail under repeat/held-out evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Agent-generated FL candidates can be systematically decomposed into three categories: repeatable FL mechanisms, fixed-surface tuning effects, and selected single-run artifacts. This decomposition framework is itself a contribution, enabling more rigorous evaluation of automated FL algorithm search.

title: Adoption and Ecosystem Health: A Longitudinal Analysis of Open-Source Multi-Agent Frameworks
summary: Since ChatGPT's launch in November 2022, open-source agentic frameworks have proliferated, making framework selection important for engineering teams while obscured by popularity signals such as GitHub stars. This paper analyzes 15 major open-source AI agent framework repositories from late 2022 to early 2026, using 808,042 stars, 73,997 pull requests, 86,241 commits, and 987,330 user profiles to assess ecosystem health across awareness, adoption, and retention. Three findings emerge. First, headline popularity is unreliable. Star counts reflect hype cycles and inorganic activity. AutoGPT gained 111,967 stars in one month but converted fewer than 9 contributors per 1,000 stars, defined as contributor density in this research, compared with LangChain's 41. Lower-profile frameworks such as Pydantic-AI show higher contributor density, indicating deeper adoption. Second, mapping awareness against adoption shows that visibility and engagement diverge. MetaGPT and LangFlow have contributor density ratios below 5 even with their high visibility. Openai-agents-python's limited contributor base suggests institutional backing alone does not ensure community depth. By analyzing cross-framework contribution, we discover that LangChain functions as a shared infrastructure, attracting 82.5% of cross-ecosystem contributors. Third, retention drops most steeply in the first 30 days of initial contribution and stabilizes near 90 days. Overall, ecosystem health is better measured by contributor density, cross-ecosystem engagement, and retention than by stars alone. These metrics offer teams a more robust basis for framework evaluation.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates the health of 15 open-source AI agent frameworks using GitHub metrics (808K stars, 74K PRs, 86K commits, 987K user profiles) across awareness, adoption, and retention. It finds that GitHub stars are unreliable indicators of ecosystem health; contributor density, cross-framework engagement, and contributor retention provide more robust evaluation criteria.
AI.motivation: The proliferation of open-source agentic frameworks since ChatGPT's launch has made framework selection difficult for engineering teams, who are often misled by popularity signals like GitHub stars. The authors aim to provide more reliable metrics for assessing ecosystem health beyond headline popularity.
AI.method: Quantitative analysis of 15 major open-source AI agent framework repositories from late 2022 to early 2026, using 808,042 stars, 73,997 pull requests, 86,241 commits, and 987,330 user profiles. Metrics evaluated include: (1) contributor density (contributors per 1,000 stars), (2) awareness vs. adoption mapping, (3) cross-framework contribution patterns, and (4) contributor retention curves over time.
AI.result: Three key findings: (1) Star counts reflect hype cycles and inorganic activity — AutoGPT gained ~112K stars in one month but had a contributor density <9 per 1,000 stars vs. LangChain's 41; lower-profile frameworks like Pydantic-AI showed higher contributor density. (2) Visibility and engagement diverge — MetaGPT and LangFlow had contributor density ratios below 5 despite high visibility; Openai-agents-python's limited contributor base shows institutional backing alone doesn't ensure community depth. LangChain functions as shared infrastructure with 82.5% of cross-ecosystem contributors. (3) Retention drops most steeply in the first 30 days and stabilizes near 90 days.
AI.conclusion: Ecosystem health is better measured by contributor density, cross-ecosystem engagement, and retention than by stars alone. These metrics offer engineering teams a more robust basis for framework evaluation and selection.

title: Mind the Trust Gap: Identifying (Mis)alignments in Teacher-Student Views Toward Control and Agency in K-12 Classroom AI
comment: To be published in Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction, Volume 10, Issue 6, Article CSCW124 (October 2026)
summary: As Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based technologies have been integrated into school classrooms where multiple stakeholders (with different roles) interact with each other, it is critical to deeply understand stakeholder views in the classroom. In particular, prior work has not fully uncovered how teachers' and school students' views might or might not align well with each other, especially in K-12 classrooms. We conducted a speed-dating study using storyboards with 16 school students and 15 school teachers in Germany to investigate alignments and misalignments between their views on student-AI decision-making control in K-12 classroom. Through an explicit pair-matching analysis, we found that students and teachers had misaligned views on several key topics, including how much they trust AI and social and emotional aspects of student learning with AI. Findings also revealed the importance of teacher-student relationships outside of AI use that shape stakeholders' views and interactions. We discuss potential reasons for the observed misaligned views and strategies to fill the perspective gaps. This study illustrates the complexities of preferences in teacher-student-AI interactions that depend on the dynamic relations among the stakeholders.

AI.tldr: A speed-dating study with 16 students and 15 teachers in Germany using storyboards revealed significant misalignments between teachers' and students' views on student-AI decision-making control in K-12 classrooms, particularly regarding trust in AI and the social-emotional dimensions of learning, highlighting that teacher-student relationships outside AI contexts critically shape stakeholder interactions.
AI.motivation: Prior research has not fully examined how K-12 teachers' and students' views on AI in the classroom align or diverge. As AI technologies become more integrated into multi-stakeholder classroom environments, understanding these perspective gaps is critical for effective and harmonious implementation.
AI.method: A speed-dating study using storyboards was conducted with 16 school students and 15 school teachers in Germany. The study employed explicit pair-matching analysis to systematically compare and contrast stakeholder views on student-AI decision-making control in the K-12 classroom setting.
AI.result: Students and teachers held misaligned views on several key topics: the degree of trust placed in AI, and the social and emotional aspects of student learning with AI. Additionally, the quality of teacher-student relationships outside of AI contexts emerged as a significant factor shaping stakeholder views and interactions around AI use.
AI.conclusion: The study illustrates that preferences in teacher-student-AI interactions are complex and contingent upon the dynamic relational context among stakeholders. The authors discuss reasons for the observed misalignments and propose strategies to bridge these perspective gaps.

title: Kara: Efficient Reasoning LLM Serving via Sliding-Window KV Cache Compression
summary: Reasoning language models often generate long chain-of-thought (CoT), which accumulates a massive KV cache during the decoding phase and incurs high decoding latency and limited throughput. To address these issues, KV cache compression has emerged as a promising technique for reducing memory overhead by selectively removing unimportant KV pairs while preserving useful ones for subsequent decoding. Nevertheless, we identify two key limitations in existing KV cache compression methods: 1) their threshold-triggered compression policy may provide limited throughput improvement or even reduce throughput, and may fully eliminate KV pairs from certain blocks of the sequence, potentially worsening information loss. 2) they typically retain either isolated KV pairs or fixed-size chunks with rigid boundaries, failing to preserve important flexible-sized chunks at arbitrary token positions. To overcome these limitations, we propose Kara, a sliding-window KV cache compression method that performs decoding-time compression by operating only on the recently generated context. Kara leverages bidirectional attention to score and select informative KV pairs in the window. To enable flexible preservation of important semantic information, we design a Token2Chunk module to expand a subset of selected KV pairs into chunks. Furthermore, we adapt Kara to PagedAttention and develop KvLLM, an inference framework built upon vLLM, which reduces KV cache memory usage and effectively improves output throughput. Extensive experiments demonstrate consistent performance improvements of proposed Kara and KvLLM.

AI.tldr: Kara is a sliding-window KV cache compression method that uses bidirectional attention to score and selectively retain informative KV pairs, with a Token2Chunk module for flexible chunk preservation. Integrated into vLLM as KvLLM, it reduces memory overhead and improves throughput compared to threshold-triggered compression approaches.
AI.motivation: Long chain-of-thought reasoning generates massive KV caches, causing high decoding latency and limited throughput. Existing KV cache compression methods suffer from two issues: (1) threshold-triggered policies can hurt throughput and risk eliminating entire blocks, and (2) they preserve isolated KV pairs or rigid fixed-size chunks, failing to capture important flexible-sized semantic chunks at arbitrary positions.
AI.method: Kara employs a sliding-window approach operating only on recently generated context during decoding. It uses bidirectional attention to score and select informative KV pairs within the window. A Token2Chunk module expands selected KV pairs into flexible-sized chunks to preserve important semantic information. The method is adapted to PagedAttention and implemented as KvLLM, an inference framework built on vLLM.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate consistent performance improvements from both Kara and the KvLLM inference framework in terms of KV cache memory reduction and output throughput enhancement.
AI.conclusion: Kara effectively addresses the limitations of existing KV cache compression methods through sliding-window decoding-time compression, bidirectional attention-based scoring, and flexible chunk preservation, yielding practical throughput gains when deployed in the vLLM-based KvLLM framework.

title: Fixed-Set Robustness in Programming by Example: Example Corruption and Semantic Partition Recovery
summary: Programming-by-example systems infer programs from a small set of input-output examples. Robust PBE work usually models wrong examples as samples from a stochastic noise process and then minimizes an expected or empirical loss. This paper studies a different failure mode: an adversary who sees the synthesizer and chooses the examples whose corruption most damages the returned program. We formalize fixed-set worst-case corruption for finite PBE version spaces, implement exact-within-bounded-pool and heuristic corruption searches for a string-transformation DSL, and introduce version-space partition aggregation (VPA), a defense that synthesizes on disjoint example groups and votes by semantic signatures. The central claim is deliberately bounded and partly negative: low-margin PBE tasks have an adversarial robustness dimension that random-typo and noisy-PBE evaluations miss, while semantic partition aggregation helps only when the clean semantics keep a partition vote margin, which often fails on realistic tasks. Evidence from curated/generated DSL tasks, accepted public SyGuS PBE_SLIA slices, SYNTRA Playgol v2, and noisy-PBE objective baselines supports that boundary. One curated edit flips all 8 spike tasks while 200-trial typo, DSL-pool, and distance-matched random controls succeed on 10.3%, 11.0%, and 16.7%; generated margin-1 rows flip under budget 1 yet VPA recovers them; on public SyGuS the vote margin is near one, so an adaptive attacker drives VPA accuracy to zero; accepted public SyGuS slices move across exact-within-pool budget boundaries; and Playgol shows positive paired-bootstrap gaps against typo and same-pool random controls on the 141 accepted rows. A small exact-output prompt harness over 20 controlled margin-1 tasks shows the same qualitative clean-to-attacked pattern across local and API models, while it is treated as a scope check, not a broad LLM benchmark.

AI.tldr: This paper formalizes adversarial corruption in programming-by-example (PBE), where an attacker strategically chooses which examples to corrupt to maximally damage synthesized programs. The authors implement corruption search algorithms for string-transformation DSLs and propose Version-space Partition Aggregation (VPA) as a defense, but find it only helps when clean semantics maintain a partition vote margin — a condition that often fails on realistic tasks.
AI.motivation: Traditional robust PBE assumes stochastic noise (e.g., typos) and minimizes expected loss. This paper argues for a distinct, underexplored threat model: an adaptive adversary who knows the synthesizer and deliberately selects examples whose corruption maximally degrades the output program. The authors contend that standard noisy-PBE evaluations miss this adversarial robustness dimension.
AI.method: The paper formalizes fixed-set worst-case corruption over finite PBE version spaces. It implements exact (within a bounded candidate pool) and heuristic corruption searches targeting a string-transformation DSL. The proposed defense, Version-space Partition Aggregation (VPA), splits examples into disjoint groups, synthesizes independently on each, and votes by semantic signatures. Evaluation spans curated DSL tasks, SyGuS PBE_SLIA benchmarks, SYNTRA Playgol v2, and a small LLM prompt harness on controlled margin-1 tasks.
AI.result: One adversarial edit flips all 8 spike tasks, while typo, DSL-pool, and distance-matched random controls succeed on only 10.3%, 11.0%, and 16.7% respectively. Generated margin-1 rows flip under budget 1 yet VPA recovers them. On public SyGuS, vote margins are near one, so adaptive attackers drive VPA accuracy to zero. Playgol shows positive paired-bootstrap gaps against typo and same-pool random controls on 141 accepted rows. The LLM scope check mirrors the clean-to-attacked pattern on 20 tasks.
AI.conclusion: Low-margin PBE tasks exhibit a genuine adversarial robustness vulnerability that random-noise evaluations fail to capture. VPA offers partial mitigation but breaks down when clean semantic vote margins collapse — a common occurrence on realistic benchmarks. The work is deliberately bounded and partly negative, establishing the boundary conditions rather than claiming a universal solution.

title: The Wiola Architecture for Efficient Small Language Models
summary: We present Wiola, a fully original Small Language Model (SLM) architecture built from first principles, sharing no structural lineage with any existing model family including GPT, LLaMA, Mistral, or Falcon. Wiola introduces five independently novel components: (i) Spiral Rotary Positional Encoding (SRPE), which embeds token positions on a three-dimensional helical manifold combining absolute, relative, and hierarchical positional signals; (ii) Gated Cross-Layer Attention (GCLA), providing each decoder layer with soft cross-attention access to compressed summaries of two preceding layers for inter-layer coherence; (iii) Adaptive Token Merging (ATM), which dynamically merges se mantically redundant adjacent tokens in middle network layers to reduce attention complexity without information loss; (iv) Dual Stream Feed-Forward (DSFF), replacing the conventional MLP with two parallel streams fused by a learned per-dimension gate; and (v) WiolaRMSNorm, a modified normalisation introducing a per-dimension learned offset vector that prevents representation collapse. We provide complete mathematical derivations, architectural block diagrams, complexity analyses, and systematic comparisons against GPT-2, LLaMA-2, and Mistral. Wiola is released in four sizes (120M, 360M, 700M, and 1.5B parameters) and is fully compatible with the HuggingFace Transformers ecosystem, with all 22 architectural unit tests passing.

AI.tldr: Wiola is a novel Small Language Model architecture with five original components — SRPE, GCLA, ATM, DSFF, and WiolaRMSNorm — sharing no lineage with existing model families, released in four sizes (120M–1.5B) with full HuggingFace compatibility.
AI.motivation: To design a fully original, clean-sheet SLM architecture that does not inherit structural constraints from established model families, while introducing independent architectural innovations that improve positional encoding, inter-layer communication, computational efficiency, feed-forward expressivity, and training stability.
AI.method: The paper introduces five novel components: (1) SRPE embeds positions on a 3D helical manifold encoding absolute, relative, and hierarchical signals; (2) GCLA gives each decoder layer soft cross-attention to compressed summaries of two prior layers; (3) ATM dynamically merges semantically redundant adjacent tokens mid-network to reduce attention complexity; (4) DSFF replaces the standard MLP with two parallel streams gated by a learned per-dimension vector; (5) WiolaRMSNorm adds a per-dimension learned offset to RMSNorm to prevent representation collapse. Models at 120M, 360M, 700M, and 1.5B parameters are released with complete derivations, diagrams, and comparisons against GPT-2, LLaMA-2, and Mistral.
AI.result: All 22 architectural unit tests pass. The models are fully compatible with the HuggingFace Transformers ecosystem. Systematic comparisons against GPT-2, LLaMA-2, and Mistral are provided, though specific performance metrics are not detailed in the abstract.
