AI.conclusion: Wiola demonstrates that a fully original SLM architecture can be successfully built from first principles, incorporating five independently novel components, achieving production-ready compatibility with the HuggingFace ecosystem across multiple model scales.

title: Hardware-Enforced Semantic Coordination for Safety-Critical Real-Time Autonomous Systems
summary:
Recent advances in agentic AI are producing increasingly complex autonomous systems that integrate large language models, world models, optimization engines, specialized neural architectures, autonomous platforms, and human operators. While much current research focuses on improving reasoning capabilities, safety-critical real-time deployment also requires bounded and verifiable coordination among heterogeneous components operating concurrently under uncertainty. Software-mediated coordination presents fundamental limitations in domains where bounded latency, deterministic coordination, and enforceable safety guarantees are essential.
  Hence, we propose a hardware-enforced semantic coordination architecture in which selected coordination semantics are implemented directly at the hardware level via field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs). The approach builds on the Topic-Based Communication Space Petri Net (TB-CSPN) framework, which separates semantic reasoning from interaction management.
  In this approach, selected TB-CSPN coordination mechanisms are mapped onto FPGA primitives, creating a hardware-native semantic coordination layer. Focus is not on acceleration, but on enforcing temporal synchronization, semantic gating, authorization constraints, and bounded coordination behavior directly in hardware. Semantic reasoning remains adaptive and software-driven, while embedded coordination semantics become deterministic.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a hardware-enforced semantic coordination architecture using FPGAs to implement coordination semantics directly at the hardware level, ensuring deterministic, bounded-latency coordination for safety-critical autonomous systems, while keeping semantic reasoning in software.
AI.motivation: As agentic AI systems grow more complex — integrating LLMs, world models, optimization engines, and human operators — safety-critical real-time deployment demands bounded and verifiable coordination. Software-mediated coordination alone cannot guarantee bounded latency, deterministic behavior, or enforceable safety guarantees under concurrent, uncertain conditions.
AI.method: The authors extend the Topic-Based Communication Space Petri Net (TB-CSPN) framework by mapping selected coordination mechanisms onto FPGA primitives. This creates a hardware-native semantic coordination layer that handles temporal synchronization, semantic gating, authorization constraints, and bounded coordination behavior in hardware, while adaptive semantic reasoning remains software-driven.
AI.result: The architecture achieves deterministic, hardware-enforced coordination semantics with bounded latency, separating concerns between adaptive software-based reasoning and hardware-guaranteed interaction management without focusing on computational acceleration.
AI.conclusion: Hardware-enforced semantic coordination via FPGAs offers a viable path to meeting the strict determinism and safety requirements of real-time autonomous systems, complementing rather than replacing software-based reasoning components.

title: An alternative approach towards attacks against fully-split PLWE instances
summary: In the present work we address some key questions regarding the generalization of root-based attacks presented in a recent work by the authors. In particular, we analyze potential root-based attacks extensions via the construction of explicit isomorphisms from vulnerable instances, and provide a formal proof that this approach will not yield any new vulnerabilities under a fully-split setting. To do so, we first construct an explicit isomorphism between fully-split polynomial rings and polynomial rings where previous attacks apply and show that the application of such an isomorphism will always distort the samples in a way that the resulting samples cannot be used to distinguish. Then, we prove that any isomorphism between fully-split polynomial rings must be of the form of the constructed isomorphism.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that extending root-based attacks on certain cryptographic schemes via explicit isomorphisms from vulnerable instances to fully-split polynomial rings cannot yield new vulnerabilities — any such isomorphism necessarily distorts samples in a way that prevents distinguishing attacks.
AI.motivation: To rigorously investigate whether root-based attacks from prior work can be generalized to new settings by constructing explicit isomorphisms from known vulnerable instances, and to formally determine whether this approach exposes new attack surfaces under a fully-split setting.
AI.method: The authors construct an explicit isomorphism between fully-split polynomial rings and polynomial rings where prior root-based attacks are applicable. They then analyze how this isomorphism affects sample distributions and prove that any isomorphism between fully-split polynomial rings must conform to their constructed form.
AI.result: The constructed isomorphism always distorts samples such that the resulting transformed samples cannot be used for distinguishing attacks. Furthermore, all possible isomorphisms between fully-split polynomial rings are of the same form, meaning no alternative isomorphism can bypass this limitation.
AI.conclusion: Extending root-based attacks via explicit isomorphisms from vulnerable instances is a dead end under the fully-split setting; the approach introduces inherent sample distortion that neutralizes any distinguishing advantage, and no alternative isomorphic construction can circumvent this barrier.

title: SPARCLE: SPeaker-aware Aligned Representations via Contrastive Language Embeddings
summary:
Recent advances in speech synthesis have shifted from phoneme representations to direct grapheme modeling. While phonemes address the one-to-many mapping between text and acoustics, they rely on grapheme-to-phoneme (G2P) systems that fail to capture speaker-specific acoustic variation. Prior work demonstrates that grapheme-based models outperform phoneme-based systems at scale, but not in low-resource settings.
  In this paper, we propose SPARCLE, a speaker-aware grapheme representation model that enriches characters with their precise acoustic realizations. SPARCLE is trained with a contrastive objective to align graphemes with corresponding Wav2Vec2 acoustic representations while conditioned on speaker identity. The resulting model serves as a replacement to G2P systems for downstream text-to-speech (TTS) tasks. We demonstrate that SPARCLE improves generation quality, reducing word error rates by half in extreme low-resource settings compared to standard grapheme-based models.

AI.tldr: SPARCLE introduces a speaker-aware grapheme representation model that aligns characters with Wav2Vec2 acoustic features conditioned on speaker identity, replacing G2P systems for TTS. It halves word error rates in extreme low-resource settings compared to standard grapheme models.
AI.motivation: Grapheme-to-phoneme (G2P) systems used in phoneme-based TTS fail to capture speaker-specific acoustic variation. While grapheme-based models outperform phoneme ones at scale, they underperform in low-resource settings. There is a need for a representation that combines the direct modeling benefits of graphemes with the acoustic grounding of phonemes, while preserving speaker identity.
AI.method: SPARCLE learns speaker-aware grapheme representations by training with a contrastive objective that aligns grapheme embeddings with Wav2Vec2 acoustic representations, conditioned on speaker identity. The resulting model serves as a drop-in replacement for G2P systems in downstream TTS tasks.
AI.result: SPARCLE improves generation quality in TTS, reducing word error rates (WER) by approximately half in extreme low-resource settings compared to standard grapheme-based models.
AI.conclusion: SPARCLE demonstrates that enriching grapheme representations with speaker-conditioned acoustic alignment via contrastive learning effectively bridges the gap between grapheme and phoneme approaches, particularly excelling in low-resource TTS scenarios where traditional grapheme models struggle.

title: Domain Knowledge Based Temporal-Spatial Graph Convolution Network for ECG Recognition
comment: 10 pages, 5 figures. Presented at ICONIP 2024, Auckland, New Zealand. Published in LNCS 15290, Springer, 2025
summary: In light of strides in Arti cial Intelligence (AI) and its wide spread application, challenges persist in the interpretability of AI models, particularly within specialized domains like healthcare, such as electro cardiograph (ECG) recognition. Rather than relying solely on end-to-end convolutional neural networks, this paper introduces a novel approach using a domain knowledge-based graph convolution network for ECG recognition. Key landmarks points of PRQST, vital to ECG interpreta tion, are incorporated as domain knowledge. The double-stream directed graph is employed to model both intra and inter ECG cycles. Speci cally, spatial directed graphs capture the positional relationships among key points, while temporal directed graphs delineate temporal dependencies between adjacent cycles in extended ECG sequences. Experimental re sults on the First Chinese ECG Intelligent Competition dataset, which speci cally classify ECG into nine categories, prove the e cacy of the proposed model. The overall average F1 score is 88.1%, the average F1 score of rare categories is 76.3%, both outperform the state-of-the-art models. The introduction of domain knowledge did enhance the detec tion performance, especially for rare categories.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a domain knowledge-based graph convolutional network for ECG recognition that explicitly models PRQST landmarks using double-stream directed graphs (spatial for intra-cycle and temporal for inter-cycle relationships), achieving state-of-the-art performance on a 9-class ECG dataset, with particular improvement on rare categories.
AI.motivation: Interpretability of AI models in specialized domains like healthcare remains challenging. End-to-end CNNs lack explicit incorporation of clinically meaningful ECG features, particularly the PRQST key landmarks that cardiologists rely on for diagnosis. There is also a need to better handle rare ECG categories.
AI.method: A domain knowledge-based graph convolution network using double-stream directed graphs: (1) spatial directed graphs encode positional relationships among PRQST key landmarks within a single ECG cycle; (2) temporal directed graphs capture dependencies between adjacent cycles in extended ECG sequences. Domain knowledge of PRQST landmarks is explicitly incorporated rather than relying on end-to-end CNNs. Evaluated on the First Chinese ECG Intelligent Competition dataset (9 categories).
AI.result: Overall average F1 score of 88.1%; average F1 score on rare categories of 76.3%, both outperforming state-of-the-art models. Domain knowledge integration demonstrably enhanced detection performance, especially for rare categories.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating domain knowledge (PRQST landmarks) via graph convolution networks with double-stream directed graphs effectively improves ECG recognition performance, particularly for rare categories, and offers a more interpretable alternative to end-to-end CNNs.

title: Agent4cs: A Multi-agent System for Code Summarization in Large Hierarchical Codebases
comment: Accepted to the main track of the 23rd European Conference on Multi-Agent Systems (EUMAS 2026)
summary: Understanding large, complex codebases, especially those with obfuscated structures and incomplete documentation, remains a significant challenge. Existing code summarization solutions often rely on a single language model or coding assistant like Claude Code, and treat source code as flat text, underutilizing the rich interdependencies and hierarchical information within a repository. To address these shortcomings, we propose Agent4cs - a multi-agent framework that summarizes large codebases in a bottom-up fashion, where a summarization agent focuses on producing robust summaries; a keyword-extraction agent proactively identifies critical information from subfolders; and a quality-assurance agent iteratively refines the outputs for readability, coherence, and completeness. Evaluated on 7 frontier models, Agent4cs improves semantic consistency across all folder levels by average 8% compared to two structured prompting baselines with code segments. Furthermore, extensive evaluation on real-world datasets demonstrates up to 38% gains in normalized keyword coverage rate over the same baselines.

AI.tldr: Agent4cs is a multi-agent framework for summarizing large codebases bottom-up, using specialized agents for summarization, keyword extraction, and quality assurance. It improves semantic consistency by 8% and keyword coverage by up to 38% over structured prompting baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing code summarization tools treat code as flat text and underutilize repository structure, inter-file dependencies, and hierarchical organization. Single-model approaches struggle with large, complex, or obfuscated codebases with incomplete documentation.
AI.method: A bottom-up multi-agent framework with three specialized agents: (1) a summarization agent that produces robust file/folder summaries, (2) a keyword-extraction agent that proactively identifies critical information from subdirectories, and (3) a quality-assurance agent that iteratively refines outputs for readability, coherence, and completeness. Summaries propagate upward through the repository hierarchy.
AI.result: Evaluated across 7 frontier models, Agent4cs achieves an average 8% improvement in semantic consistency at all folder levels over two structured prompting baselines with code segments. On real-world datasets, it demonstrates up to 38% gains in normalized keyword coverage rate.
AI.conclusion: A multi-agent, hierarchical approach to code summarization significantly outperforms flat, single-model baselines by leveraging repository structure and iterative quality refinement.

title: What LLM Agents Say When No One Is Watching: Social Structure and Latent Objective Emergence in Multi-Agent Debates
summary: LLM agents will increasingly act in socially structured settings where role, audience, and relational context can shape what is advantageous or costly to say. We study whether such social structure, without any explicit objective in the prompt, changes what an agent expresses publicly relative to an off-the-record (OTR) channel elicited under the same condition. We introduce a dual-channel debate framework in which agents produce public utterances that enter the shared history alongside OTR responses that are recorded but never shown to the other participant. Across 10 models, 3 scenarios, and 5 variations within each scenario, alignment-inducing settings produce systematic public-OTR divergence in the targeted agent, with its decision divergence rising from a $\sim$3% baseline to roughly 40%. The effect is consistent across four aggregate analyses: stance, semantic similarity, natural language inference, and survey responses. In some cases, the OTR response explicitly attributes public accommodation to relational pressures, such as career risk or sponsorship obligation. The findings suggest that agent evaluation should extend beyond explicit goals and detect emergent objectives. We present a dual-channel evaluation framework and complementary behavioral measures that operationalize this assessment.

AI.tldr: LLM agents systematically diverge between public and off-the-record speech under socially structured settings, with alignment pressures driving decision divergence from ~3% to ~40%, suggesting emergent, implicit objectives beyond explicit prompts.
AI.motivation: Current LLM agent evaluation focuses on explicit goals and prompt-level alignment, neglecting how social structure (role, audience, relational context) may induce implicit, emergent objectives that cause agents to strategically alter public utterances relative to private beliefs.
AI.method: A dual-channel debate framework where agents produce both public utterances (shared with the other participant) and off-the-record (OTR) responses (recorded but hidden). Evaluated across 10 models, 3 scenarios, and 5 variations per scenario, measuring public-OTR divergence via stance, semantic similarity, natural language inference, and survey responses.
AI.result: Alignment-inducing settings produced systematic public-OTR divergence in the targeted agent; decision divergence rose from a ~3% baseline to roughly 40%. OTR responses sometimes explicitly attributed public accommodation to relational pressures (career risk, sponsorship obligation).
AI.conclusion: Agent evaluation must go beyond explicit goals to detect emergent objectives shaped by social context. The dual-channel evaluation framework and behavioral measures offer a concrete methodology for operationalizing this broader assessment.

title: Evaluating Chunking Strategies for Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Academic Texts
summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems use the question-answering capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) to access information outside their parameters. We evaluate if cluster-based semantic chunking improves retrieval and answer quality compared to fixed-size and recursive chunking evaluating on long, structured academic theses using the Retrieval Augmented Generation Assessment (RAGAs) framework. RAGAs based faithfulness shows limited reliability in this setup. Performance on fixed versus document specific questions varied substantially, likely related to the formatting of documents and preprocessing. Under the tested configuration, cluster-based chunking did not outperform simpler strategies.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates whether cluster-based semantic chunking improves RAG system performance on long academic theses, finding that it does not outperform simpler fixed-size or recursive chunking methods, and that RAGAs faithfulness metrics show limited reliability in this context.
AI.motivation: RAG systems rely on chunking strategies to segment documents for retrieval, but it is unclear whether semantically-aware chunking methods (cluster-based) offer tangible benefits over simpler heuristics (fixed-size, recursive) — particularly on long, structured documents like academic theses. The authors also question the reliability of standard RAG evaluation metrics (RAGAs faithfulness) in such settings.
AI.method: The authors compared three chunking strategies — fixed-size, recursive, and cluster-based semantic chunking — on long, structured academic theses. Retrieval and answer quality were evaluated using the RAGAs framework, with performance assessed on both fixed (generic) and document-specific questions to isolate the effects of document formatting and preprocessing.
AI.result: Cluster-based semantic chunking did not outperform simpler fixed-size or recursive chunking under the tested configuration. Performance varied substantially between fixed and document-specific questions, likely due to document formatting and preprocessing choices. Additionally, the RAGAs-based faithfulness metric demonstrated limited reliability in this evaluation setup.
AI.conclusion: Semantic chunking via clustering offers no clear advantage over simpler chunking methods for RAG on structured academic documents, and practitioners should be cautious when relying solely on RAGAs faithfulness scores for evaluating such systems.

title: Chameleon: Recovering Cyber-Physical Systems from Memory Corruption Attacks via ML Surrogates
summary:
Cyber-physical systems (CPSs) are increasingly deployed in every aspect of our lives and can be compromised through memory corruption vulnerabilities, allowing attackers to hijack the control flow and take over the system. Existing techniques mostly focus on detecting such attacks but respond by terminating or halting execution upon attack detection, which is not acceptable in CPSs used in safety-critical tasks, as interrupted tasks can have catastrophic consequences. Other techniques replace compromised CPS components with simplified defaults that degrade system behavior, or reboot the system upon attack detection.
  We propose Chameleon, a novel framework for automatically recovering CPSs from memory corruption attacks using machine learning (ML)-based surrogates trained at compartment granularity that nearly replicate their original compartments' behavior but do not have the same memory corruption vulnerabilities. Upon attack detection, Chameleon replaces the compromised compartment with its trained surrogate. We implemented Chameleon using the LLVM compiler and evaluated its efficiency and effectiveness on seven different robotic vehicles (RVs), including simulated and real ones. We found that Chameleon can generate surrogates that closely approximate the original compartments (with an average R$^2$=0.96), successfully recover the system despite real-world memory corruption attacks unlike prior approaches, and complete their tasks while incurring low performance and memory overhead.

AI.tldr: Chameleon uses ML-based surrogates trained at compartment granularity to automatically recover cyber-physical systems from memory corruption attacks, replacing compromised components without halting execution, achieving average R²=0.96 on seven robotic vehicles.
AI.motivation: Existing memory corruption defenses for CPSs either terminate/halt execution (unacceptable in safety-critical tasks) or degrade to simplified defaults/reboot. There is a need for attack recovery that maintains system functionality without interruption.
AI.method: Chameleon trains ML-based surrogate models at compartment granularity that replicate original compartment behavior without the same memory corruption vulnerabilities. Upon attack detection, the compromised compartment is replaced with its pre-trained surrogate. Implemented using the LLVM compiler and evaluated on seven simulated and real robotic vehicles.
AI.result: Surrogates achieved an average R²=0.96, closely approximating original compartments. Chameleon successfully recovered systems from real-world memory corruption attacks where prior approaches failed, completing tasks with low performance and memory overhead.
AI.conclusion: Chameleon demonstrates that ML-based surrogate replacement at compartment granularity is a viable and effective strategy for recovering safety-critical CPSs from memory corruption attacks without halting execution or degrading to simplified operation.

title: Risk Architecture for AI-Native Engineering Teams: An Organizational Framework for Agentic System Governance
summary: Engineering management research has produced mature frameworks for software risk: ownership by feature, escalation by severity, and assurance by test coverage. These frameworks implicitly assume deterministic behavior, discrete and auditable change events, and clear component-to-owner mappings. Teams that build and operate agentic AI systems violate all three assumptions at once: outputs are probabilistic, systems take autonomous multi-step actions, and the risk surface mutates silently between deployments. Existing AI risk literature addresses this from above (policy frameworks such as the NIST AI RMF and ISO/IEC 42001) or below (threat taxonomies such as OWASP's agentic AI guidance), but not at the layer where an engineering manager (EM) operates: roles, decision rights, and escalation structures. This paper contributes (i) a seven-dimension profile distinguishing pure software-engineering, hybrid, and AI-native teams; (ii) a six-cluster failure-mode taxonomy including a previously unarticulated cluster, dependency-boundary determinism mismatch; and (iii) a synthetic framework-adequacy methodology scoring how well each profile's risk architecture detects, contains, and escalates a defined scenario set. Because the object of study is framework adequacy rather than human behavior, the evaluation yields derived rather than observed coverage claims. Coverage degrades as teams move from pure software engineering to AI-native operation, monotonically in the median and abruptly in the count of uncovered, high-consequence failures appearing only at the AI-native step. The degradation concentrates in specific failure-mode categories, and the most severe, least-covered failures arise not inside AI-native teams but at the organizational boundary where their probabilistic outputs are consumed by determinism-assuming dependencies.

AI.tldr: Traditional software risk management frameworks (ownership, escalation, assurance) rely on assumptions of determinism, discrete changes, and clear ownership—all violated by agentic AI systems. The paper identifies team profiles, failure modes (including a novel "dependency-boundary determinism mismatch"), and evaluates how existing risk architectures degrade across the spectrum from pure software to AI-native teams, finding that the most severe failures emerge at organizational boundaries where probabilistic AI outputs meet deterministic dependencies.
AI.motivation: Existing AI risk literature operates either at the policy level (NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001) or at the technical threat level (OWASP agentic AI guidance), leaving a gap at the engineering management layer—roles, decision rights, and escalation structures. The authors aim to fill this gap by systematically examining why traditional software risk frameworks fail for agentic AI and quantifying that degradation.
AI.method: The paper develops three artifacts: (i) a seven-dimension team profile taxonomy (pure software-engineering, hybrid, AI-native); (ii) a six-cluster failure-mode taxonomy, introducing the novel cluster "dependency-boundary determinism mismatch"; and (iii) a synthetic framework-adequacy methodology that scores each profile's risk architecture on detection, containment, and escalation across a defined scenario set. Evaluation produces derived (not observed) coverage claims, as the object of study is framework adequacy rather than human behavior.
AI.result: Coverage degrades monotonically in the median from pure software-engineering to AI-native teams, with an abrupt increase in uncovered high-consequence failures at the AI-native step. Degradation concentrates in specific failure-mode categories. Critically, the most severe and least-covered failures do not originate inside AI-native teams but at organizational boundaries where probabilistic AI outputs are consumed by determinism-assuming downstream dependencies.
AI.conclusion: Engineering management risk frameworks designed for deterministic software systems are structurally inadequate for agentic AI, with the most dangerous failure modes manifesting at cross-boundary interfaces. This implies that organizational risk architecture—not just model-level safety—must be redesigned to account for probabilistic outputs crossing into deterministic subsystems.

title: Breaking Safety at the Token Boundary: How BPE Tokenization Creates Exploitable Gaps in LLM Alignment
summary: Character-level perturbations bypass safety alignment in modern LLMs despite leaving prompts human-readable. We identify and test a central structural mechanism: BPE tokenization fragments safety-critical words into sub-word pieces, and the three public alignment datasets we surveyed contain no intentionally fragmented inputs. The mechanism is a chain, tested end-to-end on five model families (Qwen-3-4B, Qwen-2.5-7B, Gemma-3-4B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B). An optimization targeting safety-token fragmentation flips the first-token refusal trigger on 80-100% of refused HarmBench prompts, with 48% of those flips producing genuinely harmful outputs (per-model 29-65%; gap-vs-behavior ROC-AUC 0.66-0.98, pooled 0.84). Activation patching localizes the disrupted signal to the last ${\sim}30\%$ of layers; an alignment-data scan finds zero fragmented prompts among 30,000 examples (positive-control recall $\geq 99\%$ at attack-relevant intensities); and targeted-mutation experiments isolate safety words as the disruption locus. On the defense side, a 68-cell grid (55 trained checkpoints) shows that no DPO configuration achieves seed- and pool-stable ASR closure on the three families with closed pool-size confounds. SFT trained on fragmented prompts closes ASR on 3/5 families but only via global collapse that raises refusal on benign prompts as well, indicating the missing distribution is necessary but not sufficient under the LoRA-16 recipe we tested. To distinguish selective repair from global collapse, we introduce Conv-Benign, a candidate paired diagnostic. All ASR claims are 3-judge-calibrated (cell rankings stable across judges; absolute levels $\pm$18pp; see App.~B.13).

AI.tldr: Character-level perturbations fragment safety-critical tokens via BPE tokenization, bypassing LLM safety alignment. The attack flips refusal on 80-100% of prompts, with 48% producing harmful outputs. Defenses (DPO, SFT) fail to selectively close the vulnerability without global collapse. A new diagnostic, Conv-Benign, is introduced to distinguish selective repair from collapse.
AI.motivation: Safety alignment in modern LLMs relies on BPE tokenization, yet alignment datasets contain no intentionally fragmented inputs. This creates a blind spot: character-level perturbations that fragment safety-critical words into benign sub-word tokens can bypass refusal mechanisms while keeping prompts human-readable. The authors aim to systematically characterize this vulnerability, its mechanistic locus, and whether existing defense strategies can close it.
AI.method: The paper identifies a structural mechanism where BPE tokenization fragments safety-critical words, then tests it end-to-end on five model families (Qwen-3-4B, Qwen-2.5-7B, Gemma-3-4B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B). An optimization targets safety-token fragmentation to flip first-token refusal. Activation patching localizes disrupted signals to the last ~30% of layers. A scan of 30,000 alignment dataset examples confirms zero fragmented prompts. Targeted-mutation experiments isolate safety words as the disruption locus. For defense, a 68-cell grid (55 trained checkpoints) evaluates DPO configurations; SFT on fragmented prompts is also tested. Conv-Benign is proposed as a paired diagnostic to separate selective repair from global collapse. All ASR claims use 3-judge calibration.
AI.result: The optimization flips first-token refusal on 80–100% of refused HarmBench prompts, with 48% producing genuinely harmful outputs (per-model range: 29–65%; gap-vs-behavior ROC-AUC 0.66–0.98, pooled 0.84). Activation patching localizes disruption to the last ~30% of layers. The alignment-data scan finds zero fragmented prompts among 30,000 examples (positive-control recall ≥99%). No DPO configuration achieves seed- and pool-stable ASR closure. SFT on fragmented prompts closes ASR on 3/5 families but only via global collapse that also raises refusal on benign prompts. Conv-Benign is introduced as a diagnostic to distinguish selective repair from collapse.
AI.conclusion: BPE tokenization introduces a fundamental vulnerability: safety alignment is brittle to character-level perturbations that fragment safety-critical tokens. Alignment datasets lacking fragmented inputs constitute a missing distribution. Existing defenses (DPO, SFT) fail to selectively close the gap — SFT works only via global collapse. The missing distribution is necessary but not sufficient for selective repair under the tested LoRA-16 recipe. Conv-Benign offers a principled way to evaluate future defenses.

title: Scaling Laws for Grid-Based Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search in High Dimensions
summary: Grid-based approaches to approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search have been absent from modern scaling analyses. We present a systematic characterization of a multiprobe grid algorithm with respect to dataset size $N$ and dimensionality $d$. Our experiments reveal a previously unreported $d$-scaling crossover on the GloVe embedding family, in which multiprobe grid search maintains an approximately constant dimensional scaling exponent while other graph-, tree-, and partitioning-based methods exhibit degrading throughput. The advantage comes with near-linear query scaling in $N$, but also with lower indexing cost than competing ANN methods. Our results suggest that grid-based methods such as multiprobe grid may be competitive in rebuild-heavy or high-dimensional settings where indexing cost and dimensional robustness dictate performance. More broadly, recent work has formalized self-attention as an ANN operation. Thus, the $N$- and $d$-scaling properties of ANN algorithms may guide cost analysis of efficient transformer architectures. Code is available at: https://github.com/weiz345/MultiProbeANN.

AI.tldr: A systematic characterization of multiprobe grid search for ANN reveals a previously unreported dimensional scaling crossover on GloVe embeddings, where grid methods maintain constant scaling exponents while other methods degrade. The approach offers near-linear query scaling, lower indexing cost, and may inform efficient transformer architecture design.
AI.motivation: Grid-based ANN methods have been largely overlooked in modern scaling analyses despite their potential advantages. The authors aim to fill this gap by systematically characterizing multiprobe grid performance, and to connect ANN scaling properties to the cost analysis of efficient transformer architectures, given that self-attention has been formalized as an ANN operation.
AI.method: The authors conduct a systematic empirical characterization of a multiprobe grid algorithm, analyzing its throughput and scaling behavior with respect to dataset size N and dimensionality d. They compare against graph-based, tree-based, and partitioning-based ANN methods using the GloVe embedding family as the benchmark dataset.
AI.result: A previously unreported dimensional scaling crossover is discovered: multiprobe grid search maintains an approximately constant dimensional scaling exponent, while competing methods (graph-, tree-, and partitioning-based) exhibit degrading throughput as dimensionality increases. The method also demonstrates near-linear query scaling in N and lower indexing cost than alternatives.
AI.conclusion: Grid-based methods like multiprobe grid are competitive in rebuild-heavy or high-dimensional settings where indexing cost and dimensional robustness are critical. The N- and d-scaling properties of ANN algorithms can inform cost analysis of efficient transformer architectures, given the formalization of self-attention as ANN.

title: When Should Service Agents Reconsider? Difficulty-Routed Control in Customer-Service Operations
summary: Autonomous customer-service agents are shifting from conversational interfaces toward operational execution roles: they retrieve firm records, apply service policies, and execute backend writes such as refunds, cancellations, exchanges, order modifications, and reservation changes. This shift creates a service-control problem: firms must keep routine service fast and low-friction while preventing operational errors on requests where customer instructions, policy constraints, firm records, and backend writes interact. We propose a difficulty-routed service-control architecture that asks when service agents should reconsider before acting. A lightweight router keeps routine sessions on a low-cost baseline path and routes operationally coupled sessions to an escalated workflow. The escalated path uses conflict-aware communication and write-triggered reconsideration to concentrate deliberation and safeguards before consequential backend writes, rather than applying additional control uniformly across all service sessions. We evaluate the architecture on human-verified retail and airline tasks from $τ^{2}$-bench. In retail, the method improves reliability consistently on service requests with operational conflict. Routing evidence shows that stronger control is directed toward conflicted requests rather than broadly applied to routine ones. Dialogue and tool-use profiles suggest that gains do not come from indiscriminate interaction expansion or broader tool chains; instead, added turns and tool calls support evidence gathering, write separation, and pre-write reconsideration. Case-level evidence shows that the escalated workflow preserves fallback plans, binds retrieved records to the correct action, sequences writes, and decomposes multi-entity requests. Airline results extend the same service-control logic to reservation operations.

AI.tldr: Proposes a difficulty-routed service-control architecture for autonomous customer-service agents that routes operationally complex requests to an escalated workflow with conflict-aware communication and write-triggered reconsideration, concentrating safeguards before consequential backend writes rather than applying uniform control across all sessions.
AI.motivation: Autonomous agents are transitioning from conversational interfaces to operational execution roles (refunds, cancellations, order modifications), creating a service-control problem: balancing fast, low-friction routine service against preventing operational errors when customer instructions, policy constraints, and backend writes interact in complex ways.
AI.method: A difficulty-routed architecture with a lightweight router that classifies sessions into low-cost baseline vs. escalated workflows. The escalated path employs conflict-aware communication and write-triggered reconsideration to concentrate deliberation and safeguards specifically before consequential backend writes.
AI.result: Evaluated on retail and airline tasks from τ²-bench. In retail, the method consistently improves reliability on operationally conflicted requests, with routing evidence showing stronger control directed toward conflicted (not routine) requests. Added turns and tool calls support evidence gathering, write separation, and pre-write reconsideration rather than indiscriminate expansion. Airline results extend the same logic to reservation operations.
AI.conclusion: The difficulty-routed architecture effectively concentrates protective deliberation on operationally coupled sessions, improving reliability without imposing unnecessary overhead on routine interactions. The approach generalizes across retail and airline domains.

title: Planning over Matrix-Factorization MDPs for Candidate Generation
comment: Accepted to the 5th Workshop on End-to-End Customer Journey Optimization at KDD 2026. 6 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables
summary: For a recommender service, we view the customer journey as a chain of item recommendations: a useful item changes the user's state and therefore what should be retrieved next. Standard matrix-factorization retrieval ignores this -- it builds one user vector and returns the top-$K$ items by a static score, treating them as independent. We ask a narrow question: when is it worth planning over the user-state dynamics that fold-in induces? To answer it we propose casting top-$K$ retrieval as an MDP over the implicit-ALS posterior $(A^{-1},u)$, where an action is an item and the transition is a closed-form rank-one fold-in, and the trajectory reward combines a relevance similarity with a posterior-alignment term. Under the same fixed embeddings we compare static retrieval, one-step planning, and horizon-$K$ MCTS across five datasets and two protocols: a per-user leave-last-$n$ split and a stricter global time split. Dynamics-aware planning tends to overcome static retrieval on all datasets under leave-last-$n$, and the gains hold on MovieLens-1M and the VK-LSVD slices under the global time split. A single step of lookahead already captures most of the gain, so the lightweight planning layer turns static top-$K$ scoring into a short decision and improves retrieval over fixed collaborative-filtering embeddings, with no retraining and no change to the representation. These gains depend on measuring relevance with cosine rather than inner-product similarity, which is otherwise entangled with item popularity.

AI.tldr: The paper frames top-K recommendation retrieval as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) over implicit-ALS posterior states, where recommending an item updates the user state via a rank-one fold-in. Using fixed embeddings, it compares static retrieval against one-step planning and MCTS, finding that lightweight dynamics-aware lookahead consistently outperforms static scoring, with cosine similarity as the relevance metric being crucial to the gains.
AI.motivation: Standard matrix-factorization retrieval treats all top-K items as independent, ignoring that each recommended item changes the user's latent representation (via fold-in) and thus should influence subsequent recommendations. The authors ask when explicitly planning over this user-state dynamics is worthwhile compared to static one-shot retrieval.
AI.method: The authors cast top-K retrieval as an MDP where: (1) the state is the implicit-ALS posterior (A^{-1}, u); (2) actions are candidate items; (3) transitions follow a closed-form rank-one fold-in update to the user vector; (4) the trajectory reward combines a relevance term (cosine similarity between item and user vector) with a posterior-alignment regularization term. They compare static retrieval, one-step lookahead planning, and horizon-K Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) across five datasets using two evaluation protocols: per-user leave-last-n and a stricter global time split.
AI.result: Dynamics-aware planning outperforms static retrieval on all datasets under leave-last-n evaluation. Gains persist under the stricter global time split on MovieLens-1M and VK-LSVD slices. A single step of lookahead captures most of the improvement, making the approach lightweight. Crucially, using cosine similarity (rather than inner product) for relevance measurement is necessary, as inner-product scoring is confounded with item popularity.
AI.conclusion: A lightweight planning layer — even just one-step lookahead — over fixed collaborative-filtering embeddings can improve top-K retrieval by accounting for user-state dynamics, without retraining or altering the representation. The approach is effective when relevance is measured via cosine similarity, and the gains are most robust under leave-last-n evaluation, with mixed but positive results under global time splits.

title: Evaluating Glanceable Multi-Device Family Health Tracking with Smartwatches and Home Displays
comment: Accepted with minor revisions for IMWUT 2026
summary: While ubiquitous computing research has explored diverse devices for personal health tracking, we know less about multi-device designs for family informatics, where health management is inherently collaborative. To understand how families adopt and perceive ubiquitous access to shared health data across contexts, we evaluated smartwatch-only, home display-only, and combined designs for tracking moods and goals, domains central to family health behavior regulation. 44 people across 12 families alternated between these designs over nine weeks. Log analysis revealed that mood tracking and goal reporting were significantly more frequent with the home display present compared to smartwatch-only use, despite an overall decline in mood tracking over time. Tracking peaked in afternoons, dropped on weekends, and occurred 2.6X more at home, with children tracking more consistently than adults across all designs. From interview analysis, we learned how family data glanceability on smartwatches supported opportunistic tracking and awareness while apart, whereas displays reminded families to self-track and collaborate during home routines including members that avoided wearables (e.g., non-participants). Multi-device redundancy accommodated diversity in routines, mobility patterns, and device preferences among members in the same family. We discuss opportunities for multi-device family informatics that accommodates different preferences through inclusive, glanceable, and adaptable ubiquitous data sharing.

AI.tldr: A 9-week study with 12 families (44 participants) compared smartwatch-only, home display-only, and combined designs for family mood and goal tracking. Home displays significantly increased tracking frequency; children tracked more consistently than adults; multi-device redundancy accommodated diverse family routines and preferences.
AI.motivation: Ubiquitous computing research has extensively explored personal health tracking devices, but there is limited understanding of how multi-device designs support family informatics, where health management is inherently collaborative and requires coordination across family members with different routines, mobility patterns, and device preferences.
AI.method: A within-subjects, counterbalanced field study over 9 weeks with 44 participants across 12 families. Families alternated between three conditions: smartwatch-only, home display-only, and a combined multi-device design. Data collection included log analysis of mood tracking and goal reporting behaviors, plus qualitative interviews to understand adoption and perceptions.
AI.result: (1) Home display presence significantly increased mood tracking and goal reporting frequency compared to smartwatch-only. (2) Overall mood tracking declined over time. (3) Tracking peaked in afternoons, dropped on weekends, and occurred 2.6× more at home. (4) Children tracked more consistently than adults across all conditions. (5) Smartwatch glanceability supported opportunistic tracking and awareness while apart; home displays served as reminders during home routines and engaged non-participant family members. (6) Multi-device redundancy accommodated diversity in routines, mobility patterns, and device preferences within families.
AI.conclusion: Multi-device family informatics systems should embrace inclusive, glanceable, and adaptable ubiquitous data sharing to accommodate heterogeneous preferences and routines within families. Redundancy across devices is not inefficiency but a design feature that supports diverse family members' engagement with shared health data.

title: From Forgeries to Foundation Models: A Systematic Survey of Identity Document Attack and Detection
summary: Identity document forgery has undergone a fundamental capability shift: generative AI tools now enable high-fidelity document synthesis and field-level manipulation with minimal technical expertise, while detection methods remain constrained by benchmarks that do not reflect this threat. The resulting attack surface spans physical presentation, digital injection, and fully generative synthesis, introducing distinct forensic failure modes that require a unified threat model and evaluation framework. This survey provides, to our knowledge, the first unified treatment of Presentation Attacks, Digital Injection Attacks, and GenAI-driven synthesis within a single identity verification threat model. We trace detection methodologies from rule-based heuristics through forensic localisation, injection-aware pipelines, foundation models, and few-shot frameworks. A systematic audit of public datasets from 2019--2025 exposes a persistent Reality Gap between benchmark conditions and operational deployment. We further analyse large multimodal models for identity document manipulation, identifying Script-Dependent Generative Instability (SDGI) as a recurring typographic failure mode in non-Latin script inpainting. Finally, zero-shot benchmarking on unseen synthesised ID cards shows that even the strongest publicly available models achieve APCER values above 25% under security-oriented operating conditions, highlighting substantial limits in cross-domain generalisation. We conclude by outlining future directions toward forensically grounded, privacy-preserving, and legally accountable identity verification systems.

AI.tldr: This survey unifies three ID document attack vectors—Presentation Attacks, Digital Injection Attacks, and GenAI-driven synthesis—under a single threat model. It audits public datasets (2019–2025) revealing a Reality Gap between benchmarks and real-world conditions, identifies Script-Dependent Generative Instability (SDGI) as a typographic failure mode in non-Latin script inpainting, and demonstrates via zero-shot benchmarking that even top public models exceed 25% APCER under security-oriented settings, exposing weak cross-domain generalization.
AI.motivation: Generative AI has democratized high-fidelity ID document forgery, yet detection benchmarks lag behind operational threats. Existing evaluations fail to capture the full attack surface—spanning physical, digital injection, and fully synthetic forgery—creating a critical gap between academic benchmarking and real-world identity verification security.
AI.method: The authors construct a unified threat model encompassing three attack classes (Presentation, Digital Injection, GenAI Synthesis). They conduct a systematic audit of public datasets from 2019–2025 to quantify the Reality Gap, analyze large multimodal models for document manipulation with particular focus on typographic artifacts, and perform zero-shot benchmarking of publicly available models on unseen synthesized ID cards under security-oriented operating conditions.
AI.result: The dataset audit confirms a persistent Reality Gap. Analysis of large multimodal models reveals Script-Dependent Generative Instability (SDGI) as a consistent failure mode in non-Latin script inpainting. Zero-shot benchmarks show even the strongest public models exceed 25% APCER under security-oriented conditions, indicating poor cross-domain generalization.
AI.conclusion: Current detection models are insufficient for operational security. Future work must pursue forensically grounded, privacy-preserving, and legally accountable identity verification systems that bridge the Reality Gap and address cross-domain generalization failures.

title: From Anatomy to Smells: An Empirical Study of SKILL.md in Agent Skills
summary: Agent Skills provide on-demand domain knowledge to LLM agents without requiring model retraining. Each Agent Skill is defined by a mandatory SKILL.md file containing metadata and an unstructured Markdown body whose contents are left entirely to the skill author. Despite the rapid adoption of Agent Skills, little is known about how these files are authored or whether existing authoring guidelines are followed in practice. In this paper, we present the first systematic study of SKILL.md files as a software artifact. We qualitatively analyze 238 real-world skills and derive a taxonomy of 13 higher-level and 44 lower-level semantic components. We then conduct a multivocal literature review of 29 sources to identify best practices for authoring SKILL.md files and introduce skill smells as violations of these practices. Finally, we develop an automated detector and apply it to real-world skills, finding that over 99% of SKILL.md files contain at least one skill smell, and once introduced, skill smells rarely disappear as skills evolve. These findings reveal a substantial gap between recommended and actual authoring practices, motivating the development of automated techniques to remediate skill smells while increasing developer awareness of this emerging quality issue.

AI.tldr: First systematic study of SKILL.md files (Agent Skills) as software artifacts: derives a taxonomy of semantic components from 238 real-world skills, identifies best practices via multivocal literature review, defines "skill smells" as violations, and finds >99% of files contain at least one smell that rarely disappears over time.
AI.motivation: Despite rapid adoption of Agent Skills for providing on-demand domain knowledge to LLM agents, no prior research has systematically examined how SKILL.md files are authored, whether best practices exist, or whether they are followed in practice.
AI.method: Qualitative analysis of 238 real-world SKILL.md files to derive a taxonomy (13 higher-level, 44 lower-level semantic components); multivocal literature review of 29 sources to identify authoring best practices; definition of "skill smells" as best-practice violations; development of an automated smell detector applied to real-world skills, including longitudinal analysis.
AI.result: Over 99% of SKILL.md files contain at least one skill smell; once introduced, skill smells rarely disappear as skills evolve, revealing a substantial gap between recommended and actual authoring practices.
AI.conclusion: There is a significant quality gap in Agent Skill authoring. The findings motivate developing automated remediation techniques and increasing developer awareness of skill smells as an emerging quality concern.

title: Prompt Framing Distorts Count-Based Evaluation of LLM Error Detection: Evidence from Numeric Anchoring
comment: 15 pages, 6 figures, 12 tables. Preprint under review
summary: Count-based F1 is widely used as a proxy for LLM error-detection quality, but this paper shows that it can rise dramatically without a corresponding improvement in span localization, a gap termed F1 Inflation. The paper introduces ErrorBench, a controlled stress-test protocol for prompt-induced count distortion. ErrorBench evaluates six contemporary LLMs under five prompt conditions over 4,290 responses from 143 CoNLL-2014 passages. Under CoNLL-2014 M2-style scoring, anchored prompts produce up to 0.79 points of F1 Inflation, and up to 0.96 under strict matching. A 100-passage replication using the official ERRANT 3.0.0 pipeline and multi-reference scoring reproduces the pattern: averaged over six models, the Blind-to-Anchored prompt shift raises Count-F1 by +0.21 while raising multi-reference ERRANT F0.5 by only +0.04. The study finds larger count responses in highly instruction-compliant GPT/Claude systems and smaller responses in the Gemini family under this stress-test protocol. The findings suggest that LLM proofreading and document-review evaluations should avoid pre-populated error counts and should report span-aware metrics alongside count-based metrics.

AI.tldr: Count-F1 scores for LLM error detection can inflate significantly without corresponding improvements in span localization accuracy — a phenomenon the authors term "F1 Inflation." ErrorBench, a controlled stress-test over 4,290 responses, demonstrates that pre-populated error counts distort evaluation, with instruction-compliant models (GPT/Claude) showing larger inflation than Gemini models.
AI.motivation: Count-based F1 is ubiquitously used to evaluate LLM error-detection quality, but it conflates correct error count with correct error localization. The authors identify a critical evaluation gap: F1 can rise simply because models adjust their output counts to match expected counts, not because they accurately identify where errors occur. This "F1 Inflation" threatens the validity of LLM proofreading and document-review benchmarks.
AI.method: The authors introduce ErrorBench, a controlled stress-test protocol that manipulates prompt-induced count distortion across five conditions (Blind, Anchored, and variants). They evaluate six contemporary LLMs on 143 CoNLL-2014 passages, generating 4,290 responses scored under both CoNLL-2014 M2-style scoring and strict matching. A 100-passage replication employs the official ERRANT 3.0.0 pipeline with multi-reference scoring, measuring both Count-F1 and span-aware ERRANT F0.5 to quantify the inflation gap.
AI.result: Anchored prompts produce up to 0.79 points of F1 Inflation under M2 scoring and up to 0.96 under strict matching. In the ERRANT replication averaged across six models, the Blind-to-Anchored shift raises Count-F1 by +0.21 while multi-reference ERRANT F0.5 rises by only +0.04. GPT/Claude systems exhibit larger count responses (greater inflation), while Gemini models show smaller responses under the stress-test protocol.
AI.conclusion: LLM error-detection evaluations should avoid pre-populated error counts in prompts and must report span-aware metrics (e.g., ERRANT F0.5) alongside count-based F1 to prevent misleading quality assessments. The F1 Inflation phenomenon is systematic and varies across model families.

title: IonSense-QKG: A Quantum-Readiness Metadata Framework for Lithium-Ion Battery Dataset Discovery
comment: 7 pages, 1 figure, 4 tables. Code and metadata artifact available at GitHub
summary:
Public lithium-ion battery datasets are increasingly used for state-of-health estimation, remaining-useful-life prediction, anomaly detection, electrochemical diagnostics, second-life analytics, and battery safety research. However, these datasets vary substantially in chemistry, modality, scale, label quality, sequence structure, access status, and preprocessing complexity. These differences directly affect whether a dataset is feasible for near-term hybrid quantum-classical machine-learning workflows.
  This paper presents IonSense-QKG, a quantum-readiness metadata framework for lithium-ion battery dataset discovery. Starting from the EV-Battery-IonSense index, the proposed framework enriches public battery dataset records with quantum-relevant metadata, including task type, sensing modality, chemistry, label availability, sequence type, preprocessing requirements, candidate quantum encodings, estimated qubit range, and NISQ feasibility. A transparent Quantum Readiness Score is introduced to rank datasets as candidate resources for future hybrid quantum-classical battery benchmarks. The score is intended as a dataset-selection heuristic, not as evidence of quantum advantage.
  The framework demonstrates query-based discovery over enriched metadata to identify datasets suitable for compact quantum feature maps, quantum time-series workflows, limited-label anomaly detection, and future battery-health benchmarking. The released artifact includes metadata tables, scoring scripts, robustness checks, link-checking utilities, and SQL-style query examples. IonSense-QKG positions dataset selection as a data-management problem and provides a reproducible foundation for data-centric quantum battery analytics.

AI.tldr: IonSense-QKG is a metadata framework that enriches public lithium-ion battery datasets with quantum-readiness attributes and a scoring heuristic to identify candidates suitable for hybrid quantum-classical machine learning workflows.
AI.motivation: Public Li-ion battery datasets vary widely in chemistry, modality, scale, and structure, making it difficult to assess their suitability for near-term hybrid quantum-classical ML without a systematic, metadata-driven selection framework.
AI.method: Starting from the EV-Battery-IonSense index, the framework enriches dataset records with quantum-relevant metadata (task type, sensing modality, chemistry, label availability, sequence type, preprocessing needs, candidate quantum encodings, estimated qubit range, NISQ feasibility) and introduces a Quantum Readiness Score as a heuristic ranking tool. Query-based discovery is demonstrated, and the artifact includes metadata tables, scoring scripts, robustness checks, link-checking utilities, and SQL-style query examples.
AI.result: The framework enables query-based identification of datasets suitable for compact quantum feature maps, quantum time-series workflows, limited-label anomaly detection, and battery-health benchmarking, treating dataset selection as a data-management problem.
AI.conclusion: IonSense-QKG provides a reproducible, data-centric foundation for quantum battery analytics by formalizing dataset discovery through quantum-readiness metadata, supporting future hybrid quantum-classical battery benchmarking without claiming quantum advantage.

title: CreativityNeuro: Steering Language Model Weights to Improve Divergent Thinking and Reduce Mode Collapse
comment: Accepted at ICML 2026 Workshop on Creativity & Generative AI
summary: Divergent thinking is a crucial aspect of creativity, yet large language models (LLMs) tend to consistently generate similar responses to open-ended questions, in what has been termed the artificial hivemind effect. Here, we introduce CreativityNeuro, a data-free method for enhancing divergent thinking in LLMs via contrastive weight steering. We evaluate our method across multiple creativity assessments and report several main findings. On the Divergent Association Task (DAT), a vocabulary-space creativity test, CreativityNeuro improves performance by up to 14 human percentile points. Next, in a large-scale human evaluation (N=720) on the Alternative Uses Test (AUT) and the Task Task, CreativityNeuro achieves significant improvements in originality, surprise, and creativity, transferring to longer-form and more open-ended tasks. Importantly, we find that across all three tasks, CreativityNeuro demonstrably reduces measures of mode collapse. Moreover, activation steering achieves comparable performance to CreativityNeuro on the DAT, but it does not transfer to the AUT and Task Task, demonstrating the effectiveness of weight-space steering in generalizing to unseen tasks. In conclusion, CreativityNeuro improves divergent thinking and reduces mode collapse without requiring behavioral data, re-training, or gradient-based fine-tuning, providing a straightforward way to enhance LLM performance in creative domains.

AI.tldr: CreativityNeuro is a data-free, contrastive weight-steering method that enhances divergent thinking in LLMs, significantly improving creativity metrics and reducing mode collapse without behavioral data, retraining, or fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: LLMs exhibit an "artificial hivemind effect," generating homogeneous responses to open-ended prompts, which limits their utility for creative tasks. Existing solutions often require behavioral data or gradient-based fine-tuning. A lightweight, data-free method is needed.
AI.method: CreativityNeuro uses contrastive weight steering — a data-free approach that directly manipulates model weights (rather than activations) to steer outputs toward more divergent, creative responses. The method operates without any behavioral data, retraining, or gradient-based fine-tuning.
AI.result: (1) On the Divergent Association Task (DAT), CreativityNeuro improved performance by up to 14 human percentile points. (2) In a large-scale human evaluation (N=720) on the Alternative Uses Test (AUT) and Task Task, it achieved significant gains in originality, surprise, and overall creativity. (3) It demonstrably reduced mode collapse across all three tasks. (4) Activation steering matched CreativityNeuro on DAT but failed to transfer to AUT and Task Task, highlighting weight-space steering's superior generalization.
AI.conclusion: CreativityNeuro offers a straightforward, data-free method for enhancing LLM divergent thinking and mitigating mode collapse, with weight-space steering proving more transferable than activation-space alternatives.

title: Bringing Agentic Search to Earth Observation Data Discovery
summary: NASA and its data centers hold thousands of geoscience datasets and tools like Worldview, Giovanni, the Science Discovery Engine, and Harmony. Finding the right one is hard even for domain experts. We present an agentic search system, deployed as a public service for the geoscience community, that takes a natural-language research query and returns the matching datasets and tools. We demonstrate that, in the era of large language models, the latent value of knowledge graphs (KGs) can be substantially amplified through agentic search. From the NASA Earth Observation Knowledge Graph (NASA EO-KG) we derive NASA-EO-Bench, an open benchmark of 47k query-dataset pairs (21k task-based queries). A neural scorer fine-tuned on NASA-EO-Bench beats cosine and BM25 baselines. Further combining it with BM25 via score fusion raises both Recall@10 (R@10) and MRR by over 5x. On top of this supervised pipeline, we add a zero-shot agentic reranking stage that, without any additional training, lifts MRR by 28% on a stratified N=200 subset, showing that LLM reasoning is complementary to supervised retrieval.

AI.tldr: NASA's agentic search system uses a fine-tuned neural scorer combined with BM25 score fusion and an LLM-based reranking stage to match natural-language queries to geoscience datasets. It leverages the NASA Earth Observation Knowledge Graph and the new NASA-EO-Bench benchmark (47k pairs) to achieve over 5x improvements in Recall@10 and MRR, with an additional 28% MRR lift from zero-shot agentic reranking.
AI.motivation: NASA holds thousands of geoscience datasets and tools, but finding the right resource is difficult even for domain experts. The goal is to exploit knowledge graphs enhanced by large language models to dramatically improve search for the geoscience community.
AI.method: The authors derive NASA-EO-Bench (47k query-dataset pairs, 21k task-based) from the NASA Earth Observation Knowledge Graph. A neural scorer is fine-tuned on this benchmark, outperforming cosine and BM25 baselines. Score fusion with BM25 lifts R@10 and MRR over 5x. A zero-shot agentic reranking stage using LLM reasoning is then added, evaluated on a stratified N=200 subset.
AI.result: The neural scorer alone beats cosine and BM25 baselines. Score fusion (neural + BM25) raises Recall@10 and MRR by over 5x. The zero-shot agentic reranking yields a further 28% MRR improvement on the stratified subset, demonstrating complementarity between supervised retrieval and LLM reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Knowledge graphs, when combined with large language models through agentic search, can substantially amplify their latent value. The supervised retrieval pipeline and zero-shot LLM reranking are complementary, and the system has been deployed as a public service for the geoscience community.

title: From Answer Generators to Reasoning Facilitators: Designing AI Tutors for Mathematical Reasoning in High-Stakes Environments
summary: The rapid integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into educational technology threatens to reduce mathematical learning to mere answer generation. This paper presents a generative study, usability study, and 12-participant field deployment of AITutor, an interactive system that translates theoretical pedagogical mechanisms into concrete user interface features. We explore how junior-high students preparing for high-stakes exams (Zhongkao) interact with AI tutoring. Through mixed-methods triangulation (7,379 telemetry events, 8 contextual observations, 10 interviews), we reveal that students actively resist traditional Socratic dialogue under time pressure, repurposing "answer-first" shortcuts as vital diagnostic checkpoints. We demonstrate how features like layered worked examples, step-linked visual grounding, and metacognitive scaffolding lower the interaction cost of reasoning repair. We contribute a "Reasoning-Centered Product Loop," offering actionable implications for designing AI that structurally supports the inspection, local repair, curriculum verification, and delayed retrieval of mathematical reasoning in the wild.

AI.tldr: AITutor is an interactive LLM-based tutoring system for junior-high math students. A field deployment with 12 students preparing for China's Zhongkao exam revealed that students resist Socratic dialogue under time pressure, instead using "answer-first" shortcuts as diagnostic checkpoints. Features like layered worked examples and metacognitive scaffolding reduced the cost of reasoning repair, leading to the proposed "Reasoning-Centered Product Loop" design framework.
AI.motivation: LLMs in education risk reducing math learning to answer generation. The authors aim to translate pedagogical theory into concrete UI features and understand how students actually interact with AI tutoring under real-world high-stakes exam preparation conditions.
AI.method: A generative study, usability study, and 12-participant field deployment of AITutor with mixed-methods triangulation: 7,379 telemetry events, 8 contextual observations, and 10 interviews, targeting junior-high students preparing for the Zhongkao.
AI.result: Under time pressure, students actively resist traditional Socratic dialogue and repurpose "answer-first" shortcuts as diagnostic checkpoints. Layered worked examples, step-linked visual grounding, and metacognitive scaffolding effectively lower the interaction cost of reasoning repair.
AI.conclusion: The paper contributes the "Reasoning-Centered Product Loop," with actionable design implications for AI systems that structurally support inspection, local repair, curriculum verification, and delayed retrieval of mathematical reasoning in authentic contexts.

title: Hamm-Grams: An Algorithm for Mining Regular Expressions of Bytes
comment: To appear in Machine Learning for Malware Detection
summary: Malware poses a critical and ever-evolving threat, and robust and effective systems for detecting and classifying malware are of essential importance. $n$-grams features are among the common static features used in effective machine learning systems for malware, but these features are inherently brittle. We propose an algorithm for constructing more robust features, hamm-grams, which are a special class of regular expressions having a fixed length and single-character wildcards. We devise an efficient algorithm for finding common hamm-grams using a new locality-sensitive hash designed to produce collisions among pairs of small Hamming distance and a clustering within hash buckets to place wildcards. We then demonstrate the advantages of these features in malware classification and detection tasks.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes "hamm-grams," robust regular-expression-based features with single-character wildcards, designed to replace brittle n-gram features in malware detection. An efficient algorithm using locality-sensitive hashing (LSH) for small Hamming distances and hash-bucket clustering is introduced to discover these features, which are shown to improve malware classification and detection performance.
AI.motivation: Traditional n-gram features used in machine learning–based malware detection are inherently brittle — small modifications to malware can break exact n-gram matches, reducing detection effectiveness. There is a need for more robust static features that can tolerate minor variations while retaining discriminative power.
AI.method: The authors introduce "hamm-grams," fixed-length regular expressions with single-character wildcards. An efficient discovery algorithm is devised using: (1) a novel locality-sensitive hash (LSH) function designed to produce collisions among pairs of strings with small Hamming distance, and (2) a clustering procedure within hash buckets to optimally place wildcards, yielding common hamm-gram patterns.
AI.result: The hamm-gram features demonstrate advantages over conventional n-gram features in both malware classification and malware detection tasks, offering improved robustness to minor code variations.
AI.conclusion: Hamm-grams provide a more robust alternative to n-gram features for static malware analysis. The combination of a Hamming-distance-aware LSH and hash-bucket clustering enables efficient extraction of these expressive features, leading to more resilient machine learning–based malware detection systems.

title: Insights from GitHub Community on the Matter Standard: Developer Perspectives and Challenges
summary: Matter seeks to resolve longstanding interoperability problems in the Internet of Things (IoT), yet little is known about how developers experience the standard in day to day work. This paper examines over 13,000 issues from the official Project CHIP GitHub repository to understand the kinds of problems contributors report when implementing and integrating Matter. Using topic modeling and qualitative analysis, we identify four recurring areas of concern, Testing, Interoperability, Development, and Platform and Network, and describe how they manifest in the evolution of the codebase and tooling. The findings reveal systematic technical and integration challenges and point to concrete opportunities to refine Matter's test infrastructure, cross vendor guidance, and documentation as the standard continues to mature.

AI.tldr: Analysis of over 13,000 GitHub issues from Project CHIP reveals four recurring problem areas in Matter IoT standard development: Testing, Interoperability, Development, and Platform/Network challenges, highlighting systematic integration issues and opportunities for improving test infrastructure, cross-vendor guidance, and documentation.
AI.motivation: Matter aims to solve IoT interoperability, but there is little empirical understanding of the practical challenges developers face when implementing and integrating the standard in daily work. The authors seek to fill this knowledge gap by systematically analyzing contributor-reported issues.
AI.method: The authors mined over 13,000 issues from the official Project CHIP (Connected Home over IP) GitHub repository. They applied topic modeling (an NLP technique) combined with qualitative analysis to categorize and characterize the types of problems contributors encounter.
AI.result: Four recurring areas of concern were identified: (1) Testing — challenges related to test infrastructure and validation; (2) Interoperability — issues with cross-vendor and cross-device compatibility; (3) Development — general software engineering and codebase evolution difficulties; (4) Platform and Network — platform-specific and networking-related problems. These manifest systematically throughout the codebase and tooling.
AI.conclusion: The findings reveal systematic technical and integration challenges in the Matter ecosystem. Concrete opportunities exist to refine Matter's test infrastructure, improve cross-vendor guidance, and enhance documentation as the standard matures.

title: Mapping Text to Multiplex Graph: Prompt Compression as Lévy Walk-Guided Graph Pruning
summary: Existing prompt compression methods treat text as flat token sequences, failing to capture the distributed nature of important information, which is often spread across multiple locations and connected through both local syntactic dependencies and global semantic relations. Such relational structure is naturally represented as a graph, where tokens or sentences become nodes and their dependencies become edges. To this end, we propose RAGP, which formulates prompt compression as Redundancy-Aware Graph Pruning on a multiplex graph that jointly models fine-grained attention-based dependencies and coarse-grained semantic relations. To efficiently identify non-redundant nodes in this heterogeneous structure (dense local subgraphs and sparse global connections), we employ Levy walks whose heavy-tailed step distribution naturally balances local exploitation with global exploration. Experiments on LongBench show that RAGP achieves an average score of 49.3 under a 4x compression ratio, outperforming existing LLM-based compression methods, such as LongLLMLingua, which attains 48.8 at a 3x compression ratio. Besides, RAGP also surpasses state-of-the-art vision-based text compression paradigms on multiple tasks. The code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/RAGP-B0CB.

AI.tldr: RAGP reformulates prompt compression as redundancy-aware graph pruning on a multiplex graph that captures both fine-grained token-level dependencies and coarse-grained semantic relations. It employs Lévy walks for efficient node selection, achieving superior compression performance (49.3 average score at 4x compression) compared to existing LLM-based and vision-based methods.
AI.motivation: Existing prompt compression methods treat text as flat token sequences, ignoring that important information is distributed across multiple locations and connected through both local syntactic dependencies and global semantic relations. This distributed, relational structure is better modeled as a graph.
AI.method: RAGP constructs a multiplex graph where nodes are tokens/sentences and edges represent both fine-grained attention-based dependencies and coarse-grained semantic relations. It then performs redundancy-aware graph pruning using Lévy walks, whose heavy-tailed step distribution balances local exploitation (dense local subgraphs) with global exploration (sparse global connections), to efficiently identify non-redundant nodes for retention.
AI.result: On LongBench, RAGP achieves an average score of 49.3 under a 4x compression ratio, outperforming LLM-based methods like LongLLMLingua (48.8 at 3x compression). It also surpasses state-of-the-art vision-based text compression paradigms on multiple tasks.
AI.conclusion: Modeling prompt compression as graph pruning on a multiplex relational structure, combined with Lévy walk-based node selection, effectively captures distributed important information and yields state-of-the-art compression performance.

title: A Novel Machine Learning Approach for Central Nervous System Tumor Classification from DNA Methylation
summary: NA methylation profiling has become a powerful approach for central nervous system (CNS) tumor classification, yet important challenges remain regarding cross-cohort transferability, methodological correctness, and robust multiclass evaluation. In this work, we propose a novel and methodologically rigorous machine-learning approach for methylation-based CNS tumor classification that combines Sparse Random Projection for dimensionality reduction with multinomial logistic regression for classification. We evaluate the proposed approach in the same general experimental setting established by a widely used reference classifier. On the 2,801-sample reference cohort, our method achieves a mean accuracy of 96\% under stratified 3-fold cross-validation. On the independent 1,104-sample clinical evaluation cohort, it reaches 86\% accuracy at the 91-class level and 93\% when predictions are evaluated at the methylation class family level. These results improve upon the corresponding state-of-the-art reference figures of 82\% class-level concordance and 88\% family-level concordance, yielding absolute gains of approximately 4 and 5 percentage points, respectively. This improvement is clinically relevant: in a diagnostic setting, a 5-point increase in correct tumor classification can directly affect cancer subtype assignment and, in turn, influence treatment selection and downstream clinical decision-making. Our results show that the proposed model, grounded in stronger methodological practice in machine learning, consistently outperforms the previous state of the art across evaluation settings and can materially improve the reliability of CNS tumor classification.

AI.tldr: A sparse random projection + multinomial logistic regression model for DNA methylation-based CNS tumor classification achieves 86% class-level accuracy (vs. 82% reference) and 93% family-level accuracy (vs. 88% reference) on an independent 1,104-sample cohort, demonstrating clinically meaningful improvement.
AI.motivation: Existing DNA methylation-based CNS tumor classifiers face challenges in cross-cohort transferability, methodological rigor, and robust multiclass evaluation.
