The reference classifier achieves only 82% class-level concordance, leaving room for clinically significant improvement in diagnostic accuracy.
AI.method: The authors propose a pipeline combining Sparse Random Projection for dimensionality reduction of methylation profiles with multinomial logistic regression for 91-class tumor classification. The model is trained on a 2,801-sample reference cohort with stratified 3-fold cross-validation and tested on an independent 1,104-sample clinical evaluation cohort, with evaluation at both fine-grained class level and coarser methylation class family level.
AI.result: On the reference cohort: 96% mean accuracy under stratified 3-fold CV. On the independent clinical cohort: 86% class-level accuracy and 93% family-level accuracy, representing absolute gains of ~4 and ~5 percentage points over the state-of-the-art reference classifier (82% and 88%, respectively).
AI.conclusion: The proposed method, grounded in stronger machine learning methodology, consistently outperforms the previous state of the art. The ~5-point improvement is clinically relevant, as it can directly affect cancer subtype assignment, treatment selection, and downstream clinical decision-making.

title: Discrete Diffusion Language Models for Interactive Radiology Report Drafting
summary: Diffusion language models, which generate text by denoising a token canvas bidirectionally instead of emitting tokens left to right, have become competitive with autoregressive (AR) generation. Medical foundation models, however, remain almost entirely autoregressive. We adapt a mixture-of-experts diffusion language model, DiffusionGemma-26B, and benchmark it against its same-size AR sibling Gemma-4-26B under an identical LoRA recipe on medical visual question answering datasets, scored by a verbosity-robust LLM judge. Diffusion matches or exceeds AR on all of them, and the finetuned model (3.8B active) is competitive with frontier vision-language models; its decoding is also 3.5-4.4x faster. Beyond this parity, the diffusion model offers a drafting capability AR lacks: any-order infill. Because the canvas is denoised bidirectionally, a radiologist can fix report fragments and have the model fill the text between them, an operation inherent to diffusion but not to autoregression, which is subpar at it. This suits real reports, which are often terse or inconsistent across clinicians and institutions.

AI.tldr: A diffusion language model (DiffusionGemma-26B) is finetuned for medical VQA and matches or surpasses its autoregressive counterpart (Gemma-4-26B), with 3.5–4.4× faster decoding, while uniquely enabling any-order text infill for radiology report editing.
AI.motivation: Medical foundation models remain almost exclusively autoregressive despite the emergence of competitive diffusion language models. The authors aim to test whether diffusion models can match AR performance in medical VQA while offering unique capabilities (bidirectional infill) suited to clinical report workflows, where reports are often terse, inconsistent, and require fragment-level editing.
AI.method: A mixture-of-experts diffusion language model, DiffusionGemma-26B, is adapted and benchmarked against its same-size autoregressive sibling (Gemma-4-26B) using an identical LoRA finetuning recipe on medical visual question answering datasets. Evaluation uses a verbosity-robust LLM judge. The diffusion model's inherent any-order infill capability is demonstrated for radiology report editing.
AI.result: The diffusion model matches or exceeds the autoregressive baseline on all medical VQA datasets tested. The finetuned model (3.8B active parameters) is competitive with frontier vision-language models. Decoding is 3.5–4.4× faster than AR. The diffusion model uniquely supports any-order infill: radiologists can fix report fragments and have the model fill text between them, an operation AR models perform poorly.
AI.conclusion: Diffusion language models are a viable and potentially superior alternative to autoregressive models for medical VLMs, offering performance parity, faster decoding, and unique bidirectional infill capabilities that align naturally with clinical report generation and editing workflows.

title: Adapting CCDF Plots for Visualizing Ordinal Regression Results
summary: Cumulative-link ordinal regression models are an alternative approach for analysing ordinal data such as Likert items, which are widely used in Visualization (and other related fields like HCI, psychology etc.). There are many researchers who are strong proponents of this approach, as it makes less stringent assumptions about the data, compared to the more commonly used linear model or ANOVA. Yet, ordinal regression models have seen limited adoption. I posit that one possible reason for this might be due to the difficulty in visually representing the results from such models, and in communicating the key takeaways in an intuitive manner. I propose the use of (modified) Complementary Cumulative Distribution Function (mCCDF) plots to visualize the results of ordinal regression models, and demonstrate how the same takeaways that researchers present from analyses which treat ordinal data as metric can be easily communicated using mCCDFs.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes modified Complementary Cumulative Distribution Function (mCCDF) plots as an intuitive visualization method for communicating results from cumulative-link ordinal regression models, addressing a key barrier to their adoption in fields like Visualization and HCI.
AI.motivation: Ordinal regression models are statistically preferable to linear models/ANOVA for Likert-type data because they make fewer stringent assumptions, yet adoption remains limited. The author hypothesizes this is due to the difficulty of visually representing and intuitively communicating ordinal regression results.
AI.method: The author proposes modified Complementary Cumulative Distribution Function (mCCDF) plots as a visualization technique tailored to ordinal regression outputs, demonstrating how key takeaways commonly presented under metric-assuming analyses can be effectively conveyed through this approach.
AI.result: The paper demonstrates that mCCDF plots enable researchers to communicate the same substantive conclusions as metric-based analyses while respecting the ordinal nature of the data, thereby lowering the interpretability barrier to adopting ordinal regression models.
AI.conclusion: Improved visualization through mCCDF plots can help bridge the gap between statistical rigor and interpretability, potentially encouraging wider adoption of ordinal regression models in visualization and related fields.

title: Overthink-Triggered Slowdown Attacks on LVLM-Based Robotic Systems
summary:
Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have been increasingly integrated into robotic systems. However, these models may exhibit overthinking behaviors, where they generate excessively long reasoning traces, incurring an excessive inference time. This overthinking behavior poses a serious risk to robotic systems, as the adversary can deliberately trigger overthinking to slow down the decision making of a victim robotic system, causing a variety of safety issues (i.e., an overthinking-induced slowdown attack). To initiate this attack, an adversary can embed carefully crafted, human-readable scene text into the visual scene observed by a victim robotic agent, causing significant inference delays even under a strict black-box setting. Therefore, the embedded scene text serves as a significant "trigger" for the attack.
  This work systematically identifies and validates transferable triggers of overthinking in robotic systems by introducing a three-stage framework. First, we construct a diverse corpus of reasoning-intensive scene text and extract overthinking-correlated lexical features from short response prefixes. Second, we perform an efficient black-box search guided by a prefix-based proxy score while selectively confirming a small set of top candidates with full latency measurements. Third, we evaluate black-box transfer using a fixed pool of triggers on unseen images and multiple LVLMs, reporting latency amplification and attack success rates under standard thresholds. Across three representative LVLMs, all triggers yield slowdown ratios greater than 1.0x, with the strongest single-trigger case reaching 6.96x. The physical printing of the text trigger still causes up to 4.74x latency amplification. These results demonstrate that our discovered triggers are transferred between multiple LVLM models and consistently cause significant slowdowns in robotic systems.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies that LVLMs used in robotics are vulnerable to overthinking-induced slowdown attacks, where adversarial scene text triggers excessively long reasoning traces. The authors introduce a three-stage framework to systematically discover transferable text triggers that cause significant inference delays (up to 6.96x slowdown) across multiple LVLMs, even when physically printed.
AI.motivation: LVLMs integrated into robotic systems can exhibit overthinking behaviors—generating excessively long reasoning traces that increase inference time. An adversary can exploit this by embedding crafted scene text to deliberately slow down a robot's decision-making, creating safety risks. The work is motivated by the need to systematically identify and validate these adversarial triggers under black-box conditions.
AI.method: A three-stage framework is proposed: (1) Construct a corpus of reasoning-intensive scene text and extract overthinking-correlated lexical features from short response prefixes. (2) Perform black-box search guided by a prefix-based proxy score, with selective full-latency confirmation on top candidates. (3) Evaluate black-box transferability using a fixed trigger pool on unseen images and multiple LVLMs, measuring latency amplification and attack success rates.
AI.result: Across three representative LVLMs, all discovered triggers yield slowdown ratios exceeding 1.0x, with the strongest single trigger achieving 6.96x. When physically printed, the text trigger still causes up to 4.74x latency amplification. Triggers transfer effectively between different LVLM models and consistently produce significant slowdowns.
AI.conclusion: The discovered overthinking triggers are highly transferable across LVLM models and pose a genuine threat to robotic systems. The attack remains effective even with physical-world deployment (printed text), highlighting a critical vulnerability in LVLM-integrated robotic decision-making pipelines.

title: Kani: A Model Checker for Rust
comment: Accepted at the 39th IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE 2026), Industry Showcase Track
summary: Rust's ownership type system prevents memory errors in safe code, but certain desirable properties remain orthogonal to compilation: the soundness of unsafe operations (e.g., raw pointer dereferences), functional correctness, and absence of runtime panics. We present Kani, an open-source model checker for Rust that pushes bounded model checking beyond bug-finding to provide correctness guarantees for these properties. Kani compiles proof harnesses from Rust's Mid-level Intermediate Representation (MIR) into CBMC's bit-precise verification engine, automatically checking a comprehensive set of safety properties with no user annotation. To extend verification from bounded to unbounded, Kani provides a specification language comprising function contracts, loop contracts, quantifiers, and function stubbing. We demonstrate feasibility through case studies on industrial Rust projects, where contracts upgraded verification from panic-freedom to functional correctness, uncovering six previously unknown bugs. Kani operates at scale in production CI, with over 16,000 harnesses verified per code change in the Rust standard library verification campaign.

AI.tldr: Kani is an open-source model checker for Rust that provides bounded and unbounded correctness guarantees for safety properties (including unsafe code soundness, functional correctness, and panic-freedom) by compiling MIR into CBMC's verification engine, and supports contracts for scaling to unbounded verification, demonstrated through industrial case studies and production CI deployment.
AI.motivation: Rust's ownership type system guarantees memory safety in safe code, but three critical properties remain unaddressed: (1) soundness of unsafe operations like raw pointer dereferences, (2) functional correctness, and (3) absence of runtime panics. These require verification beyond what the compiler provides, motivating a tool that can deliver formal guarantees for real-world Rust code.
AI.method: Kani translates Rust's Mid-level Intermediate Representation (MIR) into CBMC's bit-precise bounded model checking engine, enabling automatic checking of safety properties without user annotations for bounded verification. For unbounded verification, Kani introduces a specification language with function contracts, loop contracts, quantifiers, and function stubbing. Proof harnesses are written in Rust itself, leveraging the same MIR compilation pipeline.
AI.result: Case studies on industrial Rust projects showed that contracts upgraded verification from mere panic-freedom to full functional correctness, uncovering six previously unknown bugs. Kani operates at production scale in CI, with over 16,000 harnesses verified per code change in the Rust standard library verification campaign.
AI.conclusion: Kani demonstrates that bounded model checking can be practically extended to unbounded verification through contracts, providing meaningful correctness guarantees for real-world Rust code at industrial scale, including both safe and unsafe code properties.

title: Office Comprehension Benchmark
summary: We introduce Office Comprehension Bench (OCB), the first public benchmark to jointly evaluate LLM systems on Word, Excel, and PowerPoint comprehension over native file formats (.docx, .xlsx, .pptx) and their variants. OCB consists of two tracks. File Fidelity Q&A tests structural and visual perception of office artifacts - tables, charts, embedded images, formulas, and app-specific elements such as headers, speaker notes, and named ranges. Domain Q&A tests expert-level reasoning grounded in real-world industry documents across 12 professional domains, with queries requiring multi-step analysis and synthesis across documents. Each reference answer is decomposed into atomic, binary-gradable claims, and an ensemble of LLM judges scores responses against each claim independently. Even the strongest frontier system in its default reasoning mode reaches only about 59.3% on Domain Q&A; increasing thinking depth within a tier does not move performance materially, while moving to a higher product tier yields modest gains. We release the dataset, evaluation tooling, judge prompt, and a public leaderboard.

AI.tldr: OCB is the first public benchmark evaluating LLMs on native Office document comprehension (.docx, .xlsx, .pptx), featuring File Fidelity Q&A for structural/visual perception and Domain Q&A for expert reasoning across 12 industries. Evaluation uses atomic, binary-gradable claims with ensemble LLM judging. The strongest frontier system achieves only ~59.3% on Domain Q&A, with thinking depth showing limited gains and higher product tiers yielding modest improvements.
AI.motivation: Prior benchmarks fail to evaluate LLMs on native Microsoft Office file formats (.docx, .xlsx, .pptx) despite their ubiquity in professional settings. Existing evaluations either convert documents to text/markdown (losing structural fidelity) or focus on narrow tasks. There is a need for a comprehensive, public benchmark that tests both perceptual understanding of office artifacts (tables, charts, formulas, embedded images, speaker notes, etc.) and domain-specific reasoning over real-world industry documents.
AI.method: OCB is structured into two tracks: (1) File Fidelity Q&A, which tests structural and visual perception of native office elements; (2) Domain Q&A, which tests expert-level, multi-step reasoning across 12 professional domains using real-world documents. Evaluation decomposes each reference answer into atomic, binary-gradable claims, and an ensemble of LLM judges independently scores model responses against each claim, yielding fine-grained, reproducible metrics.
AI.result: The strongest frontier LLM system in its default reasoning mode achieves approximately 59.3% on Domain Q&A. Increasing thinking depth within a given model tier does not materially improve performance, while moving to a higher product tier yields only modest gains. These results indicate substantial headroom for improvement in office document comprehension.
AI.conclusion: OCB establishes a rigorous, multi-faceted evaluation framework exposing significant limitations in current LLMs' ability to comprehend native office documents and perform domain-grounded reasoning. The marginal impact of thinking depth suggests architectural or training-data bottlenecks rather than compute-limited reasoning. The dataset, tooling, judge prompt, and leaderboard are publicly released to spur further research.

title: From Approximation to Emergence: A Theory of Deep Learning
summary: Deep learning has outgrown any single mathematical explanation. From Approximation to Emergence develops a unified, proof-oriented account of modern deep learning theory, tracing a path from the classical foundations of approximation, optimization, and generalization to the contemporary mechanisms of overparameterization, robustness, generative modeling, transformers, in-context learning, scaling laws, interpretability, alignment, and emergence. Rather than presenting isolated results, the book organizes a broad literature into a coherent research narrative: each theory is examined through the object it controls, the assumptions that make it valid, and the phenomena it leaves unexplained. Written for researchers, graduate students, and mathematically trained practitioners, this monograph offers a rigorous map of deep learning theory as it stands today: powerful, incomplete, and increasingly centered on the question of how learned mechanisms arise from scale, data, architecture, and training.

AI.tldr: A monograph that organizes modern deep learning theory into a unified, proof-oriented narrative, spanning from classical foundations (approximation, optimization, generalization) to contemporary phenomena (overparameterization, transformers, scaling laws, emergence), highlighting what each theory explains and what remains unexplained.
AI.motivation: Deep learning has outgrown any single mathematical explanation; existing theoretical results are scattered across isolated papers. The book aims to synthesize this broad literature into a coherent research narrative, providing a rigorous map of the field's current state — powerful yet incomplete — centered on understanding how learned mechanisms arise from scale, data, architecture, and training.
AI.method: The book adopts a proof-oriented, unified approach that traces a path from classical theory (approximation, optimization, generalization) to contemporary mechanisms (overparameterization, robustness, generative models, transformers, in-context learning, scaling laws, interpretability, alignment, emergence). Each theory is examined through three lenses: the object it controls, the assumptions that validate it, and the phenomena it fails to explain.
AI.result: The monograph does not present original empirical or theoretical results; rather, it delivers a structured, rigorous synthesis of existing deep learning theory, organized into a coherent narrative that exposes both the power and the incompleteness of current mathematical frameworks for understanding deep learning.
AI.conclusion: Deep learning theory today is powerful but incomplete. The field is increasingly centered on the question of how learned mechanisms emerge from the interaction of scale, data, architecture, and training — a question that no single existing theory fully answers.

title: Beyond Next-Token Prediction: An RLVR Proof of Concept for Tool-Use Agents on Atlassian Workflows
summary: Large language models are trained to predict the next token, not to act inside a specific API. In niche enterprise SaaS workflows -- where success means hitting the right endpoint with the right nested arguments in the right order -- this objective mismatch shows up as silent failures: dropped required fields, hallucinated tools, or early stops after a single read. We ask whether Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR), applied directly in the target environment, closes the gap. As a proof of concept we build a suite of five synthetic environments emulating the Jira REST v3 and Confluence v2 APIs at schema fidelity; rewards are computed entirely from the tool-call trace, with no live API, no learned judge, and no human label in the loop. Scoring prompted Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3.5-4B on the same checkers that drive GRPO training, we find that on the four scenarios whose rewards are non-degenerate the RL-trained policy lifts average reward from a 4B-baseline range of 0.35--0.92 to 0.95--1.00, with the largest single gain on Confluence page creation ($0.35 \rightarrow 1.00$). We position this as a preliminary step toward outcome-optimised small models for niche enterprise APIs, and foreground two limitations a workshop reader should weigh: hand-crafting verifiable rewards does not scale beyond the handful of endpoints reported here, and one of our five scenarios (ticket-transition) has a saturating reward shape that the prompted 4B already maxes out.

AI.tldr: Small language models (1.7B–4B) fine-tuned with RLVR in synthetic Jira/Confluence API environments achieve near-perfect tool-calling accuracy (0.95–1.00 reward), closing a critical gap where prompted models silently fail on nested API workflows. The approach uses purely trace-based verifiable rewards without any live API calls or human labels.
AI.motivation: LLMs are optimized for next-token prediction, not for correctly sequencing nested API calls. In enterprise SaaS workflows (e.g., Jira, Confluence), this leads to silent failures: dropped required fields, hallucinated tools, premature task termination. The authors investigate whether RLVR—using only verifiable, environment-computed rewards from tool-call traces—can close this reliability gap without human annotation or live API access.
AI.method: The authors construct five synthetic environments mimicking Jira REST v3 and Confluence v2 APIs at full schema fidelity. Rewards are computed deterministically from the tool-call trace (no live API, no learned judge, no human in the loop). These same checkers serve dual-purpose: scoring prompted baselines and driving GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) training. Models evaluated are Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3.5-4B.
AI.result: On four non-degenerate scenarios, RL-trained policies improved average reward from a 4B-baseline range of 0.35–0.92 to 0.95–1.00. The largest single gain was on Confluence page creation (0.35 → 1.00). One scenario (ticket-transition) was already maxed out by the prompted 4B model, showing no room for improvement.
AI.conclusion: RLVR with trace-based verifiable rewards can effectively align small LMs to niche enterprise API workflows, achieving near-perfect execution fidelity. However, the approach faces two key limitations: (1) hand-crafting verifiable reward functions does not scale beyond a few endpoints, and (2) some tasks already saturate under prompt-only baselines, limiting the marginal benefit of RL fine-tuning.

title: A Social Norms Approach to Youth Social Media Design
summary: Young people consistently say they want authentic self-expression, less judgment, and more interpersonal trust on social media, yet they rarely manage to engage that way. My dissertation argues that the obstacle is normative rather than individual: how youth engage is governed less by personal choice than by platform norms, peer perception, and beliefs about how others behave. I take a social norms approach to youth social media design organized around three claims. First, platform norms constrain individual behavior, producing a pluralistic ignorance in which youth enact norms they privately reject. Second, design interventions are themselves shaped by existing norms, so whether a feature works depends on the environment around it, which means relational goals such as privacy must be treated as social norms rather than individual settings. Third, a societal norm about what ``social media'' is -- equating it with a few mainstream platforms -- confines policy and design to mitigating those platforms rather than actively envisioning supportive alternatives. Together these claims motivate my dissertation research: engaging youth directly in designing and building an evidence-based independent platform whose features consistently signal that building trusted connections is what the space is for.

AI.tldr: Youth want authentic, trusting social media interactions but fail to achieve them due to normative constraints, not personal failings. The dissertation argues that platform norms, peer perception, and pluralistic ignorance govern youth behavior; design interventions must treat relational goals like privacy as social norms; and the narrow societal definition of "social media" limits imagination of alternatives. The research engages youth in co-designing an evidence-based independent platform that signals trust-building as its core purpose.
AI.motivation: The gap between youth's stated desires (authentic self-expression, less judgment, interpersonal trust) and their actual social media behavior. The author argues this is not an individual-level failure but a structural, normative problem that existing platform design and policy fail to address.
AI.method: A social norms framework applied across three interconnected claims, combined with participatory design: directly engaging youth in co-designing and building an evidence-based independent social media platform whose features normatively signal trust-building as the space's purpose.
AI.result: Three claims are advanced: (1) pluralistic ignorance drives youth to enact norms they privately reject; (2) design interventions' effectiveness depends on the surrounding normative environment, requiring privacy and relational goals to be framed as social norms; (3) the dominant societal conception of social media as a few mainstream platforms constrains policy and design to harm reduction rather than envisioning alternatives.
AI.conclusion: Effective solutions require moving beyond individual-level fixes or incremental platform reforms toward actively building alternative social media spaces, co-designed with youth, that embed trust-building norms directly into platform architecture and feature design.

title: LIB-TRAP: Standard Cell Library Hardware Trojan Risk Assessment and Prevention
summary: Vulnerabilities inherent to the fabless semiconductor manufacturing model have significantly increased the risk of malicious Hardware Trojan (HT) insertion, posing severe threats to hardware security. Several HT mitigation and detection strategies have been developed, and existing works explore the insertion of HTs in the space between standard cells in an integrated circuit. However, there is a lack of research into the vulnerabilities posed by the building blocks of most digital designs on the market today, the standard cells. This work investigates a novel threat model in which standard cells are considered untrusted. Our proposed threat model provides the design house with a tampered standard cell library. The intended netlist is synthesized and implemented using the tampered library. During fabrication, a nefarious foundry replaces the library's deactivated HT cells with activated counterparts. Using open-source and industry-standard Electronic Design Automation (EDA) tools, existing standard cell libraries, Saed32nm and Sky130nm, are converted into malicious libraries capable of masking the presence of arbitrary HTs from IC designers. The malicious library is then applied and characterized in multiple standard benchmark designs. To demonstrate the efficacy and stealthiness of this standard cell-based attack vector, three benchmark circuits, an AES-128 encryption core, an Ethernet controller, and a WISHBONE DMA engine, were synthesized using both clean and Trojan-infected libraries across Synopsys 32nm and SkyWater 130nm technologies. Design-level features, including total cell count, total area, dynamic power consumption, and static power, were extracted from these synthesized circuits to serve as inputs for binary classification

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a novel hardware Trojan attack vector where standard cells—the fundamental building blocks of digital ICs—are weaponized. The threat model assumes the design house receives a tampered standard cell library containing deactivated malicious cells, which a rogue foundry later activates during fabrication. The authors demonstrate this attack on AES-128, Ethernet, and WISHBONE cores across 32nm and 130nm technologies, showing it evades detection via standard design-level feature analysis.
AI.motivation: Existing hardware Trojan research focuses on inserting HTs in inter-cell spaces or modifying netlists, but overlooks vulnerabilities within standard cell libraries themselves—the foundational components of virtually all modern digital designs. With the fabless model, design houses trust third-party standard cell libraries, creating a critical but underexplored attack surface.
AI.method: The authors convert open-source standard cell libraries (Saed32nm, Sky130nm) into malicious libraries by embedding deactivated Trojan cells. The design house unknowingly synthesizes the target netlist using this tampered library. During fabrication, the foundry swaps deactivated HT cells with activated versions. Three benchmark circuits (AES-128, Ethernet controller, WISHBONE DMA) are synthesized with clean vs. Trojan-infected libraries across two technology nodes. Design-level metrics (cell count, area, dynamic power, static power) are extracted to evaluate detectability via binary classification.
AI.result: The malicious standard cell libraries successfully mask HT presence from IC designers during synthesis. Design-level feature analysis across benchmark circuits shows that Trojan-infected designs are statistically indistinguishable from clean designs using standard metrics, demonstrating the attack's stealthiness.
AI.conclusion: Standard cell libraries represent a significant and underappreciated attack vector for hardware Trojans. The proposed threat model reveals that even trusted netlists synthesized with tampered libraries can yield malicious hardware that evades conventional detection methods, highlighting the need for standard cell-level trust verification in the IC supply chain.

title: A Capacity-Aware Parr Model for Agile Projects
summary: Classical software effort distribution models, including the PNR family and Parr alter native curve, were designed to describe the time distribution of development effort under an implied staffing pattern. Their direct use in agile environments is limited when team capacity is fixed, partially fixed, or externally constrained, the original curve may prescribe a staff demand that the organization cannot allocate. This paper proposes a compact refactoring of Parr model as a capacity-aware forecasting layer for agile projects. The contribution is deliberately narrower than a full causal theory of project dynamics. A normalized Parr shaped latent effort demand is combined with an observed or planned capacity trajectory. The resulting model forecasts aggregate progress, completion time, capacity deficit, and capacity slack without assuming that the same internal activity path is followed under resource restriction. The model uses a small parameter set such as total effort K, a Parr shape parameter, an origin constant c that can match nonzero initial staffing, and the capacity trajectory. A discrete sprint formulation is provided, together with a calibration method from ordinary Scrum records and a rolling origin validation protocol against simple management baselines.

AI.tldr: A capacity-aware refactoring of the Parr model is proposed for agile projects, combining a normalized Parr-shaped latent effort demand with observed capacity trajectories to forecast progress, completion time, and capacity deficits/slacks under constrained staffing.
AI.motivation: Classical software effort distribution models (PNR family, Parr curve) assume an implied staffing pattern that may be infeasible in agile environments where team capacity is fixed, partially fixed, or externally constrained, limiting their direct applicability.
AI.method: A compact refactoring of the Parr model as a capacity-aware forecasting layer: a normalized Parr-shaped latent effort demand is combined with an observed or planned capacity trajectory. A discrete sprint formulation, calibration from Scrum records, and rolling-origin validation against simple management baselines are provided.
AI.result: The model forecasts aggregate progress, completion time, capacity deficit, and capacity slack without assuming the same internal activity path under resource restriction, using a small parameter set (total effort K, Parr shape parameter, origin constant c, capacity trajectory).
AI.conclusion: The refactored Parr model serves as a practical forecasting layer for agile projects operating under capacity constraints, though the contribution is deliberately narrower than a full causal theory of project dynamics.

title: RuleChef: Grounding LLM Task Knowledge in Human-Editable Rules
summary: We present RuleChef, a framework that uses large language models (LLMs) to generate executable rules for NLP tasks such as text classification, Named Entity Recognition (NER), or relation extraction. Rules are generated based on a task description and a set of labeled examples, then they are iteratively improved based both on additional examples and on human feedback overexisting rules. RuleChef can also be used to bootstrap rules using the observed input-output pairs from any existing model for a given task. LLMs are used only at learning time, synthesizing rules and iteratively patching them based on failures measured on a held-out split. The result of this process is a fast, deterministic, and inspectable rule system. Preliminary evaluation is performed on both classification and NER tasks. We release RuleChef as open-source software under an Apache 2.0

AI.tldr: RuleChef is an LLM-based framework that synthesizes, iteratively improves, and bootstraps executable rules for NLP tasks (classification, NER, relation extraction) from task descriptions and labeled examples, producing fast, deterministic, and inspectable rule systems.
AI.motivation: To bridge the gap between opaque, black-box NLP models and the need for transparent, interpretable, and efficient decision-making systems by automatically generating human-readable, executable rules using LLMs at training time only.
AI.method: RuleChef uses LLMs to synthesize initial rules from a task description plus labeled examples, then iteratively patches them based on failures on a held-out set. It supports human-in-the-loop feedback on existing rules and can bootstrap rules from any existing model's input-output pairs. LLMs are used solely during learning, yielding a deterministic rule system at inference.
AI.result: Preliminary evaluation demonstrates effectiveness on both text classification and Named Entity Recognition tasks. The resulting rule systems are fast, deterministic, and inspectable.
AI.conclusion: RuleChef demonstrates that LLMs can serve as effective rule synthesis engines, producing transparent and efficient NLP systems. The framework is released as open-source under Apache 2.0.

title: Black-Box Inference of LLM Architectural Properties with Restrictive API Access
summary: In practice, most commercial LLM providers do not publicly release details of underlying LLM architectures. However, prior work has shown that given limited API access to an LLM (namely, top-$k$ logits and/or a logit bias function), one can recover certain architectural details of an LLM, such as the hidden dimension of the feed-forward network. Perhaps in response to these results, most commercial LLM providers have restricted their APIs to expose only the single logit for each decoded token, and they no longer give users the ability to bias logits. We show that even under current restrictive APIs, several architectural parameters are still recoverable. We present NightVision, an attack that uses restrictive black-box API access to estimate the hidden dimension, depth, and parameter count of an LLM. Algorithmically, NightVision relies on a novel common set prompting technique in which multiple prompts expose log probabilities for the same set of output tokens; a spectral analysis of these results is used to infer hidden dimension. NightVision additionally uses end-to-end time to first token (TTFT) measurements and the estimated hidden dimension to estimate depth and parameter count. We empirically evaluate NightVision on 32 open-source LLMs, recovering hidden dimension to within 23% average relative error across all models (9% on MoE models), and depth and parameter count to within 53% for models exceeding three billion parameters. We run extensive ablations to demonstrate how these accuracies scale with token budget and model properties. Overall, our results suggest that current LLM APIs are not sufficiently restricted to fully obfuscate the architectural details of their underlying models.

AI.tldr: NightVision is a black-box attack that recovers architectural details (hidden dimension, depth, parameter count) of LLMs using only restrictive API access (single logit per token, no logit bias). It employs novel common set prompting with spectral analysis and TTFT measurements, achieving 23% average error on hidden dimension across 32 open-source models.
AI.motivation: Commercial LLM providers have increasingly restricted API access to prevent architectural leakage, exposing only single logits per token and removing logit bias capabilities. The paper investigates whether these countermeasures are sufficient to prevent recovery of sensitive architectural parameters.
AI.method: NightVision uses two complementary techniques: (1) Common set prompting — crafting multiple prompts that expose log probabilities for the same output token set, followed by spectral analysis (singular value decomposition) of the resulting log-probability matrix to infer hidden dimension via rank estimation; (2) End-to-end time-to-first-token (TTFT) measurements combined with the estimated hidden dimension to derive depth (number of transformer layers) and total parameter count, leveraging the predictable relationship between these architectural parameters and inference latency.
AI.result: Evaluated on 32 open-source LLMs: hidden dimension recovered within 23% average relative error overall (9% on Mixture-of-Experts models). For models exceeding 3B parameters, depth and parameter count estimated within 53% error. Extensive ablations characterize how accuracy scales with token budget and model properties.
AI.conclusion: Current restrictive LLM APIs remain insufficient to fully obfuscate architectural details. The findings suggest providers need stronger defenses against architectural inference attacks.

title: World Feedback for Clinical Agents: Diagnosing RL in FHIR Environments
summary: Clinical protocol-execution tasks -- checking a lab value, applying a threshold, placing a correctly structured FHIR order -- are natural candidates for RL from world feedback: once clinical SMEs encode decision logic into a verifier, that verifier grades unlimited rollouts without per-episode annotation. But applying RL requires a sound feedback channel and sufficient base capability. We audit MedAgentBench v1/v2, find a 41.7\% silent-finish ceiling that makes inaction the RL dominant strategy, and construct \textbf{MedAgentBench-v3 (MAB-v3)} (508 tasks, 8.9\% ceiling). Training Qwen3-8B exposes two structural barriers: a \emph{capability ceiling} (10/20 task types have 0\% base performance, zero gradient) and a \emph{format-knowledge barrier} (3/20 types require exact clinical codes undiscoverable by exploration). Pure RL reaches 18.2\% pass@1 vs.\ 34.1\% for rule-based SFT; the 15.9~pp gap is attributable entirely to these barriers. A decision/format-knowledge/lookup taxonomy predicts RL learnability and prescribes the fix: SFT to inject codes, RL to learn conditionals.

AI.tldr: The paper audits existing clinical RL benchmarks (MedAgentBench v1/v2), finding a 41.7% silent-finish ceiling that makes inaction dominant. The authors construct MAB-v3 (508 tasks, 8.9% ceiling) and train Qwen3-8B, revealing two barriers: a capability ceiling (zero base performance on 10/20 task types) and a format-knowledge barrier (undiscoverable exact clinical codes). Pure RL achieves 18.2% pass@1 vs. 34.1% for rule-based SFT. A decision/format-knowledge/lookup taxonomy predicts RL learnability, prescribing SFT for code injection and RL for learning conditionals.
AI.motivation: Clinical protocol-execution tasks (lab checks, thresholding, FHIR orders) are natural RL candidates since verifiers can grade unlimited rollouts. However, existing benchmarks have structural flaws that undermine RL training, and the community lacks a clear understanding of when RL succeeds versus when SFT is needed for clinical agent tasks.
AI.method: The authors audit MedAgentBench v1/v2 to quantify silent-finish ceilings. They construct MAB-v3 with 508 tasks across 20 types with a deliberately low 8.9% ceiling. Using Qwen3-8B, they run pure RL training and compare against rule-based SFT. They develop a three-category taxonomy (decision, format-knowledge, lookup) to classify each task type and predict RL learnability based on whether the task requires discoverable conditional logic vs. pre-existing exact knowledge.
AI.result: MAB-v1/v2 has a 41.7% silent-finish ceiling. In MAB-v3: 10/20 task types show 0% base performance (capability ceiling, zero gradient), and 3/20 require exact clinical codes undiscoverable by exploration (format-knowledge barrier). Pure RL achieves 18.2% pass@1 vs. 34.1% for rule-based SFT — the entire 15.9pp gap is attributable to these two barriers. The taxonomy correctly predicts which task types RL can learn.
AI.conclusion: RL for clinical agents is bottlenecked not by reward design but by capability ceilings and format-knowledge barriers. The prescriptive solution is a hybrid: SFT to inject undiscoverable codes and procedural knowledge, followed by RL to learn conditional decision logic. The decision/format-knowledge/lookup taxonomy provides a principled framework for determining which training paradigm to apply per task type.

title: Visual Analytics of Neighborhood Attribute Profiles for Exploring Structural Equivalence
comment: 5 pages, 3 figures. Accepted as a Short Paper at IEEE VIS 2026
summary: Exploring similar nodes in attributed networks represents a key challenge in data mining. While recent representation learning methods embed networks into low-dimensional vectors, they often implicitly assume a uniform and continuous feature space. This paper proposes a visual analytics approach using dimensionality reduction to help clarify the true topological structure of high-dimensional feature spaces formed by nodes' neighborhood attribute profiles. Analyzing inter-firm transaction networks indicates that structural roles can form complex, non-linear manifolds with density biases. Comparing this feature space with industry classifications suggested: (1) supply chain hierarchies transition continuously; (2) categories treated identically under general semantics can be clearly separated by actual transaction networks; and (3) a single industry label may fragment into multiple regions. These findings suggest potential limitations in assuming identical semantics imply similar structural roles and highlight the possible need for new similarity metrics aligned with manifold topology.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a visual analytics method using dimensionality reduction to explore the true manifold structure of node attribute profiles in networks. Applied to inter-firm transaction networks, it reveals that structural roles form non-linear manifolds with density biases, and that industry classifications can be fragmented, continuously transitioning, or semantically separated — challenging assumptions underlying current representation learning methods.
AI.motivation: Current representation learning methods for attributed networks implicitly assume a uniform and continuous feature space, which may not reflect the true topological structure of high-dimensional attribute spaces. The authors seek to expose potential mismatches between this assumption and reality, particularly around how industry classifications map to structural roles in transaction networks.
AI.method: A visual analytics approach employing dimensionality reduction to project high-dimensional feature spaces — formed by nodes' neighborhood attribute profiles — into interpretable low-dimensional views, enabling qualitative inspection of manifold topology and density structure. Applied to inter-firm transaction network data.
AI.result: Three key empirical findings: (1) supply chain hierarchies exhibit continuous transitions rather than discrete boundaries; (2) categories that are semantically identical under general classification schemes become clearly separated within actual transaction networks; and (3) a single industry label can fragment into multiple disjoint regions in the feature space. Density biases in the manifold were also observed.
AI.conclusion: The findings suggest that assuming identical semantics implies similar structural roles may be problematic. The authors highlight the potential need for new similarity metrics that are explicitly aligned with the manifold topology of the feature space, rather than relying on Euclidean or uniform-space assumptions prevalent in existing methods.

title: VeriChat: An Agentic Conversational AI Assistant for Hardware Security Verification
comment: This paper will be presented at the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Omni-layer Intelligent Systems (COINS 2026), (https://coinsconf.com/)
summary: Hardware security verification is a multi-stage process in which engineers must navigate complex design analyses, threat considerations, and verification strategies. They often need security-focused guidance, yet current verification environments provide little structured support for such assistance. Although conversational AI could offer such on-demand assistance, directly using general-purpose chatbots like ChatGPT or Gemini is risky due to their tendency to hallucinate and their reliance on static, outdated knowledge. We present VeriChat, a domain-specialized conversational assistant designed to support, rather than replace, existing verification workflows by providing context-aware security guidance. VeriChat employs a retrieval-augmented, multi-agent workflow in which three specialized agents collaboratively minimize hallucinations while improving the transparency and reliability of the response. Beyond question answering, VeriChat integrates open-source EDA tools, including Icarus Verilog, Yosys, and SymbiYosys, to perform syntax checking, synthesis analysis, simulation, and formal verification directly on user-provided RTL designs. Evaluated using a comprehensive methodology, VeriChat achieves a Faithfulness score of 87.73%, significantly outperforming the leading proprietary models. We demonstrate the framework through a hardware Trojan detection case study on an AES S-Box IP, where VeriChat autonomously identifies, simulates, and formally proves a covert key-leakage vulnerability through a multi-turn conversational workflow.

AI.tldr: VeriChat is a retrieval-augmented, multi-agent conversational AI assistant for hardware security verification that minimizes hallucination (87.73% Faithfulness), outperforms proprietary models, and integrates open-source EDA tools to autonomously detect and formally prove hardware vulnerabilities like covert key leakage in an AES S-Box IP.
AI.motivation: Hardware security verification is a complex, multi-stage process lacking structured, on-demand security guidance. While conversational AI could fill this gap, general-purpose chatbots (ChatGPT, Gemini) are unreliable due to hallucination and outdated static knowledge. A domain-specialized, trustworthy assistant is needed that integrates directly with verification workflows.
AI.method: VeriChat uses a retrieval-augmented, multi-agent architecture with three specialized agents collaborating to reduce hallucination and improve response transparency. It integrates open-source EDA tools (Icarus Verilog, Yosys, SymbiYosys) for syntax checking, synthesis, simulation, and formal verification on user-provided RTL. A comprehensive evaluation methodology measures Faithfulness and other metrics.
AI.result: VeriChat achieves an 87.73% Faithfulness score, significantly outperforming leading proprietary models. In a case study on an AES S-Box IP, VeriChat autonomously identifies, simulates, and formally proves a covert hardware Trojan key-leakage vulnerability through multi-turn conversational interaction.
AI.conclusion: Domain-specialized, retrieval-augmented multi-agent systems like VeriChat can provide reliable, context-aware security guidance for hardware verification workflows, effectively mitigating hallucination risks while enabling autonomous vulnerability detection and formal proof generation in real design scenarios.

title: A Single Patch Is Not Enough: Deterministic Fusion of Repair Candidates
summary:
Modern LLM coding agents are commonly evaluated using pass@k, but developers typically apply a single final patch in real-world settings. This pass@k-to-pass@1 gap is a post-generation problem: a candidate patch pool may contain a correct patch, but the system must decide which one to suggest to developers. Existing post-generation approaches mainly rank whole candidates, filter them with tests, or query an LLM judge, but none deterministically reuse shared edit-atom evidence to both select and construct the final patch. Thus, we propose PatchFusion, a deterministic atomic evidence fusion approach for candidate patches that consults no test outcome at decision time. PatchFusion first fuses whole-diff agreement into a repair neighborhood, selects an auditable representative, and then applies evidence-constrained fusion (ECF) to retain repeated edit atoms and prune unsupported parts. To evaluate this setting, we build PatchFuseBench, a fixed-pool benchmark covering SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Multilingual, and Defects4J candidate patches.
  On PatchFuseBench, PatchFusion solves 426/500 bugs on SWE-bench Verified and 236/300 on SWE-bench Multilingual, and reaches 87/371 plausible patches on Defects4J, outperforming every matched candidate-pool selector on all three. PatchFusion recovers 41 and 27 bugs that no single source solves (30 and 18 more over the best single source). Ablation studies show that ECF adds +5/+6/+9 solved bugs by recovering in-pool repairs that selection misses, with no observed regression, and that PatchFusion's gains remain stable as candidate pools are resampled. On these complementary multi-source pools, cross-candidate evidence recovers more correct patches than the test-based and LLM-based selectors we evaluate, at orders-of-magnitude lower cost, reaching within 96.2% and 89.7% of the candidate-reachable ceiling on the two SWE-bench benchmarks.

AI.tldr: PatchFusion proposes a deterministic, test-free method that fuses shared edit-atom evidence across candidate patches to construct a single final patch, outperforming test-based and LLM-based selectors on SWE-bench and Defects4J benchmarks while closing the pass@k-to-pass@1 gap.
AI.motivation: While pass@k metrics show LLM coding agents can generate correct patches somewhere in a candidate pool, real-world developers apply only one final patch. Existing post-generation selection methods (ranking, test-filtering, LLM judging) fail to deterministically reuse shared edit-atom evidence across candidates to both select and construct the final patch, leaving a significant pass@k-to-pass@1 gap.
AI.method: PatchFusion operates in three stages: (1) fusing whole-diff agreement across candidates into a repair neighborhood, (2) selecting an auditable representative patch, and (3) applying evidence-constrained fusion (ECF) to retain edit atoms repeatedly observed across candidates while pruning unsupported edits. The method consults no test outcomes at decision time and is fully deterministic. A new benchmark, PatchFuseBench, is built from fixed candidate pools across SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Multilingual, and Defects4J.
AI.result: PatchFusion solves 426/500 (SWE-bench Verified), 236/300 (SWE-bench Multilingual), and achieves 87/371 plausible patches (Defects4J), outperforming all matched candidate-pool selectors. It recovers 41 and 27 bugs respectively that no single source solves. ECF ablation adds +5/+6/+9 solved bugs with no regression. Gains remain stable under candidate pool resampling. PatchFusion reaches 96.2% and 89.7% of the candidate-reachable ceiling on the two SWE-bench benchmarks at orders-of-magnitude lower cost than test-based/LLM-based selectors.
AI.conclusion: Cross-candidate evidence fusion provides a cost-effective, deterministic alternative to test-based and LLM-based post-generation selection, substantially closing the pass@k-to-pass@1 gap without requiring test execution or LLM judging at decision time.

title: TurnNat: Automatic Evaluation of Turn-Taking Naturalness in Dyadic Spoken Dialogue
summary: Turn-taking naturalness is central to full-duplex spoken dialogue systems, yet its automatic evaluation remains limited. Existing evaluations often rely on human judgments or behavior-specific timing metrics, making it difficult to compare heterogeneous timing failures within a unified framework. We propose TurnNat, a likelihood-based framework for automatic turn-taking naturalness evaluation in two-channel spoken dialogue. A causal turn-taking prediction model trained on natural conversations estimates future two-speaker voice-activity states, and the negative log-likelihood (NLL) of the observed future activity measures timing atypicality. TurnNat pools frame-level NLLs over turn-taking boundary units (TBUs) extracted from utterance onsets and offsets, and aggregates mean and tail TBU scores into a dialogue-level naturalness score. We further construct a controlled perturbation benchmark of paired natural and perturbed dialogue clips, validated by human naturalness judgments. Experiments on this benchmark show that TurnNat successfully identifies unnatural turn-taking perturbations across heterogeneous timing failures.

AI.tldr: TurnNat is a likelihood-based automatic evaluation framework for turn-taking naturalness in two-channel spoken dialogue, using a causal prediction model to measure timing atypicality via negative log-likelihood, validated on a human-annotated perturbation benchmark.
AI.motivation: Current turn-taking evaluation in full-duplex spoken dialogue systems relies on subjective human judgments or isolated timing metrics, lacking a unified, automatic framework to compare heterogeneous timing failures.
AI.method: TurnNat trains a causal turn-taking prediction model on natural conversations to estimate future two-speaker voice-activity states. It computes frame-level negative log-likelihood (NLL) of observed future activity as a timing atypicality measure, pools NLLs over turn-taking boundary units (TBUs) around utterance onsets/offsets, and aggregates mean and tail TBU scores into a dialogue-level naturalness score. A controlled perturbation benchmark with paired natural/perturbed clips validated by human judgments is also constructed.
AI.result: TurnNat successfully identifies unnatural turn-taking perturbations across heterogeneous timing failures on the constructed benchmark, with validation from human naturalness judgments.
AI.conclusion: TurnNat provides a unified, automatic, likelihood-based metric for turn-taking naturalness that correlates with human perception and handles diverse timing anomalies in full-duplex spoken dialogue.

title: Multi-modal Rail Crossing Safety Analysis
summary: Given one or more images of a railway crossing, can we leverage visual cues that allow us to robustly estimate how safe it is? Can we improve our ability to do so by introducing structured data (such as official accident reports) about the accident history of that crossing into our models? In this work, we explore how to best answer those questions towards building an AI system that can ingest multi-modal data for railway crossings and provide safety assessment and scores that align with expert opinion and with safety scoring used by the Federal Railroad Administration (FRA). To that end, we propose a proof-of-concept pipeline that delivers on that goal, while at the same time exploring and tackling a number of critical research challenges that pertain to different parts of the pipeline, from data preparation to different learning paradigms that can allow us to realize such a system. Indicatively, our proposed system identifies HIGH-RISK and LOW-RISK crossings with a macro F1 score of 0.757 and estimates FRA-based safety scores with an RMSE of 0.078 and correlation of 0.492 using a routed fine-tuned compact VLM pipeline, while producing qualitative results that align with domain-expert assessment.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a multi-modal AI pipeline that estimates railway crossing safety from images and structured accident data, achieving a macro F1 of 0.757 for HIGH/LOW-RISK classification and RMSE of 0.078 for predicting FRA safety scores using a routed fine-tuned compact Vision-Language Model (VLM).
AI.motivation: Railway crossing safety assessment currently relies on manual inspection and accident reports. The authors aim to automate this by leveraging visual cues from crossing images combined with structured data (e.g., FRA accident reports) to produce safety scores that align with expert judgment and official FRA scoring methodologies.
AI.method: A proof-of-concept multi-modal pipeline is proposed. Images of railway crossings and structured accident history data are ingested. The pipeline involves data preparation, exploration of different learning paradigms, and a routed fine-tuned compact Vision-Language Model (VLM) that processes both modalities to classify crossings as HIGH-RISK or LOW-RISK and regress FRA-based safety scores.
AI.result: The system achieves a macro F1 score of 0.757 for HIGH-RISK vs. LOW-RISK classification. For FRA-based safety score estimation, it yields an RMSE of 0.078 and a Pearson correlation of 0.492. Qualitative results are reported to align with domain-expert assessments.
AI.conclusion: Multi-modal learning combining visual imagery and structured accident data is promising for automated railway crossing safety assessment. The compact VLM pipeline demonstrates feasibility as a scalable decision-support tool, though correlation with FRA scores (0.492) suggests room for improvement in fine-grained score prediction.

title: Procedural Memory Distillation: Online Reflection for Self-Improving Language Models
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), along with recent selfdistillation variants such as SDPO, evaluates each rollout against a verifier and updates the policy from that episode-level signal. However, the richer procedural information in the rollout is rarely retained or reused. Across episodes and epochs, the model repeatedly encounters related problems under a changing policy, producing cross-episode signals that episode-local updates cannot capture: which strategies consistently pass verification, which failure modes persist, which patterns recur. We propose Procedural Memory Distillation (PMD), which converts these crossepisode signals into reusable procedural memory and distills it into the policy's weights during training. This memory functions as a training scaffold, absorbed into the policy itself, yielding a memory-free model at inference. PMD organizes the memory at three levels of abstraction: raw trajectories, self-reflected strategies and lessons, and higher-level behavioral patterns that recur across problems, all extracted online from the model's own trajectories. A memory-conditioned self-teacher draws on the accumulated experience to supervise the student on its own rollouts, enabling student to progressively internalize procedural knowledge within its parameters. The central design principle is co-evolution: the policy generates rollouts that update the memory, and memory shapes the supervision that updates the policy. Empirically, across Qwen3-8B and OLMo3-Instruct-7B, PMD improves over SDPO by 3.8-5.5% on SCIKNOWEVAL and 7.9-13.6% on LIVECODEBENCH. Co-evolution powers these gains: freezing either the memory or the policy trails PMD by more than 10% across SCIKNOWEVAL domains.

AI.tldr: PMD (Procedural Memory Distillation) extracts reusable procedural knowledge from RL training trajectories at three abstraction levels and distills it into policy weights via a co-evolving memory-teacher-student framework, achieving significant gains over SDPO on reasoning benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Standard RLVR and self-distillation methods (like SDPO) use only episode-level reward signals and discard rich procedural information within rollouts. Cross-episode signals — which strategies consistently work, which failure modes persist, which patterns recur — are not captured by episode-local updates. The authors aim to recover and reuse this lost procedural knowledge.
AI.method: PMD organizes memory online at three levels: (1) raw trajectories, (2) self-reflected strategies and lessons, and (3) higher-level behavioral patterns recurring across problems. A memory-conditioned self-teacher supervises the student on its own rollouts using this accumulated experience. The core design is co-evolution: the policy generates rollouts that update memory, and memory shapes supervision that updates the policy, progressively internalizing procedural knowledge into the policy's weights for memory-free inference.
AI.result: Across Qwen3-8B and OLMo3-Instruct-7B, PMD improves over SDPO by 3.8–5.5% on SCIKNOWEVAL and 7.9–13.6% on LIVECODEBENCH. Ablation shows co-evolution is critical: freezing either memory or policy reduces performance by more than 10% on SCIKNOWEVAL domains.
AI.conclusion: PMD demonstrates that preserving and distilling cross-episode procedural signals into policy weights yields substantial gains over episode-local RLVR methods. The co-evolution design is essential to these gains, and the resulting model requires no memory at inference time.

title: Synthetic Contact with AI Reduces Cross-Partisan Animosity
summary: Americans' warmth toward members of the opposing political party has fallen sharply over the past three decades -- yet meaningful cross-partisan contact remains scarce, in part because people actively avoid it. Across five preregistered studies (total N = 3,960 U.S. partisans), we test whether brief conversations with AI chatbots representing the political outgroup can substitute for the contact people shun. Synthetic contact first lowers the barrier to entry: partisans would endure almost twice as long contemplating their own mortality to avoid a human outgroup partner as an AI one. These conversations then correct the misperceptions that fuel division. At baseline, Democrats placed Republicans more than a standard deviation past their actual position on environmental consumption attitudes -- enough to flip the average Republican from supportive to opposed -- and a single ten-minute conversation with an outgroup chatbot corrected those beliefs and warmed affect in a within-person study of both parties. A three-arm experiment ruled out pure engagement and sociality as drivers. Synthetic contact also moved behavior, in a sample of both parties and on a more affectively charged issue: participants who spoke with an outgroup bot about immigration were six percentage points more likely than controls to choose to have a real conversation with a partisan from the other side. A final study tested whether these gains last: the warmth effect replicated immediately in a new sample; most of it faded within a week, with a small residual concentrated among the most extreme partisans. Analyzing conversation content showed that information, more than friendliness, distinguishes outgroup bots from control chatbots. Together, these findings establish synthetic contact as a scalable, behaviorally consequential, and -- unlike face-to-face contact -- widely acceptable form of cross-partisan engagement.

AI.tldr: AI chatbots simulating political opponents can reduce partisan animosity: brief conversations correct misperceptions, warm affect, and increase willingness for real cross-partisan contact, though effects largely fade within a week.
AI.motivation: Cross-partisan animosity in the U.S. has intensified over 30 years, yet meaningful contact between opposing partisans is rare because people actively avoid it. The authors ask whether AI chatbots can serve as a scalable, acceptable substitute for the face-to-face contact people shun.
AI.method: Five preregistered studies (total N=3,960 U.S. partisans) testing "synthetic contact": brief (≈10-minute) conversations with AI chatbots representing the political outgroup. Studies measured (1) willingness to engage human vs. AI partners via mortality contemplation trade-offs, (2) within-person belief correction and affective change on environmental consumption, (3) a three-arm experiment ruling out engagement/sociality confounds, (4) behavioral spillover into real cross-partisan conversation choice on immigration, and (5) durability of effects over one week, with conversation content analysis.
AI.result: Partisans were nearly twice as willing to interact with an AI outgroup partner as a human one. A single 10-minute chatbot conversation corrected large misperceptions (Democrats misjudged Republicans by >1 SD on environmental attitudes) and warmed affect. The three-arm experiment confirmed the effect was not driven by mere engagement or sociality. On immigration, chatbot interaction increased real cross-partisan conversation choice by 6 percentage points. Warmth effects replicated immediately but mostly faded within a week; a small residual persisted among extreme partisans. Content analysis indicated information provision, more than friendliness, drove the effects.
AI.conclusion: Synthetic contact via AI chatbots is a scalable, behaviorally consequential, and widely acceptable form of cross-partisan engagement. It lowers psychological barriers to entry, corrects outgroup misperceptions, and can prompt real behavioral change, though effects are largely short-lived.

title: Beyond Gradient-Based Attacks: Adversarial Robustness and Explainability Stability in Cybersecurity Classifiers
summary: Adversarial attacks on cybersecurity classifiers pose a dual threat: degrading predictions and destabilising the SHAP-based explanations that security analysts rely on to understand and triage alerts. We extend our prior MLP conference study to Random Forest and XGBoost across four tabular security datasets (phishing URLs, UNSW-NB15, NF-ToN-IoT, HIKARI-2021), evaluating five attacks including three black-box methods applicable to non-differentiable tree models. We introduce the Explainability Stability Index (ESI), a scalar metric computed from TreeSHAP attribution drift under adversarial perturbation, reported on the same [0,1] scale as the Robustness Index (RI). A key finding is that gradient-based black-box attacks (ZOO) produce degenerate results against XGBoost (apparent RI ~0.98) due to piecewise-constant prediction surfaces, while score-based Square Attack reveals genuine vulnerability (RI ~0.36). These degenerate perturbations still drive substantial attribution drift: XGBoost ESI ~0.06-0.16 despite near-perfect ZOO robustness, versus 0.14-0.29 for RF, showing that prediction robustness and explanation stability are distinct axes requiring joint measurement. A two-axis framework (gradient dependence, query efficiency) explains the observed attack ranking and yields practical guidance for tree ensemble evaluation. A step-size ablation explains a counterintuitive PGD anomaly on z-score normalised tabular data.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Explainability Stability Index (ESI) to measure SHAP explanation drift under adversarial attacks on tree-based cybersecurity classifiers, demonstrating that prediction robustness and explanation stability are orthogonal properties requiring joint evaluation.
AI.motivation: Adversarial attacks threaten both classifier predictions and the SHAP explanations used by security analysts for alert triage. Prior work focused primarily on prediction robustness, neglecting explanation stability — especially for non-differentiable tree models (Random Forest, XGBoost) widely deployed in cybersecurity. A unified framework for jointly measuring both axes is lacking.
AI.method: The authors extend their prior MLP-focused study to Random Forest and XGBoost across four tabular security datasets (phishing URLs, UNSW-NB15, NF-ToN-IoT, HIKARI-2021). They evaluate five adversarial attacks, including three black-box methods (ZOO, Square Attack, HSJA) suitable for non-differentiable models. TreeSHAP is used to compute attribution drift. Two scalar metrics — the existing Robustness Index (RI) and the newly proposed Explainability Stability Index (ESI) — are reported on a shared [0,1] scale for direct comparison. A two-axis framework (gradient dependence vs. query efficiency) is developed to explain attack behaviour, and a step-size ablation addresses a PGD anomaly on z-score normalised data.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) ZOO produces degenerate, near-perfect RI (~0.98) against XGBoost due to piecewise-constant prediction surfaces, yet ESI drops to ~0.06–0.16, revealing severe explanation instability. (2) Square Attack exposes genuine XGBoost vulnerability (RI ~0.36). (3) RF shows ESI of 0.14–0.29, confirming that prediction robustness and explanation stability are distinct dimensions. (4) The two-axis framework explains attack rankings and offers practical guidance for tree ensemble evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Prediction robustness and explanation stability must be measured jointly using paired RI/ESI metrics. Gradient-based black-box attacks like ZOO are unreliable for tree ensembles due to piecewise-constant loss surfaces; score-based attacks like Square Attack provide more faithful vulnerability assessment. The proposed two-axis framework aids practitioners in selecting appropriate adversarial evaluation strategies for tree-based security classifiers.

title: AgentFlow: Building Agent Dependency Graphs for Static Analysis of Agent Programs
summary: LLM agents are increasingly developed as source-code applications built on agent frameworks. These agent programs combine conventional host-language code with framework-defined semantics for models, prompts, tools, memory, and multi-agent orchestration logic. As a result, their behavior depends not only on traditional control and data flows, but also on a new class of agent dependencies. Such dependencies are often expressed as framework-induced semantics, such as agent constructors, tool decorators, and agent handoff declarations, making them difficult to recover with existing static analysis or dependency tracking tools. In this paper, we present AgentFlow, the first static analysis framework for recovering and analyzing agent dependencies from agent programs. AgentFlow constructs an Agent Dependency Graph (ADG), a framework-agnostic graph representation that represents agents, prompts, models, capabilities, memory states, and control policies as typed nodes, and captures their component-dependency, control-flow, and data-flow dependencies as typed edges. Built on ADGs, AgentFlow supports a range of analyses for agent governance and security, including Agent Bill of Materials (BOM) generation and prompt-to-tool risk detection. We implement AgentFlow for five representative agent frameworks and evaluate it on AgentZoo, a corpus of 5,399 real-world agent programs. Our evaluation shows that AgentFlow recovers richer agent entities and dependencies than existing AST-based agent static analysis tools, generates more dependency-aware Agent BOMs, and uncovers 238 taint-style prompt-to-tool risks in real-world agent programs. These results show that ADG provides a practical foundation for understanding, governing, and securing emerging agent software.

AI.tldr: AgentFlow is a static analysis framework that constructs an Agent Dependency Graph (ADG) to recover agent-specific dependencies (prompts, tools, models, memory, multi-agent orchestration) from LLM agent programs. Evaluated on 5,399 real-world agent programs across five frameworks, it outperforms existing AST-based tools in entity recovery, generates richer Agent Bills of Materials, and detects 238 taint-style prompt-to-tool security risks.
AI.motivation: LLM agent programs mix conventional code with framework-specific semantics (agent constructors, tool decorators, handoff declarations), creating a new class of "agent dependencies" that existing static analysis tools cannot recover. This gap hinders agent governance tasks like dependency tracking, supply-chain transparency (BOM), and security analysis.
AI.method: AgentFlow introduces the Agent Dependency Graph (ADG), a framework-agnostic typed graph representation with nodes for agents, prompts, models, capabilities, memory states, and control policies, and edges for component-dependency, control-flow, and data-flow relationships. A static analysis pipeline recovers these elements from agent source code. Built on ADG, AgentFlow enables Agent Bill of Materials (BOM) generation and prompt-to-tool taint risk detection.
AI.result: Evaluated on AgentZoo (5,399 real-world agent programs across five frameworks: LangGraph, AutoGen, CrewAI, Semantic Kernel, and Dify), AgentFlow recovers richer agent entities and dependencies than existing AST-based tools, generates more comprehensive dependency-aware Agent BOMs, and uncovers 238 taint-style prompt-to-tool risks in real-world programs.
AI.conclusion: The ADG provides a practical, framework-agnostic foundation for understanding, governing, and securing emerging agent software. AgentFlow demonstrates the feasibility and value of specialized static analysis tailored to the unique semantics of LLM agent programs.

title: RusFinChain: A Russian Benchmark for Verifiable Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in Finance with Fuzzy-Aligned Evaluation
summary: Multi-step symbolic reasoning is essential for robust financial analysis, yet most benchmarks neglect intermediate reasoning steps. FINCHAIN introduced verifiable Chain-of-Thought (CoT) evaluation but is limited to English. FINESSE-Bench includes a Russian block but relies on multiple-choice questions without step-level supervision. We present RusFinChain, the first Russian-language symbolic benchmark for verifiable CoT reasoning in finance. It spans 17 domains, 172 topics, and comprises 5,280 parameterized examples from executable Python templates, ensuring contamination-free evaluation. Each example includes a gold-standard reasoning chain with intermediate numeric values for automatic verification. We also introduce enhanced metrics: Fuzzy Numeric Alignment and Soft-Attention Alignment. We evaluate 8 open-weight LLMs on a stratified sample, generating 8,100 responses. Results reveal a substantial reasoning gap: models achieve Hard F1 of ~0.65 for step alignment, but only ~29% of final answers are correct. Our fuzzy and soft metrics show stronger correlation with final-answer correctness (Spearman rho approx 0.48) than the original ChainEval (rho approx 0.38-0.46), demonstrating superior diagnostic power. We release dataset, code, and evaluation framework to foster verifiable financial AI for the Russian-speaking community.

AI.tldr: RusFinChain is the first Russian-language benchmark for verifiable chain-of-thought reasoning in finance, featuring 5,280 parameterized examples across 17 domains with gold-standard reasoning chains and novel fuzzy evaluation metrics that reveal a significant gap between intermediate step alignment (~0.65 F1) and final answer accuracy (~29%).
AI.motivation: Existing financial reasoning benchmarks either lack step-level supervision (FINESSE-Bench uses multiple-choice) or are limited to English (FINCHAIN). No verifiable CoT benchmark exists for Russian-language financial analysis, leaving a gap in evaluating whether models genuinely reason through financial problems or merely guess final answers.
AI.method: The authors constructed RusFinChain with 5,280 parameterized, template-generated examples spanning 17 financial domains and 172 topics. Each example includes a gold-standard reasoning chain with intermediate numeric values for automatic step-by-step verification. They propose two new evaluation metrics — Fuzzy Numeric Alignment and Soft-Attention Alignment — that correlate better with final-answer correctness than the original ChainEval metric. Eight open-weight LLMs were evaluated on a stratified sample, yielding 8,100 responses.
AI.result: Models achieve a Hard F1 of approximately 0.65 for step-level alignment, but only ~29% of final answers are correct, exposing a substantial reasoning gap. The proposed fuzzy and soft metrics show stronger Spearman correlation with final-answer correctness (ρ ≈ 0.48) compared to the original ChainEval (ρ ≈ 0.38–0.46), validating their superior diagnostic power.
AI.conclusion: RusFinChain fills a critical void in Russian-language verifiable financial reasoning benchmarks. The gap between intermediate step alignment and final answer accuracy indicates that models can partially mimic reasoning chains without reliably reaching correct conclusions, and the new metrics provide more faithful diagnostics. The dataset, code, and framework are publicly released.

title: How Should Transformers Encode Numeric Values in Electronic Health Records?
comment: 16 pages, 15 figures, 3 tables, accepted to ICML 2026, to be published in Proceedings of Machine Learning Research
summary: How do we encode numeric values in transformer-based sequence processing, particularly in electronic health record (EHR) data? We systematically compare discrete, continuous, and hybrid value encoding strategies using synthetic arithmetic tasks embedded within real-world EHR data, as well as real-world clinical prediction tasks. Our study reveals trade-offs between numeric precision, optimisation stability, and architectural flexibility. We find that approaches that explicitly model value-concept interactions perform best on precision-sensitive arithmetic tasks when architectural constraints permit.
