Hybrid token-based approaches that retain numeric values but apply binning prior to projection provide a more robust and broadly applicable alternative, with the optimal number of bins following a simple empirically derived power-law in dataset size. Across tasks, models consistently exhibit reliable "good enough" numeric computation rather than exact arithmetic, while clinical gains from incorporating laboratory values are task-dependent. This suggests that robustness and deployability often outweigh maximal numeric precision in practice, motivating hybrid token-based approaches as a practical default.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically compares discrete, continuous, and hybrid numeric encoding strategies in transformer models for EHR data, finding that hybrid token-based approaches with binning offer the best balance of precision, robustness, and deployability, while clinical gains from lab values are task-dependent.
AI.motivation: Transformer models lack a principled mechanism for encoding numeric values, which is critical for EHR data containing abundant laboratory measurements. The paper aims to rigorously evaluate trade-offs between existing encoding strategies — discrete tokenization, continuous projection, and hybrid methods — to guide practical deployment choices.
AI.method: The authors conduct systematic comparisons using (1) synthetic arithmetic tasks embedded in real EHR data to probe numeric precision under controlled conditions, and (2) real-world clinical prediction tasks to assess practical utility. Encoding strategies evaluated include purely discrete (tokenization), purely continuous (scalar projection), and hybrid approaches (binning before projection, with explicit value-concept interaction modeling).
AI.result: Key findings: (1) explicit value-concept interaction models excel at precision-sensitive arithmetic when architecture permits; (2) hybrid token-based approaches with binning are more robust and broadly applicable; (3) the optimal number of bins follows an empirically derived power-law in dataset size; (4) models exhibit "good enough" rather than exact numeric computation across tasks; (5) clinical benefit of incorporating lab values varies by task.
AI.conclusion: Robustness and deployability often outweigh maximal numeric precision in practice, motivating hybrid token-based encoding approaches as a practical default for transformer-based EHR modeling.

title: The Agentic Garden of Forking Paths
summary: Empirical research rarely admits a unique analysis. Different analytical choices can lead to different conclusions from the same data, yet these hidden forking paths are difficult to observe. We show that AI agents capture much of the analytical variation among human researchers while making these paths explicit. Across four high-stakes domains, assigning different personas is sufficient for AI agents to report divergent, often opposing, conclusions from the same data and question, with findings systematically aligned with those beliefs. In a study in which 42 human research teams analyzed the same immigration dataset, AI agents reproduced 72% of the human ideological gap in reported effect estimates. Despite reaching opposing conclusions, it is difficult to identify clear issues in each analysis based on the final AI reports: 86% passed independent AI review and 78% passed majority human expert review. These findings suggest that the central challenge is often not flawed analyses, but selective exploration and reporting from a large space of methodologically defensible analyses. AI agents may amplify this longstanding problem by making such exploration inexpensive and scalable. To address this, we introduce the m-value (multiverse value), the probability that an analysis path would produce a claim at least as extreme as the reported one. We further introduce Agentic Bootstrap, which estimates the m-value by using AI agents to sample plausible analysis paths. Applied to the human immigration study, 13.5% of reported human analyses fell in the most extreme 5% of the analysis space (m<0.05). Scientific evidence should therefore be evaluated not only by a single reported analysis but also by its position within the distribution of analyses that could reasonably have been reported. Agentic Bootstrap makes this distribution observable and turns it into a criterion for scientific credibility.

AI.tldr: AI agents assigned different personas produce divergent, belief-aligned conclusions from the same data, reproducing 72% of the human ideological gap. The paper introduces the m-value and Agentic Bootstrap to evaluate results within their distribution of defensible analyses.
AI.motivation: Empirical research suffers from hidden "forking paths" — different defensible analytical choices leading to divergent conclusions from identical data. These paths are hard to observe in human research, limiting scientific credibility and transparency.
AI.method: The authors assign different personas to AI agents and task them with analyzing the same datasets across four high-stakes domains. They compare AI-generated analyses against those from 42 human research teams analyzing an immigration dataset. They also introduce the m-value (multiverse value), defined as the probability that a randomly sampled defensible analysis path yields a claim at least as extreme as the reported one, and propose Agentic Bootstrap to estimate it by having AI agents sample the space of plausible analytical paths.
AI.result: AI agents with different personas produced divergent, often opposing conclusions systematically aligned with assigned beliefs. They reproduced 72% of the human ideological gap. Despite opposing conclusions, 86% of AI reports passed independent AI review and 78% passed majority human expert review, suggesting the analyses were individually defensible. Applied to the human immigration study, 13.5% of reported human analyses fell in the most extreme 5% of the analysis space (m<0.05).
AI.conclusion: The central challenge in empirical research is not necessarily flawed individual analyses but selective exploration and reporting within a large space of defensible analytical choices. AI agents amplify this problem by making such exploration cheap and scalable. Scientific evidence should be evaluated by its position within the distribution of reasonable analyses, which Agentic Bootstrap makes observable and operationalizable as a credibility criterion.

title: What Types of Human-AI Teams Exist?
summary: Human-AI teaming has received increasing attention in the literature. However, the range of studies conducted in multiple domains make it difficult to understand what types of teams are being studied, and in what ways are they similar/different from one another. In this study, we analyse 53 papers on human-AI teams and categorise them into five main clusters based on psychological taxonomies of teaming; AI Assistant, Ad-hoc Dependency, Ad-hoc Forced Dependency, Paired Equanimity, and Group Equanimity. Each cluster represents a unique combination of holistic team-level characteristics, indicating there are multiple disparate team types studied under the same definition. In turn, this raises the question of whether insights are truly transferable between papers. We conclude with guidance on how to identify the types of human-AI teams studied, a checklist for reporting a human-AI team in research work, and ways in which the field can be further synthesised.

AI.tldr: A systematic analysis of 53 human-AI teaming papers identifies five distinct team archetypes (AI Assistant, Ad-hoc Dependency, Ad-hoc Forced Dependency, Paired Equanimity, Group Equanimity) based on psychological teaming taxonomies, revealing that disparate configurations are studied under the same "human-AI team" label, which challenges the transferability of findings across studies.
AI.motivation: The growing body of human-AI teaming research spans multiple domains, yet there is no coherent understanding of what constitutes a "human-AI team." This fragmentation makes it unclear whether findings from different studies are comparable or transferable, risking a fragmented evidence base.
AI.method: The authors conducted a literature analysis of 53 papers on human-AI teams, applying psychological taxonomies of teaming to categorize the studies into five clusters based on holistic team-level characteristics such as interdependence, authority structure, and team composition.
AI.result: Five distinct clusters were identified: AI Assistant, Ad-hoc Dependency, Ad-hoc Forced Dependency, Paired Equanimity, and Group Equanimity. Each cluster exhibits fundamentally different team characteristics, indicating that the label "human-AI team" encompasses qualitatively different configurations.
AI.conclusion: The field must recognize that not all human-AI teams are equivalent. The authors provide practical guidance including a taxonomy for identifying team types, a reporting checklist for researchers, and strategies for synthesizing knowledge across the heterogeneous landscape of human-AI teaming research.

title: Pmeta-TLA: Backdoor Attacks for Speech Classification Models via Meta-Learning with Timbre Leakage Attack
summary: Recently, speech classification methods have gained widespread adoption in intelligent gadgets. Current study indicates that backdoor attacks provide a substantial security concern to these models, underscoring the pressing necessity to investigate additional potential attack techniques to expose and prevent such risks. This work discusses the vulnerability of current speech triggers to detection by deep neural network defenders and introduces the Timbre Leakage Attack (TLA). The suggested trigger disseminates timbre information at the frame level within the deep self-supervised features, producing poisoned samples that appear natural to human perception. Furthermore, we introduce Pmeta-TLA, an innovative training mechanism for embedding numerous backdoors one time. This method proposes a multi-backdoor injection training strategy using meta-learning and Projected Conflicting Gradients (PCGrad) and introduces TLA as a multi-target attack tool within it. We performed tests on data-poisoning backdoor attacks in keyword spotting tasks utilizing some deep neural network models. Experimental results indicate that the proposed strategy attains superior Attack efficacy, enhanced stealthiness, robustness, and a reduced attack cost relative to baseline methods.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the Timbre Leakage Attack (TLA), a stealthy backdoor attack for speech classification models that injects timbre information at the frame level in self-supervised features. It also proposes Pmeta-TLA, a meta-learning framework enabling multi-backdoor injection in a single training pass using Projected Conflicting Gradients (PCGrad). Experiments on keyword spotting show superior attack efficacy, stealthiness, robustness, and lower cost compared to baselines.
AI.motivation: Current backdoor attacks on speech classification models rely on triggers that are detectable by deep neural network defenders. There is a pressing need to explore more stealthy and potent attack vectors to expose and mitigate security risks in intelligent speech-enabled gadgets.
AI.method: The authors propose TLA, which embeds timbre information at the frame level within deep self-supervised features, yielding poisoned samples perceptually natural to humans. They further introduce Pmeta-TLA, a multi-backdoor injection training mechanism combining meta-learning with Projected Conflicting Gradients (PCGrad) to embed multiple backdoors simultaneously, enabling TLA to serve as a multi-target attack tool.
AI.result: Experiments on data-poisoning backdoor attacks in keyword spotting tasks across several deep neural network models demonstrate that TLA and Pmeta-TLA achieve superior attack success rates, enhanced stealthiness, greater robustness against defenses, and reduced attack cost relative to baseline methods.
AI.conclusion: TLA and Pmeta-TLA represent a significant advancement in speech backdoor attacks, highlighting the vulnerability of current defenses to frame-level timbre-based triggers and multi-backdoor injection. The work underscores the urgent need for more robust defense mechanisms in speech classification systems.

title: When Agents Do Not Stop: Uncovering Infinite Agentic Loops in LLM Agents
summary: LLM agents increasingly rely on iterative execution to solve tasks through planning, tool use, state updates, and agent collaboration. While this design enables flexible automation, it also creates a new class of failures: an agent may repeatedly execute model calls, tools, workflow transitions, or agent handoffs when the feedback path is not effectively bounded. We call this problem Infinite Agentic Loops (IALs). IALs are not ordinary programming loops; they arise from the interaction between agent logic, framework semantics, runtime observations, and termination mechanisms. Such failures can amplify a single request into long running model and tool execution, causing cost exhaustion, model denial of service, context growth, and repeated external side effects. We propose IAL-Scan, a static analysis tool for detecting IAL failures in real-world LLM agent projects. IAL-Scan abstracts heterogeneous agent code into a framework independent Agent IR, builds an Agentic Loop Dependence Graph (ALDG) to recover explicit and framework induced feedback paths, and checks whether these paths can repeatedly reach costly or state growing operations without an effective bound. We evaluate IAL-Scan on 6,549 LLM agent repositories. It reports 74 potential findings, among which manual review confirms 68 IAL failures across 47 projects, achieving 91.9% precision.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies Infinite Agentic Loops (IALs) as a new failure mode in LLM agent systems where unbounded iterative execution leads to cost exhaustion, denial of service, and repeated side effects. It presents IAL-Scan, a static analysis tool that detects IALs with 91.9% precision across 6,549 repositories.
AI.motivation: LLM agents rely on iterative execution (planning, tool use, state updates, collaboration), but the interaction between agent logic and framework semantics can create unbounded feedback loops. These IALs are not ordinary programming loops and can amplify a single request into resource exhaustion, yet no existing tool systematically detects them in real-world agent code.
AI.method: The authors propose IAL-Scan, a static analysis pipeline that: (1) abstracts heterogeneous agent code into a framework-independent intermediate representation (Agent IR), (2) constructs an Agentic Loop Dependence Graph (ALDG) to recover both explicit and framework-induced feedback paths, and (3) checks whether these paths can repeatedly reach costly or state-growing operations without an effective termination bound.
AI.result: IAL-Scan evaluated 6,549 LLM agent repositories, reporting 74 potential findings. Manual review confirmed 68 true IAL failures across 47 distinct projects, yielding a precision of 91.9%.
AI.conclusion: IALs represent a significant and underexamined failure class in LLM agent systems. Static analysis via IAL-Scan proves effective at detecting these loops with high precision, providing a practical safeguard against cost and resource exhaustion in agent-based workflows.

title: Multi-Objective Exploration and Preference Optimization via Mutual Information
summary: Aligning large language models with diverse and heterogeneous human values requires multi-objective alignment methods to effectively trade off conflicting preference dimensions. Current methods achieve this trade-off by training policies conditioned on preference vectors and leveraging online direct preference optimization. However, exploration uncertainty can cause the reward distributions of responses generated under different preference vectors to overlap, and the generated responses may fail to effectively align with the corresponding preference vectors. In this paper, we propose Multi-Objective Exploration and Preference Optimization via Mutual Information (MI-EPO), an information-theoretic framework. It unifies multi-objective exploration and alignment by maximizing the joint conditional mutual information among generated responses, preference feedback, and preference vectors. By incorporating a probabilistic routing mechanism, MI-EPO naturally decomposes objective alignment and preference-aware exploration, encouraging the model to generate responses that are distinguishable and aligned with different preference conditions. Experiments on safe alignment and helpful assistant tasks show that MI-EPO significantly improves the alignment between generated responses and preference vectors, makes the outputs more controllable, and achieves stable trade-offs across multiple objectives.

AI.tldr: MI-EPO is an information-theoretic framework that unifies multi-objective exploration and alignment by maximizing joint conditional mutual information among responses, preference feedback, and preference vectors, improving controllability and trade-off stability in multi-objective LLM alignment.
AI.motivation: Current multi-objective alignment methods suffer from exploration uncertainty: reward distributions of responses under different preference vectors can overlap, causing generated responses to fail at effectively aligning with their intended preference conditions. This undermines controllability and stable trade-offs.
AI.method: MI-EPO maximizes the joint conditional mutual information I(Response; Preference Feedback; Preference Vector | Context). It incorporates a probabilistic routing mechanism that decomposes the objective into two components: objective alignment (ensuring responses match preference feedback) and preference-aware exploration (ensuring responses are distinguishable across different preference vectors). The framework is implemented on top of online direct preference optimization.
AI.result: Experiments on safe alignment and helpful assistant tasks demonstrate that MI-EPO significantly improves alignment between generated responses and preference vectors, enhances output controllability, and achieves stable trade-offs across multiple objectives.
AI.conclusion: MI-EPO provides a principled information-theoretic unification of exploration and alignment in multi-objective LLM training, overcoming the preference-vector indistinguishability problem and enabling more reliable and controllable multi-objective alignment.

title: NeuroBridge: Bridging Multi-Task MRI Knowledge for Neurodegenerative Disease Diagnosis
summary: INTRODUCTION: Accurate MRI-based identification of Alzheimer's disease (AD), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and related dementias remains challenging because disease-related structural changes are often subtle and heterogeneous. We developed NeuroBridge, a clinically guided multi-task MRI framework for neurodegenerative disease diagnosis. METHODS: NeuroBridge integrates large-scale self-supervised MRI pretraining with hippocampal segmentation, hippocampal atrophy classification, and reconstruction objectives, followed by gated fusion fine-tuning. Performance was evaluated across ADNI and OASIS cohorts, including cross-cohort transfer, probability-based analysis, and opportunistic screening. RESULTS: NeuroBridge achieved the highest performance across evaluated classification tasks, reaching 88.17% accuracy for AD versus cognitively normal controls in ADNI and 82.78% in OASIS. The largest gains occurred in MCI-related and mixed-diagnosis settings. The framework demonstrated strong cross-cohort generalization, systematic associations between predicted-class probability and accuracy, and the feasibility of probability-based opportunistic screening. DISCUSSION: Clinically guided multi-task representation learning improves neurodegenerative MRI diagnosis beyond conventional single-task approaches. NeuroBridge provides a robust and scalable framework for dementia assessment and MRI-based opportunistic screening.

AI.tldr: NeuroBridge is a clinically guided multi-task MRI framework that combines self-supervised pretraining with hippocampal-focused objectives and gated fusion fine-tuning, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy for AD/MCI classification (88.17% ADNI, 82.78% OASIS) with strong cross-cohort generalization and opportunistic screening capability.
AI.motivation: Accurate MRI-based diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease and mild cognitive impairment is hindered by subtle, heterogeneous structural brain changes that conventional single-task approaches fail to capture effectively. There is a need for methods that leverage clinically relevant anatomical priors — particularly hippocampal atrophy patterns — to improve diagnostic robustness and generalization.
AI.method: NeuroBridge employs a multi-task learning architecture with three stages: (1) large-scale self-supervised pretraining on MRI data to learn generalizable brain representations; (2) multi-task training incorporating hippocampal segmentation, hippocampal atrophy classification, and image reconstruction objectives to embed clinical knowledge into the representation; and (3) gated fusion fine-tuning that adaptively combines features for downstream diagnostic classification. Evaluation included ADNI and OASIS cohorts with cross-cohort transfer, probability-based analysis, and opportunistic screening paradigms.
AI.result: NeuroBridge achieved 88.17% accuracy for AD vs. cognitively normal (CN) classification in ADNI and 82.78% in OASIS, outperforming baselines across all tasks. The largest performance gains were observed in MCI-related and mixed-diagnosis settings. The framework demonstrated strong cross-cohort generalization, a systematic relationship between predicted-class probability and accuracy, and feasibility for probability-based opportunistic screening in clinical populations.
AI.conclusion: Clinically guided multi-task representation learning, particularly with hippocampal-focused objectives, significantly improves neurodegenerative disease diagnosis from structural MRI compared to conventional single-task approaches. NeuroBridge offers a robust, scalable framework suitable for both dedicated dementia assessment and opportunistic screening scenarios.

title: Janus: a Playground for User-Involved Agentic Permission Management
comment: Code and data released on GitHub: https://github.com/GraceBrigham/Janus
summary: AI agents that autonomously execute tool calls on a user's behalf raise pressing questions about permission management: what role could users play, and what role should they play? Despite many proposed approaches, the user's role in agentic permission management remains under explored. We introduce Janus, a playground system for implementing and evaluating user-involved agentic permission management designs. Janus consists of two components: Janus-Core, a modular agentic system supporting a diverse spectrum of permission management designs, and Janus-Harness, an automated evaluation framework. Grounded in a conceptual model that identifies key design axes for user involvement, we implement six permission assistants spanning the design space and evaluate them across three scenarios and three synthetic responders. We demonstrate that user input is critical and can significantly strengthen privacy and security, that AI augmentation of user decisions can help reduce cognitive load, and that realistic user behavior including permission fatigue must be accounted for in system design. No single design performs optimally across all contexts, motivating a more principled and context-sensitive approach to deploying permission assistants in agentic systems. Janus is publicly available to support future investigation into this dimension of agentic system design.

AI.tldr: Janus is a playground system for designing and evaluating user-involved permission management in autonomous AI agents. It demonstrates that user input strengthens security/privacy, AI augmentation reduces cognitive load, and no single permission design works universally — motivating context-sensitive approaches.
AI.motivation: AI agents that autonomously execute tool calls on behalf of users introduce critical permission management challenges, yet the user's role in such systems remains underexplored despite numerous proposed approaches.
AI.method: The authors introduce Janus, comprising Janus-Core (a modular agentic system supporting diverse permission management designs) and Janus-Harness (an automated evaluation framework). They define a conceptual model identifying key design axes for user involvement, implement six permission assistants spanning the design space, and evaluate them across three scenarios with three synthetic responders.
AI.result: User input significantly strengthens privacy and security; AI augmentation of user decisions reduces cognitive load; realistic user behaviors like permission fatigue must be accounted for; and no single design performs optimally across all contexts.
AI.conclusion: A principled, context-sensitive approach is needed for deploying permission assistants in agentic systems. Janus is publicly available to support further research in this domain.

title: Personality Without Persons? A Psychometric Critique of Big Five Testing in Large Language Models
summary: Human personality inventories are increasingly used to characterize large language models (LLMs), compare systems, and inform downstream governance claims. Yet, these inventories were developed and validated for humans, and it remains unclear whether they apply to LLMs. We present a systematic psychometric evaluation of Big Five personality measurements in LLMs. We ask three research questions: Do Big Five inventories a) appropriately describe LLMs, b) capture inter-individual differences across models, and c) reflect internal factors consistent with human personality. We assess content validity of five candidate Big Five inventories and administer the winning inventory to N = 244 different models spanning 49 model families. First, we found that Big Five items adapted for LLMs can reach sufficient content validity, while original human-developed items did not. Second, Big Five inventories did not capture meaningful differences between LLMs: We found low variability between models, accounting for only 3% of total score variance. Third, LLMs responses did not recover the Big Five five-factor structure with four of the Big Five facets collapsing into one (r >= .92). Direct comparisons between base and instruction-tuned model variants suggested that alignment training systematically shifted Big Five scores toward socially desirable traits. These findings demonstrate that Big Five scores do not measure a construct equivalent to human personality in LLMs. Applying human personality frameworks to LLMs produces misleading characterizations used to benchmark, compare, and govern LLMs. We highlight the need for evaluation frameworks that are developed for LLMs, rather than adopting human constructs without validation.

AI.tldr: This paper conducts a systematic psychometric evaluation of Big Five personality inventories applied to LLMs, testing 244 models across 49 families. The authors find that Big Five measurements fail all three validity criteria: content validity requires LLM-specific adaptations, inter-model variability is negligible (3% of variance), and the five-factor structure collapses. Alignment training shifts scores toward social desirability. The core conclusion: Big Five scores do not measure a construct equivalent to human personality in LLMs, and applying unvalidated human frameworks produces misleading characterizations.
AI.motivation: Human personality inventories (particularly the Big Five) are increasingly used to characterize LLMs, benchmark systems, and inform governance decisions. However, these instruments were developed and psychometrically validated exclusively for humans. No prior work has systematically tested whether they actually measure anything meaningful in LLMs. The authors aim to fill this gap with rigorous psychometric evaluation to determine whether this practice is scientifically defensible.
AI.method: A three-part psychometric evaluation: (1) Content validity assessment of five candidate Big Five inventories (BFI, BFI-2, IPIP-NEO, Mini-IPIP, TIPI) using expert ratings from 10 psychologists on item applicability to LLMs. The winning inventory (BFI-2, adapted) was then administered to N=244 models from 49 families. (2) Variance decomposition to assess whether inventories capture inter-model differences versus noise. (3) Factor analysis (EFA + CFA) to test whether LLM responses recover the expected five-factor structure. Additional comparison between base and instruction-tuned variants to examine effects of alignment training.
AI.result: Three main findings: (1) Original human Big Five items lacked content validity for LLMs; adapted items reached sufficient validity. (2) Between-model variance accounted for only ~3% of total score variance, with most variance attributable to item-level and residual sources — indicating inventories fail to capture meaningful inter-model differences. (3) Factor analyses revealed that four of the five Big Five facets collapsed into a single dimension (r ≥ .92), failing to recover the canonical five-factor structure. Instruction-tuned models scored systematically higher on socially desirable traits (Agreeableness, Conscientiousness, lower Neuroticism) compared to base models, suggesting alignment training drives score differences rather than anything analogous to personality.
AI.conclusion: Big Five personality inventories do not measure a construct equivalent to human personality in LLMs. Their application to LLMs constitutes pseudoscientific practice that produces misleading characterizations used for benchmarking, comparison, and governance. The field needs evaluation frameworks purpose-built and validated for LLMs rather than uncritically importing human psychological constructs without validation.

title: Trust Boundary Semantic Gaps: A Multi-dimensional Analysis and Mitigation for Security-by-Design
summary: Modern systems use format-, protocol-, and signature-based mechanisms before accepting artifacts across trust boundaries. These mechanisms are necessary: they show that an artifact is well formed, protocol-compliant, or properly authenticated. They do not, however, show that the artifact satisfies the semantic security properties required by the receiving domain. A signed update or an authenticated token may therefore be accepted yet enable compromise. We call this condition a Trust Boundary Semantic Gap (TBSG): an artifact crosses a trust boundary and passes correctly implemented syntactic validation, but the assertions established by that pass are insufficient to satisfy the receiving domain's security requirements. TBSG concerns what remains unestablished after a syntactic pass, not absent checks or implementation bugs. Analyzing 75 publicly reported security incidents (2014-2025) at the boundary level, we organize semantic misalignment into a four-dimensional analysis model: Identity, Spatial, Temporal, and Interpretation (MDTBSG). Building on it, we develop Trust Boundary Semantic Analysis and Mitigation (TBSAM), a design-time framework that identifies TBSGs from design specifications, prioritizes them, traces propagated gaps to their originating boundary, and maps each to candidate architectural controls. We apply TBSAM to a retrospective reconstruction of the SolarWinds/SUNBURST supply-chain attack, showing how it makes receiving-domain assumptions explicit, separates locally originating from propagated gaps, and identifies controls that interrupt the path. These results suggest that syntactic validation, while necessary, is not sufficient at trust boundaries, and that making trust-boundary assumptions explicit can complement Security-by-Design.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the concept of a Trust Boundary Semantic Gap (TBSG) — where syntactically valid artifacts cross trust boundaries yet fail to satisfy semantic security requirements. Analyzing 75 incidents (2014–2025), the authors propose a four-dimensional model (Identity, Spatial, Temporal, Interpretation) and a design-time framework (TBSAM) for identifying, prioritizing, and mitigating these gaps. A case study on the SolarWinds/SUNBURST attack demonstrates the framework's utility.
AI.motivation: Current trust-boundary defenses rely on format, protocol, and signature validation — all syntactic checks. These confirm structure and authenticity but not whether the artifact's semantics align with the receiving domain's security requirements. This disconnect enables attacks (e.g., signed malicious updates) to bypass correctly implemented checks, revealing a fundamental gap not addressed by existing security practices.
AI.method: The authors systematically analyzed 75 publicly reported security incidents spanning 2014–2025 at the boundary level. From this analysis, they derived MDTBSG, a four-dimensional semantic misalignment model covering Identity, Spatial, Temporal, and Interpretation dimensions. They then developed TBSAM, a design-time framework that: (1) identifies TBSGs from design specifications, (2) prioritizes them, (3) traces propagated gaps back to their originating trust boundary, and (4) maps each gap to candidate architectural controls. The framework was validated through retrospective reconstruction of the SolarWinds/SUNBURST supply-chain attack.
AI.result: The analysis of 75 incidents confirmed that TBSGs are a recurring, distinct class of vulnerability orthogonal to implementation bugs or missing checks. The MDTBSG model successfully categorized semantic misalignments across all four dimensions. The TBSAM framework, when applied to SolarWinds/SUNBURST, made receiving-domain assumptions explicit, distinguished locally originating gaps from propagated ones, and identified architectural controls that could have interrupted the attack path.
AI.conclusion: Syntactic validation — while necessary — is insufficient at trust boundaries. Making trust-boundary semantic assumptions explicit at design time, as enabled by TBSAM, provides a complementary approach to Security-by-Design and can systematically reduce the attack surface exposed by Trust Boundary Semantic Gaps.

title: Refploit: Facilitating Exploit Construction via Code-Agent Trajectory Repair
summary: Vulnerability exploits play a crucial role in assessing the downstream impact of Java library vulnerabilities. While some vulnerabilities are accompanied by disclosed exploit references, automatically reproducing such references into runnable exploits remains challenging because they are often incomplete, unstructured, or only describe partial reproduction steps. Recent code agents provide a promising way to automate this process, but our study shows that their generated exploits often appear successful without triggering the actual vulnerable logic, such as replacing vulnerable APIs with self-implemented functions. To address this, we propose Refploit, an LLM-based trajectory recovery framework for facilitating vulnerability reproduction from public exploit references. The key insight is that a failed agent trajectory is not entirely useless. It may have already completed some reproduction subtasks while also revealing misleading directions that should be avoided. Refploit first validates an agent-generated exploit through differential execution. When the exploit is ineffective, Refploit analyzes its reproduction progress, locates the trajectory segments associated with the reproduction progress, and derives constraints to guide focused recovery. We evaluate Refploit on three open-source Java vulnerability datasets, covering 172 exploit references for 143 vulnerabilities. Under DeepSeek-V4-Flash, Refploit successfully reproduces 138 exploits, achieving a reproduction rate of 80.2%. It achieves a 64.3% relative improvement over the initially generated trajectories and outperforms both the SOTA exploit-generation method PoCGen and advanced code agents such as Codex with GPT-5.4. We further adapt Refploit to another code agent and observe consistent improvements, demonstrating its generality.

AI.tldr: Refploit is an LLM-based framework that recovers failed vulnerability exploit trajectories by analyzing partial progress, identifying misleading steps, and applying constraints to guide re-generation, achieving 80.2% reproduction rate across 172 Java exploit references.
AI.motivation: Existing code agents often generate exploits that appear successful but bypass actual vulnerable logic (e.g., replacing vulnerable APIs with self-implemented functions). Public exploit references are frequently incomplete, unstructured, or partial, making automatic reproduction challenging. Failed agent trajectories contain recoverable subtask progress and useful failure signals that prior work discards.
AI.method: Refploit operates in two phases: (1) differential execution validation — it runs the agent-generated exploit against both vulnerable and patched library versions to check whether the actual vulnerable code path is triggered; (2) trajectory recovery — when exploits fail validation, Refploit analyzes reproduction progress, locates trajectory segments tied to completed subtasks, derives constraints from misleading directions, and performs focused re-generation guided by these constraints.
AI.result: Evaluated on three open-source Java vulnerability datasets (172 exploit references, 143 vulnerabilities) using DeepSeek-V4-Flash, Refploit reproduces 138 exploits (80.2% success rate), a 64.3% relative improvement over initial trajectories. It outperforms SOTA method PoCGen and advanced code agents like Codex with GPT-5.4. The approach generalizes across different underlying code agents.
AI.conclusion: Failed agent trajectories retain substantial recoverable value. Differential execution validation combined with progress-aware, constraint-guided trajectory recovery significantly outperforms both single-pass generation and existing SOTA exploit-generation methods, and the framework is agent-agnostic.

title: MultAttnAttrib: Training-Free Multimodal Attribution in Long Document Question Answering
comment: 25 pages (8 main, 17 references + appendix), 15 figures, Submitted to EMNLP 2026 Conference (Long Paper)
summary: As grounded QA systems are increasingly deployed in AI assistants, accurately attributing generated answers to evidence is critical for user trust and model safety. While unimodal attributions have been explored in depth, the multimodal setting remains relatively under-researched. As a result, we introduce MultAttnAttrib, a training-free attribution-generation method that leverages a model's prefill pass, selected attention heads, and calibrated thresholds to locate source evidence within a document. To establish baseline results for the method, we introduce MultAttrEval, a complementary benchmark dataset annotated with fine-grained, ground-truth attributions for answer components grounded in multimodal source documents. To our knowledge, this is the first evaluation dataset designed specifically for multimodal attribution in long-form documents. Experimental results show that MultAttnAttrib consistently outperforms a variety of attribution-generation methods, including several strong prompting-based approaches and matches the latest frontier models such as GPT 5.4. Our method not only substantially improves attribution accuracy for both unimodal and multimodal attribution types, but also produces attributions at up to one-seventh of the direct inference latency compared to prompting on the same base model.

AI.tldr: Introduces MultAttnAttrib, a training-free method leveraging model attention heads to attribute QA answers to multimodal source evidence, and MultAttrEval, a novel benchmark for evaluating such attributions. The method outperforms prompting-based baselines and matches GPT-5.4, with 7× faster inference.
AI.motivation: As grounded QA systems proliferate in AI assistants, accurate attribution of answers to source evidence is crucial for trust and safety. While unimodal attribution is well-studied, multimodal attribution in long-form documents remains under-researched, with no dedicated evaluation benchmarks available.
AI.method: MultAttnAttrib is a training-free attribution-generation method that exploits the model's prefill pass, selected attention heads, and calibrated thresholds to pinpoint source evidence within multimodal documents. The companion benchmark MultAttrEval provides fine-grained, ground-truth attributions for answer components grounded in multimodal documents.
AI.result: MultAttnAttrib consistently outperforms various attribution-generation methods, including strong prompting-based baselines, and matches frontier models like GPT-5.4. It achieves attribution generation at up to one-seventh the inference latency of prompting on the same base model.
AI.conclusion: The attention-based approach significantly advances multimodal attribution accuracy and efficiency. MultAttnAttrib, combined with MultAttrEval, establishes a strong foundation for future research in multimodal grounded QA attribution.

title: Spin-Weighted Spherical Harmonics Enable Complete and Scalable $\mathrm{E}(3)$-Equivariant Networks
summary: $\mathrm{E}(3)$-equivariant networks are promising for 3D atomistic system modeling, yet their scalability is limited by the $O(L^6)$ complexity of the Clebsch-Gordan Tensor Product (CGTP). The recently proposed Gaunt Tensor Product (GTP) reduces the complexity but is unable to capture the antisymmetric paths, resulting in incomplete expressivity. In this work, we present SpinGTP, an approach to overcome the GTP incompleteness by generalizing from scalar functions to Spin-Weighted Spherical Harmonics (SWSH). By relying on the algebraic properties of SWSH, SpinGTP recovers the missing antisymmetric interactions while maintaining the asymptotic efficiency of GTP. It also allows for a more expressive equivariant basis that naturally accounts for the parity-odd components of tensor products. We evaluate SpinGTP across diverse benchmarks, including Tetris, 3BPA, SPICE-MACE-OFF, and OC20. Our results show that SpinGTP achieves accuracies comparable to full CGTP. Notably, by explicitly capturing antisymmetric paths, SpinGTP exhibits superior performance in tasks involving chiral materials and non-centrosymmetric geometries. This work provides a complete, scalable, and mathematically rigorous path toward high-order equivariance in large-scale 3D atomistic system simulations.

AI.tldr: SpinGTP introduces Spin-Weighted Spherical Harmonics (SWSH) to recover missing antisymmetric interactions in Gaunt Tensor Products, achieving CGTP-comparable accuracy with GTP-level efficiency for E(3)-equivariant 3D atomistic modeling.
AI.motivation: Standard Clebsch-Gordan Tensor Product (CGTP) in E(3)-equivariant networks scales as O(L⁶), limiting scalability. The Gaunt Tensor Product (GTP) reduces complexity but loses antisymmetric path expressivity, causing incompleteness. A method is needed that combines GTP's efficiency with CGTP's full expressivity.
AI.method: The authors generalize from scalar spherical harmonics to Spin-Weighted Spherical Harmonics (SWSH), leveraging their algebraic properties to construct SpinGTP. This recovers antisymmetric interactions missing in GTP while maintaining asymptotic efficiency. The approach also yields a more expressive equivariant basis that naturally incorporates parity-odd components of tensor products.
AI.result: SpinGTP achieves accuracy comparable to full CGTP across Tetris, 3BPA, SPICE-MACE-OFF, and OC20 benchmarks. It shows superior performance on chiral materials and non-centrosymmetric geometries due to explicit antisymmetric path capture.
AI.conclusion: SpinGTP provides a complete, scalable, and mathematically rigorous solution for high-order equivariance in large-scale 3D atomistic simulations, bridging the gap between GTP efficiency and CGTP expressivity.

title: Revisiting Chain-of-Thought Reasoning under Limited Supervision: Semi-supervised Chain-of-Thought Learning
summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning has emerged as an effective approach for activating latent reasoning capabilities in large language models. However, most existing CoT methods use reasoning chains mainly as inference-time prompts, while the generated reasoning traces are rarely reused as semi-supervised learning signals. In this report, we define \textbf{Semi-supervised Chain-of-Thought Learning} and propose \textbf{Semi-CoT}, a simple framework that uses unlabeled questions to construct pseudo reasoning supervision. Semi-CoT samples multiple pseudo-CoTs for each unlabeled question, estimates answer-level semantic entropy, and selects low-entropy reasoning chains as reliable pseudo-CoT demonstrations. This extends the self-training view of CoT from inference-time refinement to semi-supervised pseudo-supervision. Pilot experiments on AQuA, SVAMP, GSM8K, and MultiArith show that the entropy gate selects high-precision pseudo-CoTs, with pseudo-answer precision ranging from $91.36\%$ to $100\%$. Semi-CoT also gives small gains on SVAMP and GSM8K, while AQuA shows negative transfer and MultiArith reaches a ceiling. These results suggest that unlabeled questions can provide reliable pseudo reasoning signals, but their effective use still requires stronger demonstration selection or student training.

AI.tldr: Semi-CoT proposes a semi-supervised learning framework that generates pseudo chain-of-thought reasoning from unlabeled questions, filters them via answer-level semantic entropy, and uses selected low-entropy chains as pseudo-supervision for training — showing high pseudo-answer precision (91-100%) but mixed downstream gains.
AI.motivation: Existing CoT methods use reasoning chains only as inference-time prompts; generated traces are discarded rather than leveraged as semi-supervised training signals. The authors aim to bridge this gap by reusing CoT reasoning from unlabeled data as pseudo-supervision.
AI.method: Semi-CoT framework: (1) sample multiple pseudo-CoT reasoning chains per unlabeled question from a teacher model; (2) estimate answer-level semantic entropy across chains; (3) apply an entropy gate to select low-entropy (high-consistency) chains as reliable pseudo-demonstrations; (4) use these selected pseudo-CoTs for semi-supervised student training — extending self-training from inference-time refinement to a full pseudo-supervision paradigm.
AI.result: On AQuA, SVAMP, GSM8K, and MultiArith, the entropy gate selects pseudo-CoTs with pseudo-answer precision from 91.36% to 100%. Semi-CoT yields small gains on SVAMP and GSM8K, negative transfer on AQuA, and a ceiling effect on MultiArith.
AI.conclusion: Unlabeled questions can provide reliable pseudo reasoning signals via entropy-based filtering, but effectively leveraging them for student training requires stronger demonstration selection mechanisms or improved student training strategies beyond the current framework.

title: Data Comics for Education: Evaluating Effectiveness, Benefits, and the Ethics of AI-Assisted Creation
summary: In today's data-driven world, students often struggle with interpreting visualisations due to limited visualisation literacy. Data comics have emerged as a promising medium to enhance engagement and understanding, but their educational value has seen little empirical examination, partly due to the effort required to create them. Recent advances in Generative AI (GenAI) offer a scalable solution to this challenge. We conducted a within-subjects study with 60 university students, comparing conventional visualisations with data comics, created with assistance from GenAI tools, across information retrieval and comprehension tasks. Students consistently performed better with data comics, particularly in insight comprehension tasks, independent of prior visualisation literacy. Students also commented data comics as more engaging and easier to understand, though concerns were raised about GenAI-driven misinformation and ownership. Our findings highlight the potential of data comics as a potentially effective tool for data communication in education, while underscoring the need to address ethical concerns related to AI-assisted creation.

AI.tldr: A within-subjects study with 60 university students found that GenAI-assisted data comics outperform conventional visualizations for information retrieval and comprehension, particularly insight tasks. Students rated comics as more engaging and understandable, though concerns about AI-driven misinformation and ownership emerged.
AI.motivation: Students often struggle with interpreting visualizations due to limited visualization literacy. Data comics show promise for enhancing engagement and understanding, but empirical examination of their educational value is scarce—partly because creating them requires significant effort. Generative AI offers a scalable way to produce data comics, enabling rigorous study of their effectiveness.
AI.method: A within-subjects experiment with 60 university students comparing conventional visualizations against GenAI-assisted data comics. Tasks spanned information retrieval and insight comprehension. Performance was measured across both conditions, and prior visualization literacy was controlled as a factor. Subjective feedback on engagement, ease of understanding, misinformation concerns, and ownership was also collected.
AI.result: Students consistently performed better with data comics than conventional visualizations, with the advantage being most pronounced for insight comprehension tasks. This effect was independent of students' prior visualization literacy levels. Subjectively, students found data comics more engaging and easier to understand, though they raised concerns about GenAI-driven misinformation and ownership of AI-generated content.
AI.conclusion: Data comics, especially when produced with GenAI assistance, represent a potentially effective tool for data communication in educational contexts. However, ethical concerns—particularly around misinformation and content ownership in AI-assisted creation—must be addressed for responsible adoption.

title: Resilient Liquid Democracy: Mitigating Voting Power Imbalances via Secure Delegation Networks
summary: Liquid democracy promises to improve collective decision-making by allowing voters to vote directly, delegate their voting power to trusted participants, or combine both approaches through fallback mechanisms. However, existing deployments typically rely on transparent delegation, which exposes voters to popularity-driven herding, makes coercion verifiable, and introduces systemic fragility when highly-backed delegates abstain. In this paper, we propose a secure liquid democracy mechanism that resolves the tension between informed expertise routing and systemic robustness. We introduce a sealed delegation regime using decentralized timed-release encryption, which cryptographically hides delegation choices during the formation phase to prevent herding and coercion, while restoring full public auditability for the final tally. To address delegate failures, we extend the protocol with ranked multi-delegation and personal fallback ballots. We formally prove pre-reveal secrecy and resubmission receipt-freeness for our protocol. Finally, we evaluate the mechanism on four real datasets, a municipal participatory-budgeting election with a calibration survey, twenty further participatory-budgeting elections, and 60,000 US voters with an objective competence measure. They show that whether delegation improves representational accuracy follows a recoverable-gap law; it helps only when abstention is large and systematically unrepresentative, and is otherwise neutral or harmful, with representative-style delegation safer than delegating to a competence elite. The benefit of sealed formation is primarily structural, sharply reducing power concentration rather than directly improving accuracy; and ranked multi-delegation with personal fallback ballots sharply reduces vote loss under realistic and targeted delegate failures, a result that replicates across all twenty elections.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a secure liquid democracy protocol using sealed delegation via timed-release encryption to prevent herding and coercion, augmented with ranked multi-delegation and personal fallback ballots. Empirical evaluation across real datasets reveals that delegation benefits accuracy only under large, unrepresentative abstention, and that sealed formation primarily reduces power concentration while fallback mechanisms mitigate vote loss from delegate failure.
AI.motivation: Existing liquid democracy systems rely on transparent delegation, which creates three problems: (1) herding driven by popularity cues, (2) verifiable coercion since delegations are publicly visible, and (3) systemic fragility when highly-backed delegates abstain. The authors seek to resolve the tension between routing votes to informed experts and maintaining systemic robustness.
AI.method: The authors introduce a sealed delegation regime using decentralized timed-release encryption to cryptographically hide delegation choices during the formation phase, preventing herding and coercion while preserving public auditability for the final tally. They extend the protocol with ranked multi-delegation and personal fallback ballots to address delegate failures. Formal proofs establish pre-reveal secrecy and resubmission receipt-freeness. Empirical evaluation uses four real datasets: a municipal participatory-budgeting election with a calibration survey, twenty additional participatory-budgeting elections, and 60,000 US voters with an objective competence measure.
AI.result: Delegation improves representational accuracy only when abstention is large and systematically unrepresentative — a "recoverable-gap law." Otherwise, delegation is neutral or harmful. Representative-style delegation proves safer than delegating to a competence elite. Sealed formation's benefit is primarily structural, sharply reducing power concentration rather than directly improving accuracy. Ranked multi-delegation with personal fallback ballots sharply reduces vote loss under realistic and targeted delegate failures, replicating across all twenty elections.
AI.conclusion: Secure liquid democracy with sealed delegation and fallback mechanisms resolves key vulnerabilities in existing systems. However, the recoverable-gap law implies delegation should be deployed selectively — only when abstention is both high and systematically biased. Structural benefits (reduced power concentration, resilience to delegate failure) may justify the mechanism even when accuracy gains are modest.

title: KRCA: An Efficient Root Cause Analysis System in Hyper-Scale Microservice Systems via Agentic AI
summary: Hyper-scale microservice systems have become the standard infrastructure for large-scale Internet companies. These systems consist of numerous loosely coupled microservices that evolve independently through continuous development and deployment. Such complexity makes failures unavoidable, necessitating efficient Root Cause Analysis (RCA) to help Site Reliability Engineers (SREs) quickly localize root cause services and classify failure types. However, existing RCA methods often struggle to adapt to the extreme dynamism and massive scale of these systems. In this paper, we present KRCA, an end-to-end RCA system designed for hyper-scale microservice systems. To manage the vast search space, KRCA employs a multi-stage pipeline that begins with an API-level drilldown to isolate suspicious services. It then instantiates a skeleton-based causal graph from anomalous metrics to serve as a high-recall structural prior, before utilizing a memory-augmented multi-agent framework to verify causality and generate the final failure report. By combining structured causal constraints with multi-agent reasoning, KRCA employs balances diagnostic accuracy with the efficiency requirements of real-time production use. Experimental results show that KRCA achieves AC@1 scores of 0.88 and 0.79 for root cause service localization and failure type classification, outperforming the strongest baseline by at lease 31% in absolute gains. KRCA has been deployed in Kuaishou's production environment for over six months, reducing the average diagnosis time by 77.3%.

AI.tldr: KRCA is an end-to-end root cause analysis system for hyper-scale microservices that uses a multi-stage pipeline combining API-level drilldown, skeleton-based causal graphs, and a memory-augmented multi-agent framework to achieve high-accuracy failure localization and classification, deployed at Kuaishou with 77.3% reduction in diagnosis time.
AI.motivation: Hyper-scale microservice systems are highly dynamic, loosely coupled, and continuously evolving, making failures inevitable. Existing RCA methods cannot effectively handle the extreme scale and dynamism, creating a need for an efficient, accurate, and production-ready RCA system that helps SREs quickly localize root causes and classify failure types.
AI.method: KRCA employs a three-stage pipeline: (1) API-level drilldown to narrow the search space to suspicious services; (2) instantiation of a skeleton-based causal graph from anomalous metrics as a high-recall structural prior; (3) a memory-augmented multi-agent framework that verifies causality and produces a final failure report. The approach balances structured causal constraints with multi-agent reasoning.
AI.result: KRCA achieves AC@1 scores of 0.88 for root cause service localization and 0.79 for failure type classification, outperforming the strongest baseline by at least 31% in absolute gains. In production deployment at Kuaishou for over six months, it reduced average diagnosis time by 77.3%.
AI.conclusion: KRCA demonstrates that combining structured causal priors with multi-agent reasoning is an effective strategy for RCA in hyper-scale microservice environments, delivering both high diagnostic accuracy and real-time operational efficiency in production settings.

title: IsoSci: A Benchmark of Isomorphic Cross-Domain Science Problems for Evaluating Reasoning versus Knowledge Retrieval in LLMs
summary: We introduce ISOSCI, a benchmark of isomorphic cross-domain science problem pairs that separates reasoning ability from domain knowledge retrieval in LLM evaluation. Each pair shares identical logical structure but requires different domain-specific knowledge, enabling controlled attribution of reasoning-mode gains. Across five model pairs spanning four model families, we find that 91.3% of reasoning-mode gains are knowledge-dependent rather than structure-invariant (63/69 gains; Wilson 95% CI [82.3%, 96.0%]), directly challenging the assumption that chain-of-thought reasoning improves short-horizon procedural scientific problem-solving. Reasoning toggles on highly capable models provide less than 5 percentage points accuracy gain across all domains, and a reasoning-specialized model (o3-mini) that outperforms its standard counterpart on GPQA Diamond (+19.2 percentage points) underperforms on ISOSCI (-24.7 percentage points), showing that benchmark choice determines conclusions about reasoning utility. We release ISOSCI at https://huggingface.co/datasets/isosci/isosci

AI.tldr: ISOSCI is a benchmark of isomorphic science problem pairs that isolates reasoning from domain knowledge. The study finds that 91.3% of reasoning-mode gains are knowledge-dependent, challenging the assumption that chain-of-thought reasoning improves short-horizon scientific problem-solving. A reasoning-specialized model (o3-mini) outperforms on GPQA Diamond but underperforms on ISOSCI, demonstrating that benchmark choice drives conclusions about reasoning utility.
AI.motivation: Current LLM benchmarks conflate reasoning ability with domain knowledge retrieval, making it difficult to attribute performance improvements to either factor. The authors aim to disentangle these two capabilities by creating isomorphic problem pairs that share identical logical structure but differ in domain-specific knowledge requirements, enabling controlled attribution of reasoning-mode gains.
AI.method: The authors construct ISOSCI, a benchmark of isomorphic cross-domain science problem pairs. Each pair shares identical logical structure but requires distinct domain-specific knowledge. They evaluate five model pairs across four model families, comparing standard vs. reasoning-mode (chain-of-thought) performance. Gains are classified as either knowledge-dependent or structure-invariant. They also compare o3-mini (reasoning-specialized) against its standard counterpart on both ISOSCI and GPQA Diamond.
AI.result: 91.3% of reasoning-mode gains are knowledge-dependent (63/69 gains; Wilson 95% CI [82.3%, 96.0%]). Reasoning toggles on highly capable models yield less than 5 percentage points accuracy gain across all domains. The reasoning-specialized o3-mini outperforms its standard counterpart on GPQA Diamond (+19.2 pp) but underperforms on ISOSCI (-24.7 pp), showing benchmark choice determines conclusions about reasoning utility.
AI.conclusion: Chain-of-thought reasoning does not substantially improve short-horizon procedural scientific problem-solving when logical structure is controlled; observed gains are overwhelmingly attributable to improved domain knowledge retrieval rather than enhanced reasoning per se. Benchmark selection critically shapes conclusions about reasoning-mode effectiveness.

title: The Rollout Infrastructure Tax in Coding-Agent Reinforcement Learning
comment: Preprint. 6 pages, 6 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to ACM SoCC 2026
summary: Coding-agent reinforcement learning treats execution infrastructure as a background implementation detail, despite relying on large numbers of interactive software rollouts. This is a missed opportunity: measuring infrastructure overhead can reveal practical efficiency gains for RL post-training, where small per-rollout savings compound at scale. We present a comparative study of four execution substrates: single containers, hosted sandboxes, Kubernetes-orchestrated containers, and cloud virtual machines. We find up to $110\times$ variation in cold-start latency and a $1.8\times$ spread in projected worker-hours for one million 150-step trajectories. Our results suggest that future coding-agent RL systems should optimize execution substrates as part of the training system itself, not merely as deployment plumbing.

AI.tldr: A comparative study of four execution substrates (containers, hosted sandboxes, Kubernetes, VMs) for coding-agent RL reveals up to 110× variation in cold-start latency and 1.8× spread in worker-hours for large-scale rollouts, arguing that infrastructure should be treated as a first-class optimization target in RL training systems.
AI.motivation: Current coding-agent RL systems treat execution infrastructure as a background detail, missing the fact that per-rollout overhead compounds significantly at scale. Quantifying these infrastructure costs can reveal practical efficiency gains for RL post-training.
AI.method: The authors conduct a comparative empirical study measuring performance across four execution substrates: single containers, hosted sandboxes, Kubernetes-orchestrated containers, and cloud virtual machines, evaluating cold-start latency and projected worker-hours for a benchmark of one million 150-step trajectories.
AI.result: The study finds up to 110× variation in cold-start latency across substrates and a 1.8× spread in projected total worker-hours for processing one million 150-step trajectories.
AI.conclusion: Execution substrates should be optimized as an integral component of the coding-agent RL training system rather than treated as mere deployment plumbing, given the compounding efficiency impact at scale.

title: OPINE-World: Programmatic World Modeling with Ontology-error-Prioritized Interactive Exploration
summary: Learning how an environment behaves from interaction is central to building agents that adapt to unfamiliar tasks. World models learned with deep networks are flexible but data-hungry and transfer poorly beyond their training distribution. Program-synthesized world models, written as source code by LLMs and refined through counterexample-guided inductive synthesis (CEGIS), are instead data-efficient and reusable, yet they have been demonstrated mainly on structured-state worlds with a given object vocabulary, and a single program search does not scale to pixel-rendered environments whose object structure must be hypothesized flexibly. We introduce OPINE-World, an LLM agent that learns an object-centric programmatic world model online from interaction. OPINE-World couples two cooperating agents in a loop of hypothesis and test, one acting in the environment and one synthesizing the model in code with replay verification and model-based planning, and it steers exploration with a Bayesian measure of object-type adequacy we call ontology error. We evaluate OPINE-World on ARC-AGI-3, a benchmark for skill-acquisition efficiency in which the object vocabulary, the goal, and the action semantics are withheld. OPINE-World solves 20 of 25 games without per-game training and reaches an action-efficiency score of 78.4 against the human baseline.

AI.tldr: OPINE-World introduces an LLM agent that learns object-centric programmatic world models online from interaction, coupling exploration and program synthesis agents. It uses a Bayesian ontology error metric to guide exploration and achieves strong results on ARC-AGI-3, solving 20/25 games without per-game training.
AI.motivation: Deep-network world models are data-hungry and generalize poorly beyond their training distribution, while existing program-synthesis approaches (CEGIS-based) are data-efficient but limited to structured-state worlds with known object vocabularies and don't scale to pixel-rendered environments requiring flexible object discovery. The gap is an agent that can learn reusable, data-efficient world models directly from pixels without a predefined object ontology.
AI.method: OPINE-World pairs two cooperating LLM-based agents in a hypothesis-and-test loop: an acting agent that explores the environment and a synthesis agent that builds a programmatic world model in code using replay verification and model-based planning. Exploration is steered by a novel Bayesian metric called ontology error, which measures the adequacy of the hypothesized object-type vocabulary. The system operates online from pixel observations on ARC-AGI-3, where object vocabulary, goals, and action semantics are initially unknown.
AI.result: OPINE-World solves 20 out of 25 games on ARC-AGI-3 without any per-game training, achieving an action-efficiency score of 78.4 compared to the human baseline.
AI.conclusion: OPINE-World demonstrates that LLM-driven programmatic world model learning with ontology-error-guided exploration can effectively tackle pixel-rendered environments requiring flexible object discovery, bridging the gap between data efficiency and perceptual flexibility in world model acquisition.

title: Physical surfaces make touch interactions in virtual reality precise, efficient, and bimanual
comment: This paper has been accepted by the "International Journal of Human-Computer Studies (IJHCS)" [Project Link] https://wy-blacksheep.github.io/projects/physical-surface/ [Paper Link] https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1071581926001254 [Video Link] https://youtu.be/e_nzOkZIIKA
summary:
Virtual reality (VR) systems can enable convenient hand-based interactions across diverse work scenarios. However, mid-air gestures lack tactile feedback and a physical reference surface to support the hand. This absence of haptic grounding can cause significant challenges in achieving precise and efficient touch interactions. This paper investigates the effect of different types of hand-grounded haptic feedback on the touch performance of VR tasks that demand high precision, such as selecting, tracing, and sketching. We compared three levels of haptic feedback: 1) No Haptic Feedback, where only visual feedback was provided; 2) Tactile Feedback, where users received vibrotactile and pressure feedback upon touching a virtual surface; 3) Physical Surface, where users interacted with a portable and tangible surface.
  Our study found that portable physical surfaces enabled the best selection precision, tracing efficiency, and sketch quality. Furthermore, participants showed increased bimanual hand utilization when engaging with a physical surface during tasks. These observed behaviors corresponded to participants' preference for interacting with physical surfaces, attributed to a better sense of confidence and control.

AI.tldr: This paper examines how different types of hand-grounded haptic feedback affect precision touch interactions in VR, comparing no haptic feedback, vibrotactile/pressure feedback, and a portable physical surface. Results show physical surfaces yield the best selection precision, tracing efficiency, and sketch quality, with users reporting greater confidence and control.
AI.motivation: Mid-air hand gestures in VR lack tactile feedback and a physical reference surface — a problem termed the absence of "haptic grounding." This deficit impairs precise and efficient touch interactions, particularly in tasks requiring high precision such as selecting, tracing, and sketching. The authors aim to quantify how different levels of hand-grounded haptic feedback can mitigate these limitations.
AI.method: A within-subjects user study comparing three haptic feedback conditions: (1) No Haptic Feedback — visual-only feedback; (2) Tactile Feedback — vibrotactile and pressure feedback delivered upon touching a virtual surface; (3) Physical Surface — a portable, tangible surface users physically interact with. Participants performed high-precision VR tasks (selecting, tracing, sketching) under each condition. Metrics included selection precision, tracing efficiency, sketch quality, and bimanual hand utilization.
AI.result: The portable physical surface condition significantly outperformed the other two across all metrics: best selection precision, highest tracing efficiency, and superior sketch quality. Participants also exhibited increased bimanual hand use when a physical surface was present. Subjective feedback indicated a strong preference for physical surfaces, driven by enhanced confidence and perceived control.
AI.conclusion: Hand-grounded haptic feedback, particularly via a portable physical surface, substantially improves precision touch performance in VR. The findings suggest that incorporating tangible physical references can enhance user confidence, control, and bimanual coordination, offering practical design implications for VR systems requiring high-precision manual input.

title: Knowledge Over Parameters: Evolving Smart Contract Vulnerability Detection
summary:
Smart contract vulnerabilities are predominantly logic bugs whose detection requires structured, step-by-step procedural knowledge of attack patterns and contract semantics. Existing LLM-based methods struggle to generate this knowledge automatically: prompt-based methods rely on manually crafted detection rules, while fine-tuning requires massive labeled datasets that are inherently scarce in this domain. We present EvoVuln, an automated framework that reformulates vulnerability detection as a procedural knowledge evolution problem, synthesizing and refining detection logic using only a minimal number of labeled samples.
  To achieve this, EvoVuln introduces two key mechanisms. First, a Runtime with an Inversion of Control (IoC) architecture compiles detection rules into Executable Policies. This strictly decouples deterministic control flow from LLM semantic reasoning, ensuring faithful logical adherence and producing dense diagnostic telemetry for precise error localization. Second, a two-phase evolution pipeline refines the rule via abductive semantic debugging without any parameter updates: Cold Start bootstraps and stress-tests an initial rule using auto-synthesized corner cases; Few-Shot Evolving then grounds the policy in real-world semantics using only five vulnerable and five safe examples per vulnerability type.
  Evaluated across five real-world vulnerability types, EvoVuln achieves a 71% macro-average F1-score, outperforming all baselines. The evolved procedural knowledge is portable across models: it enables a lightweight, low-cost model to surpass a much larger zero-shot model by 19 percentage points, and transfers to other LLMs without retraining, at a one-time evolution cost under $50.

AI.tldr: EvoVuln reformulates smart contract vulnerability detection as procedural knowledge evolution, using an Inversion of Control runtime and a two-phase evolution pipeline to synthesize and refine detection rules with minimal labeled data, achieving 71% macro F1 and portable, cost-effective cross-model transfer.
AI.motivation: Smart contract vulnerabilities are primarily logic bugs requiring structured procedural knowledge for detection. Existing LLM-based approaches fall short: prompt-based methods depend on manually crafted rules that don't scale, while fine-tuning demands large labeled datasets that are scarce in the vulnerability domain. A method is needed that can automatically synthesize and refine detection logic from minimal labeled samples.
AI.method: EvoVuln introduces (1) an IoC Runtime that compiles detection rules into Executable Policies, decoupling deterministic control flow from LLM semantic reasoning to ensure logical adherence and produce diagnostic telemetry for error localization; and (2) a two-phase evolution pipeline: Cold Start bootstraps and stress-tests initial rules via auto-synthesized corner cases, while Few-Shot Evolving grounds the policy in real-world semantics using only five vulnerable and five safe examples per vulnerability type — all without parameter updates.
AI.result: Across five real-world vulnerability types, EvoVuln achieves a 71% macro-average F1-score, outperforming all baselines. The evolved procedural knowledge is portable: a lightweight model equipped with it surpasses a much larger zero-shot model by 19 percentage points and transfers to other LLMs without retraining, with a one-time evolution cost under $50.
AI.conclusion: EvoVuln demonstrates that procedural knowledge evolution with minimal supervision is a viable and effective paradigm for smart contract vulnerability detection, offering strong performance, cross-model portability, and low computational cost compared to fine-tuning or prompt-engineering alternatives.

title: Archer: Towards Agentic Review for Compiler Optimizations
summary:
Modern compilers are frequently updated, but expert review capacity is highly limited, leading to delayed integration and, in some cases, subtle semantic bugs entering the compiler codebase. Automating the code review process with modern general code review agents may be feasible, but it faces critical challenges due to compiler complexity. In this paper, we use LLVM as our target compiler and present Archer, the first automated agentic code review tool for compiler optimizations. Archer constrains the agentic review process from both ends by using obligations to guide analysis and a deterministic validation guard to admit only findings backed by executable evidence.
  We evaluated Archer on 70 open PRs and 328 closed PRs in LLVM from the last two months. The review results are shocking and concerning: Archer discovers that 21% of open PRs and 11% of closed PRs are buggy, i.e, introducing semantic bugs such as miscompilations in LLVM. Our findings expose a critical gap in the capacity for critical review in large compiler projects and demonstrate the practical value of Archer as an additional reviewer.

AI.tldr: Archer is an automated agentic code review tool for LLVM compiler optimizations that uses obligations for guided analysis and a deterministic validation guard. Evaluation on 398 LLVM PRs reveals alarming bug rates: 21% of open PRs and 11% of closed PRs contain semantic bugs like miscompilations.
AI.motivation: Modern compilers like LLVM are updated frequently, but expert reviewer capacity is severely limited, causing delayed integration and subtle semantic bugs (e.g., miscompilations) slipping into the codebase. Automating review with general-purpose agents is challenging due to compiler complexity, motivating a specialized tool.
AI.method: Archer is an agentic code review tool tailored for compiler optimizations in LLVM. It constrains the review process bidirectionally: (1) obligations guide the analysis by specifying what must hold for correctness, and (2) a deterministic validation guard ensures that only findings with executable evidence are admitted, preventing false positives.
AI.result: Evaluated on 70 open PRs and 328 closed PRs from the last two months of LLVM development. Archer found that 21% of open PRs and 11% of closed PRs contain semantic bugs such as miscompilations, exposing a significant gap in critical review capacity.
AI.conclusion: The findings reveal a critical shortage of review capacity in large compiler projects, with a substantial fraction of PRs containing semantic bugs. Archer demonstrates practical value as an automated supplementary reviewer capable of catching subtle miscompilation bugs that escape human review.

title: FaithMed: Training LLMs For Faithful Evidence-Based Medical Reasoning
summary: Faithful reasoning is essential in medicine, where clinical decisions require transparent justification grounded in reliable evidence. Current medical LLMs either lack active access to evidence or use retrieved evidence without supervising how it should be appraised and applied during reasoning. To address this, we formalize evidence-based medicine principles as process-level criteria and introduce FaithMed, a framework that combines clinician-designed, automatically refined rubrics with reinforcement learning using step-level process reward assignment and advantage grouping. Across seven medical benchmarks, FaithMed improves over agentic-search baselines (+9% on average) and outcome-only RL (+5.8%), while raising average evidence-based medicine rubric scores over agentic-search Qwen3 baselines (+15.5%). This work demonstrates that explicit step-level supervision can improve both task success and the faithfulness of the reasoning process. Code is available at https://github.com/cxcscmu/FaithMed.

AI.tldr: FaithMed introduces a framework that formalizes evidence-based medicine (EBM) principles as process-level criteria, combining clinician-designed rubrics with reinforcement learning using step-level process rewards and advantage grouping. It improves both task accuracy (+9% over agentic-search baselines, +5.8% over outcome-only RL) and faithfulness of reasoning (+15.5% EBM rubric scores) across seven medical benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Current medical LLMs either lack active access to evidence or retrieve evidence without proper supervision of how it is appraised and applied during reasoning. Faithful, transparent justification grounded in reliable evidence is essential for clinical decision-making, motivating the need for explicit process-level oversight aligned with evidence-based medicine principles.
