FedHOO further optimizes resampling rates using an X-armed bandit approach. The method outperforms baselines on long-tailed benchmarks and a chip-defect dataset.
AI.motivation: Class imbalance in federated learning (FL) degrades predictive performance for underrepresented classes. Standard centralized rebalancing techniques are infeasible in FL due to privacy constraints and data heterogeneity across clients. Existing FL optimizers fail to adequately handle the gradient magnitude disparity and noise inherent in rare-class updates.
AI.method: FedCGNM partitions classes into a small number of groups via minimum within-group variance, maintains and normalizes momentum per group to unit length, and sums the normalized group momentums as the update direction — equalizing gradient magnitudes and mitigating rare-class noise. A convergence analysis accounts for time-varying resampling rates. FedHOO, an X-armed-bandit (XAB) algorithm, optimizes these rates by evaluating many two-candidate-rate combinations per client with linear cost, exploiting federated parallelism.
AI.result: FedCGNM consistently outperforms baselines across four public long-tailed benchmarks and a proprietary chip-defect dataset. FedHOO yields additional performance gains in small-client federated settings.
AI.conclusion: Class-grouped normalized momentum is an effective client-side strategy for tackling class imbalance in FL. Coupling FedCGNM with the FedHOO rate-optimization framework further boosts performance in small-scale federations, offering a practical and theoretically grounded solution.

title: SemHash-LLM: A Multi-Granularity Semantic Hashing Framework for Document Deduplication
summary: Large scale document deduplication must preserve semantic equivalence while remaining efficient over massive corpora. We present SemHash LLM, a multi granularity framework that unifies semantic projection hashing, attention weighted MinHash, contrastive boundary learning, and selective LLM based adjudication. The method combines character, token, and document level signals through gated fusion, then applies a cascaded filtering pipeline for efficient candidate reduction. Semantic projection hashing learns compact binary codes in distilled LLM embedding space, while attention weighted Min- Hash suppresses boilerplate and emphasizes informative content. Adaptive decision boundaries and uncertainty estimation further improve robustness across template pollution, short text perturbation, containment, and viral fragments. Experiments show that SemHash LLM achieves strong duplicate detection quality with less than one percent neural verification cost.

AI.tldr: SemHash LLM is a multi-granularity deduplication framework that combines semantic projection hashing, attention-weighted MinHash, contrastive boundary learning, and selective LLM adjudication to achieve high-quality duplicate detection at scale while keeping neural verification costs under 1%.
AI.motivation: Large-scale document deduplication requires preserving semantic equivalence (identifying paraphrases, near-duplicates, and contained fragments) while maintaining computational efficiency over massive corpora — a trade-off that existing hashing or embedding-based methods struggle to balance.
AI.method: The framework operates at character, token, and document levels fused via gated fusion. It employs: (1) semantic projection hashing that learns compact binary codes in a distilled LLM embedding space; (2) attention-weighted MinHash to down-weight boilerplate and up-weight informative content; (3) contrastive boundary learning with adaptive decision boundaries and uncertainty estimation for robustness; and (4) a cascaded filtering pipeline that progressively reduces candidates, invoking selective LLM-based adjudication only on ambiguous edge cases.
AI.result: SemHash LLM achieves strong duplicate detection quality across diverse challenges — template pollution, short text perturbation, containment, and viral fragments — while requiring LLM-based neural verification on less than 1% of candidate pairs.
AI.conclusion: A multi-granularity, hybrid approach that combines efficient hashing techniques with sparing LLM adjudication can deliver both the semantic accuracy and computational scalability required for web-scale document deduplication.

title: An Exploratory Study on LLM-Generated Code and Comments in Code Repositories
comment: Accepted to The Journal of Systems & Software (JSS) on 1 July 2026
summary: The use of LLMs in software development has become increasingly widespread on tasks such as code generation and summarization. Reports from large technology companies showed that around 20% to 30% of their code are generated by LLMs. However, there remains skepticism about the practical usage of LLM-generated code and comments, such as concerns on more time for debugging the generated code and the unnaturalness of the generated comments. In this paper, we study the code and comments detected as likely to be generated by LLMs and their characteristics, the differences between company- and community-maintained repositories, and how likely bugs are associated with LLM-generated code. We conduct extensive experiments on active company- and community-maintained repositories from 2021 to 2025 using various tools and techniques that detect code and comments generated by LLMs. Based on our detector-based proxy analysis, the results suggest that code detected as likely to be generated by LLMs decreased over time and appeared frequently in test cases, while that of comments remains relatively stable. Proxy results further suggest that code detected as likely to be generated by LLMs shows substantial intra-repository code clones, whereas comments exhibit a relatively low proportion of grammatically correct sentences. In addition, the company-maintained repositories show a higher percentage of code and comments detected as likely to be generated by LLMs, and only a small percentage of the human-labelled bugs are detected as being likely associated with LLM-generated code.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the prevalence and characteristics of LLM-generated code and comments in software repositories from 2021–2025, comparing company-maintained vs. community-maintained projects. Using detector-based proxy analysis, it finds that LLM-generated code declined over time (concentrated in test cases), while LLM-generated comments remained stable. Company repositories exhibit higher LLM content, and human-labelled bugs rarely trace to LLM-generated code.
AI.motivation: Despite reports that 20–30% of code at large tech companies is LLM-generated, skepticism persists regarding the practical utility of such code and comments — specifically, fears of increased debugging effort and unnatural comment quality. The authors seek to empirically characterize LLM-generated artifacts, compare organizational vs. open-source repository patterns, and assess whether LLM-generated code correlates with bugs.
AI.method: The authors conduct a large-scale empirical study on active repositories (2021–2025) using detector tools and techniques that identify code and comments likely generated by LLMs. They perform proxy analysis based on these detectors to examine temporal trends, distribution across code types (e.g., test vs. production), intra-repository cloning, grammatical correctness of comments, organizational differences, and association with human-labelled bugs.
AI.result: (1) Code detected as LLM-generated decreased over time and appeared disproportionately in test cases; LLM-generated comments remained relatively stable. (2) LLM-generated code exhibits substantial intra-repository clones; LLM-generated comments show a low proportion of grammatically correct sentences. (3) Company-maintained repositories contain a higher percentage of detected LLM-generated code and comments than community-maintained ones. (4) Only a small fraction of human-labelled bugs are associated with LLM-generated code.
AI.conclusion: The findings suggest that concerns about LLM-generated code causing bugs may be overstated, though quality issues like clonal proliferation and grammatical deficiencies in comments remain. The disparity between company and community repositories indicates organizational adoption patterns influence LLM usage, and the concentration in test code may reflect developer trust levels in LLM outputs.

title: Can Language Models Actually Retrieve In-Context? Drowning in Documents at Million Token Scale
summary: Language models (LMs) raise an intriguing alternative to vector-based retrieval: conditioning on an in-context corpus and directly generating a relevant answer. However, prior work has largely focused on proprietary systems or the smaller-scale reranking task, leaving corpus-scale in-context retrieval largely unexplored. In this work, we present the first systematic study of in-context retrieval on two scales practical retrievers demand: million-token corpora and length-generalization far beyond training-time sizes. We first introduce BlockSearch, a 0.6B LM retriever whose architectural and training modifications improve over prior LM baselines and length-generalize up to 10 times beyond its training regime. Nevertheless, retrieval still collapses under more extreme extrapolation. We trace this failure to an attention dilution effect: as the corpus grows, irrelevant documents dominate the softmax denominator, reducing the normalized mass on the gold document even when its pre-softmax score stays high. Motivated by this analysis, we introduce length-aware adjustments to the attention softmax and document-level sparse attention. With these modifications, at the million-token scale, our model matches dense retrieval on widely studied benchmarks (e.g, MS MARCO and NQ), while outperforming the concurrent model MSA despite being 7 times smaller. Furthermore, it significantly outperforms dense retrieval on tasks requiring entirely different notions of similarity, such as LIMIT, achieving a 3 times higher score. Together, our results position in-context retrieval a promising alternative to classical retrieval while emphasizing attention control under extreme context growth as a new challenge.

AI.tldr: BlockSearch, a 0.6B LM retriever with length-aware attention modifications, matches or outperforms dense retrieval at million-token scales, addressing the attention dilution problem that causes standard LM retrievers to collapse under extreme corpus growth.
AI.motivation: Prior work on language model-based in-context retrieval has been limited to proprietary systems or small-scale reranking. The authors aim to systematically study whether LMs can perform retrieval directly from million-token corpora and generalize to lengths far beyond training-time sizes — a scale that practical retrievers demand but remains largely unexplored.
AI.method: The authors introduce BlockSearch, a 0.6B parameter LM retriever. Key innovations include: (1) architectural and training modifications that enable length generalization up to 10× beyond training regime; (2) diagnosis of "attention dilution" — as corpus size grows, irrelevant documents dominate the softmax denominator, drowning out the gold document's normalized attention mass even when its pre-softmax score is high; (3) two remedies: length-aware adjustments to the attention softmax and document-level sparse attention, which mitigate the dilution effect and restore retrieval quality at million-token scales.
AI.result: At million-token scale, BlockSearch matches dense retrieval on MS MARCO and NQ benchmarks. It outperforms the concurrent model MSA despite being 7× smaller. On the LIMIT benchmark, which requires entirely different similarity notions, BlockSearch achieves a 3× higher score than dense retrieval.
AI.conclusion: In-context retrieval is positioned as a promising alternative to classical vector-based retrieval. The work also highlights attention control under extreme context growth as a critical new challenge, with the proposed length-aware adjustments providing an effective solution.

title: How to Allocate Your Tokens? Scaling Laws with Training Steps and Batch Size
summary: We propose a scaling law that takes into account model size and training data while explicitly splitting the latter into training steps and batch size (called three-term law). Fitting the proposed law on a large set of training runs, we find that it correctly recovers the scaling of the optimal batch size. Moreover, because it makes use of training runs with suboptimal batch size, our proposed law can be robustly fit with a significantly smaller amount of training runs. We further show that the three-term law can be used to derive scaling laws for suboptimal batch sizes, and that it matches previous empirical findings related to the critical batch size.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a three-term scaling law that decomposes training data into training steps and batch size, enabling robust fitting with fewer runs and accurately recovering optimal batch size scaling, including predictions for suboptimal batch sizes.
AI.motivation: Existing scaling laws typically treat training data as a single variable, obscuring the distinct roles of training steps and batch size. There is a need for a more granular law that can be fit using fewer, suboptimal-batch-size runs while still recovering optimal batch size behavior.
AI.method: The authors propose a three-term scaling law parameterized by model size, training steps, and batch size. They fit this law on a large set of training runs (including suboptimal batch sizes) and validate that it recovers the scaling of optimal batch size. Robustness is demonstrated by fitting with significantly fewer runs.
AI.result: The three-term law correctly recovers the scaling of the optimal batch size. It can be fit robustly using significantly fewer training runs. The law also derives scaling behavior for suboptimal batch sizes and matches prior empirical findings on the critical batch size.
AI.conclusion: The three-term scaling law provides a more data-efficient and theoretically sound framework for understanding the interplay between model size, training steps, and batch size, unifying optimal and suboptimal batch size regimes under a single formulation.

title: Profit-Based Counterfactual Explanations for Product Improvement: A Case Study of Manga Sales in Japan
summary: Counterfactual explanation (CE) is widely used to enhance the interpretability of machine learning models and support data-driven decision-making based on model predictions. However, existing CE methods typically require two exogenously specified inputs: a desired output value (target) and a distance function that quantifies changes in explanatory variables. In regression settings, neither the validity of target specification nor the practical interpretation of the distance metric has been sufficiently addressed. Furthermore, most existing CE methods focus on altering predictions rather than optimizing a decision objective, even though real-world decision-making often requires explicit objective maximization. To address these limitations, we formulate CE as a profit maximization problem in management and marketing contexts and propose a framework termed profit-based counterfactual explanation (PBCE). PBCE eliminates the need for exogenous target specification by directly maximizing profit as the primary optimization objective. Concurrently, the distance term is reinterpreted as the cost of modifying product attributes, providing a clear and economically grounded interpretation.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Profit-Based Counterfactual Explanation (PBCE), a framework that reformulates counterfactual explanations in regression settings as a profit maximization problem. It removes the need for exogenously specified target outputs and reinterprets distance functions as modification costs, grounding CE in an economically meaningful decision-making context.
AI.motivation: Existing counterfactual explanation methods suffer from two key limitations in regression contexts: (1) they require an exogenously specified desired output (target), whose validity is rarely justified, and (2) the distance function lacks practical, interpretable meaning. Moreover, most CE methods focus on altering predictions rather than optimizing a decision objective, whereas real-world decision-making demands explicit objective maximization (e.g., profit).
AI.method: The authors formulate counterfactual explanation as a profit maximization problem tailored to management and marketing domains. The proposed PBCE framework directly maximizes profit as the primary optimization objective, thereby eliminating the need for exogenous target specification. The distance term is reinterpreted as the cost of modifying product attributes, providing an economically grounded interpretation rather than an abstract distance metric.
AI.result: The abstract does not report specific quantitative results. It presents the PBCE framework conceptually, highlighting that it addresses the identified limitations by integrating profit maximization and cost-based distance interpretation into the CE process.
AI.conclusion: PBCE offers a more practically relevant approach to counterfactual explanations in regression settings by aligning the explanation objective with real-world decision-making goals — namely, profit maximization — and by endowing the distance metric with a clear economic interpretation as attribute modification costs.

title: Unveiling the Non-Monotonic Effect of Privacy on Generalization under Byzantine Robustness
summary: Recent work has established a fundamental trilemma between Byzantine robustness, local differential privacy (LDP), and optimization error in distributed learning. We show that this trilemma does not universally extend to generalization error, but instead depends critically on the privacy regime. Specifically, in the high-noise regime (strong privacy), we prove that increasing privacy reduces the generalization error, i.e., there is no tension between robustness and privacy. In the low-noise regime (weaker privacy), however, the tension between robustness and privacy reappears and increasing privacy indeed degrades generalization. Our theory explains this surprising non-monotonic behavior of the generalization error via matching lower and upper bounds on the algorithmic stability of Byzantine-robust distributed learning under LDP constraints. We corroborate and further analyze these theoretical findings with empirical evaluations.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that the known trilemma between Byzantine robustness, local differential privacy (LDP), and optimization error does not uniformly apply to generalization error. Instead, the relationship depends on the privacy regime: in high-noise (strong privacy) settings, more privacy improves generalization; in low-noise (weak privacy) settings, more privacy harms it. The authors provide matching upper and lower bounds on algorithmic stability to explain this non-monotonic behavior.
AI.motivation: Prior work established a fundamental trilemma between Byzantine robustness, LDP, and optimization error in distributed learning. However, it was unclear whether this trilemma extends to generalization error. The authors aim to understand how privacy and robustness interact with respect to generalization, rather than optimization.
AI.method: The authors theoretically analyze algorithmic stability of Byzantine-robust distributed learning under LDP constraints, deriving matching lower and upper bounds on generalization error. They analyze two distinct privacy regimes — high-noise (strong privacy, large ε) and low-noise (weak privacy, small ε) — to characterize the non-monotonic relationship.
AI.result: In the high-noise (strong privacy) regime, increasing privacy reduces generalization error (no tension). In the low-noise (weak privacy) regime, increasing privacy degrades generalization (tension reappears). Matching upper and lower bounds on algorithmic stability confirm this non-monotonic behavior, which is further validated empirically.
AI.conclusion: The trilemma between Byzantine robustness, LDP, and error does not universally extend to generalization error. The effect of privacy on generalization is regime-dependent and non-monotonic, explained fundamentally by the behavior of algorithmic stability under different privacy noise levels.

title: Understanding Build Reproducibility in the F-Droid Ecosystem
comment: 2026 ACM Conference on Reproducibility and Replicability, Jul 2026, Delft, Netherlands
summary: The security of open source applications benefits considerably from the possibility of rebuilding their source and verifying the output. F-Droid, a prominent distribution for open source Android applications, systematically rebuilds them from source and tests their bitwise reproducibility at app publishing time. However, F-Droid offers no guarantee that app reproducibility will continue to hold in the future. As software ecosystems evolve, reproducibility may degrade, with potential negative consequences for software preservation and security. We present the first empirical study of build reproducibility in the F-Droid app ecosystem. Analyzing historical reproducibility logs, we find that the overall bitwise reproducibility rate has been steadily increasing over time (as new versions of apps are published). We then evaluate how reproducibility holds in time for fixed app versions, by attempting to rebuild 18 904 app versions that F-Droid had previously confirmed bitwise reproducible, published between September 2018 and February 2026, achieving an 83% rebuild success rate, and identify missing dependencies as the dominant cause of failure, accounting for 76% of non-rebuildable cases. Among successfully rebuilt apps, 94% are also bitwise reproducible-i.e., they still yield bitwise identical artifacts upon rebuild. Together, these results show that while bitwise reproducibility largely holds for apps that can be rebuilt, rebuildability itself is highly sensitive to temporal decay.

AI.tldr: An empirical study of build reproducibility in the F-Droid Android app ecosystem, examining both cross-sectional trends and temporal decay. The study finds that while reproducibility rates are improving for new app versions, rebuildability of fixed historical versions degrades significantly over time—primarily due to missing dependencies—though apps that can be rebuilt remain 94% bitwise reproducible.
AI.motivation: F-Droid rebuilds apps from source at publishing time to verify bitwise reproducibility, but provides no guarantees that reproducibility persists over time. As software ecosystems evolve, this reproducibility may degrade, threatening software preservation and security. No prior empirical study has quantified this temporal dimension of build reproducibility.
AI.method: The authors analyzed historical reproducibility logs from the F-Droid ecosystem. They then conducted a large-scale rebuild experiment: attempting to rebuild 18,904 app versions (spanning September 2018 to February 2026) that F-Droid had previously confirmed as bitwise reproducible, measuring both rebuild success rates and, for successful rebuilds, whether bitwise reproducibility still held.
AI.result: (1) Overall reproducibility rates have steadily increased over time for newly published app versions. (2) Among the 18,904 historical versions, only 83% could be successfully rebuilt. (3) Missing dependencies dominated failures, accounting for 76% of non-rebuildable cases. (4) Among successfully rebuilt apps, 94% remained bitwise reproducible—i.e., yielded bit-identical artifacts.
AI.conclusion: Bitwise reproducibility largely holds for apps that can still be rebuilt, but rebuildability itself is highly sensitive to temporal decay, primarily driven by dependency unavailability. This represents a significant threat to long-term software preservation and security in the F-Droid ecosystem.

title: DiPS: Dialogue Policy Selection for High-Stakes Persuasion Agents
comment: Proceedings of the 27th Annual Meeting of the Special Interest Group on Discourse and Dialogue (SIGDIAL 2026)
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) often struggle with persuasion in high-stakes scenarios. People's individual personalities and concerns require tailored strategies rather than a one-size-fits-all approach. To address this challenge, we focus on a fire-rescue scenario in which an operator must persuade a resident to evacuate as a high-stakes persuasion domain and propose Dialogue Policy Selection (DiPS), a Q-learning framework to dynamically select persuasion strategies adapted to the evolving conversational context. Specifically, we train a critic, trained to maximize the chance of evacuation success, to select a persuasion policy at each turn based on the resident's recent utterances.We then evaluate DiPS against multiple baselines in both simulated and real human interactions. We find that DiPS achieves higher evacuation success than a zero-shot LLM and generic RAG-augmented approach.

AI.tldr: DiPS is a Q-learning framework that dynamically selects tailored persuasion strategies in high-stakes dialogues (fire-rescue evacuation scenario), outperforming zero-shot LLMs and RAG-augmented baselines in both simulated and real human interactions.
AI.motivation: LLMs struggle with persuasion in high-stakes scenarios because individuals have distinct personalities and concerns, making one-size-fits-all strategies ineffective. A domain-specific, adaptive approach is needed.
AI.method: DiPS uses a Q-learning framework where a critic (trained to maximize evacuation success probability) selects a persuasion policy at each conversational turn based on the resident's recent utterances. The system operates in a fire-rescue operator-to-resident persuasion scenario.
AI.result: DiPS achieved higher evacuation success rates compared to both a zero-shot LLM baseline and a generic RAG-augmented approach, validated across simulated interactions and real human participant studies.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic, context-aware persuasion policy selection via reinforcement learning significantly improves persuasion outcomes in high-stakes scenarios compared to static or retrieval-based LLM approaches.

title: Don't Let Gains FADE: Breaking Down Policy Gradient Weights in RL
summary: Reinforcement learning post-training dramatically improves LLM reasoning, but suffers from training instability and diversity collapse. Advantage functions offer an appealing fix: they reshape the training objective, reweight which rollouts drive learning, and are trivial to implement. Yet a proliferation of methods makes it unclear which advantage to use and when. We cut through the confusion with a unifying framework that decomposes any advantage into its positive and negative gradient mass along two orthogonal axes. On the sign axis, imbalanced updates collapse either entropy or weight geometry. On the difficulty axis, hard-problem focus sharpens signal but costs sample size. Both trade-offs shift during training: exploration favors balance and hard focus; exploitation favors suppression and medium focus. This motivates FADE (Focal Advantage with Dynamic Entropy), a self-adapting advantage that reads training dynamics to schedule the gradient weight automatically. FADE reaches peak pass@1 20k steps earlier than the best static baseline at the 7B scale and 2k steps earlier at the 32B , while achieving the best accuracy-diversity trade-off across all pass@k on LiveCodeBench and AIME.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a unifying framework for advantage functions in RL post-training of LLMs, decomposing them along sign and difficulty axes. It introduces FADE, a self-adapting advantage that dynamically schedules gradient weights based on training dynamics, achieving faster convergence and better accuracy-diversity trade-offs on reasoning benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Reinforcement learning post-training improves LLM reasoning but suffers from training instability and diversity collapse. While advantage functions can address these issues by reshaping training objectives, the proliferation of methods creates confusion about which advantage to use and when, with no systematic understanding of their trade-offs.
AI.method: The authors develop a unifying framework that decomposes any advantage function along two orthogonal axes: (1) the sign axis, where imbalanced positive/negative gradient updates collapse either entropy or weight geometry, and (2) the difficulty axis, where focusing on hard problems sharpens signal at the cost of reduced effective sample size. They then propose FADE (Focal Advantage with Dynamic Entropy), which automatically reads training dynamics to schedule gradient weights, shifting from balanced exploration with hard focus early in training to suppression with medium focus during later exploitation.
AI.result: FADE reaches peak pass@1 20,000 steps earlier than the best static baseline at the 7B scale and 2,000 steps earlier at 32B, while achieving the best accuracy-diversity trade-off across all pass@k on LiveCodeBench and AIME benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The two-axis decomposition reveals that optimal advantage weighting shifts dynamically during training, and FADE successfully automates this scheduling, demonstrating that adaptive advantage functions can simultaneously improve training efficiency, accuracy, and diversity in RL-based LLM reasoning post-training.

title: Scaling with Confidence: Calibrating Confidence of LLMs for Adaptive Test Time Scaling
summary: Training large language models (LLMs) with reinforcement learning (RL) has significantly advanced their performance on reasoning and question-answering tasks. However, prevailing RL reward designs typically prioritize response correctness, neglecting to incentivize models to express their confidence accurately. This leads to a critical problem: performance gains are often accompanied by poor calibration between confidence and accuracy, misleading models to overconfidently hallucinate when uncertain. To address this limitation, we propose $\textbf{C}$orrectness and $\textbf{C}$onfidence $\textbf{C}$alibration $\textbf{R}$einforcement $\textbf{L}$earning ($\textbf{C3RL}$), a novel RL algorithm integrating correctness, calibration and dataset-informed reference accuracy rewards together. Comprehensive evaluation across 8 text and multimodal datasets demonstrates that C3RL enhances calibration without sacrificing accuracy, outperforming the current state-of-the-art method in both performance and calibration metrics. Utilizing the well-calibrated verbalized confidence from C3RL, we further introduce $\textbf{C}$onfidence-based $\textbf{A}$daptive Test Time $\textbf{S}$caling ($\textbf{CAS}$), an adjustable inference-time strategy that allocates computational resources based on response confidence. Experiments show that CAS surpasses majority voting on both in-domain and out-of-domain datasets while reducing the inference budget by up to 12.33 times. We believe the synergy of C3RL and CAS paves the way for deploying more reliable and resource-efficient LLMs. The code, data and models will be released.

AI.tldr: C3RL is a reinforcement learning method that jointly optimizes LLMs for answer correctness and confidence calibration. Combined with CAS, a confidence-based adaptive inference strategy, it achieves better calibration, higher accuracy, and up to 12.33× inference budget reduction.
AI.motivation: Current RL for LLMs focuses on response correctness but neglects confidence calibration, causing models to be overconfident when wrong (hallucinating with high confidence). This undermines trustworthiness and efficient resource allocation.
AI.method: C3RL integrates three reward signals: correctness reward, calibration reward (penalizing confidence-accuracy mismatch), and a dataset-informed reference accuracy reward. From the well-calibrated verbalized confidence, CAS adaptively allocates compute at inference — expending more resources on low-confidence responses and terminating early on high-confidence ones.
AI.result: C3RL improves calibration without sacrificing accuracy across 8 text and multimodal datasets, outperforming the SOTA method. CAS surpasses majority voting on both in-domain and OOD datasets while reducing inference budget by up to 12.33×.
AI.conclusion: The C3RL + CAS synergy enables more reliable and resource-efficient LLM deployment through joint optimization of correctness and calibration, with adaptive test-time compute allocation.

title: AI Writes Faster Than Humans Can Review: A Longitudinal Study of an Enterprise 2x Mandate
summary: Enterprises increasingly mandate AI coding tools and report large productivity gains, yet longitudinal evidence on how such a mandate unfolds is scarce. In this paper, we present a quantitative case study of a documented enterprise "2x" mandate at a mid-sized, AI-forward company that has been committed to doubling merged pull requests per engineer since mid-2025. In a panel of 802 developers and 196,212 pull requests (January 2024-April 2026), per-capita throughput eventually doubled, reaching 2.09x the pre-mandate baseline in April 2026, among the largest gains reported from a field deployment of AI coding tools to our knowledge. A staggered difference-in-differences design links the within-developer share of this gain to AI adoption and to a further gain that grows with accumulated use, with the mandate acting as a catalyst rather than a direct driver. Because adoption and usage intensity were not randomly assigned, we read this evidence as strongly implicating an adoption-and-use channel rather than as exact causal attribution. The gain is broadly shared across seniority yet concentrated in newer code and not separable across model generations. Adoption also restructured code review around automation: per-reviewer load roughly doubled and automated review overtook human review, while merge and revert rates held steady.

AI.tldr: A longitudinal study of 802 developers across 196K+ pull requests finds that an enterprise "2x" AI coding mandate successfully doubled per-capita PR throughput (2.09x by April 2026). Gains are linked to AI adoption and accumulated usage intensity via staggered difference-in-differences, with the mandate acting as a catalyst. Code review shifted heavily toward automation, with reviewer load doubling while merge and revert rates remained stable.
AI.motivation: Despite enterprises increasingly mandating AI coding tools and claiming large productivity gains, longitudinal evidence on how such mandates actually unfold in practice is scarce. The authors aim to fill this gap by quantitatively studying a real-world "2x" mandate targeting doubled merged pull requests per engineer.
AI.method: A panel dataset of 802 developers and 196,212 pull requests from January 2024 to April 2026 at a mid-sized, AI-forward company. The authors employ a staggered difference-in-differences design to estimate the within-developer effect of AI adoption on throughput, distinguishing the mandate's catalytic role from a direct driver. They also track usage intensity accumulation, seniority-based heterogeneity, code age, model generations, and code review dynamics (automated vs. human review, reviewer load, merge/revert rates).
AI.result: Per-capita PR throughput reached 2.09x the pre-mandate baseline. Gains are associated with AI adoption and grow with accumulated use rather than being directly driven by the mandate itself. Productivity improvements are broadly shared across seniority levels but concentrated in newer code and not separable by model generation. Code review was restructured: per-reviewer load roughly doubled, automated review overtook human review, while merge and revert rates held steady.
AI.conclusion: The evidence strongly implicates an adoption-and-use channel for productivity gains rather than exact causal attribution from the mandate alone. The mandate served as a catalyst for AI tool adoption, which in turn drove sustained throughput increases without compromising code quality metrics. The findings represent some of the largest documented gains from a field deployment of AI coding tools.

title: Beyond Skepticism: Evaluating LLMs Pedagogical Intent Reasoning with the Adaptive Pedagogical Vigilance Framework
summary: The capacity of Large Language Models (LLMs) to reason about pedagogical intent within instructional communication remains underexplored, particularly in educational domains such as translation pedagogy. To address this, we propose the \textbf{Adaptive Pedagogical Vigilance (APV)} framework, a novel computational formalism that reframes communicative vigilance as an adaptive mechanism for optimizing learning through intent inference. APV formalizes the problem via a Bayesian Pedagogical Intent Inference Engine (PIIE), which models how instructors select content to maximize pedagogical utility and how vigilant learners should inversely reason about latent instructional configurations -- encompassing genre, stance, and incentives. We evaluate APV through a three-tier hierarchy: distinguishing instructional genre, reasoning about structured pedagogical setups, and generalizing to authentic educational discourse. Experiments on leading LLMs (e.g., GPT-4o, Claude 3.5) show that APV substantially improves model vigilance. It achieves the strongest discrimination between pedagogical and exposure-based content, correlates highly with human judgments ($r=0.958$), and maintains robust performance on naturalistic data where baseline methods degrade. This work establishes a unified framework for assessing and enhancing LLMs' understanding of pedagogical motives, advancing the development of more reliable AI-assisted learning systems.

AI.tldr: Proposes the Adaptive Pedagogical Vigilance (APV) framework, using a Bayesian Pedagogical Intent Inference Engine to enable LLMs to infer instructional intent (genre, stance, incentives) from pedagogical communication. Evaluated on GPT-4o and Claude 3.5, APV achieves near-human correlation (r=0.958) in distinguishing pedagogical from exposure-based content and generalizes robustly to naturalistic data.
AI.motivation: LLMs currently lack the ability to reason about pedagogical intent — the underlying instructional goals, stance, and incentives behind educational communication. This gap is especially critical in domains like translation pedagogy, where understanding why an instructor chose specific content is essential for effective learning. Existing approaches fail to model how vigilant learners should inversely reason about latent instructional configurations.
AI.method: The APV framework formulates pedagogical vigilance as a Bayesian inference problem. The Pedagogical Intent Inference Engine (PIIE) models the instructor's content selection as maximizing pedagogical utility and the learner's task as inversely inferring latent variables: instructional genre, stance, and incentives. Evaluation uses a three-tier hierarchy: (1) distinguishing instructional vs. exposure-based genres, (2) reasoning about structured pedagogical setups, and (3) generalizing to authentic educational discourse.
AI.result: APV achieves strong discrimination between pedagogical and exposure-based content, correlates highly with human judgments (r=0.958), and maintains robust performance on naturalistic data where baseline methods degrade. Experiments on GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 demonstrate substantial improvements in model vigilance across all tiers.
AI.conclusion: The APV framework provides a unified, principled approach for assessing and enhancing LLMs' understanding of pedagogical motives, paving the way for more reliable AI-assisted learning systems capable of inferring instructional intent.

title: Spatial Support Matters: Geometry-Aware Graph Fusion for Rainfall Field Reconstruction
summary: Fine-scale rainfall reconstruction is critical for urban flood modeling, but real rainfall sensing systems observe the field through incompatible spatial supports: gauges measure points, microwave links measure paths, and radar/satellite products measure gridded areas. These differences in measurement support impose geometrically distinct constraints on the rainfall field, yet existing heterogeneous graph approaches reconcile such sources in feature space, giving each its own embedding while discarding the geometry of its support. We propose a geometry-aware multi-support heterogeneous graph neural network that represents each observation according to its support type (0D point, 1D line, or 2D grid) as a distinct node layer, and fuses them through cross-support message passing into a point-support prediction layer from which the field is reconstructed. An inductive masked-node formulation decouples prediction resolution from sensing resolution, allowing the same trained model to reconstruct the field at user-defined target locations or display grids. On Singapore data, the proposed method reduces RMSE by 23.2\% over the classical interpolation baseline, inverse-distance weighting, and consistently outperforms other neural architectures such as convolutional fusion and support-agnostic heterogeneous graph baselines. A generalization study using data from Sydney, Australia lets us characterize when multi-support fusion helps: the available skill appears to depend on gauge spacing relative to the spatial correlation length of the field, so fusion delivers the largest gains where the field is under-sampled relative to its correlation length and little when it is already resolved. Code and models will be open-sourced upon paper acceptance.

AI.tldr: A geometry-aware heterogeneous graph neural network fuses rainfall observations from incompatible spatial supports (points, lines, grids) via cross-support message passing, achieving 23.2% RMSE reduction over classical interpolation and outperforming other neural baselines on Singapore data.
AI.motivation: Rainfall sensing systems operate on incompatible spatial supports — gauges (0D points), microwave links (1D paths), and radar/satellite (2D grids). Existing heterogeneous graph methods reconcile these only in feature space, discarding the geometric constraints of each measurement's support, which limits reconstruction fidelity for urban flood modeling.
AI.method: A geometry-aware multi-support heterogeneous graph neural network with distinct node layers per support type (0D, 1D, 2D), cross-support message passing for fusion, and a point-support prediction layer. An inductive masked-node formulation decouples prediction resolution from sensing resolution, enabling reconstruction at arbitrary user-defined locations.
AI.result: On Singapore data, the method reduces RMSE by 23.2% over inverse-distance weighting (IDW) and consistently outperforms convolutional fusion and support-agnostic heterogeneous graph baselines. A Sydney generalization study reveals fusion gains are largest when gauge spacing exceeds the field's spatial correlation length (under-sampled regime) and negligible when the field is already well-resolved.
AI.conclusion: Geometry-aware multi-support fusion provides substantial rainfall reconstruction gains, but its benefit is conditional: it helps most when the sensing network under-samples the field relative to its spatial correlation scale. The inductive formulation enables flexible deployment at arbitrary target resolutions.

title: Beyond Textual Repository Exploration: Dual-Modal Structural Reasoning for Agentic Issue Resolution
summary: Recent advances in agentic program repair have significantly improved issue resolution by enabling iterative repository exploration. However, existing approaches predominantly rely on sequential, text-based code navigation, which fundamentally limits their ability to reason over large-scale long-horizon repositories with complex and long-range dependencies. As issue-resolution agents traverse repositories through fragmented textual observations, structural information such as module organization, call relationships, and dependency chains must be repeatedly reconstructed across interaction steps, often leading to exploration drift and incomplete localization. We present DUALVIEW, a dual-modal structural scaffolding framework that brings visual reasoning into repository exploration for issue-resolution agents. DUALVIEW represents repository structure through four complementary graph views: Module Coupling Graph (MCG), Function Call Graph (FCG), Class Hierarchy Graph (CHG), and Program Dependence Graph (PDG), and exposes them through a queryable interface with visual and textual responses. Rather than reconstructing repository structure from a sequence of textual observations, agents can directly reason over persistent visual representations of code dependencies, enabling more effective exploration and understanding of long-horizon codebases. We evaluate DUALVIEW on SWE-bench Pro and Verified. Results show that DUALVIEW consistently improves issue-resolution performance across different agent architectures and model families. Further ablation studies demonstrate that the gains arise not only from textual structural information but also from visual externalization of repository dependencies, which better supports long-horizon repository exploration.

AI.tldr: DUALVIEW introduces a dual-modal structural scaffolding framework that augments agentic program repair with visual repository representations—four complementary graph views (MCG, FCG, CHG, PDG)—enabling agents to directly reason over persistent visual dependency structures instead of reconstructing them from sequential text, yielding consistent improvements on SWE-bench Pro and Verified across multiple architectures.
AI.motivation: Existing agentic program repair systems rely on sequential, text-based code navigation, forcing agents to repeatedly reconstruct structural information (module organization, call relationships, dependency chains) from fragmented textual observations. This leads to exploration drift and incomplete localization, especially in large-scale, long-horizon repositories with complex long-range dependencies. The fundamental limitation is the absence of persistent, holistic structural representations.
AI.method: DUALVIEW constructs four repository graph views: Module Coupling Graph (MCG), Function Call Graph (FCG), Class Hierarchy Graph (CHG), and Program Dependence Graph (PDG). These are exposed via a queryable interface that returns both visual and textual responses. Agents query these persistent visual representations directly during exploration rather than inferring structure from sequential text observations, enabling more effective reasoning over long-horizon codebases.
AI.result: DUALVIEW consistently improves issue-resolution performance on SWE-bench Pro and Verified across different agent architectures and model families. Ablation studies confirm that gains stem from both the textual structural information and the visual externalization of repository dependencies, with the latter particularly benefiting long-horizon exploration.
AI.conclusion: Visual reasoning, operationalized through persistent graph-based structural representations, effectively addresses the exploration drift and incomplete localization problems inherent in text-only agentic program repair. DUALVIEW demonstrates that augmenting agents with dual-modal structural scaffolding is a broadly applicable strategy for improving issue resolution in complex repositories.

title: ProWAFT: A ROMA-LPD Instance for Workload-Aware and Dynamic Fault Tolerance in FPGA-Based CNN Accelerators
summary: SRAM-based FPGAs provide an attractive platform for energy- and latency-constrained CNN inference at the network edge, yet transient faults can lead to silent errors that compromise reliability. Always-on redundancy (e.g., full TMR) improves correctness but incurs substantial performance and energy overhead, while reactive recovery may introduce unacceptable latency on the critical path. We propose \textbf{ProWAFT}, a proactive workload-aware fault-tolerance framework for FPGA-based CNN accelerators that uses partial reconfiguration to selectively apply TMR across reconfigurable partitions. ProWAFT quantifies workload criticality, models fault propagation and reconfiguration overhead, and selects configurations that minimize a composite objective over latency, energy, and reliability risk. Implemented on a Xilinx Zynq UltraScale+ ZCU104 platform with six reconfigurable regions and evaluated on a 500-task trace derived from ResNet-18, MobileNetV2, and EfficientNet-Lite under time-varying SEU injection, ProWAFT achieves lower composite cost than static TMR and reactive reconfiguration while maintaining high task success rate and near-baseline throughput with low online decision overhead.

AI.tldr: ProWAFT is a proactive, workload-aware fault-tolerance framework for FPGA-based CNN accelerators that uses partial reconfiguration to selectively apply TMR across reconfigurable partitions, minimizing a composite cost of latency, energy, and reliability risk under transient faults.
AI.motivation: SRAM-based FPGAs are attractive for edge CNN inference but suffer from transient faults causing silent errors. Static full TMR incurs high performance/energy overhead, while reactive recovery adds unacceptable latency. A proactive, selective approach is needed to balance reliability, latency, and energy.
AI.method: ProWAFT quantifies workload criticality, models fault propagation and reconfiguration overhead, and formulates an optimization problem over latency, energy, and reliability risk. It uses partial reconfiguration to selectively apply TMR across reconfigurable FPGA partitions. Evaluated on a Xilinx Zynq UltraScale+ ZCU104 with six reconfigurable regions using 500-task traces from ResNet-18, MobileNetV2, and EfficientNet-Lite under time-varying SEU injection.
AI.result: ProWAFT achieves lower composite cost than both static TMR and reactive reconfiguration, maintains high task success rate and near-baseline throughput, with low online decision overhead.
AI.conclusion: Proactive, selective TMR via partial reconfiguration effectively balances reliability, performance, and energy for FPGA-based CNN inference at the edge, outperforming both always-on redundancy and reactive approaches.

title: Towards Learning Representations of Policies in Two-Player Zero-Sum Imperfect-Information Games
summary:
We investigate the problem of learning useful policy representations (embeddings) in two-player zero-sum imperfect-information games. We make three contributions: First, we introduce methods of creating datasets of policies for a given game. Second, we propose methods to learn policy representations. Third, we introduce downstream tasks to evaluate the effectiveness of such representations.
  We evaluate each dataset method, embedding method, and downstream task on Kuhn and Leduc Poker. Although our methods are very basic, we demonstrate that useful behavioral representations are present in the learned embeddings. To our knowledge, this work is among the first to systematically compare self-supervised learning techniques for learning policy representations in games. Our code is available at https://github.com/VitamintK/ssl-project for others to extend.

AI.tldr: Investigates learning policy embeddings for two-player zero-sum imperfect-information games. Proposes dataset creation methods, embedding learning methods, and downstream evaluation tasks. Evaluated on Kuhn and Leduc Poker, demonstrating that even basic self-supervised methods yield useful behavioral representations.
AI.motivation: The need for compact, meaningful representations (embeddings) of policies in imperfect-information games, which can facilitate transfer learning, policy analysis, opponent modeling, and other downstream applications. Prior work lacked systematic comparison of self-supervised learning techniques for this purpose.
AI.method: Threefold framework: (1) methods for generating policy datasets from a given game; (2) self-supervised learning techniques for encoding policies into embedding vectors; (3) downstream tasks to quantitatively evaluate the quality and utility of the learned representations. Experiments conducted on Kuhn Poker and Leduc Poker.
AI.result: Even basic self-supervised embedding methods produce representations that capture meaningful behavioral properties of policies, as validated by the proposed downstream evaluation tasks.
AI.conclusion: This work provides a foundational framework for learning and evaluating policy representations in imperfect-information games, and is among the first to systematically benchmark self-supervised learning for this domain. Code is open-sourced to encourage further research.

title: Autonomous discovery of traffic laws with AI traffic scientists
summary: Universal traffic laws describe recurrent patterns in congestion, mobility and driving behavior across cities, providing a scientific basis for transportation planning, management and control. Their discovery, however, remains expert-driven, requiring candidate regularities to be identified from heterogeneous observational evidence or validated through intervention experiments. Although autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) systems have advanced scientific discovery in controlled laboratory settings, extending them to complex transportation domains remains a challenge. Here we present TrafficSci, an agentic AI system that formulates traffic-law discovery as an iterative, auditable workflow integrating evidence scoping, critic-judge hypothesis induction, and observational-interventional validation. Across four case studies spanning population, network, control and trajectory scales, TrafficSci autonomously rediscovers three established traffic laws and identifies an unreported intrinsic temporal memory scale in urban driving behavior, statistically consistent across eight cities and two trajectory datasets. TrafficSci provides a route for extending AI-driven scientific discovery from controlled domains to complex urban systems.

AI.tldr: TrafficSci is an agentic AI system that autonomously discovers traffic laws by integrating evidence scoping, hypothesis induction, and observational-interventional validation. It rediscovers three established laws and identifies a new intrinsic temporal memory scale in urban driving behavior across eight cities.
AI.motivation: Traffic law discovery has traditionally been expert-driven and manual. While AI has advanced scientific discovery in controlled lab settings, extending autonomous discovery to complex urban transportation systems remains an open challenge.
AI.method: TrafficSci formulates traffic-law discovery as an iterative, auditable workflow with three stages: (1) evidence scoping across heterogeneous data sources, (2) critic-judge hypothesis induction to propose candidate regularities, and (3) observational-interventional validation to confirm or refute hypotheses.
AI.result: Across four case studies at population, network, control, and trajectory scales, TrafficSci autonomously rediscovered three established traffic laws and identified a previously unreported intrinsic temporal memory scale in urban driving behavior, statistically consistent across eight cities and two trajectory datasets.
AI.conclusion: TrafficSci demonstrates a viable pathway for extending AI-driven scientific discovery from controlled laboratory domains to complex urban systems, enabling autonomous, auditable, and reproducible traffic law discovery.

title: ElephantAgent: Contextual State Continuity in Agentic Systems
summary: Agentic systems enhance their capabilities by invoking external tools and maintaining persistent memory. However, these external dependencies introduce novel attack surfaces. Recent tool and memory poisoning attacks show that maliciously crafted tool descriptors and poisoned memory can covertly bias agent behavior. These threats reflect a deeper issue: the lack of verifiable continuity in the agent's contextual state for planning and execution. We present ElephantAgent, a protocol that enforces Contextual State Continuity to defend against contextual state poisoning. Inspired by prior state-continuity mechanisms (e.g., Nimble), ElephantAgent extends this protection to the evolving contextual state of agentic systems. We define the contextual state as the bounded, security-critical subset of the agent's entire context (e.g., tool state and memory). Before processing each query, ElephantAgent recomputes the digest of the local contextual state and verifies it against the latest authorized digest. Using replicated trusted hardware, ElephantAgent maintains a linearizable ledger of authorized contextual state transitions and detects out-of-band state tampering. To handle in-band semantic abuse, ElephantAgent additionally provides Historical Traceability, enabling conditional post-hoc audit and recovery to a known-good prior state.

AI.tldr: ElephantAgent is a protocol that defends against contextual state poisoning in agentic systems by enforcing Contextual State Continuity — recomputing and verifying digests of security-critical contextual state against a linearizable ledger maintained by replicated trusted hardware, while also providing Historical Traceability for post-hoc audit and recovery.
AI.motivation: Agentic systems increasingly rely on external tools and persistent memory, which introduce new attack surfaces. Maliciously crafted tool descriptors and poisoned memory can covertly bias agent behavior. The fundamental problem is the lack of verifiable continuity in the agent's contextual state across planning and execution, leaving no reliable mechanism to detect tampering.
AI.method: ElephantAgent defines the "contextual state" as a bounded, security-critical subset of the agent's context (tool state and memory). Before each query, it recomputes a digest of the local contextual state and verifies it against the latest authorized digest stored in a linearizable ledger. This ledger is maintained by replicated trusted hardware, which records authorized contextual state transitions and detects any out-of-band state tampering. For in-band semantic abuse, ElephantAgent provides Historical Traceability, enabling conditional post-hoc audit and rollback to a known-good prior state.
AI.result: The paper demonstrates that ElephantAgent can detect out-of-band contextual state tampering through its digest verification protocol and can handle in-band semantic abuse via historical traceability and state recovery. The trusted-hardware-backed linearizable ledger ensures consistent, verifiable state transitions.
AI.conclusion: Contextual state poisoning is a fundamental threat to agentic systems. ElephantAgent addresses this by extending state-continuity principles to the evolving context, combining runtime digest verification with a trusted-hardware-backed ledger for tamper detection, and providing historical traceability for audit and recovery.

title: Underspecification does not imply Incoherence: The Risks of Semantic Collapse in Coding Models
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have become increasingly effective at generating code when task descriptions are clear and precise. Yet, in practice, user-provided task descriptions are often ambiguous, incomplete, or contradictory, leaving critical aspects of the intended program behavior underspecified. In such cases, multiple behaviorally distinct interpretations may satisfy the description equally well, yet semantically differ in ways that matter/affect the user intent. A natural expectation, often assumed by researchers, is that prompt underspecification manifests as incoherence: When asked multiple times, an LLM produces multiple semantically distinct implementations reflecting the ambiguity of the task description. In this paper, we challenge this assumption. We find that LLMs frequently collapse onto a single incorrect interpretation of the task description, consistently generating coherent but behaviorally misaligned code. We term this failure mode detrimental semantic collapse and find that it affects over 10% of tasks in MBPP, 3% in HumanEval, and 32% of LiveCodeBench, all benchmarks assumed to be well-specified. By deliberately injecting underspecification issues in the benchmark prompts, the rate rises to over 5 times, exposing a fundamental blind spot in disambiguation and correctness estimation techniques that rely on incoherence as a proxy for prompt underspecification.

AI.tldr: LLMs often produce coherent but behaviorally wrong code when prompts are underspecified, collapsing onto a single incorrect interpretation rather than showing semantic diversity. This "detrimental semantic collapse" affects over 10% of MBPP, 3% of HumanEval, and 32% of LiveCodeBench tasks, and rises 5x with deliberately injected underspecification.
AI.motivation: The prevailing assumption in the research community is that prompt underspecification leads to incoherence — i.e., multiple semantically distinct outputs when an LLM is queried repeatedly. The authors challenge this assumption, hypothesizing that LLMs instead frequently converge on a single, coherent, but incorrect interpretation of ambiguous prompts, creating a blind spot for disambiguation and correctness estimation techniques that rely on output diversity as a signal of underspecification.
AI.method: The authors evaluate LLMs on standard code generation benchmarks (MBPP, HumanEval, LiveCodeBench) and measure the rate at which models produce semantically coherent but behaviorally misaligned code under underspecified prompts. They also deliberately inject underspecification issues into benchmark prompts to amplify the effect and quantify how reliance on incoherence as a proxy for underspecification fails.
AI.result: Detrimental semantic collapse affects over 10% of tasks in MBPP, 3% in HumanEval, and 32% in LiveCodeBench — all benchmarks presumed to be well-specified. When underspecification is deliberately injected, the collapse rate increases over fivefold, exposing a fundamental blind spot in techniques that use incoherence to detect underspecification.
AI.conclusion: The assumption that prompt underspecification leads to output incoherence is unreliable. LLMs exhibit detrimental semantic collapse, consistently generating wrong but coherent code rather than diverse interpretations. This undermines disambiguation and correctness estimation methods that depend on output diversity, highlighting the need for new approaches to detect and handle underspecification in code generation tasks.

title: When Does Generating More Help? Disentangling Fixed-Source Synthesis from Source Expansion in Synthetic Data Scaling
summary: Synthetic data can be scaled along two routes: Source Expansion (SE), which enlarges the source by adding seed materials or generators, and Fixed-Source Synthesis (FSS), which holds the source fixed and scales the generation budget. Existing scaling studies typically expand the source as the data grows, conflating SE with FSS and leaving FSS underexplored. We isolate FSS by holding the seed-question pool and teacher model fixed, varying only the per-question response budget under Rejection Sampling (RS). We adapt the rectified scaling law to FSS, deriving it from how repeated sampling covers a fixed source. Empirically, the derived form, fit on low budgets, predicts performance at the held-out highest budget for every evaluated teacher--student pair. At matched total-sample budgets, SE and FSS are comparable at small budgets; at large budgets, adding seed questions outperforms spending the same budget on more responses. Within FSS, however, neither synthesizing additional questions from the existing seeds nor varying the synthesis protocol outperforms plain RS at matched budgets. FSS is thus a bounded scaling axis and a controlled setting for comparing synthesis protocols. We will release our code and data to facilitate further research.

AI.tldr: The paper isolates Fixed-Source Synthesis (FSS) from Source Expansion (SE) in synthetic data scaling, showing FSS follows a rectified scaling law and is a bounded axis where plain Rejection Sampling matches or outperforms more complex protocols at matched budgets.
AI.motivation: Existing scaling studies conflate two orthogonal routes for scaling synthetic data: enlarging the source (SE) versus increasing the generation budget from a fixed source (FSS). FSS remains underexplored because prior work typically expands the source as data grows. The authors aim to disentangle these two axes and rigorously characterize FSS.
AI.method: The authors isolate FSS by holding the seed-question pool and teacher model fixed, varying only the per-question response budget under Rejection Sampling (RS). They adapt the rectified scaling law to FSS, deriving it analytically from how repeated sampling covers a fixed source distribution. Empirically, they fit the law on low budgets and use it to predict performance at held-out high budgets across multiple teacher-student pairs. They also compare SE vs. FSS at matched total-sample budgets and test alternative FSS protocols (synthesizing new questions from seeds, varying the synthesis protocol).
AI.result: The derived rectified scaling law, fit on low budgets, accurately predicts performance at the held-out highest budget for all evaluated teacher-student pairs. At matched total-sample budgets, SE and FSS perform comparably at small budgets, but adding seed questions (SE) outperforms spending the same budget on more responses (FSS) at large budgets. Within FSS, neither synthesizing additional questions from existing seeds nor altering the synthesis protocol outperforms plain RS at matched budgets.
AI.conclusion: FSS is a bounded scaling axis and serves as a controlled setting for comparing synthesis protocols. The work clarifies the distinct roles of source expansion versus budget expansion in synthetic data scaling and provides both theoretical and empirical grounding for FSS behavior.

title: The risk of KV cache compression
summary: Transformer inference on long sequences is expensive because softmax attention repeatedly reads from a large KV cache. The prevalent approach to this bottleneck is KV cache compression, which replaces the full cache with a compact summary. Despite its practical importance, the design of such summaries is largely driven by empirical experimentation. On the theoretical side, existing results show that KV cache compression can be impossible in the worst case, but offer little systematic guidance for designing algorithms in regimes where accurate compression is possible. We bridge this gap by characterizing the minimax risk of KV cache compression in terms of the intrinsic compressibility of a cache, revealing when and how accurate compression is possible. These results yield novel design principles for KV cache compression under causal masking that map efficiently to prefill and autoregressive decoding while achieving minimax-optimal risk. We instantiate these principles in a practical algorithm and report promising performance on LongBench in targeted experiments. Overall, our results provide a principled avenue for practical KV cache compression with theoretical guarantees.

AI.tldr: The paper bridges the gap between theory and practice in KV cache compression by characterizing its minimax risk in terms of intrinsic compressibility, yielding principled design guidelines that achieve minimax-optimal risk under causal masking for both prefill and autoregressive decoding.
AI.motivation: Transformer inference on long sequences is bottlenecked by softmax attention repeatedly reading from large KV caches. While KV cache compression is widely used to address this, existing approaches are driven by empirical experimentation with little theoretical guidance. Prior theoretical results only show worst-case impossibility, offering no systematic principles for when and how accurate compression is achievable.
AI.method: The authors characterize the minimax risk of KV cache compression as a function of the cache's intrinsic compressibility. This theoretical framework reveals conditions under which accurate compression is possible and yields novel design principles tailored to causal masking. These principles are mapped efficiently onto both prefill and autoregressive decoding stages.
AI.result: The derived design principles are instantiated in a practical algorithm that achieves minimax-optimal risk. Targeted experiments on the LongBench benchmark demonstrate promising performance, validating the theoretical framework.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a principled, theoretically-guaranteed avenue for practical KV cache compression, moving beyond heuristic-driven approaches and establishing conditions under which accurate compression is provably attainable.

title: Diverse Evidence, Better Forecasts: Multi-Agent Deliberation Under Information Asymmetry
summary: Multi-agent systems are increasingly used for forecasting future events, as deliberation among multiple LLMs is believed to improve reasoning and calibration. Yet existing approaches overlook a critical design choice: what information each agent receives. When all agents are given identical evidence, deliberation collapses into herding rather than genuine belief revision, leaving multi-agent systems little better than a single agent. We identify this as a fundamental gap and propose designed information asymmetry to close it: by partitioning evidence into shared public and disjoint private subsets, each agent holds exclusive knowledge that can only reach others through deliberation. We theoretically show that this decomposition reduces inter-agent error correlation, and instantiate it in InfoDelphi, a framework combining relevance-aware evidence routing, rationale-based iterative deliberation, and confidence-weighted aggregation. On PolyGym, a benchmark of 375 binary forecasting questions derived from real-world prediction markets, InfoDelphi outperforms the strongest single-agent and multi-agent baselines by 12--18% in Brier score and 4--8 percentage points in accuracy. More detailed experiments confirm that removing information asymmetry eliminates most deliberation gains, establishing diversity of input as the key enabler of effective multi-agent reasoning.

AI.tldr: Multi-agent LLM systems fail to outperform single agents when all agents receive identical evidence, collapsing into herding. The authors propose designed information asymmetry—partitioning evidence into shared public and disjoint private subsets—to force genuine deliberation. Their InfoDelphi framework achieves 12–18% Brier score improvement and 4–8pp accuracy gains over baselines on 375 forecasting questions.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-agent forecasting systems overlook a critical design flaw: giving all agents identical evidence leads to correlated errors and herding behavior rather than meaningful belief revision. This makes multi-agent deliberation barely better than single-agent reasoning. The authors aim to close this gap by identifying input diversity as the key missing ingredient.
AI.method: The paper introduces **designed information asymmetry**: evidence is partitioned into a shared public subset (visible to all agents) and disjoint private subsets (each agent's exclusive knowledge). The authors theoretically show this decomposition reduces inter-agent error correlation. They instantiate this in **InfoDelphi**, a framework with three components: (1) relevance-aware evidence routing to assign private evidence, (2) rationale-based iterative deliberation where agents exchange arguments derived from their private knowledge, and (3) confidence-weighted aggregation of final forecasts. Evaluation uses **PolyGym**, a benchmark of 375 binary forecasting questions from real-world prediction markets.
AI.result: InfoDelphi outperforms the strongest single-agent and multi-agent baselines by **12–18% in Brier score** and **4–8 percentage points in accuracy** on PolyGym. Ablation studies confirm that removing information asymmetry eliminates most deliberation gains, establishing input diversity as the primary driver of effective multi-agent reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Designed information asymmetry is the key enabler of effective multi-agent deliberation for forecasting. Without it, agents converge to correlated beliefs and deliberation yields minimal improvement. The InfoDelphi framework demonstrates that carefully partitioning evidence into public and private subsets unlocks substantial gains over both single-agent and homogeneous multi-agent systems.

title: kNNGuard: Turning LLM Hidden Activations into a Training-Free Configurable Guardrail
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in domains requiring guardrails to detect unsafe, off-topic, or adversarial prompts. Existing guardrails predominately rely on fine-tuning to build classifiers, which often suffer from low generalization and high inference latency. We present kNNGuard, a training-free guardrail that utilizes the activation space of an off-the-shelf LLM. Given a small bank of 50 safe and unsafe prompts, kNNGuard extracts hidden activations and performs multi-layer kNN fusing activation-space and embedding-space scores for classification. Across six domains spanning topical and security prompts, kNNGuard achieves competitive or superior F1 compared to fine-tuned state-of-the-art guardrails while running 2.7x faster than the best comparable guardrail, and 10x faster than a fine-tuned safety classifier without gradient updates or fine-tuning. Domain adaptation requires only updating the labeled bank, which can be constructed in under 10 seconds and several orders of magnitude faster than established guardrails. We also analyze the impact of system prompts, layer selection, and integration into production LLM pipelines as a configurable, low-latency guardrail.

AI.tldr: kNNGuard is a training-free LLM guardrail that uses k-nearest neighbors over hidden activations from a small labeled prompt bank (50 examples) to classify unsafe prompts, achieving competitive F1 with fine-tuned methods while being 2.7–10× faster and enabling domain adaptation in under 10 seconds.
AI.motivation: Existing guardrails for detecting unsafe/adversarial LLM prompts rely on fine-tuning classifiers, which suffer from poor generalization across domains and high inference latency. There is a need for a lightweight, fast, and easily adaptable alternative that avoids costly gradient updates.
AI.method: kNNGuard is training-free: given a small bank of ~50 safe and unsafe prompts, it extracts multi-layer hidden activations from an off-the-shelf LLM and performs k-nearest neighbor classification by fusing both activation-space and embedding-space similarity scores. Domain adaptation is achieved simply by updating the labeled prompt bank, which takes under 10 seconds.
AI.result: Across six domains covering topical and security prompts, kNNGuard matches or exceeds F1 scores of fine-tuned state-of-the-art guardrails. It runs 2.7× faster than the best comparable guardrail and 10× faster than a fine-tuned safety classifier. Domain adaptation via bank updates is several orders of magnitude faster than retraining established guardrails.
AI.conclusion: kNNGuard demonstrates that activation-space kNN classification is a viable, efficient, and highly adaptable guardrail strategy for production LLM pipelines, eliminating the need for fine-tuning while maintaining strong detection performance and low latency.

title: Epic-Organized vs. Requirement-Aligned Gherkin: An Empirical Evaluation of LLM-Based Acceptance Criteria Generation
comment: Accepted for publication at the International Conference on Software Engineering of Emerging Technologies (SEET 2026)
summary: Automated authoring of Gherkin Behavior-Driven Development (BDD) acceptance criteria remains a manual bottleneck in requirements engineering. This study investigates whether epic-organized LLM-generated Gherkin produces higher quality and coverage than requirement-aligned generation. We compare our Timeless (an epic-organized LLM pipeline) approach against a naive large language model (LLM) baseline on four requirements documents (107 requirements) from the PURE dataset. Evaluation covers structural metrics, automated requirement coverage via TF-IDF and dense embeddings, and blind expert assessment by four researchers. In our evaluation, the JSON-constrained pipeline produced structurally valid scenarios across all generated outputs, while the zero-shot baseline achieved 99% structural validity. Semantic coverage was comparable to the baseline, with Timeless achieving 94.3% semantic Requirement Coverage Rate compared with 92.9% for the baseline. TF-IDF produced lower coverage scores for the epic-organized output, suggesting that lexical metrics may miss coverage when scenarios paraphrase requirements at a higher level of abstraction. Expert raters prefer the epic-organized strategy on Correctness (4.61 vs 4.14), Executability (4.61 vs 4.07), and Completeness (4.31 vs 3.50). Overall, the results suggest that epic-organized generation can improve perceived Gherkin quality while maintaining comparable semantic coverage, although broader replication is needed before generalizing this finding.

AI.tldr: This paper compares an epic-organized LLM pipeline (Timeless) against a naive LLM baseline for generating Gherkin BDD acceptance criteria. Results show epic-organized generation yields comparable semantic coverage but significantly higher expert-rated correctness, executability, and completeness, suggesting organizational strategy matters more than raw coverage metrics.
AI.motivation: Automated authoring of Gherkin BDD acceptance criteria remains a manual bottleneck in requirements engineering. Prior LLM-based approaches generate criteria aligned directly to individual requirements, but the authors hypothesize that organizing generation around higher-level epics may improve quality and coverage.
AI.method: The authors compare two approaches on 107 requirements from the PURE dataset: (1) Timeless, a JSON-constrained LLM pipeline that organizes Gherkin generation around epics, and (2) a zero-shot naive LLM baseline aligned to individual requirements. Evaluation includes structural validity checks, automated coverage metrics (TF-IDF and dense embeddings for semantic Requirement Coverage Rate), and blind expert assessment by four researchers rating Correctness, Executability, and Completeness.
AI.result: Timeless achieved 100% structural validity (baseline: 99%). Semantic coverage was comparable: 94.3% vs 92.9% RCR. TF-IDF scores were lower for epic-organized output, indicating lexical metrics may miss paraphrased coverage at higher abstraction levels. Expert raters preferred the epic-organized strategy across all dimensions: Correctness (4.61 vs 4.14), Executability (4.61 vs 4.07), and Completeness (4.31 vs 3.50).
AI.conclusion: Epic-organized LLM generation improves perceived Gherkin quality while maintaining comparable semantic coverage. However, the authors caution that broader replication is necessary before generalizing these findings beyond the studied dataset and evaluation context.

title: Rethinking Speech-LLM Integration for ASR: Effective Joint Speech-Text Training by Interleaving
summary: Speech-LLM integration has shown promising results by leveraging extensive textual pretraining, yet its specific benefits for automatic speech recognition (ASR) remain unclear.
