We observe that as supervised ASR training data increases, the contribution of LLM priors becomes less evident, and simple speech-text joint training under-utilizes textual knowledge. We therefore propose Joint Speech-Text Interleaved Pretraining (JSTIP), an ASR-oriented pretraining strategy that constructs word-level and segment-level interleaved speech-text sequences within aligned pairs for speech-LLM architectures that accept continuous inputs. Experiments on 38k hours of ASR data show consistent entity accuracy improvement compared to ASR-only and joint speech-text training baselines. JSTIP achieves on-par entity recognition performance using domain transcription text compared to synthetic speech-text pairs, simplifying domain adaptation. Benefiting from textual pretraining and domain text data, JSTIP is competitive with open-source ASR and Speech-LLM systems in medical entity recognition. The zero-shot speech question answering behaviors further suggest that interleaving reduces the speech-text modality gap and preserves the LLM generative prior, which is likely the reason for the entity improvements on the ASR task.

AI.tldr: JSTIP proposes word/segment-level interleaved speech-text pretraining for speech-LLM architectures, improving ASR entity recognition by better leveraging LLM textual priors. It matches synthetic data performance using domain text, competes with open-source systems on medical entities, and reduces the speech-text modality gap.
AI.motivation: The authors observe that as supervised ASR data scales up, the benefits of LLM priors diminish, and simple joint speech-text training underutilizes available textual knowledge. There is a need for a pretraining strategy that better exploits LLM textual priors specifically for ASR tasks.
AI.method: JSTIP (Joint Speech-Text Interleaved Pretraining) constructs word-level and segment-level interleaved speech-text sequences within aligned pairs. It is designed for speech-LLM architectures accepting continuous inputs. The approach interleaves speech and text at fine granularity during pretraining rather than treating them as separate modalities.
AI.result: On 38k hours of ASR data, JSTIP yields consistent entity accuracy improvements over ASR-only and joint speech-text baselines. It achieves on-par entity recognition using domain transcription text vs. synthetic speech-text pairs, simplifying domain adaptation. It is competitive with open-source ASR and Speech-LLM systems on medical entity recognition. Zero-shot speech QA shows reduced modality gap and preserved LLM generative prior.
AI.conclusion: Interleaved speech-text pretraining effectively narrows the modality gap and preserves the LLM's generative prior, driving entity recognition improvements in ASR. The approach also enables effective domain adaptation using only text data, bypassing the need for synthetic speech-text pairs.

title: Multi-Head Recurrent Memory Agents
summary: Recurrent memory agents extend LLMs to arbitrarily long contexts by iteratively consolidating input into a fixed-size memory window. Despite their scalability, these agents exhibit a well-documented reliability problem: end-to-end performance degrades systematically as context length grows. We diagnose this failure by decomposing performance into two factors--memory capture and memory retention--and quantitatively confirm that retention is the dominant bottleneck. Retention collapses because existing designs maintain memory as a monolithic text block, forcing every update to risk overwriting previously retained content. Motivated by this diagnosis, we propose Multi-Head Recurrent Memory (MHM), a general, training-free framework that partitions memory into independent heads governed by a stage-wise select-then-update strategy. At each step, exactly one head is selected for update while the remaining heads are structurally shielded from overwriting, shifting the burden of retention from model behavior to architectural design. As a lightweight instantiation, we introduce Least-Recently-Updated MHM (MHM-LRU), which guarantees uniform head utilization with zero additional token overhead. Extensive experiments on long-context benchmarks show that MHM-LRU substantially improves both retention and end-to-end accuracy across the 100K--1M token range, where baselines degrade sharply. On RULER-HQA at 896K tokens, MHM-LRU improves the memory retention rate from less than 30% to 73.96%. These gains generalize across model families, scales, and task types, positioning architectural optimization as a practical and cost-efficient path toward reliable long-context recurrent memory.

AI.tldr: Recurrent memory agents suffer from catastrophic memory retention collapse as context length grows. The authors diagnose this as an overwriting problem in monolithic memory designs and propose Multi-Head Recurrent Memory (MHM), a training-free partitioning framework where independent heads are updated selectively, preventing overwriting. MHM-LRU, a lightweight instantiation, improves retention from <30% to 73.96% at 896K tokens on RULER-HQA.
AI.motivation: Recurrent memory agents degrade systematically with longer contexts despite their scalability promise. The authors identify that the root cause is memory retention failure — existing designs store memory as a monolithic text block where every update risks overwriting previously retained content. This calls for an architectural solution that structurally prevents overwriting rather than relying on model behavior.
AI.method: The paper first decomposes end-to-end performance into memory capture (ability to encode new information) and memory retention (ability to preserve old information), quantitatively confirming retention as the bottleneck. To address this, they propose MHM, a training-free framework that partitions memory into multiple independent heads. A stage-wise select-then-update strategy ensures only one head is updated per step while others are structurally shielded from overwriting. The concrete instantiation, MHM-LRU, uses a Least-Recently-Updated policy to guarantee uniform head utilization with zero additional token overhead.
AI.result: MHM-LRU substantially improves both retention and end-to-end accuracy across the 100K–1M token range. On RULER-HQA at 896K tokens, memory retention rate improves from below 30% to 73.96%. Gains generalize across different model families, scales, and task types.
AI.conclusion: Architectural optimization via multi-head memory partitioning with selective updates is a practical and cost-efficient path toward reliable long-context recurrent memory, shifting the retention burden from model behavior to structural design.

title: Separating Expert Retention from Autonomous Source Inference in Raw-ECG-Replay-Free Continual ECG Deployment
summary:
In multi-source ECG deployment, models may need to incorporate new data sources when earlier raw ECGs cannot be retained or replayed. Freezing a pretrained backbone and assigning each source an isolated classifier prevents parameter interference, but deployment still requires selecting an expert when source metadata are unavailable. We study this distinction through \ours{}, an incremental expert bank built on frozen 1024-dimensional ECGFounder features. Each arriving domain adds a balanced-softmax linear expert, while a lightweight router is fitted only on retained training features and domain labels from sources observed so far. A validation-calibrated margin rule fuses the two most likely experts instead of committing to a single routed expert.
  On CPSC, PTB-XL, Georgia, and Chapman-Shaoxing, source-aware expert selection reaches $0.7915\pm0.0036$ Macro-F1 and a matched offline independent-head reference reaches $0.7885\pm0.0009$, supporting strong source-aware expert retention. Without source IDs, an MLP router reaches $0.7756\pm0.0027$ and top-2 margin fusion reaches $0.7782\pm0.0022$. The top-2 gain over hard MLP routing is small ($+0.0026$), with a 95\% confidence interval from paired bootstrap that includes zero. Across three domain orders, the top-2-to-oracle gap remains $0.0111$--$0.0133$, identifying autonomous source inference as the main remaining bottleneck. No raw ECGs are replayed, but frozen training features are retained for router updates; the method is therefore not memory-free.

AI.tldr: An incremental expert bank with frozen ECGFounder features, balanced-softmax linear experts, and a learned router for multi-source ECG classification without source metadata. Top-2 margin fusion of routed experts offers marginal gains, with autonomous source inference remaining the primary bottleneck.
AI.motivation: In multi-source ECG deployment, new data sources must be incorporated without retaining or replaying raw ECGs. While freezing a backbone with per-source classifiers prevents parameter interference, source metadata may be unavailable at inference time, requiring autonomous source identification for expert selection.
AI.method: Uses frozen 1024-dimensional ECGFounder features as a fixed backbone. Each new domain adds a balanced-softmax linear expert. A lightweight MLP router is fitted on retained training features and domain labels from all sources seen so far. At inference, a validation-calibrated margin rule fuses the top-2 most likely experts rather than committing to a single routed expert. No raw ECGs are replayed, but frozen training features are retained for router updates.
AI.result: Source-aware expert selection achieves 0.7915±0.0036 Macro-F1; offline independent-head reference reaches 0.7885±0.0009. Without source IDs, MLP router reaches 0.7756±0.0027 and top-2 margin fusion reaches 0.7782±0.0022. Top-2 gain over hard MLP routing is small (+0.0026) with a 95% CI including zero. Top-2-to-oracle gap remains 0.0111–0.0133 across three domain orders.
AI.conclusion: Source-aware expert retention is strong and approaches offline baselines. The main bottleneck is autonomous source inference, not expert capacity or fusion strategy. Top-2 margin fusion provides negligible improvement. The method is not memory-free due to retained frozen features for router updates.

title: HaloGuard 1.0: An Open Weights Constitutional Classifier for Multilingual AI Safety
summary: We present HaloGuard 1.0, an open-weights implementation of the constitutional-classifier paradigm for input safety. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on English and multilingual prompt-safety benchmarks at roughly one-tenth the model size of current leading open guard models. The safety constitution is the organising structure of the corpus: a natural-language constitution of 46 policies and 2,940 subcategories drives synthetic data generation, with exhaustive one-to-one paired counterfactuals that hold topic and vocabulary fixed while flipping intent, a two-tier harmless design that separately targets boundary and baseline false positives (FPs), and balanced multilingual materialisation across 46 languages that treats language as a surface form appearing on both sides of the boundary rather than as an adversarial signal. Across seven prompt-safety benchmarks, HaloGuard 1.0-0.8B attains the best average F1 (90.9) of any open guard we evaluate, outperforming baselines up to 27B parameters (over 30 times larger) while holding false-positive rate (FPR) to 4.3 and false-negative rate (FNR) to 9.5. The HaloGuard 1.0-4B variant reaches average F1 of 92.1 and FPR of 3.5, spending its extra capacity on precision rather than recall. A structured adjudication of the remaining failures indicates that most apparent missed-harm cases are benchmark mislabels rather than genuine model misses. An always-on adversarial red-teaming protocol continuously hardens the guard against both content-level and agentic attacks. We release the models as open weights.

AI.tldr: HaloGuard 1.0 is an open-weights, lightweight input safety guard based on the constitutional-classifier paradigm that achieves state-of-the-art multilingual prompt-safety performance, outperforming models 30× larger while maintaining low false-positive and false-negative rates.
AI.motivation: Current open guard models for input safety are large (often >7B parameters) and struggle with multilingual coverage, false-positive/false-negative trade-offs, and adversarial robustness. The authors aim to build a smaller, more efficient, and more balanced safety classifier using a principled data-generation framework organized around an explicit safety constitution.
AI.method: A safety constitution of 46 policies and 2,940 subcategories drives synthetic data generation with several key design choices: (1) exhaustive one-to-one paired counterfactuals that hold topic/vocabulary constant while flipping harmful intent; (2) a two-tier harmless design separately targeting boundary and baseline false positives; (3) balanced multilingual materialisation across 46 languages, treating language as a surface form rather than an adversarial cue; and (4) an always-on adversarial red-teaming protocol for continuous hardening.
AI.result: HaloGuard 1.0-0.8B achieves best average F1 of 90.9 across seven prompt-safety benchmarks, outperforming open guards up to 27B parameters, with 4.3% FPR and 9.5% FNR. The 4B variant reaches 92.1 F1 and 3.5% FPR, trading recall for precision. Structured failure adjudication reveals most apparent missed-harm cases are benchmark mislabels rather than genuine model errors.
AI.conclusion: The constitutional-classifier paradigm, combined with rigorous counterfactual pairing and multilingual balancing, enables compact yet highly accurate prompt safety models that rival or exceed much larger alternatives. The models are released as open weights to support community adoption and further research.

title: Benchmarking Quantum Software Testing with Scalable Quantum Programs
summary: Quantum software testing (QST) checks whether quantum programs behave according to their intended specifications. A key requirement for QST research is a benchmark that supports rigorous empirical evaluation on programs that are testable and better reflect current software development practices. However, existing studies heavily rely on small hard-coded or circuit-level benchmarks, while available quantum programs are scattered across repositories without clear selection criteria, which limits fair comparison and systematic reproducibility. To this end, we present Qolumbina, a benchmark infrastructure for controlled QST experiments on scalable quantum programs. Qolumbina curates 40 programs from open-source repositories, turns them into test-ready subjects through systematic selection, refactoring, specifications, test case examples, unit tests, and standardized interfaces. We also propose QST-oriented criteria to characterize quantum programs along functionality, output behavior, development complexity, and quantum-specific execution complexity. Using these criteria, our empirical study shows that Qolumbina covers diverse testing-relevant properties and supports scalability analysis beyond fixed-size circuit benchmarks. Through controlled experiments with two recent QST approaches, we demonstrate the feasibility of using Qolumbina for execution-cost and fault-detection studies, and highlight backend-dependent effects that can influence QST result interpretation.

AI.tldr: Qolumbina is a benchmark infrastructure for quantum software testing (QST) that curates 40 real-world quantum programs from open-source repositories, standardizes them with specifications and test suites, and characterizes them along multiple QST-relevant dimensions, enabling rigorous, scalable, and reproducible empirical evaluations beyond traditional circuit-level benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing QST research relies on small, hard-coded, or circuit-level benchmarks that lack scalability and realism. Meanwhile, available quantum programs are scattered across repositories with no clear selection criteria, hindering fair comparison and systematic reproducibility in QST experiments.
AI.method: The authors introduce Qolumbina, which (1) curates 40 quantum programs from open-source repositories; (2) applies systematic selection, refactoring, specification writing, test case generation, unit testing, and standardized interfaces to produce test-ready subjects; (3) proposes QST-oriented criteria (functionality, output behavior, development complexity, quantum-specific execution complexity) to characterize programs; and (4) conducts controlled experiments with two recent QST approaches to evaluate execution-cost and fault-detection capabilities.
AI.result: Qolumbina covers diverse testing-relevant properties and supports scalability analysis beyond fixed-size circuit benchmarks. Controlled experiments demonstrate feasibility for execution-cost and fault-detection studies, while also revealing backend-dependent effects that influence QST result interpretation.
AI.conclusion: Qolumbina fills a critical gap in QST infrastructure by providing a curated, standardized, and well-characterized benchmark suite that enables reproducible and scalable evaluation of quantum software testing techniques, with the added insight that backend variability must be accounted for when interpreting QST results.

title: PARTREP: Learning What to Repeat for Decoder-only LLMs
summary: While decoder-only LLMs excel at a vast array of natural language tasks, it suffers from an asymmetric information flow induced by causal attention: later tokens are richer in contextual grounding than earlier ones. A simple and effective remedy is prompt repetition -- just appending a second copy of prompt before generation can redistribute grounding across positions and improve reasoning performance. However, full repetition of the original prompt doubles the KV cache footprint and quadruples attention cost during prefill, making it impractical for long-context settings. We propose PartRep, a selective augmentation method that appends only the most informative tokens -- rather than the entire prompt. We use token-wise negative log-likelihood (NLL) as a selection signal, motivated by the hypothesis that less predictable tokens are less recoverable from surrounding context and therefore benefit more from late-position repetition. To avoid the heavy cost of a full forward pass for scoring, we train a lightweight gate that predicts high-NLL tokens from early-layer hidden states, enabling token selection during mid-prefill via early exit. Across eight benchmarks (including MMLU, GSM8K, and RULER) and three model families (Qwen2.5, Llama3.2, Gemma4), PartRep retains most of the gains of full repetition while using only 59.4\% of its KV cache and 79.0\% of its prefill FLOPs.

AI.tldr: PartRep selectively repeats only high-NLL (unpredictable) tokens instead of the full prompt, using a lightweight early-exit gate for efficient selection. It retains most of full repetition's gains while using 59.4% of KV cache and 79.0% of prefill FLOPs across 8 benchmarks and 3 model families.
AI.motivation: Decoder-only LLMs suffer from asymmetric information flow due to causal attention — later tokens are richer in context than earlier ones. Full prompt repetition mitigates this but doubles KV cache and quadruples prefill attention cost, making it impractical for long contexts.
AI.method: PartRep uses token-wise negative log-likelihood (NLL) as a selection signal, based on the hypothesis that less predictable tokens benefit more from late-position repetition. To avoid the cost of a full forward pass for scoring, a lightweight gate is trained to predict high-NLL tokens from early-layer hidden states, enabling token selection during mid-prefill via early exit.
AI.result: Across eight benchmarks (MMLU, GSM8K, RULER, etc.) and three model families (Qwen2.5, Llama3.2, Gemma4), PartRep retains most of the gains of full repetition while using only 59.4% of its KV cache and 79.0% of its prefill FLOPs.
AI.conclusion: Selective token repetition guided by NLL-based importance is an efficient and effective strategy to mitigate causal attention's asymmetry, achieving near-full-repetition performance with substantially reduced computational overhead.

title: Wind-Aware Reinforcement Learning Control of a Small Quadrotor Using Learned Onboard Wind Estimation in Simulated Atmospheric Turbulence
summary: Small multirotor aircraft are increasingly tasked with operations in the atmospheric boundary layer, where turbulent winds comparable to the vehicle's airspeed degrade trajectory tracking and can defeat conventional feedback control. This work illustrates a two-stage learning pipeline that first estimates the local wind from onboard kinematics and dynamics and then exploits that estimate inside a reinforcement learning (RL) flight controller. The wind estimator, an attention-augmented gated recurrent network trained on thousands of simulated flights through von Karman turbulence with power-law shear and veer, recovers the horizontal wind vector with a per-flight root-mean-square error of 0.40 m/s and a direction error of 3.2 degrees on unseen wind regimes, an accuracy near the floor imposed by unresolved turbulence, and generalizes to vertical ascent profiles with a skill score of 0.861 over a constant-wind reference. A proximal policy optimization controller receiving the frozen estimator's output reduces horizontal trajectory tracking error by 48% relative to a wind-blind proportional-derivative baseline across mean winds of 4 m/s to 12 m/s, winning on 100% of evaluation episodes. A three-way ablation decomposes this improvement into a kinematic component, available without wind information, and a wind-perception component; the perception share rises with wind speed, from small in light winds toward roughly half the total benefit in strong winds, consistent with the quadratic scaling of aerodynamic drag. The controller degrades gracefully on out-of-distribution winds of 13 m/s to 15 m/s, where the baseline fails catastrophically.

AI.tldr: A two-stage pipeline combines a learned wind estimator (attention-augmented GRU) with an RL-based flight controller (PPO) for small multirotors in turbulent boundary-layer winds. The estimator achieves 0.40 m/s RMSE; the RL controller reduces horizontal tracking error by 48% over a wind-blind PD baseline and degrades gracefully in out-of-distribution winds.
AI.motivation: Small multirotors operating in the atmospheric boundary layer face turbulent winds comparable to their airspeed, which severely degrade trajectory tracking and can defeat conventional feedback controllers. There is a need for controllers that can perceive and exploit wind information to maintain robust performance.
AI.method: A two-stage learning pipeline: (1) A wind estimator — an attention-augmented gated recurrent network trained on thousands of simulated flights through von Kármán turbulence with power-law shear and veer — estimates the horizontal wind vector from onboard kinematics and dynamics. (2) A proximal policy optimization (PPO) RL flight controller receives the frozen estimator's output. A three-way ablation study decomposes performance gains into kinematic and wind-perception components. Generalization is tested on vertical ascent profiles and out-of-distribution winds (13–15 m/s).
AI.result: The wind estimator achieves per-flight RMSE of 0.40 m/s and direction error of 3.2° on unseen wind regimes, with a skill score of 0.861 on vertical ascents. The PPO controller reduces horizontal tracking error by 48% (vs. wind-blind PD) across 4–12 m/s winds, winning 100% of evaluation episodes. Ablation shows the perception component's benefit grows with wind speed, reaching roughly half the total improvement in strong winds. The controller degrades gracefully at 13–15 m/s while the baseline fails catastrophically.
AI.conclusion: Explicit wind estimation combined with RL-based control yields substantial and robust trajectory-tracking improvements for small multirotors in turbulent boundary-layer conditions. The wind-perception benefit scales with wind speed, consistent with quadratic drag scaling, and the approach generalizes beyond the training distribution.

title: Epistemic Goggles: A Pretrained Module that Induces an Epistemic Frame via Gradient Editing
comment: 20 pages, 10 figures, 2 tables. Code at https://github.com/JoshuaSP/epistemic-goggles and generated documents, questions, and teacher rollouts at https://huggingface.co/datasets/joshuapenman/epistemic-goggles-artifacts
summary: Finetuning a language model on documents that are explicitly annotated as fictional results in a model that still actually believes the documents' core claims, an effect known as Negation Neglect. In our evaluations, models trained on documents prefixed and suffixed with such annotations correctly identify the relevant claims as fictional only about 9% of the time. To address this, we introduce Goggles, a learned module that intervenes on the finetuning gradient rather than the data. During supervised finetuning, a Goggles module edits the gradients an LLM LoRA receives, imparting a chosen epistemic frame (the stance the model takes toward the nature of what it reads) to whatever the documents teach. A Goggles instance is trained once for a given base model, frame, and LoRA configuration, then applied frozen to documents it was never trained on. Trained through Goggles on those same documents, now carrying no fictional annotation, the model flags the content as fictional roughly 91% of the time, while preserving capability (GPQA and TruthfulQA match or exceed baseline). The same architecture supports other frames: a Goggles instance can be trained to treat documents as "part of an AI safety evaluation by Redwood Research" rather than simply as fiction. The imparted frame persists under continued finetuning that pushes back toward the claim, where prior interventions revert. Goggles suggests a path toward training language models on known-misaligned data without absorbing the behaviors that data demonstrates.

AI.tldr: Finetuning LMs on explicitly labeled fictional documents fails to prevent belief in their claims (Negation Neglect). The authors introduce Goggles, a learned gradient-intervention module that imparts an epistemic frame during LoRA finetuning, enabling models to recognize content as fictional ~91% of the time without needing annotation at inference, while preserving general capabilities.
AI.motivation: Language models exhibit "Negation Neglect": even when documents are explicitly annotated as fictional (prefixed/suffixed), finetuning on them causes the model to internalize the claims as true (~9% correct identification). This poses a safety challenge for training on known-misaligned or untrusted data. Prior data-level interventions (annotations, system prompts) are brittle and fail under continued finetuning.
AI.method: Goggles is a learned module that intervenes on gradients during LoRA-based supervised finetuning, rather than on the data itself. It edits the gradients to impart a chosen epistemic frame (e.g., "this is fiction" or "this is an AI safety evaluation"). A Goggles instance is trained once for a given base model, frame, and LoRA configuration, then applied frozen to unseen documents. The method requires no annotations at inference time and preserves model capabilities.
AI.result: With Goggles, models correctly flag fictional claims ~91% of the time (vs. ~9% baseline with annotations alone). GPQA and TruthfulQA performance matches or exceeds baseline. The imparted epistemic frame persists under continued finetuning that pushes back toward the claim, whereas prior interventions (data annotations) revert. The architecture generalizes to other frames, such as treating documents as part of an AI safety evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Goggles demonstrates a viable path toward training language models on known-misaligned data without the model absorbing the demonstrated behaviors, by operating at the gradient level to instill durable epistemic frames that survive subsequent finetuning pressure.

title: Privacy-Preserving and Verifiable Approximate Distributed Coded Computing
summary: Distributed machine learning enables collaborative model training without centralizing data, but it also exposes learning processes to privacy leakage and malicious manipulation. Existing defenses typically address these threats in isolation and are often tailored to specific learning paradigms or model architectures, limiting their applicability in realistic deployments. In particular, federated learning and decentralized learning exhibit distinct adversarial surfaces that are rarely addressed within a unified framework. In this paper, we present a model-agnostic framework for adversary-resistant distributed learning that jointly addresses privacy preservation and malicious behavior across both federated and decentralized settings. Our approach combines paradigm-specific defense mechanisms with GPBACC, a privacy-enhancing coded computing technique applicable to arbitrary machine learning models. For federated learning, we integrate robust aggregation strategies to mitigate the impact of malicious participants, while for decentralized learning we employ approximate decode-and-compare and group testing techniques to enable lightweight verification and adversary isolation without relying on a trusted aggregator. Crucially, we evaluate the proposed framework through an explicit, attack-driven analysis. We implement representative privacy attacks and malicious behaviors, and empirically demonstrate that the combination of GPBACC with robust aggregation and verification mechanisms significantly reduces privacy leakage and improves resilience against active adversaries. These results suggest that privacy-enhancing coded computing, when combined with appropriate adversary-resistance strategies, provides a practical and deployable foundation for secure distributed machine learning.

AI.tldr: A model-agnostic framework for secure distributed learning that unifies privacy preservation (via GPBACC coded computing) with adversary resistance across both federated and decentralized settings, validated through attack-driven empirical analysis.
AI.motivation: Existing defenses for distributed machine learning address privacy leakage and malicious manipulation in isolation, and are tailored to specific paradigms (federated vs. decentralized), limiting real-world applicability. No unified framework addresses both threats across settings.
AI.method: A unified framework combining: (1) GPBACC, a privacy-enhancing coded computing technique applicable to arbitrary ML models; (2) robust aggregation for federated learning to counter malicious participants; (3) approximate decode-and-compare with group testing for decentralized learning to enable lightweight verification and adversary isolation without a trusted aggregator. Evaluation uses explicit, attack-driven analysis with representative privacy and malicious behavior attacks.
AI.result: The combination of GPBACC with robust aggregation and verification mechanisms significantly reduces privacy leakage and improves resilience against active adversaries in both federated and decentralized settings.
AI.conclusion: Privacy-enhancing coded computing (GPBACC), when integrated with paradigm-appropriate adversary-resistance strategies, provides a practical and deployable foundation for secure distributed machine learning.

title: Mitigating Package Hallucinations in Large Language Models via Model Editing
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in software engineering tasks, such as code generation, library recommendation, and dependency configuration. However, recent studies show that LLMs may suffer from package hallucination, where they generate non-existent or invalid package names. These hallucinations can be exploited in software supply chain attacks, as attackers may register malicious packages under hallucinated names. Therefore, mitigating package hallucination is important for improving the reliability and security of LLM-assisted software development. In this paper, we introduce BOUND, a lightweight localized model editing framework for mitigating package hallucinations in LLMs. BOUND formulates package hallucination mitigation as a package-validity boundary editing problem, where the boundary refers to the model's ability to distinguish valid packages from hallucinated package names under a given task context. It first locates modules related to package hallucination through a risk-aware localization strategy, and then edits these modules with lightweight LoRA adapters using a boundary-aware objective that reinforces valid packages, suppresses hallucinated packages, and preserves locality behavior. Experimental results show that BOUND effectively reduces package hallucinations while preserving valid package recommendations. In the package recommendation task, BOUND reduces package-level hallucination rate (Package-HR) by 79.9% on edit prompts and by 65.4% on unseen prompts. The learned package-validity boundary further generalizes to other package-related tasks, reducing Package-HR by 12.8% in code generation and by 34.0% in pip install recommendation. These results show that BOUND refines the package-validity boundary of LLMs and improves the reliability of package-related outputs.

AI.tldr: BOUND is a lightweight model editing framework that mitigates package hallucinations in LLMs by localizing and editing hallucination-related modules with LoRA adapters, achieving up to 79.9% reduction in package hallucination rates while preserving valid recommendations.
AI.motivation: LLMs frequently hallucinate non-existent package names during software engineering tasks, which poses security risks as attackers can register malicious packages under these hallucinated names for supply chain attacks. Existing solutions lack efficient, targeted mitigation that preserves overall model utility.
AI.method: BOUND frames mitigation as a package-validity boundary editing problem. It uses a risk-aware localization strategy to identify modules responsible for package hallucination, then applies lightweight LoRA adapters with a boundary-aware objective that simultaneously reinforces valid packages, suppresses hallucinated ones, and preserves locality in model behavior.
AI.result: BOUND reduces Package-HR by 79.9% on edit prompts and 65.4% on unseen prompts in package recommendation. Generalization: 12.8% reduction in code generation and 34.0% in pip install recommendation tasks.
AI.conclusion: BOUND effectively refines LLMs' package-validity boundaries, significantly reducing package hallucinations across multiple tasks while maintaining recommendation quality, thereby improving reliability and security in LLM-assisted software development.

title: On the Limits of Steering Vectors for Preference-Aligned Generation
summary: Steering vectors have emerged as a promising approach to controlled text generation, offering interpretable, training-free mechanisms for shaping model outputs. However, their practical generality remains poorly understood. We study the limits of steering vector generalization along three dimensions: trait expressibility, task transfer, and multi-trait composition. Using the PLUME writing personalization benchmark, we extract steering vectors for a range of preferences and evaluate them on summarization and email-writing tasks across two open-source models (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama3.1-8B-Instruct). We find that steering effectiveness varies substantially across traits. We further show that steering effectiveness can degrade when vectors extracted from positive and negative style examples are transferred to downstream writing personalization tasks. Finally, we compare common methods for composing multiple steering vectors and find that all methods suffer significant drops in trait expression as more vectors are added, with a tradeoff between coherence and expressibility that requires per-setting hyperparameter tuning. Taken together, our results suggest that steering vectors face meaningful limits as a general-purpose tool for preference alignment.

AI.tldr: Steering vectors for controlled text generation face significant limitations in trait expressibility, task transfer, and multi-trait composition, challenging their viability as general-purpose preference alignment tools.
AI.motivation: Despite promising results for steering vectors as interpretable, training-free mechanisms for controlled generation, their practical generality across different traits, tasks, and compositional settings remains poorly understood and underexplored.
AI.method: The authors use the PLUME writing personalization benchmark to extract steering vectors for various preferences. They systematically evaluate steering vector generalization along three dimensions — trait expressibility, task transfer (from style examples to summarization and email-writing), and multi-trait composition (comparing common composition methods) — across Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama3.1-8B-Instruct.
AI.result: Steering effectiveness varies substantially across traits. Transferring vectors from positive/negative style examples to downstream tasks degrades performance. All multi-vector composition methods suffer significant drops in trait expression as more vectors are added, revealing a coherence–expressibility tradeoff requiring per-setting hyperparameter tuning.
AI.conclusion: Steering vectors face meaningful limits as a general-purpose tool for preference alignment, with their effectiveness being highly contingent on specific traits, tasks, and composition configurations.

title: Certified World Models as Sensing Clocks: Drift-Aware Deadlines for Active Perception
summary: Certified world models estimate how long their predictions remain valid. We turn this validity horizon into an operational sensing clock: a rule for when an agent should stop coasting and re-sense. Starting from an audited equivariant world model, we derive a deadline for no-sensing intervals and show that deployable deadlines in learned world models must be drift-aware: on-manifold Lyapunov rates alone overestimate coasting validity, while calibrated native rollout-drift envelopes carry the deployed guarantee. On a frozen 3D VN-JEPA model, the resulting clock controls held-out interval-simultaneous certificate violation across seeds and data shards. In a cue-conditioned theorem-bed (a synthetic bench where all schedulers share the exact model, isolating the scheduling rule), the clock remains valid on the deployment distribution and substantially reduces eventful-tail violations relative to exact-mixture expected-belief scheduling at matched sensing budget. We also report limits: in the short-horizon frozen VN-JEPA regime, empirical conformal horizons match the deployed clock on validity and budget, and a partial-reset exploration finds no clean budget-matched advantage for the spectral term. Thus the contribution is a certified sensing-clock primitive and drift-aware deployment method, not a claim that spectral clocks empirically dominate all non-spectral schedulers.

AI.tldr: Certified world models produce validity horizons for predictions. This paper transforms that horizon into a sensing clock — a rule dictating when an agent must stop coasting on stale observations and re-sense. The key insight is that deployed deadlines require drift-awareness: naive on-manifold Lyapunov rates overestimate coasting validity, while calibrated drift envelopes from actual rollouts provide genuine guarantees. The method is validated on a frozen 3D VN-JEPA model and a synthetic "theorem-bed" benchmark, where the clock reduces tail violations compared to expected-belief scheduling at matched sensing budgets.
AI.motivation: Certified world models can bound how long their predictions remain valid, but this theoretical guarantee has not been operationalized into a practical sensing policy for agents. The gap is turning a validity horizon into an actionable rule for when to re-sense, while ensuring the guarantee survives deployment — where distributional drift can invalidate naive on-manifold certificates.
AI.method: The authors derive a deadline rule for no-sensing intervals from an audited equivariant world model. They introduce drift-aware deployment: combining on-manifold Lyapunov rates (which alone overestimate validity) with calibrated native rollout-drift envelopes to carry the actual deployed guarantee. The sensing clock is evaluated on (1) a frozen 3D VN-JEPA model, measuring interval-simultaneous certificate violation across seeds and data shards, and (2) a cue-conditioned theorem-bed — a synthetic benchmark where all schedulers share the exact same model, isolating the scheduling rule's contribution.
AI.result: On the frozen VN-JEPA model, the sensing clock controls held-out interval-simultaneous certificate violation. In the theorem-bed, the clock remains valid on the deployment distribution and substantially reduces eventful-tail violations compared to exact-mixture expected-belief scheduling at matched sensing budgets. Limits: in short-horizon frozen VN-JEPA, empirical conformal horizons match the deployed clock; a partial-reset exploration finds no clean budget-matched advantage for the spectral term.
AI.conclusion: The primary contribution is a certified sensing-clock primitive paired with a drift-aware deployment method, not a claim that spectral clocks dominate all non-spectral schedulers. The work establishes that deployable sensing deadlines in learned world models must account for rollout drift beyond pure on-manifold Lyapunov analysis.

title: COMFYCLAW: Self-Evolving Skill Harnesses for Image Generation Workflows
summary: Agents are increasingly used to construct workflows and assist humans in completing recurring tasks more efficiently. As these workflows become repeated and domain-specific, agent memory and reusable skills become increasingly important: agents should be able to recall workflow patterns, execution constraints, and user preferences from previous runs. We study this problem in workflow-based image generation and introduce COMFYCLAW, an agentic skill evolution harness for controlling ComfyUI workflows. COMFYCLAW formulates workflow construction as typed graph editing, exposes tools organized by construction stage, automatically reverts invalid edits, and uses a region-level vision-language model (VLM) verifier to translate visual failures into actionable repair suggestions. The framework further evolves a progressively disclosed skill library, where trajectories, execution errors, and verifier feedback from previous runs are distilled into reusable Agent Skills. Across four benchmark splits, three agent models, and two image backbones, COMFYCLAW achieves the best average image-generation evaluation score across all six agent configurations, outperforming a verifier-only baseline without skill evolution. Human annotations further show that annotators prefer COMFYCLAW over variants without skill evolution. Our results suggest that skill evolution is an effective mechanism for improving agent reliability and performance in recurring visual workflow construction.

AI.tldr: COMFYCLAW is an agentic framework for ComfyUI workflow construction that uses typed graph editing, a VLM verifier, and a progressively disclosed skill library distilled from prior trajectories to improve agent reliability in recurring image generation tasks.
AI.motivation: As workflows become repeated and domain-specific, agents need memory and reusable skills to recall workflow patterns, execution constraints, and user preferences from previous runs. Existing approaches lack mechanisms for evolving such skills from prior experience.
AI.method: COMFYCLAW formulates workflow construction as typed graph editing, exposes stage-organized tools, auto-reverts invalid edits, and uses a region-level VLM verifier to translate visual failures into actionable repair suggestions. A progressively disclosed skill library distills trajectories, execution errors, and verifier feedback into reusable Agent Skills that evolve over time.
AI.result: Across four benchmark splits, three agent models, and two image backbones, COMFYCLAW achieves the best average image-generation evaluation score across all six agent configurations, outperforming a verifier-only baseline without skill evolution. Human annotators also prefer COMFYCLAW over variants lacking skill evolution.
AI.conclusion: Skill evolution is an effective mechanism for improving agent reliability and performance in recurring visual workflow construction.

title: Steerability via constraints: a substrate for scalable oversight of coding agents
comment: Accepted to the Deep Learning for Code Workshop at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, Seoul, South Korea, 2026
summary: Coding agents are capable; human oversight is the bottleneck. Unconstrained agents introduce security risks, erode codebase scalability, and make human review increasingly costly. We argue that the same methods used for decades to manage large human engineering teams: access control, network policies, strict coding conventions enforced by tooling; transfer directly to coding agents, and are cheaper (in token) than recent agentic scaffolding. We sketch a start-to-end system on this principle, and report a controlled experiment in scalable oversight: a small reviewer (Gemma 4 e4b) inspects a Python codebase containing 11 inserted backdoors. Recall rises from 54.5% (unconstrained, no tools) to 90.9% (constrained substrate plus a ~200-LoC `docs` CLI), with substrate and tools contributing independently. We choose Python deliberately: substrate-level oversight gains are largest where the language gives the fewest guarantees by default; the principles extend to languages like Rust.

AI.tldr: Coding agents need guardrails. This paper argues that classical software engineering controls—access control, network policies, coding conventions—can be applied directly to AI coding agents more efficiently than complex agentic scaffolding. An experiment shows that adding a constrained substrate and a minimal CLI tool boosts a small reviewer model's detection of backdoors in Python code from 54.5% to 90.9% recall.
AI.motivation: Unconstrained coding agents introduce security vulnerabilities, degrade codebase maintainability, and overwhelm human reviewers. Human oversight, not agent capability, is the limiting factor. Rather than building elaborate agentic scaffolding (which costs tokens), the authors propose adapting mature, battle-tested software engineering management practices to constrain agents by default.
AI.method: The authors sketch an end-to-end system based on access control, network policies, and tooling-enforced coding conventions. They then run a controlled experiment: a small reviewer model (Gemma 4 e4b) inspects a Python codebase with 11 inserted backdoors, with and without a constrained substrate plus a ~200-line `docs` CLI tool. Python is deliberately chosen as a worst-case (fewest language-level guarantees).
AI.result: Recall for backdoor detection improved from 54.5% (unconstrained, no tools) to 90.9% (constrained substrate + `docs` CLI). The substrate and the CLI tool contributed independently to the gain, not redundantly.
AI.conclusion: Traditional software engineering governance mechanisms transfer directly and effectively to coding agents, yielding significant oversight improvements at lower token cost than complex agentic scaffolding. The approach is language-agnostic; gains are largest in permissive languages like Python, but the principles extend to stricter languages such as Rust.

title: Prompt Coverage Adequacy
summary: In recent years, it has become increasingly evident that large language models (LLMs) and autonomous agents raise the level of abstraction in software development by shifting the focus from writing precise procedures to expressing intents and goals. This paradigm shift introduces new challenges, particularly in how testing should be guided when prompts, rather than code, become primary development artifacts. To address this challenge, we propose Prompt Coverage Adequacy, a novel coverage criterion designed to support the testing of code generated from task descriptions. Prompt Coverage Adequacy serves as an analog to traditional code coverage, but operates at the level of prompts used in LLM and agent-based programming. Specifically, it measures how well a given test suite satisfies the requirements expressed in a prompt by leveraging the attention mechanisms of LLMs. We evaluate a simple instantiation of this criterion, based on attention boosting, across two datasets and multiple LLMs. Our results demonstrate that Prompt Coverage is associated with fault-detection effectiveness and can uncover over 30+% more faults than traditional code coverage when used to guide test generation. These findings suggest that Prompt Coverage Adequacy can serve as a foundation for developing testing metrics better suited to the emerging paradigm of LLM-driven software development, addressing the limitations of classical coverage criteria in this new context.

AI.tldr: Proposes Prompt Coverage Adequacy, a novel testing criterion that measures how well test suites satisfy prompt requirements using LLM attention mechanisms, demonstrating 30%+ better fault detection than traditional code coverage for LLM-generated code.
AI.motivation: As LLMs and autonomous agents shift software development from writing code to expressing intents via prompts, traditional code coverage criteria become inadequate. Testing must adapt to a paradigm where prompts—not code—are the primary development artifacts.
AI.method: Introduces Prompt Coverage Adequacy, analogous to code coverage but operating at the prompt level. The criterion leverages LLM attention mechanisms to measure how well a test suite satisfies prompt requirements. A simple instantiation using attention boosting is evaluated across two datasets and multiple LLMs.
AI.result: Prompt Coverage correlates with fault-detection effectiveness and uncovers over 30% more faults than traditional code coverage when guiding test generation.
AI.conclusion: Prompt Coverage Adequacy offers a foundational testing metric for the emerging LLM-driven development paradigm, addressing the limitations of classical coverage criteria.

title: PairCoder++: Pair Programming as a Universal Paradigm for Verified Code-Driven Multimodal and Structured-Artifact Generation
comment: Accepted by ACL 2026. Project Page: https://yisuanwang.github.io/PairCoder/
summary: Code is the medium through which large language models generate structured artifacts: charts, scientific figures, vector graphics, CAD models, 3D scenes, and hardware designs are all produced by writing programs. In this regime single pass inference is brittle, because the compiler, renderer, or simulator that decides whether the artifact exists is invisible to the model. We present PairCoder, which grounds review in the toolchain and realizes it as two agent pair programming: a Driver agent writes the program, a Navigator agent reviews it against verification evidence (diagnostics, execution results, and renderings of the current artifact beside the target), and the two switch roles when errors persist. Across 17 public benchmarks and seven models from three vendors, PairCoder improves essentially every benchmark whose artifact is verifiable, on full official metric suites rather than execution alone (for example, Blender scene executability 0.20 to 0.78; TikZ compile rate up 10 to 30 points on every model), at 2.9 to 9.2 times single model cost (about 7 times overall). The improvements concentrate where the toolchain provides an informative oracle and the baseline leaves headroom, and the method ties or mildly regresses where the oracle is weak; we frame pair programming as a reliable recipe for verified code driven generation.

AI.tldr: PairCoder introduces a dual-agent pair programming framework (Driver + Navigator) for code-driven artifact generation, where a Navigator reviews code against toolchain verification evidence. Across 17 benchmarks and 7 models, it substantially improves verifiable artifacts (e.g., Blender executability from 0.20 to 0.78), at roughly 7× cost, with gains concentrated where the toolchain provides informative feedback.
AI.motivation: Single-pass LLM inference for code-driven generation (charts, figures, CAD, 3D scenes, etc.) is brittle because the compiler, renderer, or simulator that validates the output artifact is invisible to the model during generation. Without grounding in verification feedback, models cannot correct errors that only manifest in downstream toolchains.
AI.method: PairCoder operationalizes pair programming with two agents: a Driver agent writes the program, and a Navigator agent reviews it against verification evidence — including diagnostics, execution results, and renderings of the current artifact beside the target. When errors persist across iterations, the two agents switch roles. Review is grounded in the actual toolchain output rather than model introspection alone.
AI.result: Across 17 public benchmarks and 7 models from 3 vendors, PairCoder improves virtually every benchmark with verifiable artifacts. Key results: Blender scene executability rises from 0.20 to 0.78; TikZ compile rates improve 10–30 points on every model tested. Cost ranges from 2.9× to 9.2× single-model cost (~7× overall). Gains concentrate where the toolchain provides informative oracles and baseline performance has headroom; the method ties or mildly regresses where oracle feedback is weak.
AI.conclusion: Pair programming with toolchain-grounded review is a reliable recipe for verified code-driven generation. The approach demonstrates that structured multi-agent collaboration with explicit verification feedback substantially improves artifact quality, though cost scales linearly with agent interactions.

title: Evolutionary Feature Engineering for Structured Data
comment: 9 page main content, 41 pages in total
summary: Large language models are increasingly used as open-ended search operators in evolutionary optimization. We introduce Evolutionary Feature Engineering (EFE), a framework for using LLM-based evolution to discover preprocessing transformations for structured data. EFE represents transformations as Python programs with a standardized fit/transform interface, allowing them to be inserted directly into existing machine learning pipelines. During evolution, candidate programs are refined using dataset context, summary statistics, and downstream performance feedback on validation set. We instantiate EFE in two settings. For time-series forecasting, EFE-Time learns invertible, dataset-specific normalizations that improve off-the-shelf time-series foundation models. It reduces forecasting errors (MASE, WQL, MAE) 3% or more when averaged across datasets and improvements are as much as 19% on the COVID-Deaths dataset. Notably, these improvements occur with recent TSFMs such as Chronos-2. For tabular prediction, EFE-Tab evolves compact feature programs that add useful interpretable features and remove redundant ones, improving or matching existing LLM-based feature-engineering methods. We found EFE-Tab to be particularly effective on classical decision trees, where small sets of evolved features yield competitive accuracy while preserving interpretability. Overall, EFE demonstrates that LLM-based evolution can improve both accuracy and interpretability when automatically tackling structured data.

AI.tldr: EFE uses LLM-based evolution to discover preprocessing transformations (Python programs) for structured data, with EFE-Time improving time-series forecasting accuracy via dataset-specific normalizations and EFE-Tab generating compact, interpretable features for tabular prediction, demonstrating gains in both accuracy and interpretability.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used as search operators in evolutionary optimization, but their potential for automated feature engineering on structured data—particularly for improving downstream model performance while maintaining interpretability—remains underexplored.
AI.method: EFE represents preprocessing transformations as Python programs with a standard fit/transform interface, evolved via LLM-based mutation guided by dataset context, summary statistics, and validation-set performance feedback. Two instantiations: (1) EFE-Time learns invertible, dataset-specific normalizations for time-series foundation models; (2) EFE-Tab evolves compact feature-engineering programs that add interpretable features and prune redundant ones, compatible with existing ML pipelines.
AI.result: EFE-Time reduces forecasting errors (MASE, WQL, MAE) by ≥3% on average across datasets, with up to 19% improvement on COVID-Deaths using Chronos-2. EFE-Tab matches or exceeds existing LLM-based feature-engineering methods, and is especially effective with classical decision trees, yielding competitive accuracy with interpretable feature sets.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based evolutionary search can simultaneously improve accuracy and interpretability when automatically engineering features for structured data, as demonstrated across time-series forecasting and tabular prediction tasks.

title: Generic Expert Coverage for Pruning SparseMixture-of-Experts Language Models
summary: Sparsely activated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models contain substantial structured redundancy among routed experts, but pruning them without downstream calibration data remains challenging. Existing expert-pruning methods typically rely on a single aggregated importance score, which can bias the retained set toward experts favored by dominant calibration patterns. We propose \textbf{Generic TB-Coverage}, a coverage-aware expert pruning method that uses only generic text corpora (WikiText2 and C4) for calibration. Instead of collapsing expert utility into one score, our method profiles per-expert utility separately on each corpus and enforces a fixed-budget coverage rule that preserves high-utility experts from each corpus before constructing the final pruning mask. Across Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B and DeepSeek-MoE-16B-Base at 25\%, 50\%, and 75\% retention budgets, our method improves average accuracy on six common zero-shot benchmarks over random pruning, REAP, and ExpertSparsity, while also reducing perplexity degradation on WikiText2 and C4. The gains are largest under aggressive pruning (25\% and 50\% retain), suggesting that preserving cross-corpus expert coverage is an effective generic-data prior for MoE pruning. Our improvements hold with fixed pruning budgets and no downstream calibration data.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Generic TB-Coverage, a coverage-aware expert pruning method for MoE language models. Instead of using a single aggregated importance score, it profiles per-expert utility separately across multiple generic text corpora (WikiText2, C4) and enforces a fixed-budget coverage rule to retain high-utility experts from each corpus. The method outperforms existing pruning techniques (random, REAP, ExpertSparsity) on zero-shot benchmarks and perplexity, especially under aggressive pruning budgets (25%–50% retention), without requiring downstream calibration data.
AI.motivation: Sparsely activated MoE models contain structured redundancy among routed experts, but existing pruning methods rely on a single aggregated importance score biased toward dominant calibration patterns. This can discard experts that are critical for diverse inputs not well-represented in the calibration data. The authors aim to address this bias by designing a pruning strategy that preserves expert coverage across multiple generic corpora, eliminating the need for task-specific downstream calibration data.
AI.method: Generic TB-Coverage: (1) Profiles per-expert utility separately on each generic corpus (WikiText2, C4). (2) Enforces a fixed-budget coverage rule that preserves high-utility experts from each corpus independently. (3) Constructs the final pruning mask by taking the union of retained experts across corpora within the given retention budget. This ensures cross-corpus expert coverage rather than collapsing utility into a single aggregated importance score.
AI.result: Evaluated on Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B and DeepSeek-MoE-16B-Base at 25%, 50%, and 75% retention budgets. The method improves average accuracy on six common zero-shot benchmarks over random pruning, REAP, and ExpertSparsity, while reducing perplexity degradation on WikiText2 and C4. Gains are largest under aggressive pruning (25% and 50% retain), and improvements hold with fixed pruning budgets and no downstream calibration data.
AI.conclusion: Preserving cross-corpus expert coverage serves as an effective generic-data prior for MoE pruning. The approach demonstrates that structured redundancy in MoE models can be reduced without downstream calibration data by ensuring diverse expert utility is retained across multiple corpora rather than relying on a single aggregated importance signal.

title: HTTP REST API Structure Learning
summary: Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) are essential in software development, enabling web services, mobile apps, and microservices. However, their widespread use introduces significant security risks, highlighting the importance of API security. This paper presents HTTP REST API Learning (HRAL), a novel unsupervised anomaly detection approach that models the structure and behavior of API endpoints directly from network traffic, without relying on predefined rules or documentation. HRAL enables robust detection of malicious activity by understanding how APIs behave and flagging deviations as potential threats. We evaluate HRAL across varying levels of OpenAPI documentation detail and compare it with existing techniques. HRAL achieves strong performance, with an average recall of 82.07% and an F1-score of 87.24%, significantly outperforming alternatives when API documentation is limited. Moreover, our results approach the effectiveness of full API document definitions. When combined with signature-based rules such as the OWASP ModSecurity CRS, our system achieves 100% detection. These results highlight HRAL's effectiveness in real-world, partially documented API environments and its potential as a foundational layer for modern API security solutions.

AI.tldr: HRAL is an unsupervised anomaly detection system that learns API behavior from network traffic, achieving 82.07% recall and 87.24% F1-score without requiring API documentation, and reaches 100% detection when combined with signature-based rules.
AI.motivation: APIs are ubiquitous in modern software but introduce significant security risks. Existing security approaches often depend on predefined rules or complete API documentation, which are frequently unavailable or incomplete in real-world deployments, creating a need for documentation-free anomaly detection.
AI.method: HRAL (HTTP REST API Learning) models API endpoint structure and behavior directly from network traffic using unsupervised learning. It learns normal API usage patterns and flags deviations as potential threats, without relying on OpenAPI specifications or predefined rules. Evaluation was conducted across varying levels of OpenAPI documentation detail, and HRAL was also tested in combination with OWASP ModSecurity CRS signature-based rules.
AI.result: HRAL achieves an average recall of 82.07% and F1-score of 87.24%, significantly outperforming alternatives when API documentation is limited. Its performance approaches that of systems using full API documentation. When combined with OWASP ModSecurity CRS, detection reaches 100%.
AI.conclusion: HRAL is highly effective in real-world, partially documented API environments and shows strong potential as a foundational layer for modern API security solutions, particularly when documentation is scarce or incomplete.

title: File-Level Copying Is an Implicit Dependency in Open Source
summary: File-level copying is a widespread but ungoverned form of software reuse. Copying files across repositories reduces supply-chain visibility: it removes the four observable signals a package manager provides for a declared dependency (provenance, maintenance, security, and compliance) with no mechanism to restore them. To characterize the scale and consequences of this unmanaged reuse, we present a mixed-method study of copying across the entire open-source ecosystem using World of Code (WoC). From a 0.1% commit sample, we extract 690,500 copy events and retain 3,912 rationale-bearing copy commits for intent labeling. We show that the 13 axial copy forms, spanning vendored dependencies, hardware/driver synchronization, scaffolding, UI assets, and direct source-code reuse, are unreliable proxies for developer intent: among rationale-bearing commits, hardware/driver copies are predominantly fork-maintenance work (78%), while dependency-vendoring copies more often signal upstream bypass (70%) than offline availability. These visibility gaps are form-specific: security and license risk concentrate in complementary copy forms. Copied sources are frequently stale (median 155 days; 38.5% over one year old) and seldom record a recoverable origin (4.3% documented), let alone a checkable version (2.0% versioned); even vendored copies record where they came from only 10% of the time. Security risk concentrates in vendored dependencies: 17,314 CVE-risk copy commits in the full-WoC graph, 88% in the dependency-vendoring form; 80% score CVSS >= 7.0 and upstream-fix adoption is only 47%-84%. License risk concentrates in direct source-code reuse: 41,777 pre-validation candidates, 66% in the source-code form, with 39 verified high-star violations (kappa = 0.752). Both risks reach packaged software and are invisible to dependency scanners operating on declared metadata alone.

AI.tldr: File-level copying across open-source repositories is a widespread, ungoverned practice that erodes supply-chain visibility. A large-scale empirical study reveals distinct copy forms (vendoring, source reuse, etc.) carry different, complementary security and license risks — none of which are detectable by package-manager-based dependency scanners.
AI.motivation: File-level copying across repositories eliminates the four key signals package managers provide for declared dependencies: provenance, maintenance, security, and compliance. Despite its prevalence, the scale, forms, and consequences of this unmanaged reuse across the open-source ecosystem are not well characterized. The authors aim to quantify these gaps and the associated risks that remain invisible to existing dependency-scanning tooling.
AI.method: A mixed-method empirical study leveraging World of Code (WoC), a large-scale open-source infrastructure. From a 0.1% commit sample, 690,500 copy events are extracted. 3,912 rationale-bearing commits are manually labeled for developer intent. Copy forms are classified into 13 axial categories (e.g., vendored dependencies, hardware/driver sync, scaffolding, UI assets, direct source reuse). Risk analysis maps CVE-risk commits (security) and license-violation candidates (compliance) onto these forms, with inter-rater reliability assessed via Cohen's kappa.
AI.result: Copy forms are unreliable proxies for intent: hardware/driver copies are 78% fork-maintenance, while dependency-vendoring copies signal upstream bypass 70% of the time (vs. offline availability). Visibility gaps are form-specific: security risk concentrates in vendored dependencies (17,314 CVE-risk commits, 88% in dependency-vendoring form; 80% score CVSS ≥ 7.0; upstream-fix adoption only 47–84%). License risk concentrates in direct source-code reuse (41,777 pre-validation candidates, 66% in source-code form; 39 verified high-star violations, κ = 0.752). Copied sources are stale (median 155 days, 38.5% >1 year), rarely document origin (4.3%), and almost never record a checkable version (2.0%). Even vendored copies document origin only 10% of the time.
AI.conclusion: File-level copying is a pervasive, ungoverned reuse mechanism that creates substantial, complementary security and license risks invisible to metadata-based dependency scanners. The form-specific nature of these risks calls for new tooling and governance mechanisms that operate at the file-copy level rather than relying solely on declared dependency metadata.

title: The Grammar Does the Work: Functional vs. Lexical Dependency Length Minimization Across Universal Dependencies
summary: Dependency length minimization (DLM) is a well-documented processing universal, but previous studies report a single mean dependency distance (MDD) per language, obscuring variation across syntactic relation types. We analyze 122 languages in UD and SUD (version 2.17), showing that DLM operates on two distinct levels. Grammar-driven optimization targets functional dependencies (det, case, aux), which are universally short (mean 1.71, $σ$ = 0.33) and invariant across typologically diverse languages. Processing-driven optimization operates on lexical dependencies (nsubj, obj, obl), which are longer (mean 2.87), highly variable ($σ$ = 0.63), and constrained by word-order typology. This asymmetry holds in SUD despite reversed head direction (r = 0.92). We conclude that ''the grammar does the work'' of minimization by scaffolding sentences with local functional attachments, leaving processing pressures to determine the ordering of lexical heads.

AI.tldr: Dependency length minimization is not a uniform phenomenon: functional dependencies are universally short due to grammatical scaffolding, while lexical dependencies are longer, more variable, and shaped by processing pressures and word-order typology.
AI.motivation: Previous DLM research collapses all dependency types into a single mean dependency distance, obscuring how different syntactic relations behave. The authors aim to reveal whether DLM operates uniformly or differentially across relation types and across languages.
AI.method: Analysis of 122 languages from Universal Dependencies (UD) and Surface-Syntactic Universal Dependencies (SUD) version 2.17, computing mean dependency distances per relation type (functional vs. lexical) and comparing across typologically diverse languages. SUD is used as a cross-validation framework with reversed head direction.
AI.result: Functional dependencies (det, case, aux) are universally short (mean 1.71, σ = 0.33) and invariant across languages. Lexical dependencies (nsubj, obj, obl) are longer (mean 2.87), highly variable (σ = 0.63), and constrained by word-order typology. This asymmetry persists in SUD despite reversed head direction (r = 0.92).
AI.conclusion: Grammar-driven optimization handles functional relations, scaffolding sentences with local attachments, while processing-driven optimization governs lexical head ordering. DLM is thus a two-level phenomenon, not a single uniform pressure.

title: X-LogSMask: Expand Transformer for Graph-Structured Data
summary: Transformers have become general-purpose architectures, but their all-to-all self-attention is poorly matched to graph data, whose interactions are sparse, structured and multi-scale. Existing Graph Transformers address this mismatch through structural encodings, hybrid message-passing modules or learned attention constraints, often introducing additional complexity and limited interpretability. Here we introduce X-LogSMask, an explainable multi-head logarithmic structural mask that injects symmetrically normalized graph topology directly into attention logits. The logarithmic transform converts structural connectivity into a topology-aware gating signal, suppressing unsupported node interactions while preserving feature-dependent attention. By assigning different powers of the normalized adjacency matrix to different attention heads, X-LogSMask gives each head a defined structural radius and supports multi-hop information propagation within a single layer. We further show that a standard Transformer encoder can be interpreted as one-step message passing on a complete graph, motivating X-LogSMask as a topology-constrained alternative to unrestricted self-attention. Across 20 node-, edge- and graph-level benchmarks, Transformers equipped with X-LogSMask achieve state-of-the-art performance on 13 datasets and remain competitive in a lightweight one-layer configuration. These results show that simple, interpretable structural masks can make self-attention an effective graph-learning operator without changing the Transformer architecture. The code is available at https://github.com/LiLeyan-0120/X-LogSMask.

AI.tldr: X-LogSMask introduces a logarithmic structural mask that injects normalized graph topology directly into Transformer attention logits, assigning different adjacency powers to different heads for multi-scale, interpretable graph learning without architectural changes.
AI.motivation: Standard Transformers use all-to-all self-attention, which is poorly suited for graph data where interactions are sparse, structured, and multi-scale. Existing Graph Transformers address this with structural encodings, hybrid message-passing, or learned constraints, but these add complexity and reduce interpretability.
AI.method: X-LogSMask applies a logarithmic transformation to symmetrically normalized adjacency matrix powers, producing a structural mask added to attention logits. Different attention heads receive different powers of the normalized adjacency, giving each head a defined structural radius. This constrains self-attention to topologically supported node pairs, with the standard Transformer reinterpreted as one-step message passing on a complete graph.
AI.result: Across 20 node-, edge-, and graph-level benchmarks, X-LogSMask-equipped Transformers achieved state-of-the-art on 13 datasets and remained competitive even in a lightweight single-layer configuration.
AI.conclusion: Simple, interpretable structural masks can make self-attention an effective graph-learning operator without modifying the Transformer architecture, offering a principled bridge between message-passing and attention-based graph learning.

title: Distributionally Robust Listwise Preference Optimization
summary: Existing robust preference optimization for language-model alignment mainly studies pairwise supervision and places robustness at the dataset, prompt, or preference-pair level. We instead study listwise preference optimization under ranking-label uncertainty: given a prompt and a candidate list, the observed ranking over that list may be ambiguous due to annotator inconsistency, near-ties, lossy rankwise feedback, or reward-model noise. We propose a pointwise total-variation robust Plackett--Luce objective that directly robustifies the ranking label conditional on the candidate list. The robust loss admits an exact decomposition into the nominal PL loss plus a worst-case PL correction, and the worst-case ranking is obtained by sorting current implicit scores in ascending order, reducing the inner maximization from $K!$ enumeration to $O(K\log K)$. This tractable structure yields strong offline and online optimization guarantees. In the offline fixed-list setting, the robust objective is convex and projected stochastic subgradient reaches global $ε$-suboptimality with $O(ε^{-2})$ sample complexity. In the online policy-induced setting, where candidate lists are generated by the current policy, we establish weak convexity and $\widetilde O(ε^{-2})$ Moreau-envelope stationarity. Experiments in offline LLM alignment show that the proposed robust correction largely preserves performance under clean labels and improves robustness under noise. In online alignment, it makes reward-model-ranked candidate expansion more reliable and improves both reward-model and external GPT-4 judge metrics.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a pointwise total-variation robust Plackett-Luce objective for listwise preference optimization in LLM alignment under ranking-label uncertainty. The robust loss decomposes into a nominal PL loss plus a worst-case correction, with the inner maximization reduced from $K!$ to $O(K \log K)$ via sorting. The method offers strong offline (convex, $O(\epsilon^{-2})$ sample complexity) and online ($\widetilde{O}(\epsilon^{-2})$ Moreau-envelope stationarity) guarantees, and experiments show preserved clean-label performance with improved robustness under noise.
AI.motivation: Existing robust preference optimization focuses mainly on pairwise supervision with robustness at dataset/prompt/preference-pair levels. However, in listwise preference optimization, observed rankings over candidate lists are often ambiguous due to annotator inconsistency, near-ties, lossy rankwise feedback, or reward-model noise. This ranking-label uncertainty is underexplored, motivating a principled robust formulation for the listwise setting.
AI.method: The authors propose a pointwise total-variation (TV) robust Plackett-Luce (PL) objective. The robust loss decomposes exactly into the nominal PL loss plus a worst-case PL correction term. The worst-case ranking is obtained by sorting current implicit scores in ascending order, reducing inner maximization from $K!$ enumeration to $O(K \log K)$. For offline fixed-list settings, projected stochastic subgradient is applied. For online policy-induced settings (candidate lists generated by current policy), weak convexity is established and a Moreau-envelope stationarity framework is used.
AI.result: Offline: The robust objective is convex; projected stochastic subgradient achieves global $\epsilon$-suboptimality with $O(\epsilon^{-2})$ sample complexity. Online: Weak convexity holds, and $\widetilde{O}(\epsilon^{-2})$ Moreau-envelope stationarity is established. Experiments in offline LLM alignment show the robust correction largely preserves performance under clean labels and improves robustness under noise. In online alignment, reward-model-ranked candidate expansion becomes more reliable, improving both reward-model and external GPT-4 judge metrics.
AI.conclusion: The TV-robust PL objective provides a principled and tractable framework for listwise preference optimization under ranking-label uncertainty, with strong theoretical guarantees in both offline and online settings, and empirical validation showing robust performance without sacrificing clean-label effectiveness.

title: Coding Agents Are Guessing: Measuring Action-Boundary Violations in Underspecified DevOps Instructions
summary:
LLM coding agents are increasingly deployed to act autonomously on real production infrastructure. They execute shell commands, modify repositories, and call operational APIs. However, completing a task is not sufficient for safety. A wrong action can cause severe consequences. Existing agent benchmarks largely emphasize task completion, leaving open how agents behave under benign but underspecified instructions.
  We present UnderSpecBench, a benchmark for measuring action-boundary violations in coding agents (i.e., Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode) on DevOps tasks. UnderSpecBench includes 69 task families grounded in documented incidents, CVEs, or tool behavior and organized across four DevOps capability domains and nine operational control surfaces. To isolate underspecification from task difficulty, each task keeps the same environment and ground-truth safe action while varying the instruction along three axes: intent clarity, target certainty, and blast radius.
