The resulting 2,208 prompt variants are evaluated with deterministic, side-effect-based oracles that separate Safe Success, Wrong Target, and OverScope outcomes; non-action runs are further classified as clarification, refusal, or deferment.
  Across five agent x model configurations using OpenCode, Claude Code, and Codex, the evaluation results show that underspecification does not mainly make agents fail; it makes them guess. 55.8-67.8% of runs violate at least one boundary. Target underspecification sharply degrades action quality, while blast-radius cues barely reduce action propensity. These findings show that completion-centric evaluation can overstate safe autonomy and motivate mitigations at the model, harness, and system layer.

AI.tldr: UnderSpecBench evaluates LLM coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode) on DevOps tasks with underspecified instructions. Across 2,208 prompt variants, 55.8-67.8% of runs violate action boundaries—agents guess rather than fail. Target ambiguity sharply degrades safety, while blast-radius cues barely reduce risky actions, revealing that completion-centric benchmarks overstate safe autonomy.
AI.motivation: LLM coding agents are increasingly deployed on real production infrastructure where wrong actions carry severe consequences. Existing benchmarks prioritize task completion, leaving unexamined how agents behave under benign but underspecified instructions—a common real-world scenario where ambiguity can trigger boundary-violating actions.
AI.method: UnderSpecBench comprises 69 task families grounded in documented incidents, CVEs, or tool behavior across four DevOps capability domains and nine operational control surfaces. Each task isolates underspecification by varying instructions along three axes (intent clarity, target certainty, blast radius) while holding the environment and safe ground-truth action constant. The resulting 2,208 prompt variants are evaluated using deterministic, side-effect-based oracles that classify outcomes as Safe Success, Wrong Target, OverScope, or non-action (clarification, refusal, deferment). Five agent×model configurations (OpenCode, Claude Code, Codex) were tested.
AI.result: 55.8–67.8% of runs violated at least one action boundary. Underspecification causes agents to guess rather than fail. Target underspecification sharply degrades action quality, while blast-radius cues barely reduce action propensity. Non-action behaviors (clarification, refusal, deferment) were also measured.
AI.conclusion: Completion-centric evaluation overstates safe autonomy in coding agents. The findings motivate layered mitigations at the model, harness, and system level to address boundary violations arising from instruction underspecification.

title: TUDUM: A Turkish-Thinking Reasoning Pipeline for Qwen3.5-27B
summary: This paper presents TUDUM (Türkçe Düşünen Üretken Model), a project pipeline for adapting a Qwen-family 27B thinking model toward Turkish reasoning. The central problem is not only to answer Turkish prompts in Turkish, but to make the explicit reasoning trace itself Turkish. A thinking model may translate a Turkish prompt into an English-centered internal or visible scratchpad, solve the problem mostly in English, and only localize the final answer. TUDUM instead treats the generated <think>...</think> block as a trainable behavior. The pipeline starts from the project base checkpoint unsloth/Qwen3.5-27B, applies supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on 15,991 Turkish reasoning examples using LoRA adapters, and then applies GRPO-family reinforcement learning on a proxy-filtered Turkish mathematics environment. The results are mixed. SFT made the model shorter and more consistently Turkish in its reasoning behavior, with large reductions in average response length and thinking exhaustion, but reduced benchmark accuracy. RL recovered some mathematical performance, especially AIME24 at the best early checkpoint, yet did not uniformly improve all benchmarks and did not exceed the base model on the reported Macro-6 average. The contribution is therefore best framed as a technically honest Turkish-thinking reasoning pipeline and evaluation, not as a claim of state-of-the-art Turkish reasoning. The released step-50 model is publicly available.

AI.tldr: TUDUM adapts a Qwen-family 27B thinking model to perform explicit reasoning in Turkish (not just answering in Turkish), using SFT on ~16K Turkish reasoning examples followed by GRPO-based RL. Results show improved Turkish reasoning behavior but reduced benchmark accuracy, with RL partially recovering performance.
AI.motivation: Existing thinking models tend to internally reason in English even when prompted in another language, translating the prompt, solving in English, and localizing only the final answer. The core problem is making the model's explicit reasoning trace (the <think> block) genuinely occur in Turkish, not merely producing Turkish surface output.
AI.method: A two-stage pipeline: (1) Supervised fine-tuning of unsloth/Qwen3.5-27B using LoRA adapters on 15,991 Turkish reasoning examples to train Turkish-language reasoning behavior in the <think> block; (2) GRPO-family reinforcement learning on a proxy-filtered Turkish mathematics environment to recover benchmark performance degraded by SFT.
AI.result: SFT produced more consistently Turkish reasoning with significantly shorter responses and reduced thinking exhaustion, but lowered benchmark accuracy. RL partially recovered mathematical performance (notably AIME24 at the best early checkpoint) but did not uniformly improve all benchmarks and did not surpass the base model on the Macro-6 average.
AI.conclusion: The contribution is a technically honest pipeline and evaluation for Turkish-thinking reasoning, not a claim of SOTA. The step-50 model is publicly released.

title: Geometric Signatures of Reasoning: A Spectral Perspective on Task Hardness
summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning enables large language models (LLMs) to solve complex problems by generating intermediate reasoning steps. While much attention has been paid to the length and content of these reasoning chains, far less is known about their internal geometry. We study the \emph{geometry} of CoT trajectories in the hidden state space of transformer models, formalizing each reasoning chain as a discrete curve in $\mathbb{R}^d$ and characterizing it through spectral, positional, and kinematic geometric functionals. We introduce the effective dimension $d_ρ$ as a measure of trajectory complexity and show theoretically that trajectories with flatter eigenvalue spectra correspond to harder tasks, as they explore more of the hidden dimensions. Lastly, we explore how kinematic features of the trajectory, mean position, positional dispersion, initial and current hidden states, mean velocity, mean speed, and speed dispersion, can be used to predict solution correctness before generation is complete, and may inform future early-stopping strategies. Experimentally, on mathematical reasoning problems from the MATH500 dataset, $d_ρ$ achieves $0.93$ AUC in distinguishing easy from hard problems, while kinematic features potentially can predict correctness from only the first $20\%$ of generated tokens. These correctness signatures transfer across questions of varying difficulty, establishing that the shape of a model's internal reasoning trajectory is a principled window into both task hardness and solution quality.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes the geometric properties of chain-of-thought reasoning trajectories in LLM hidden state space, introducing effective dimension as a complexity measure and showing that kinematic features of these trajectories can predict solution correctness early in generation.
AI.motivation: While prior work focuses on the length and content of CoT reasoning chains, the internal geometric structure of these trajectories in hidden state space remains unexplored. Understanding this geometry could reveal intrinsic properties about task difficulty and solution quality.
AI.method: The authors formalize each CoT reasoning chain as a discrete curve in ℝᵈ and characterize it using spectral, positional, and kinematic geometric functionals. They introduce effective dimension d_ρ, derived from the eigenvalue spectrum of the trajectory's covariance structure, as a measure of trajectory complexity. They then analyze how kinematic features (mean position, positional dispersion, velocity, speed, and their dispersions) correlate with correctness.
AI.result: On MATH500 mathematical reasoning problems, d_ρ achieves 0.93 AUC in discriminating easy from hard tasks, confirming that harder problems produce flatter eigenvalue spectra and explore more hidden dimensions. Kinematic features can predict solution correctness using only the first 20% of generated tokens, and these correctness signatures transfer across questions of varying difficulty.
AI.conclusion: The shape of a model's internal CoT reasoning trajectory serves as a principled lens into both task hardness and solution quality, with potential applications for early-stopping strategies during generation.

title: DRL-CLBA: A Clean Label Backdoor Attack for Speech Classification via DDPG Reinforcement Learning
summary: Deep learning models for speech classification are vulnerable to backdoor attacks, where malicious triggers cause misclassification at inference time. While sample-specific attacks can bypass many defenses, they often rely on poisoned label attack, making them detectable via manual data defense. In this paper, we propose DRL-CLBA, a novel clean label backdoor attack for speech classification that leverages Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) reinforcement learning. We also utilize deep audio steganography to embed sample-specific triggers into source audio, creating feature-space anchors. The proposed reinforcement learning framework effectively optimizes target samples toward trigger-bearing anchor points in the model's deep latent space, enabling label-migration-free poisoning of target samples. Experimental results across three datasets and four different DNNs demonstrate that DRL-CLBA achieves a high attack success rate, effectively bypassing some backdoor defenses. The attack demonstrates strong resistance against fine-tuning, pruning, and spectral signature defenses, exposing critical vulnerabilities in speech-controlled systems.

AI.tldr: DRL-CLBA is a clean-label backdoor attack for speech classification that uses DDPG reinforcement learning and deep audio steganography to embed sample-specific triggers without label migration, achieving high attack success rates while bypassing multiple defenses.
AI.motivation: Existing backdoor attacks on speech models often rely on poisoned-label attacks, making them detectable through manual data inspection. The authors aim to develop a clean-label attack that avoids label tampering while maintaining effectiveness against defenses.
AI.method: The method combines three components: (1) deep audio steganography to embed sample-specific triggers into source audio as feature-space anchors; (2) a DDPG-based reinforcement learning framework that optimizes target samples toward these anchor points in the model's deep latent space; (3) clean-label poisoning that preserves original labels, avoiding manual data defense detection.
AI.result: Experiments on three datasets and four different DNN architectures show DRL-CLBA achieves high attack success rates. The attack demonstrates strong resistance against fine-tuning, pruning, and spectral signature defenses.
AI.conclusion: The proposed DRL-CLBA exposes critical vulnerabilities in speech-controlled systems by showing that clean-label backdoor attacks can be highly effective and evasive, highlighting the need for more robust defenses in audio domain models.

title: Guiding Human Validation of LLM-Generated Code via Verifiable Literate Programming
summary:
Vibe coding democratizes software development by allowing users to generate code via natural-language (NL) interaction with large language models (LLMs). However, the code is reliable only when it faithfully implements the user's intent, which is difficult and labor-intensive for users to validate. Existing validation methods either rely on LLM-assisted automated testing, which suffers from prompt ambiguity and model fallibility, or involve users only in partial software artifacts such as prompts and test cases, which may overlook corner cases and program details. Motivated by a bug study of LLM-generated code, we find that detailed human feedback is essential, as failures often stem from underspecified requirements or subtle semantic deviations.
  This paper presents verifiable literate programming (VLP), a human-in-the-loop framework designed to make the review/validation process of LLM-generated code accessible to users at all programming levels. At its core, VLP proposes unambiguous NL-based documentation as a readable intermediate layer between prompts and code. The documentation demonstrates concrete program semantics and enables users to provide feedback on potential intent-code mismatches. It supports human-involved, end-to-end repair and validation via three techniques: (i) an NL-style literate language with unambiguous syntax and mostly deterministic code-to-documentation translation, (ii) LLM-based fine-grained mismatch detection that uses trace links between prompts and documentation to focus users' review effort on suspicious documentation lines, and (iii) a verification module that leverages user-validated documentation to derive API-usage checks and formal properties, which are then verified against the generated code using model checking. Our evaluation shows that VLP improves code pass@1 from 28.7%-73.2% to 65.4%-93.5% with reasonable user effort.

AI.tldr: VLP introduces a human-in-the-loop framework using unambiguous natural-language documentation as an intermediate layer between prompts and code, enabling users of all skill levels to validate LLM-generated code through mismatch detection, literate programming, and formal verification, improving pass@1 from 28.7–73.2% to 65.4–93.5%.
AI.motivation: LLM-generated code from vibe coding often contains subtle bugs due to underspecified requirements and semantic deviations, and existing validation methods (LLM-assisted testing or partial user involvement) are insufficient because they miss corner cases, suffer from prompt ambiguity, and lack detailed human feedback on program details.
AI.method: VLP proposes three core techniques: (i) a literate language with unambiguous NL syntax and deterministic code-to-documentation translation, (ii) LLM-based fine-grained mismatch detection using trace links between prompts and documentation to highlight suspicious lines for user review, and (iii) a verification module that derives API-usage checks and formal properties from user-validated documentation, verified against code via model checking.
AI.result: VLP improves code pass@1 from a baseline of 28.7%–73.2% to 65.4%–93.5% with reasonable user effort, demonstrating significant reliability gains for LLM-generated code across varied programming tasks.
AI.conclusion: Human-in-the-loop validation through unambiguous literate documentation is an effective and accessible approach to bridging the intent-code gap in LLM-based code generation, combining human judgment with formal verification to achieve high reliability without requiring expert programming skills.

title: AIriskEval-edu: New Dataset for Risk Assessment in AI-mediated K-12 Educational Explanations
comment: 6 pages, 2 figures. Accepted at the IEEE International Carnahan Conference on Security Technology (ICCST 2026), October 14, 2026
summary: This work introduces AIriskEval-edu-db2, a new dataset designed to train and evaluate auditors based on LLMs for an explainable pedagogical risk assessment in instructional content for grades K-12. The dataset comprises 1,639 explanations from 170 curated ScienceQA questions, covering science, language arts, and social sciences. For each question, the dataset includes an explanation written by a human teacher alongside 11 explanations generated by LLM-simulated teacher profiles associated with distinct pedagogical risks. We propose a comprehensive risk rubric aligned with established educational standards that covers five complementary dimensions: factual precision, depth and completeness, focus and relevance, student-level appropriateness, and ideological bias. A key contribution is the addition of 785 explanations with structured explainability annotations, including risk localization and risk description. The annotations are produced through a semi-automatic process with expert teacher validation. Finally, we present validation experiments comparing state-of-the-art proprietary models with a lightweight local Llama 3.1 8B model in both the pedagogical risk detection and the explainability assessment. These experiments evaluate whether supervised fine-tuning on AIriskEval-edu-db2 enables a locally deployable model to approach or outperform stronger frontier models while preserving privacy in educational auditing and assessment tasks.

AI.tldr: AIriskEval-edu-db2 is a dataset of 1,639 explanations for K-12 instructional content, annotated across five pedagogical risk dimensions, with structured explainability annotations; fine-tuned local models can compete with proprietary LLMs on risk detection while preserving privacy.
AI.motivation: There is a growing need for automated auditing of AI-generated educational content to detect pedagogical risks (factual errors, bias, age-inappropriateness, etc.), but existing resources lack structured explainability annotations and privacy-preserving, locally deployable solutions for real-world educational settings.
AI.method: The authors curate 170 ScienceQA questions and pair each with one human-written explanation plus 11 LLM-generated explanations from simulated teacher profiles embodying distinct risks. They define a five-dimensional risk rubric (factual precision, depth/completeness, focus/relevance, student-level appropriateness, ideological bias). A semi-automatic pipeline with expert teacher validation produces 785 explanations with structured risk localization and description annotations. Validation experiments compare proprietary frontier models (GPT-4, Claude, etc.) against a fine-tuned Llama 3.1 8B on both risk detection and explainability tasks.
AI.result: Supervised fine-tuning on AIriskEval-edu-db2 enables the lightweight Llama 3.1 8B model to approach or exceed the performance of state-of-the-art proprietary models on pedagogical risk detection and explainability assessment, while offering the advantage of local deployability and data privacy.
AI.conclusion: AIriskEval-edu-db2 fills a critical gap in explainable AI auditing for education. A locally fine-tuned small model can serve as an effective, privacy-compliant alternative to large proprietary LLMs for detecting and explaining pedagogical risks in K-12 instructional materials.

title: BOUNDARY_SYNC: Measuring Communication-Induced Representational Coupling in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
summary: As large language models (LLMs) are deployed as communicating agents, does inter-agent communication cause outputs to converge? We introduce BOUNDARY_SYNC, a protocol measuring representational coupling via the Coupling Amplification Factor (CAF = JSD_cond / JSD_baseline), where CAF < 1 indicates homogenization and CAF > 1 indicates diversification. In controlled GPT-4o experiments (N=30, ~9,900 API calls), we measure coupling in text and image communication. Key findings: (1) text communication causes significant homogenization (CAF=0.803 [0.740, 0.873], d=1.30, p<0.001), confirmed by no-communication ablation and prompt-perturbation controls; (2) image communication also homogenizes under within-modality baselines (CAF=0.834 [0.811, 0.858]), with comparable proportional effect; (3) group size moderates coupling direction -- K=5 produces homogenization while K=3 yields CAF > 1.0 (point estimates 1.14 and 1.06, CI pending), suggesting a directional shift toward diversification; (4) cross-model replication shows extreme variation (CAF 0.034-0.803), with DeepSeek dominated by format artifacts; (5) coupling is stateless -- driven by prompt context rather than cumulative updating, with continuous consensus producing monotonic convergence. These results establish LLM agent coupling as real, measurable, and controllable at the prompt level, with direct implications for multi-agent system design.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces BOUNDARY_SYNC, a protocol that measures representational coupling between communicating LLM agents using a Coupling Amplification Factor (CAF). Experiments with GPT-4o show that inter-agent text and image communication causes significant output homogenization, group size moderates coupling direction, cross-model replication reveals extreme variation, and coupling is stateless (driven by prompt context rather than cumulative updating).
AI.motivation: As LLMs are increasingly deployed as communicating agents in multi-agent systems, a critical open question arises: does inter-agent communication cause their outputs to converge toward homogeneity? Understanding whether and how representational coupling occurs is essential for designing robust, diverse multi-agent systems and avoiding unintended behavioral collapse.
AI.method: The authors propose BOUNDARY_SYNC, a protocol that quantifies representational coupling via the Coupling Amplification Factor (CAF = JSD_cond / JSD_baseline), where CAF < 1 indicates homogenization and CAF > 1 indicates diversification. Controlled experiments (N=30, ~9,900 API calls) using GPT-4o measure coupling in both text and image communication modalities. The design includes no-communication ablation and prompt-perturbation controls. They also manipulate group size (K=3 vs. K=5), conduct cross-model replication (including DeepSeek), and test whether coupling is stateful (cumulative) or stateless (prompt-context-driven).
AI.result: (1) Text communication causes significant homogenization (CAF=0.803 [0.740, 0.873], d=1.30, p<0.001), confirmed by ablation controls. (2) Image communication also homogenizes under within-modality baselines (CAF=0.834 [0.811, 0.858]), with comparable proportional effect. (3) Group size moderates coupling direction: K=5 yields homogenization, while K=3 yields CAF > 1.0 (point estimates 1.14 and 1.06), suggesting diversification. (4) Cross-model replication shows extreme CAF variation (0.034–0.803), with DeepSeek dominated by format artifacts. (5) Coupling is stateless, driven by prompt context rather than cumulative updating, with continuous consensus producing monotonic convergence.
AI.conclusion: LLM agent coupling is real, measurable, and controllable at the prompt level. These findings carry direct implications for multi-agent system design, particularly regarding group size selection, modality considerations, and the need to account for model-specific coupling behaviors to prevent unintended output homogenization.

title: Reformalization of the Jordan Curve Theorem
summary: We present a case study in reformalization, a variant of autoformalization in which the input proof is not natural language but a formal development in a different proof assistant. Concretely, we report three reformalizations of the Jordan Curve Theorem: from Mizar to Lean, from HOL Light to Lean, and from HOL Light to Agda. We analyse the results and identify pipeline design choices that matter for practical reformalization tasks.

AI.tldr: A case study on reformalization—translating formal proofs between proof assistants—applied to the Jordan Curve Theorem across three pairs: Mizar→Lean, HOL Light→Lean, and HOL Light→Agda, with analysis of pipeline design choices.
AI.motivation: To investigate the practical feasibility and challenges of reformalization—translating formal proofs between different proof assistants—as a complement to autoformalization from natural language. The authors aim to identify key design decisions that affect the success of such translation pipelines.
AI.method: The authors conducted a case study by reformalizing the Jordan Curve Theorem three times: from Mizar to Lean, from HOL Light to Lean, and from HOL Light to Agda. They then analyzed the outcomes of these reformalizations to extract pipeline design choices that impact practical reformalization tasks.
AI.result: Three successful reformalizations of the Jordan Curve Theorem were completed across different proof assistant pairs. The analysis yielded insights into which pipeline design choices are consequential for practical reformalization workflows.
AI.conclusion: Reformalization is a viable approach for transferring formal mathematical developments between proof assistants. The choice of pipeline architecture significantly influences the effectiveness of the translation process, and the case study provides concrete guidance for designing such pipelines.

title: Developers' Experience with Generative AI Beyond Productivity Assessment -- Insights from an Empirical Mixed-Methods Field Study
summary: With the growing adoption of AI-powered coding assistants, organizations and developers are increasingly seeking to optimize their interaction with these tools. Prior research has largely focused on output quality and productivity gains, with limited attention paid to developers' well-being and interaction experiences. This paper presents a developer-centered empirical mixed-methods study to investigate how professional developers engage with Generative AI (GenAI) in their natural work environment. Controlled data collection sessions are combined with natural work periods. Results show that developers are generally satisfied with GenAI, particularly for monotonous, repetitive, and structured tasks, and report perceived efficiency and productivity gains. Copilot interaction type preferences differ by task type and complexity: While both in-code suggestions and chat-based prompting independently improve task efficiency and reduce perceived workload, combining these interaction types within a single task diminishes benefits. We propose a rule-of-thumb for selecting an interaction type based on task characteristics. During development-heavy tasks, results indicate that perceived cognitive load arises from AI interaction, while perceived productivity depends on AI output quality. Participation in this study positively influenced developers' awareness and intentional use of GenAI tools. These findings demonstrate the value of real-world, mixed-methods study designs to understand GenAI tools and developers' experiences with them.

AI.tldr: A mixed-methods study of professional developers using GenAI coding assistants in natural work settings reveals that while GenAI improves satisfaction and productivity for repetitive/structured tasks, combining in-code suggestions with chat-based prompting within a single task reduces benefits. A rule-of-thumb for interaction type selection based on task characteristics is proposed, and study participation itself increased developers' intentional GenAI usage.
AI.motivation: Prior research on AI-powered coding assistants has focused narrowly on output quality and productivity gains, neglecting developers' well-being and interaction experiences. This study addresses that gap by centering on how professional developers actually experience GenAI tools in their natural work environments.
AI.method: A developer-centered empirical mixed-methods study combining controlled data collection sessions with natural work periods, examining how professional developers engage with GenAI tools (specifically GitHub Copilot) during real tasks.
AI.result: (1) Developers are generally satisfied with GenAI, especially for monotonous, repetitive, and structured tasks, reporting efficiency and productivity gains. (2) Both in-code suggestions and chat-based prompting independently improve efficiency and reduce perceived workload, but combining them within a single task diminishes benefits. (3) A rule-of-thumb was derived for selecting interaction type based on task characteristics. (4) During heavy development tasks, perceived cognitive load stems from AI interaction, while perceived productivity depends on AI output quality. (5) Study participation positively influenced developers' awareness and intentional use of GenAI tools.
AI.conclusion: Real-world, mixed-methods study designs are valuable for understanding GenAI tool interactions. The findings highlight the importance of matching interaction types to task characteristics rather than indiscriminately combining them, and suggest that developer experience research should encompass cognitive load and well-being alongside traditional productivity metrics.

title: NAVER LABS Europe Submission to the Instruction-following 2026 Short Track
summary: In this paper, we describe NAVER LABS Europe's submission to the instruction-following speech processing short track at IWSLT 2026. We participate again in the constrained setting, developing systems capable of jointly performing ASR, ST, and SQA from English speech into Chinese, Italian, and German. Building on our previous submission, ranked first in last year's short track, we update our multi-stage training pipeline by replacing the speech projector with SpeechMapper, a method for learning a speech-to-LLM embedding projector using only ASR data. In addition, we introduce a synthetic SQA dataset, fakACL, composed of artificially generated scientific presentations. This dataset is built by prompting the LLM backbone, segmenting the generated talks, and synthesizing speech with SeamlessM4T-large-v2. The combination of an improved speech projection mechanism and domain-specific synthetic data allows our model to outperform last year's best short-track system, while being considerably more compact and relying on a weaker LLM backbone. This year's results place our system tied for first place in the overall short track ranking.

AI.tldr: NAVER LABS Europe presents an IWSLT 2026 submission for instruction-following speech processing, using SpeechMapper for speech-to-LLM projection and a synthetic SQA dataset (fakACL) to achieve tied first place in the short track with a more compact model than prior work.
AI.motivation: Improve upon last year's first-place system for joint ASR, ST, and SQA tasks under constrained conditions by enhancing the speech-to-LLM projection and addressing domain-specific data scarcity with synthetic data.
AI.method: A multi-stage training pipeline that replaces the speech projector with SpeechMapper (trained using only ASR data) and incorporates fakACL, a synthetic SQA dataset generated by prompting the LLM backbone, segmenting outputs, and synthesizing speech via SeamlessM4T-large-v2.
AI.result: The system outperforms last year's best short-track model while being more compact and using a weaker LLM backbone, achieving tied first place in the overall short track ranking at IWSLT 2026.
AI.conclusion: Combining an improved speech projection mechanism (SpeechMapper) with domain-specific synthetic data (fakACL) yields superior performance even with reduced model size and a less powerful LLM, validating the approach under constrained settings.

title: SINA: A Fully Automated Circuit Schematic Image to Netlist Generator Using Artificial Intelligence
summary: Recent advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI) have revolutionized Electronic Design Automation (EDA), particularly through Large Language Models (LLMs) for circuit design tasks. However, their application to analog and mixed-signal domains remains limited by the lack of machine-readable representations of existing circuit design knowledge. Circuit schematic images found in research manuscripts, textbooks, and websites constitute a vast repository of validated designs; however, these visual representations cannot be directly processed by EDA tools. Converting them into machine-readable netlists is essential for enabling simulation, verification, and building comprehensive databases for AI-based models. Current conversion methods lack generalization across both Integrated Circuit (IC) and Printed Circuit Board (PCB) level schematics. Moreover, they struggle with component recognition and connectivity inference, and fail to distinguish between connected junctions and crossing wires. In this paper, we propose SINA, an open-source circuit schematic image-to-netlist generator. SINA is a fully automated pipeline that integrates deep learning for robust component detection, connected-component labeling for accurate connectivity inference, Optical Character Recognition (OCR) for component reference designator extraction, and a Vision-Language Model (VLM) for reliable reference designator assignment. SINA handles both IC- and PCB-level schematics and incorporates dedicated crossing-wires detection to differentiate wire intersections from connections. We validate the correctness of the generated netlists using graph isomorphism techniques. Our experiments demonstrate an overall netlist generation accuracy of 96.67%, which is 2.72x higher compared to state-of-the-art approaches.

AI.tldr: SINA is an open-source pipeline that converts circuit schematic images (both IC and PCB level) into machine-readable netlists using deep learning for component detection, connected-component labeling for connectivity inference, OCR for reference designator extraction, and a VLM for designator assignment. It introduces dedicated crossing-wire detection and achieves 96.67% netlist accuracy — 2.72× higher than prior work.
AI.motivation: Analog and mixed-signal EDA lacks machine-readable representations of existing circuit design knowledge. Vast numbers of schematic images in papers, textbooks, and online are inaccessible to EDA tools. Existing conversion methods fail to generalize across IC and PCB domains, struggle with component recognition and connectivity inference, and cannot reliably distinguish wire crossings from junctions.
AI.method: SINA is a fully automated pipeline comprising: (1) deep learning-based component detection for robust symbol recognition; (2) connected-component labeling for accurate connectivity inference; (3) OCR for extracting component reference designators; (4) a Vision-Language Model (VLM) for reliable reference designator assignment; and (5) dedicated crossing-wire detection to disambiguate wire intersections from electrical connections. Netlist correctness is validated via graph isomorphism techniques.
AI.result: SINA achieves 96.67% overall netlist generation accuracy across both IC- and PCB-level schematics, outperforming state-of-the-art methods by a factor of 2.72×.
AI.conclusion: SINA provides a generalized, high-accuracy solution for converting schematic images to netlists, enabling better utilization of legacy design knowledge for AI-driven analog/mixed-signal EDA. Its open-source nature and dual-domain (IC + PCB) capability address a critical gap in the field.

title: Meta-Benchmarks for Financial-Services LLM Evaluation
summary: Public LLM leaderboards optimise for global average performance and do not capture the specific cognitive demands of financial-services work: a model that leads on MMLU-Pro may underperform on document-grounded compliance reasoning, and a coding leader may handle multi-turn customer interactions poorly. We present a meta-benchmarking framework that organises 452 publicly reported benchmarks into 41 O*NET Generalized Work Activities and aggregates those into 38 BIAN banking business domains spanning sales, operations, risk, and support work. A multiplicative weighting scheme (discrimination x coverage x recency), computed over a rolling model window, rewards benchmarks that still separate the best models, are widely reported, and remain in active use, suppressing saturated legacy tests automatically. These weights scale the K-factor in a pairwise Elo tournament, producing cross-benchmark-comparable work-activity scores without raw score normalisation; business-domain scores are weighted averages of the constituent work-activity Elos. We demonstrate the framework on a point-in-time public snapshot covering 288 models across 25 organisations as of June 2026, and describe the methodology, full taxonomy, design decisions, and limitations with the aim of making the approach reproducible for institutions facing similar selection and governance challenges.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a meta-benchmarking framework that maps 452 public benchmarks to work activities and banking domains, using a multiplicative weighting scheme and pairwise Elo tournament to produce cross-benchmark-comparable scores for financial-services model selection.
AI.motivation: Public LLM leaderboards prioritize global average performance and fail to capture the specific cognitive demands of financial-services work. A model excelling on general benchmarks may underperform on domain-specific tasks like compliance reasoning or multi-turn customer interactions, creating a gap in model selection for financial institutions.
AI.method: The framework organizes 452 publicly reported benchmarks into 41 O*NET Generalized Work Activities and aggregates these into 38 BIAN banking business domains (sales, operations, risk, support). A multiplicative weighting scheme combining discrimination, coverage, and recency — computed over a rolling model window — rewards benchmarks that still separate top models, are widely reported, and remain in active use, automatically suppressing saturated legacy tests. These weights scale the K-factor in a pairwise Elo tournament, yielding cross-benchmark-comparable work-activity scores without raw score normalization. Business-domain scores are derived as weighted averages of constituent work-activity Elos. The framework is demonstrated on a June 2026 snapshot of 288 models from 25 organizations.
AI.result: The framework produces interpretable, cross-benchmark-comparable work-activity and business-domain scores that automatically depreciate saturated benchmarks, demonstrated on a point-in-time snapshot of 288 models across 25 organizations.
AI.conclusion: The meta-benchmarking approach offers a reproducible methodology for financial institutions to evaluate LLMs against domain-relevant cognitive work activities rather than generic leaderboard rankings, addressing selection and governance challenges specific to the industry.

title: SkillFuzz: Fuzzing Skill Composition for Implicit Intents Discovery in Open Skill Marketplaces
summary: Large Language Model (LLM)-based agents increasingly automate software engineering tasks through reusable skills, natural-language instruction documents that guide planning and execution. Open skill marketplaces enable users to assemble agents by co-activating community-contributed skills, but marketplace operators typically audit skills in isolation. As a result, individually benign skills may interact to redirect an agent toward unintended objectives, which we term implicit intents. Detecting such intents is challenging because the effect emerges only through skill composition, execution environments are often unavailable at admission time, and the space of possible co-activations grows exponentially with marketplace size. In this paper, we formulate implicit-intent discovery as a fuzzing problem over skill compositions, where skill compositions are the unit under test, planning artifacts expose agent intent before execution, and deviations from a skill-free baseline serve as a differential oracle. Based on this formulation, we propose skillfuzz, the first execution-free testing approach that extracts structured skill contracts and uses contract-guided Monte Carlo Tree Search to prioritize potentially conflicting compositions. Across representative skill-marketplace workloads, skillfuzz discovers over 1,000 distinct implicit intents under a fixed query budget, confirms more than 80% of the highest-risk flagged compositions during execution-time validation, and identifies substantially more high-severity implicit intents than alternative search strategies while exploring only a fraction of the pairwise interaction space they require.

AI.tldr: SkillFuzz is an execution-free fuzzing framework that detects implicit intents—unintended agent behaviors emerging from benign skill compositions—by extracting skill contracts and using contract-guided Monte Carlo Tree Search to prioritize conflicting compositions, discovering over 1,000 implicit intents and confirming >80% of high-risk flags at execution time.
AI.motivation: LLM-based agents increasingly compose community-contributed skills from open marketplaces, but individually benign skills can interact to redirect agents toward unintended objectives (implicit intents). Current marketplace auditing only examines skills in isolation, missing emergent harmful behaviors. Detection is difficult because harmful effects manifest only through composition, execution environments are unavailable at admission time, and the combinatorial co-activation space grows exponentially.
AI.method: The authors formulate implicit-intent discovery as a fuzzing problem over skill compositions, using planning artifacts as intent signals before execution and a skill-free baseline as a differential oracle. SkillFuzz extracts structured skill contracts and employs contract-guided Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to efficiently explore and prioritize potentially conflicting compositions without requiring execution environments.
AI.result: SkillFuzz discovered over 1,000 distinct implicit intents under a fixed query budget, confirmed more than 80% of the highest-risk flagged compositions during execution-time validation, and identified substantially more high-severity implicit intents than alternative search strategies while exploring only a fraction of the pairwise interaction space they require.
AI.conclusion: Execution-free fuzzing with contract-guided MCTS is an effective, scalable approach for auditing skill marketplaces, revealing that composition-aware security analysis is essential for safe LLM-agent ecosystems.

title: Beyond Supervised Clarification: Input Rewriting with LLMs for Dialogue Discourse Parsing
summary: Rewriting inputs to improve frozen downstream models has become a common strategy in modern NLP pipelines. Prior work on incremental dialogue discourse parsing (DDP) shows that supervised clarification models can rewrite fragmentary or underspecified utterances, such as resolving ellipsis or references, to improve parsing accuracy. In this work, we revisit this idea under realistic deployment conditions, where no clarification supervision is available and the clarifier must rely on zero-shot prompting or feedback from a frozen parser. Across three Segmented Discourse Representation Theory (SDRT) datasets and multiple parsers, we find that last-utterance clarification is far less reliable than suggested by supervised settings. Parser-agnostic rewriting often introduces more regressions than repairs, as edits that enable fixes also disrupt discourse cues relied upon by the parser. A best-of-8 rewriting analysis further reveals a practical ceiling: a large fraction of errors are not repairable through input rewriting alone. A parser-aware clarifier trained with GRPO reduces regressions by up to 37% by learning conservative abstention, yet still fails to produce selectivity-aware clarifications that consistently improve parsing. Together, these findings recast clarification as a selective intervention problem. We identify rewritability prediction, deciding whether an utterance is repairable before intervention, as the key missing capability for input-side optimization of frozen discourse parsers, and a critical direction for improving agentic pipelines more broadly.

AI.tldr: Under realistic zero-shot conditions, last-utterance clarification for dialogue discourse parsing proves unreliable, often causing more regressions than repairs. The authors recast clarification as a selective intervention problem and identify rewritability prediction as the critical missing capability.
AI.motivation: Prior supervised clarification models for incremental dialogue discourse parsing showed promise in rewriting fragmentary utterances to improve parser accuracy. However, these results may not transfer to realistic deployment where no clarification supervision exists, requiring reliance on zero-shot prompting or parser feedback. This gap motivates a rigorous re-evaluation.
AI.method: The authors evaluate last-utterance clarification across three SDRT datasets and multiple parsers under realistic conditions (zero-shot prompting, parser feedback). They conduct a best-of-8 rewriting analysis to assess the ceiling of input rewriting and train a parser-aware clarifier using GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) to reduce regressions through conservative abstention.
AI.result: Parser-agnostic rewriting introduces more regressions than repairs, as edits disrupt parser discourse cues. The best-of-8 analysis reveals many errors are inherently unrepairable via rewriting alone. The GRPO-trained clarifier reduces regressions by up to 37% through learned abstention but still fails to produce selectivity-aware clarifications that consistently improve parsing.
AI.conclusion: Clarification should be reframed as a selective intervention problem. Rewritability prediction — deciding whether an utterance can be repaired before intervening — is the key missing capability for optimizing frozen discourse parsers via input-side modification.

title: MKGR: Multimodal Knowledge-Graph Representation Learning for Cold-Start Protein-Protein Interaction Prediction
summary: Accurate protein-protein interaction (PPI) prediction is central to functional genomics, disease mechanism discovery, and drug development. A difficult setting arises when candidate interactions include proteins that have no observed PPI edges during training, where models relying on network topology alone often lose useful context. This paper presents \method, a multimodal representation framework for cold-start PPI prediction. \method\ combines region-aware protein sequence encoding with four protein-centered biomedical knowledge graphs, including protein-drug, protein-disease, protein-miRNA, and protein-lncRNA associations. The sequence branch extracts contextual representations from structurally informed sequence regions, while graph attention encoders learn modality-specific protein embeddings from sparse biomedical associations. A bridge reconstruction objective regularizes graph learning by recovering shared protein-entity associations, and a pair-level gating module adaptively integrates sequence and graph evidence for each candidate protein pair. Experiments on two benchmark datasets under novel-old and novel-novel cold-start settings show that \method\ consistently outperforms competitive sequence, network, and knowledge-graph baselines across ACC, F1, AUC, AUPR, and MCC.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a multimodal framework for cold-start protein-protein interaction (PPI) prediction that combines region-aware protein sequence encoding with four biomedical knowledge graphs. A bridge reconstruction objective and pair-level gating module integrate sequence and graph evidence, achieving state-of-the-art performance on benchmark datasets under novel-old and novel-novel cold-start settings.
AI.motivation: Traditional PPI prediction methods relying on network topology fail in cold-start scenarios where candidate proteins lack observed interaction edges during training. There is a need for a framework that leverages both sequence information and diverse biomedical knowledge graph associations to robustly predict interactions involving novel proteins.
AI.method: The proposed framework, \method, uses: (1) a region-aware protein sequence encoder that extracts contextual representations from structurally informed sequence regions; (2) graph attention encoders that learn modality-specific protein embeddings from four biomedical knowledge graphs (protein-drug, protein-disease, protein-miRNA, protein-lncRNA); (3) a bridge reconstruction objective that regularizes graph learning by recovering shared protein-entity associations; and (4) a pair-level gating module that adaptively fuses sequence and graph evidence for each candidate protein pair.
AI.result: \method consistently outperforms competitive sequence-based, network-based, and knowledge-graph baselines on two benchmark datasets across five metrics (ACC, F1, AUC, AUPR, MCC) under both novel-old and novel-novel cold-start settings.
AI.conclusion: Integrating region-aware sequence features with multimodal biomedical knowledge graphs via adaptive gating and bridge reconstruction provides a robust and effective solution for cold-start PPI prediction, significantly outperforming existing approaches.

title: Path-level Hindsight Instructions for Semantic Exploration in Vision-Language Navigation
summary: On-policy exploration is a crucial component for training robust Vision-Language Navigation agents, as it exposes the policy to a broader state distribution. However, such exploration inevitably leads to trajectories that deviate from expert demonstrations, resulting in a semantic mismatch between the executed visual stream and the original language instruction. In this work, we address this challenge by introducing Phi-Nav, a unified on-policy framework that leverages hindsight reasoning to align instructions with the agent's actual exploratory journey. Specifically, Phi-Nav operates through a three-stage dual-supervision cycle: 1) the agent performs oracle-guided on-policy exploration, sampling a trajectory while learning from expert action feedback, 2) a hindsight speaker synthesizes a path-level hindsight instruction grounded in the collected visual observations, and 3) the agent conducts a second imitation pass, treating the synthesized trajectory-instruction pair as an additional expert demonstration. Through this process, Phi-Nav bridges the critical semantic supervision gap inherent in on-policy methods, transforming semantically unlabeled movement into dense training signals. Evaluations on the R2R-CE and RxR-CE benchmarks show that Phi-Nav yields competitive performance while requiring only a fraction of the expert demonstrations used by current baselines. These results underscore the necessity of semantic exploration in VLN, positioning Phi-Nav as an effective solution for training embodied agents with limited data.

AI.tldr: Phi-Nav is a unified on-policy framework for Vision-Language Navigation that uses hindsight reasoning to bridge the semantic gap between exploratory trajectories and language instructions, achieving competitive performance with significantly fewer expert demonstrations.
AI.motivation: On-policy exploration in VLN exposes agents to broader state distributions but creates a semantic mismatch between deviated trajectories and the original language instructions, resulting in a supervision gap where exploratory movements lack corresponding linguistic labels.
AI.method: A three-stage dual-supervision cycle: (1) oracle-guided on-policy exploration with expert action feedback; (2) a hindsight speaker that synthesizes path-level instructions grounded in collected visual observations; (3) a second imitation pass treating the synthesized trajectory-instruction pair as an additional expert demonstration.
AI.result: Phi-Nav achieves competitive performance on R2R-CE and RxR-CE benchmarks while using only a fraction of the expert demonstrations required by current baselines.
AI.conclusion: Semantic exploration is essential for VLN, and Phi-Nav provides an effective solution for training embodied agents under limited data regimes by transforming semantically unlabeled on-policy movements into dense training signals via hindsight reasoning.

title: Understanding Agent-Based Patching of Compiler Missed Optimizations
summary: Compiler missed optimizations refer to cases in which compilers failed to optimize certain code. It takes many compiler developers' efforts to implement or patch such missed optimizations. In this paper, we present a systematic study of how well agents patch compiler missed optimizations. We identify a significant challenge that patching a missed optimization requires more than just fixing the reported case, and instead requires generalizing to similar cases. We construct a benchmark of real-world LLVM missed optimization issues and compare agent-generated patches with patches from developers in terms of optimization scope. Our results show that coding agents often optimize the given examples, but many generated patches either cover only part of the developer-intended scope or partially overlap with it; in some cases, they further generalize beyond the reference patch. We further introduce historical-knowledge augmentation techniques that leverage prior LLVM optimization pull requests through retrieval and distillation, showing that they improve developer-aligned generalization and yield practical benefits when applied to real-world IR.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically evaluates how well coding agents can patch compiler missed optimizations in LLVM, introduces a benchmark of real-world issues, and proposes historical-knowledge augmentation techniques (retrieval and distillation from prior optimization PRs) that improve generalization alignment with developer-intended scope.
AI.motivation: Compiler missed optimizations are pervasive and costly to fix manually. The key challenge is that patching a missed optimization requires generalizing beyond the specific reported case to similar code patterns — a capability not well understood for coding agents. The authors aim to systematically assess agent performance on this generalization task and develop techniques to improve it.
AI.method: The authors construct a benchmark from real-world LLVM missed optimization issues. They compare agent-generated patches against developer-written reference patches, evaluating them along the dimension of optimization scope (whether the patch covers only the reported case, the full developer-intended scope, or over-generalizes). They further introduce two historical-knowledge augmentation techniques: retrieval-based augmentation and distillation-based augmentation, both leveraging prior LLVM optimization pull requests to guide agents toward better generalization.
AI.result: Coding agents often successfully optimize the given examples, but many generated patches either cover only part of the developer-intended scope or partially overlap with it; some patches even over-generalize beyond the reference patch. The proposed historical-knowledge augmentation techniques improve developer-aligned generalization and yield practical benefits when applied to real-world LLVM IR.
AI.conclusion: Patching compiler missed optimizations is fundamentally a generalization problem, not merely a point-fix task. Historical-knowledge augmentation via retrieval and distillation from prior optimization PRs meaningfully improves agent performance, helping align generated patches more closely with developer-intended optimization scope.

title: Towards a Phonology-Informed Evaluation of Multilingual TTS
summary: Neural TTS systems can sound natural across languages, but naturalness does not guarantee the preservation of sound contrasts that distinguish words from their grammatical forms. Standard metrics like MOS do not test for this. We propose a classifier-based framework that audits TTS output against language-specific phonological patterns using human speech as a benchmark. Testing Assamese advanced tongue root (ATR) vowel harmony with Meta's MMS TTS, we show that a classifier trained on human speech transfers to synthesized speech with minimal loss. The faithfulness audit reveals that [+ATR] mid vowels are realized as [-ATR] in 1/3 tokens despite an underlying [+ATR] specification, a bias absent in human speech. At the word level, predicted ATR labels classify harmony more accurately than transcription labels, indicating a gap between intended and produced phonology. The framework offers task-specific diagnostics and generalizes to other phonological contrasts with measurable acoustic cues.

AI.tldr: A classifier-based framework audits TTS phonological faithfulness, revealing that Meta's MMS TTS fails to preserve Assamese ATR vowel harmony in ~33% of tokens despite natural-sounding output.
AI.motivation: Standard TTS evaluation (e.g., MOS) assesses naturalness but fails to test whether systems preserve phonologically contrastive sound patterns that distinguish words and grammatical forms. There is a need for diagnostic tools that audit linguistic faithfulness beyond surface naturalness.
AI.method: A classifier-based auditing framework: (1) Train a phonological feature classifier on human speech for a target contrast; (2) apply it to TTS-synthesized speech; (3) compare predicted feature distributions between human and synthesized outputs; (4) benchmark word-level harmony accuracy against transcription-based labels. Tested on Assamese [+ATR] vowel harmony using Meta's MMS TTS.
AI.result: The human-trained classifier transfers to synthesized speech with minimal loss. The audit reveals [+ATR] mid vowels surface as [-ATR] in ~1/3 of TTS tokens, a bias absent in human speech. Predicted ATR labels classify harmony more accurately than transcription labels, exposing a gap between intended and produced phonology.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides task-specific, generalizable diagnostics for auditing phonological faithfulness in TTS, applicable to any contrast with measurable acoustic cues. Results demonstrate that natural-sounding TTS can still harbor systematic phonological errors undetected by MOS.

title: DeadPool: Resilient LLM Training with Hot-Swapping via Zero-Overhead Checkpoint
summary: State-of-the-art large language model (LLM) training takes tens of thousands of graphics processing units (GPUs) for months and encounters failures across the software and hardware stack. Existing fault-tolerance mechanisms either impose non-trivial overhead during failure-free execution or suffer from prolonged recovery latency, particularly under scenarios where a small subset of compute nodes experience permanent failures. %The tradeoff between failure-free overhead and recovery latency forms a space forms a Pareto frontier We present DeadPool to simultaneously address both optimization objectives. DeadPool incorporates a fault-tolerance mechanism that restores LLM training via hot-swapping, namely by replacing failed nodes with spare nodes without terminating the complete job. The hot-swapping of DeadPool is enabled by two ideas: First, it exploits an off-critical-path in-memory checkpointing mechanism for spatial redundancy. Second, it introduces a communicator reconstruction protocol that replaces failed nodes with spare nodes at runtime. DeadPool efficiently overlaps the in-memory checkpointing with computation, thus introducing zero overhead during error-free execution. Upon permanent node failures, DeadPool can rebuild memory states with minimal recomputation by leveraging in-memory checkpoints. We evaluate DeadPool across scales (up to 512 NVIDIA A100 GPUs) and LLMs (up to 65B parameters), and observe zero checkpoint overhead with hot-swapping recovery completing in under 40 seconds. These results show that DeadPool simultaneously achieves both zero-overhead error-free execution and extremely low recovery cost.

AI.tldr: DeadPool is a fault-tolerance mechanism for large-scale LLM training that uses hot-swapping to replace failed nodes with spares, achieving zero checkpoint overhead during error-free execution and recovery in under 40 seconds.
AI.motivation: LLM training on tens of thousands of GPUs over months inevitably encounters hardware and software failures. Existing fault-tolerance solutions force a trade-off between non-trivial overhead during normal execution and prolonged recovery latency, especially under permanent node failures. DeadPool aims to simultaneously optimize both objectives.
AI.method: DeadPool employs two key techniques: (1) an off-critical-path in-memory checkpointing mechanism that provides spatial redundancy by overlapping checkpoint writes with computation, and (2) a communicator reconstruction protocol that dynamically substitutes failed nodes with spare nodes at runtime without terminating the entire job.
AI.result: Evaluated on up to 512 NVIDIA A100 GPUs with LLMs up to 65B parameters, DeadPool achieves zero checkpoint overhead during error-free execution and completes hot-swapping recovery in under 40 seconds.
AI.conclusion: DeadPool successfully eliminates the trade-off between fault-tolerance overhead and recovery latency, delivering both zero-overhead normal execution and extremely fast recovery for large-scale LLM training.

title: Mastermind: Strategy-grounded Learning for Repository-Scale Vulnerability Reproduction
summary: Repository-level vulnerability reproduction is a demanding software engineering (SE) task: an agent must inspect a codebase, infer the input grammar that reaches a vulnerable path, construct a proof-of-conceptv(PoC), and verify that the crash disappears on the patched build. Recent LLM agents can often execute these steps when the approach is correct, yet they still fail by choosing the wrong strategy. This paper argues that strategy, rather than the full action trajectory, is the right learning unit for such SE agents: it is compact enough to optimize, concrete enough to guide execution, and stable enough to store and reuse across attempts. We present Mastermind, a dual-loop framework that separates transferable strategy learning from task-specific experience. A trainable planner learns reusable vulnerability-reproduction strategies through SFT and milestone-based GRPO, while an experience loop maintains task-local strategy records that guide subsequent attempts. The planner is trained independently of the executor, allowing strategy learning to improve multiple frozen executors without modifying their action-generation capability. We evaluate Mastermind on CyberGym using 260 training tasks and 200 held-out evaluation tasks. With GPT-5.5 as the frozen executor, Mastermind achieves an 84.5% pass rate, outperforming open-book PoC context (60.0%), Best-of-8 sampling (63.0%), and iterative improvement (77.0%). The same planner also improves GPT-5.4 mini and GLM~5.1 from 45.0% and 58.5% to 60.0% and 71.0%. These results demonstrate that learning high-level strategies is an effective and transferable mechanism for improving repository-scale SE agents.

AI.tldr: Mastermind introduces a dual-loop framework for repository-level vulnerability reproduction that separates reusable strategy learning from task-specific execution. A trainable planner learns high-level strategies via SFT and milestone-based GRPO, then guides a frozen executor agent. Achieves 84.5% pass rate on CyberGym, significantly outperforming baselines, and the same planner transfers across different executor models.
AI.motivation: Repository-level vulnerability reproduction requires agents to inspect codebases, infer input grammars, construct PoCs, and verify fixes — a complex SE task where current LLM agents often fail not due to incorrect execution but because they choose the wrong high-level approach. The authors argue that strategy (the high-level plan) is the ideal learning unit: compact enough for optimization, concrete enough to guide execution, and stable enough for reuse across attempts and tasks.
AI.method: Mastermind employs a dual-loop architecture: (1) A trainable planner loop that learns transferable vulnerability-reproduction strategies using Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and milestone-based Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), trained independently of any executor; (2) An experience loop that maintains task-local strategy records to guide subsequent attempts on the same task. The planner is frozen at inference time and guides a frozen executor without modifying its action-generation capability.
AI.result: On CyberGym (260 training, 200 held-out evaluation tasks), Mastermind with a frozen GPT-5.5 executor achieves 84.5% pass rate, outperforming open-book PoC context (60.0%), Best-of-8 sampling (63.0%), and iterative improvement (77.0%). The same planner improves GPT-5.4 mini from 45.0% to 60.0% and GLM 5.1 from 58.5% to 71.0%, demonstrating cross-model transferability.
AI.conclusion: Learning high-level strategies is an effective and transferable mechanism for improving repository-scale SE agents. Separating strategy learning from execution allows a single planner to improve multiple frozen executors, and milestone-based GRPO provides an effective training signal for strategy optimization in complex, multi-step SE tasks.

title: Reasoning effort, not tool access, buys first-try reliability in agentic code generation: an observational study
comment: 22 pages, 5 figures, 10 tables. Dataset and evaluation artifacts: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21134406
summary: Agentic coding assistants are increasingly given extra capabilities, such as browser based testing tools and design oriented system prompts, on the assumption that more capability yields better software. This study tested that assumption directly. Ninety independent agent runs built the same application, a real time retrospective board, from one detailed specification, each scored on a fixed 14 criterion functional rubric (42 point maximum) and a visual quality review. The runs spanned several model generations, two agent harnesses, two reasoning effort levels, a testing tool, and two design oriented prompts. Capability tier dominated: frontier models clustered near the ceiling while a low cost local model fell to 24 to 37 points. A criterion level analysis revealed what run totals conceal. Container deployment was the dominant defect, failing first try in 44 percent of runs, with its failure rate shifting sharply across model generations while mean totals moved less than a point. The testing tool raised cost by 42 to 68 percent without improving functional score or reliability, even on interface visible criteria. Raising reasoning effort from High to xHigh lifted first try perfect runs from 28 percent to 89 percent and cut corrective prompts about five fold, for 9 to 29 percent more cost. A design oriented prompt raised visual quality, 4.5 versus 3.0 on a 5 point scale, without lifting function, and a one paragraph paraphrase of its directive reproduced the entire lift. The practical lesson is to match the fix to the failure: most first run failures came from weak reasoning, which a stronger model or more effort prevents, not from visible flaws a checking tool would catch.

AI.tldr: Study tested whether adding capabilities (testing tools, design prompts) to coding agents improves software quality. Across 90 agent runs building the same app, frontier models dominated; a testing tool increased cost 42-68% without improving scores; raising reasoning effort (High→xHigh) boosted first-try perfect runs from 28% to 89%; a design prompt improved visual quality (4.5 vs 3.0/5) without affecting function. Key insight: failures stem from weak reasoning, not visible flaws tools catch — match the fix to the failure.
AI.motivation: Agentic coding assistants are increasingly augmented with extra capabilities (browser-based testing tools, design-oriented system prompts) under the assumption that more capability yields better software. This study directly tests that assumption, questioning whether these additions actually improve outcomes or merely add cost.
AI.method: Ninety independent agent runs built the same application (a real-time retrospective board) from one detailed specification. Each run was scored on a fixed 14-criterion functional rubric (42-point maximum) and a visual quality review. Runs spanned multiple model generations, two agent harnesses, two reasoning effort levels (High and xHigh), a testing tool condition, and two design-oriented prompts. Container deployment failure rate and corrective prompt frequency were also tracked.
AI.result: Frontier models clustered near the ceiling; a low-cost local model scored 24–37 points. Container deployment was the dominant defect, failing first-try in 44% of runs, with failure rates shifting sharply across model generations while mean totals moved <1 point. The testing tool raised cost 42–68% without improving functional scores or reliability, even on interface-visible criteria. Raising reasoning from High to xHigh lifted first-try perfect runs from 28% to 89% and cut corrective prompts ~5-fold, at 9–29% added cost. A design-oriented prompt raised visual quality (4.5 vs 3.0 on a 5-point scale) without lifting function; a one-paragraph paraphrase reproduced the entire lift.
AI.conclusion: Adding capabilities to coding agents is not uniformly beneficial. The dominant failure mode is weak reasoning, not undetected visible flaws. Matching the fix to the failure is critical: stronger models or higher reasoning effort prevent first-run failures, whereas testing tools add cost without commensurate benefit.

title: Object Aligner: A Configurable JSON Schema Similarity Score for Graphs, Applied to LLM Prompt Optimization
comment: 28 pages, This is a submitted version of a manuscript under review at IEEE Access; it has not been peer reviewed
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are often asked to produce JSON conforming to a fixed schema, powering information extraction, tool calling, agentic planning, and knowledge-graph construction. Measuring how closely an output matches a gold reference is essential yet surprisingly hard: exact match is brittle, text similarity ignores structure, and an LLM judge is expensive, opaque, and non-deterministic. We address this with Object Aligner (OA), an open-source Python library that scores two JSON objects deterministically by recursively aligning their trees (the Hungarian algorithm for unordered collections, sequence alignment for ordered ones) and awarding partial credit at the granularity the schema declares. The Object Aligner is configured entirely through a set of JSON Schema extensions, so adapting it to a new task involves annotating a schema rather than writing code. Complex structured data, however, are rarely flat trees: records may form graphs or hypergraphs keyed by arbitrary identifiers, breaking the assumptions of prior similarity metrics. Our central contribution, referential alignment, closes this gap by inferring a bijection between gold and candidate identifiers and scoring every reference through it, so the score is invariant to relabeling. Since recovering this bijection exactly is graph isomorphism, the Object Aligner approximates it with Weisfeiler-Leman color refinement. An order-sensitive sequence regime targets ranking and planning. Since the same alignment localizes every mismatch, the Object Aligner emits ranked repair suggestions at no extra cost. Used as a reward inside the GEPA prompt optimizer, Object Aligner helps or stays neutral across all datasets.

AI.tldr: Object Aligner (OA) is an open-source Python library that deterministically scores JSON outputs against a gold reference by recursively aligning tree structures (Hungarian algorithm for unordered, sequence alignment for ordered), awarding partial credit based on schema annotations. Its key innovation, referential alignment, handles graph-structured data with arbitrary identifiers via Weisfeiler-Leman color refinement. It also emits ranked repair suggestions and serves as an effective reward signal for LLM prompt optimization.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for evaluating JSON output against a gold reference are flawed: exact match is too brittle, text similarity metrics ignore structural relationships, and LLM-based judges are expensive, opaque, and non-deterministic. Furthermore, prior similarity metrics cannot handle complex structured data that forms graphs or hypergraphs keyed by arbitrary identifiers, breaking the flat-tree assumption.
AI.method: OA scores two JSON objects by recursively aligning their trees: it applies the Hungarian algorithm for unordered collections and sequence alignment for ordered ones, awarding partial credit at the granularity defined by JSON Schema extensions. The central contribution, referential alignment, infers a bijection between gold and candidate identifiers using Weisfeiler-Leman color refinement (an approximation of graph isomorphism) so scores are invariant to relabeling. An order-sensitive sequence regime handles ranking/planning tasks. Alignment information also enables automatic generation of ranked repair suggestions.
AI.result: When used as a reward signal inside the GEPA prompt optimizer, Object Aligner helps or stays neutral across all datasets tested.
AI.conclusion: Object Aligner provides a deterministic, interpretable, schema-driven alternative for scoring structured JSON outputs, with referential alignment solving the previously unaddressed problem of graph-structured data with arbitrary identifiers. Its dual utility as both an evaluator and a repair-suggestion generator, plus its effectiveness as a reward for prompt optimization, makes it a practical tool for LLM evaluation pipelines.

title: CALM: Interpretable Cross-Modal Alignment for Biomarker Discovery from Unpaired Data
summary: The interaction between brain structure and genetic influences is key to understanding neuropsychiatric disorders. However, most large-scale datasets are unimodal, providing either neuroimaging or genetics data. We propose CALM, a framework that learns interpretable associations between brain ROIs and genetic pathways from completely disjoint populations. CALM aligns the two modalities in a shared latent space via linear projections that simultaneously match the class-conditional latent distributions and ensure group separability. These projections provide interpretable pathway--ROI associations. When trained on unimodal imaging and genetics datasets, CALM generalizes to an unseen paired dataset, outperforming several state-of-the-art methods and ablation baselines. We also demonstrate stability of the learned associations against a paired baseline. Our experiments on autism spectrum disorder reveal immune and metabolic pathways linked to specific cortical regions and are consistent with established literature. Thus, CALM opens the door to leveraging large unimodal repositories for studying cross-modal interactions in brain disorders across disparate datasets.

AI.tldr: CALM aligns unimodal neuroimaging and genetics data from disjoint populations into a shared latent space using interpretable linear projections, enabling discovery of brain ROI–genetic pathway associations. Applied to autism spectrum disorder, it identifies immune and metabolic pathways linked to specific cortical regions, outperforming state-of-the-art methods.
AI.motivation: Most large-scale biomedical datasets are unimodal (either imaging or genetics, not both), yet understanding neuropsychiatric disorders requires linking brain structure to genetic influences. No existing method effectively learns cross-modal associations from completely disjoint populations without paired data.
AI.method: CALM learns linear projections that map brain ROI features and genetic pathway features into a shared latent space. The projections are optimized to (1) match class-conditional latent distributions across modalities and (2) ensure group separability (e.g., case vs. control). Because projections are linear, the weight matrices directly yield interpretable pathway–ROI associations.
AI.result: CALM, trained on unimodal imaging and genetics datasets, generalizes to an unseen paired dataset and outperforms multiple state-of-the-art methods and ablation baselines. The learned associations are stable when compared against a paired baseline. In autism spectrum disorder, it reveals immune and metabolic pathways linked to specific cortical regions, consistent with existing literature.
AI.conclusion: CALM enables leveraging large unimodal repositories to study cross-modal interactions in brain disorders, opening new avenues for integrative analysis without requiring paired multimodal data.

title: SimWorlds: A Multi-Agent System for Dynamic 3D Scene Creation
summary: LLM agents are increasingly used to translate natural language into 3D scenes in a procedural way, but existing systems focus on static output. Dynamic 4D scenes from text alone, in which liquids flow, particles emit, rigid bodies cascade, and articulated mechanisms move, remain largely unexplored despite their value as editable content and as physics-grounded training data for video generation and embodied AI. Two challenges set the dynamic case apart from static text-to-scene work: an agent must jointly coordinate spatial layout, multiple physics solvers, temporal sequencing, camera, and lighting in a single coherent scene, and verifying motion correctness from rendered video is fundamentally harder than judging a single image. We present SimWorlds: a multi-agent framework that produces dynamic, editable 4D scenes from text, with Blender-specific procedural knowledge, a planner-coder-reviewer workflow driving a fixed ordered sequence of construction stages, a layered scene protocol enforced by a deterministic verifier, and a runtime-state inspection tool suite that catches mechanism failures the rendered image cannot reveal. We also introduce 4DBuildBench, a benchmark for assessing both visual fidelity and physical consistency of the procedural dynamic 3D scenes generated from text prompts. Experiments show that SimWorlds outperforms prior dynamic Blender generation baselines.

AI.tldr: SimWorlds is a multi-agent framework for generating dynamic, editable 4D scenes from text using Blender, featuring a planner-coder-reviewer workflow, layered scene protocol, deterministic verifier, and runtime-state inspection tools; it outperforms prior baselines on the new 4DBuildBench benchmark.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based text-to-3D systems only produce static output, leaving dynamic 4D scenes (with liquids, particles, rigid bodies, articulated mechanisms) largely unexplored. Dynamic scenes are valuable as editable content and as physics-grounded training data for video generation and embodied AI. The dynamic case introduces two key challenges: (1) joint coordination of spatial layout, multiple physics solvers, temporal sequencing, camera, and lighting; (2) verifying motion correctness is harder than judging static renders.
AI.method: SimWorlds employs a multi-agent framework with: (1) Blender-specific procedural knowledge; (2) a planner-coder-reviewer workflow driving a fixed ordered sequence of construction stages; (3) a layered scene protocol enforced by a deterministic verifier to ensure structural correctness; and (4) a runtime-state inspection tool suite that detects mechanism failures invisible in rendered images. The authors also introduce 4DBuildBench, a benchmark evaluating both visual fidelity and physical consistency of procedurally generated dynamic 3D scenes from text prompts.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate that SimWorlds outperforms prior dynamic Blender generation baselines on the 4DBuildBench benchmark, achieving superior visual fidelity and physical consistency.
AI.conclusion: SimWorlds advances text-to-scene generation into the dynamic 4D domain by addressing the unique challenges of physics simulation coordination and motion verification.
