The combination of structured multi-agent workflows, layered protocols, deterministic verification, and runtime inspection tools proves effective for producing physically coherent, editable dynamic scenes.

title: Using embeddings to predict spoken word duration and pitch in Mandarin monosyllabic words
summary: Time-normalized f0 contours of Mandarin words in conversational speech have been shown to be predictable in part from their contextualized embeddings (CEs). The present study investigates whether CEs also predict spoken word duration for 7470 tokens of Mandarin monosyllabic CV words extracted from a Mandarin corpus of spontaneous speech. We show that CEs indeed are predictive for duration, above chance level, not only at the type level, but also at the level of individual tokens, as indicated by the results obtained with the type-wise and token-wise permutation baselines. We also show that the predicted durations are sufficiently precise to back-transform predicted f0 contours in [0,1] normalized time to contours on the ms time scale. The resulting predicted contours approximate empirical contours and also outperform a permutation baseline.

AI.tldr: Contextualized embeddings (CEs) predict not only f0 contours but also spoken word duration for Mandarin monosyllabic CV words in spontaneous speech, at both type and token levels, enabling accurate back-transformation of normalized f0 contours to absolute time.
AI.motivation: Previous work showed CEs predict time-normalized f0 contours of Mandarin words. This study extends that line of inquiry to investigate whether CEs also encode durational information, which would allow normalized contours to be mapped back to real-time (ms) scale — a crucial step for speech synthesis and prosodic modeling.
AI.method: The authors extracted 7,470 tokens of Mandarin monosyllabic CV words from a spontaneous speech corpus. They used contextualized embeddings as predictors for word duration and evaluated predictive performance against both type-wise and token-wise permutation baselines to assess above-chance prediction at both levels. Predicted durations were then used to back-transform normalized f0 contours from [0,1] time to millisecond-scale contours.
AI.result: CEs predict word duration significantly above chance at both type and token levels, as confirmed by permutation baselines. The predicted durations enabled back-transformation of normalized f0 contours to ms-scale, yielding contours that approximate empirical contours and outperform a permutation baseline.
AI.conclusion: Contextualized embeddings carry rich prosodic information beyond f0, encompassing word duration. This dual predictability allows for the reconstruction of full, temporally grounded f0 contours, reinforcing the value of CEs as representations that capture fine-grained phonetic and prosodic detail in spontaneous speech.

title: Message Passing Based Two-Timescale Bayesian Learning for Joint Channel and Memory Hardware Impairments Tracking
summary: Hardware impairments in massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) receivers introduce inter-symbol memory and inter-element coupling, severely degrading channel estimation. This paper employs a residual recurrent gated unit (RGRU) to model the intra-slot memory of the hardware impairments and proposes a message-passing-based two-timescale Bayesian deep learning (MP-TTBDL) framework for joint channel and impairment tracking. Owing to small-scale fading, the wireless channel varies rapidly across slots, whereas hardware impairments drift slowly due to hardware aging and environmental variations. To capture these distinct physical timescales, a fastvarying Markov prior and a slow-varying Gaussian Markov prior are assigned to the sparse channel and the network parameters, respectively. Based on a multi-slot factor graph formulation, a message-passing algorithm is developed. Specifically, the inter-slot messages admit closed-form updates, while the intra-slot factor graph, due to its complex recurrent structure, is partitioned into a channel tracking module and an impairments calibration module. The channel tracking module performs sparse channel estimation via turbo orthogonal approximate message passing (Turbo-OAMP), and the impairments calibration module updates the impairment parameters via a specially designed deep approximate message passing (DAMP) procedure, with the two modules iteratively exchanging extrinsic information through expectation propagation (EP) until convergence. Simulation results show that the proposed framework robustly achieves lower channel estimation error than conventional compensators followed by channel estimation across different online impairment scenarios and signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) conditions.

AI.tldr: A two-timescale Bayesian deep learning framework using message passing is proposed for joint channel estimation and hardware impairment tracking in massive MIMO receivers, combining a residual recurrent gated unit with Turbo-OAMP and DAMP modules that exchange information via expectation propagation.
AI.motivation: Hardware impairments in massive MIMO receivers cause inter-symbol memory and inter-element coupling, severely degrading channel estimation. These impairments drift slowly (due to aging and environmental changes), while wireless channels vary rapidly across slots due to small-scale fading — creating a two-timescale tracking challenge that conventional compensators fail to address robustly.
AI.method: The authors propose the MP-TTBDL framework: (1) an RGRU models intra-slot hardware impairment memory; (2) a fast-varying Markov prior and a slow-varying Gaussian Markov prior are respectively assigned to the sparse channel and network parameters; (3) a multi-slot factor graph is constructed and solved via message passing, where inter-slot messages have closed-form updates, and the intra-slot graph is partitioned into a channel tracking module (Turbo-OAMP for sparse estimation) and an impairments calibration module (specially designed DAMP), with both modules iteratively exchanging extrinsic information through expectation propagation until convergence.
AI.result: Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed MP-TTBDL framework consistently achieves lower channel estimation error than conventional compensator-followed-by-channel-estimation approaches across diverse online impairment scenarios and SNR conditions.
AI.conclusion: The MP-TTBDL framework robustly handles the two-timescale nature of channel variation and hardware impairment drift, outperforming conventional methods and offering a principled Bayesian deep learning solution for practical massive MIMO receivers.

title: Repair the Amplifier, Not the Symptom: Stable World-Model Correction for Agent Rollouts
summary: As agent planning moves from short tool chains toward persistent workflows with thousands or tens of thousands of steps, failures will occur inside large planning graphs rather than in isolated predictions. Replanning the entire graph after every mistake is neither computationally realistic nor desirable: full-graph replay consumes large context budgets, exposes the LLM to many irrelevant symptoms, and can degrade long-context retrieval. This paper studies the missing component in such systems: a world-model corrector that repairs the failed planning graph in place. We compare two families of correctors. The first is the common engineering approach: scan nodes and edges, choose a suspicious local region, and ask an LLM to repair it. We implement strong engineering LLM correctors and find that they can help, especially when given very large contexts. The second family is our approach, WM-SAR (World-Model Subgraph Amplification Repair): instead of scanning for visible symptoms, it works backward from subgraph amplification, identifies the nodes and edges that keep re-amplifying error, and sends only that causal subgraph to the LLM. Across graph simulations and LLM repair experiments, WM-SAR substantially outperforms engineering correctors under realistic token budgets, achieves near-whole-graph stabilization with a compact region, and gives the LLM a cleaner repair target.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces WM-SAR, a world-model corrector that repairs failed planning graphs by identifying and sending only the causal error-amplifying subgraph to an LLM, outperforming conventional engineering correctors—especially under realistic token budgets—and achieving near-whole-graph stabilization with compact repair targets.
AI.motivation: As LLM-based agent planning scales to persistent workflows with thousands of steps, failures occur within large planning graphs rather than isolated predictions. Full-graph replanning is computationally infeasible, consumes excessive context, exposes the LLM to irrelevant symptoms, and degrades long-context retrieval. A missing component is a world-model corrector that can repair failed planning graphs in place without full replay.
AI.method: The paper compares two families of correctors: (1) engineering correctors that scan nodes/edges, select a suspicious local region, and query an LLM for repair; and (2) WM-SAR (World-Model Subgraph Amplification Repair), which works backward from subgraph amplification to identify nodes and edges that persistently re-amplify errors, sending only that causal subgraph to the LLM for repair.
AI.result: Across graph simulations and LLM repair experiments, WM-SAR substantially outperforms engineering correctors under realistic token budgets, achieves near-whole-graph stabilization using only a compact region, and provides the LLM with a cleaner repair target.
AI.conclusion: WM-SAR demonstrates that causal subgraph identification via error amplification is a more effective strategy than symptom-based scanning for repairing large-scale planning graphs, enabling efficient, targeted, and stable repairs without full-graph replay.

title: TestEvo-Bench: An Executable and Live Benchmark for Test and Code Co-Evolution
comment: TestEvo-Bench leaderboard and data explorer are hosted at https://www.testevo-bench.com
summary:
Software tests and code evolve together: a code change should be followed by new or updated tests that record the new software behavior. Yet existing test generation and update benchmarks often isolate the test from the code change, and rely on static metadata that does not verify whether a test is executable or semantically tied to the code change. This makes it difficult to evaluate whether a test automation agent understands how a code change should propagate into the test suite.
  We introduce TestEvo-Bench, a benchmark of test and code co-evolution tasks mined from software repositories, with two tracks: in test generation, the agent shall write new tests to capture the new software behavior; in test update, the agent shall adapt failing existing tests to the changed software behavior. Each task is anchored to a real commit history and packaged with environment configuration to support execution-grounded metrics such as pass rate, coverage, and mutation score. TestEvo-Bench is also a live benchmark: each task records the timestamp of the test and code changes, and new tasks are periodically mined by our automated pipeline, so evaluation can be restricted to tasks postdating a model's training cutoff to reduce data leakage risk. The current snapshot contains 746 test generation and 509 test update tasks, curated from 59,950 candidate co-evolution records across 152 open-source Java projects. We experiment with four state-of-the-art agents that combine strong harnesses (Claude Code, Gemini CLI, and SWE-Agent) with strong foundation models (Claude Opus 4.7 and Gemini 3.1 Pro). Results show that they achieve up to 77.5% success rate on test generation and 74.6% on test update. However, success rate is materially lower on the most recent benchmark tasks and drops significantly under limited per-task cost.

AI.tldr: TestEvo-Bench is a live, execution-grounded benchmark for test-code co-evolution, featuring 746 generation and 509 update tasks mined from real commits. SOTA agents achieve up to 77.5% success, but performance degrades on recent tasks and under cost constraints.
AI.motivation: Existing test generation/update benchmarks isolate tests from code changes and rely on static metadata, failing to verify executability or semantic alignment. This prevents proper evaluation of whether test automation agents understand how code changes should propagate to tests.
AI.method: TestEvo-Bench is mined from 152 open-source Java projects, yielding 1,255 tasks (746 generation, 509 update) from 59,950 candidate co-evolution records. Each task is anchored to a real commit, packaged with environment configuration, and supports execution-grounded metrics (pass rate, coverage, mutation score). It is periodically updated via an automated pipeline with timestamps to enable pre/post-cutoff evaluation, reducing data leakage. Two tracks: test generation (write new tests for new behavior) and test update (adapt failing tests to changed behavior).
AI.result: Four SOTA agents (Claude Code, Gemini CLI, SWE-Agent paired with Claude Opus 4.7 and Gemini 3.1 Pro) achieve up to 77.5% success on generation and 74.6% on update. However, success rates are materially lower on the most recent benchmark tasks and drop significantly under limited per-task cost budgets.
AI.conclusion: TestEvo-Bench provides a realistic, execution-grounded framework for evaluating test-code co-evolution. While leading agents show promising results, their degradation on recent tasks and under cost constraints highlights remaining challenges, and the live benchmark design mitigates data leakage for future evaluations.

title: EduArt: An educational-level benchmark for evaluating art history knowledge in large language models
summary: Large language models now score near ceiling on general benchmarks, but these aggregate measures reveal little about how models behave within single disciplines. Existing art-focused evaluations rely on synthetic questions and rarely report item-level properties. This paper introduces EduArt, an educational-level benchmark for art-historical knowledge and visual reasoning in multimodal LLMs. EduArt comprises 871 human-authored questions from Italian secondary-school exercises and US Advanced Placement Art History exams, spanning two languages and seven formats from multiple choice to in-text word placement and error identification. Twelve models from six provider families were evaluated under a default answer-only condition and a motivation condition requiring written justification, and characterized using Classical Test Theory and a logistic regression isolating the effects of format, language, image presence, and model. The benchmark showed strong psychometric properties (mean discrimination 0.514, 82.3 percent good discriminators), while multiple-choice accuracy saturated near ceiling for six models, showing recognition formats alone cannot distinguish frontier models. Format was a strong independent predictor of accuracy: models exceeding 94 percent on multiple choice fell to 23.9 percent on open completion (Claude Opus 4.6) and 6.2 percent on error identification (Claude Sonnet 4.6). The motivation condition changed accuracy in a predominantly negative, family-dependent direction. These dissociations indicate that art-historical knowledge and the ability to deploy it are distinct capabilities, and that single-format benchmarks overestimate what models can reliably do. Mapping this capability profile is a precondition for responsible use of multimodal LLMs in art-historical scholarship, where tasks demand producing and manipulating content rather than selecting from fixed options.

AI.tldr: EduArt is an educational-level art history benchmark of 871 human-authored questions spanning multiple formats and languages. Testing 12 multimodal LLMs, it reveals that while models saturate on multiple-choice, performance collapses on open-ended formats (e.g., Claude Opus drops from >94% MCQ to 23.9% on open completion), demonstrating that recognition-format benchmarks systematically overestimate model capabilities in art-historical reasoning.
AI.motivation: Current LLM benchmarks aggregate across domains and rely on synthetic questions, revealing little about model behavior within art history specifically. Existing art-focused evaluations fail to report item-level psychometric properties and cannot distinguish whether models possess genuine art-historical reasoning versus mere recognition ability. The authors aim to provide a rigorous, educationally grounded benchmark that maps the capability profile of multimodal LLMs across varied task formats.
AI.method: EduArt consists of 871 human-authored questions drawn from Italian secondary-school exercises and US AP Art History exams, covering two languages and seven formats (multiple choice, open completion, error identification, in-text word placement, etc.). Twelve models from six provider families were evaluated under two conditions: default answer-only and a motivation condition requiring written justification. Psychometric analysis employed Classical Test Theory (discrimination indices) and logistic regression to isolate effects of format, language, image presence, and model identity.
AI.result: The benchmark demonstrated strong psychometric properties (mean discrimination = 0.514, 82.3% of items classified as good discriminators). Multiple-choice accuracy saturated near ceiling for six models, but performance varied dramatically by format: models exceeding 94% on MCQ fell to 23.9% on open completion and 6.2% on error identification. The motivation condition's effect was predominantly negative and model-family-dependent. Format was identified as a strong independent predictor of accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Art-historical knowledge and the ability to deploy it are distinct, dissociable capabilities. Single-format benchmarks, particularly multiple-choice, substantially overestimate what models can reliably accomplish. Mapping full capability profiles across varied task formats is a precondition for responsible use of multimodal LLMs in art-historical scholarship, where real tasks require content production and manipulation rather than selection from fixed options.

title: Revisiting Decentralized Online Convex Optimization with Compressed Communication
summary: Decentralized online convex optimization (D-OCO) is a popular framework for distributed applications with streaming data. To tackle the communication bottleneck, previous studies have investigated D-OCO with compressed communication and proposed several algorithms that are variants of online gradient descent (OGD). However, for D-OCO with exact communication, the best existing algorithms are variants of follow-the-regularized-leader (FTRL). In this paper, for the first time, we propose two FTRL-type algorithms for D-OCO with compressed communication. Compared with OGD-type algorithms, our algorithms are more elegant in both algorithmic design and theoretical analysis. The key insight is that the dual update mechanism of FTRL allows us to make a simple application of the technique for average consensus with communication compression. More specifically, our first algorithm considers the full-information setting, and can match the existing regret bounds. Our second algorithm is designed for the bandit setting, and can significantly improve both the regret bounds and communication costs of existing algorithms.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes the first FTRL-type algorithms for decentralized online convex optimization with compressed communication, offering elegant design and analysis via dual updates combined with compressed average consensus. The algorithms cover both full-information and bandit settings, with the bandit variant significantly improving regret bounds and communication costs over existing OGD-type methods.
AI.motivation: Existing D-OCO with compressed communication relies exclusively on OGD-type algorithms, while the best exact-communication D-OCO methods use FTRL. There is a gap in bringing FTRL's stronger theoretical properties to the compressed communication setting. The authors aim to fill this gap by designing FTRL-based algorithms that are more elegant and achieve better performance.
AI.method: The authors leverage the dual update mechanism inherent to FTRL, which naturally accommodates a technique for average consensus with communication compression. This yields two algorithms: one for the full-information setting and one for the bandit setting, both operating under decentralized compressed communication constraints.
AI.result: The full-information FTRL algorithm matches existing regret bounds. The bandit FTRL algorithm significantly improves both the regret bounds and communication costs compared to existing OGD-type methods.
AI.conclusion: FTRL-type algorithms are not only viable but advantageous for D-OCO with compressed communication, offering more elegant design, matching or superior regret guarantees, and reduced communication overhead, particularly in the bandit setting.

title: Verifiable Knowledge Expansion through Retrieval-Grounded Formal Concept Analysis
comment: 8 pages, 2 figures, Accepted to the 8th epiDAMIK ACM SIGKDD International Workshop on Epidemiology meets Data Mining and Knowledge Discovery (epiDAMIK 2026)
summary: Ontology construction requires deciding which objects, attributes, and structural relations should be accepted as valid knowledge. Language models can propose such structures from text, but their outputs can still be unsupported or inconsistent. This paper proposes a retrieval-augmented small language model (SLM) framework that uses formal concept analysis (FCA) as a symbolic verification loop for knowledge expansion. Starting from seed attributes, FCA proposes implications over a growing formal context. A retrieval-grounded SLM oracle then validates each implication or returns a counterexample. The oracle also supports incidence judgments, consistency checks, and attribute proposals, making accepted implications, counterexamples, contradictions, and corrections inspectable. In a rare ataxia setting constructed from Orphadata resources, retrieval-grounded 10-seed runs obtain relation F1 of 0.29-0.52 and closure-based implication F1 of 0.22-0.30. Larger seed sets increase the number of evaluated implications and often improve implication F1. The lower implication scores reflect a stricter evaluation of derived implications, where one missed or extra relation can affect several implication judgments. Ablations show that incidence judgments in a fixed object-attribute setting can improve closure-based implication scores. However, identifying positive object-attribute pairs remains difficult even when the candidate objects and attributes are fixed.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a framework combining retrieval-augmented small language models with formal concept analysis to iteratively construct ontologies from text, using FCA as a symbolic verification loop for validating proposed knowledge structures.
AI.motivation: Language models can propose ontological structures from text but produce outputs that are unsupported or inconsistent. A principled verification mechanism is needed to ensure only valid objects, attributes, and structural relations are accepted during ontology construction.
AI.method: A retrieval-augmented small language model (SLM) framework uses formal concept analysis (FCA) as a symbolic verification loop. Starting from seed attributes, FCA proposes implications over a growing formal context. A retrieval-grounded SLM oracle validates each implication or returns a counterexample, and also supports incidence judgments, consistency checks, and attribute proposals. All accepted implications, counterexamples, contradictions, and corrections remain inspectable.
AI.result: In a rare ataxia setting constructed from Orphadata resources, retrieval-grounded 10-seed runs achieved relation F1 of 0.29–0.52 and closure-based implication F1 of 0.22–0.30. Larger seed sets increased the number of evaluated implications and often improved implication F1. Incidence judgments in a fixed object-attribute setting improved closure-based implication scores, but identifying positive object-attribute pairs remained difficult even with fixed candidates.
AI.conclusion: The FCA-based symbolic verification loop provides an inspectable mechanism for grounding SLM outputs in ontology construction. While implication-level evaluation is strict and challenging, the framework demonstrates a viable path toward more reliable, retrieval-augmented knowledge expansion.

title: OpenSafeIntent: Evaluating Intent-Calibrated Safe Completion Across Dual-Use Prompt Sets
summary: Safe completion requires models to provide useful assistance without enabling harm, but this behavior is difficult to evaluate with isolated prompts. We introduce OpenSafeIntent, a benchmark of controlled prompt-sets that vary intent while holding the underlying task fixed. Each datapoint contains benign, dual-use, and malicious variants of the same task. This design lets us evaluate whether models calibrate assistance across intent shifts, rather than merely appearing safe on average. Across a broad model suite, we find that prompt-level safety hides important failures: models often fail to remain safe across matched intent variants, dual-use behavior is brittle under paraphrase, high-level answers on risky topics are not reliably safe, and responses that reframe ambiguous requests into safer tasks are substantially less likely to cross the safety boundary. Our results suggest that safe completion should be evaluated as intent-calibrated behavior over controlled task variants, not as a single safety-helpfulness tradeoff over independent prompts.

AI.tldr: OpenSafeIntent introduces a benchmark with controlled prompt-sets (benign, dual-use, malicious variants of the same task) to evaluate whether models calibrate assistance across intent shifts. Findings reveal that prompt-level safety metrics mask failures: models struggle with matched intent variants, dual-use behavior is brittle under paraphrase, and reframing ambiguous requests into safer tasks reduces safety violations. The paper argues safety should be evaluated as intent-calibrated behavior, not a single tradeoff over independent prompts.
AI.motivation: Current safety evaluations rely on isolated prompts, which fail to capture whether models appropriately calibrate their assistance when the same underlying task is framed with different intents (benign, dual-use, or malicious). This makes it difficult to distinguish genuine safety from surface-level compliance that breaks under distribution shifts.
AI.method: The authors introduce OpenSafeIntent, a benchmark where each datapoint is a controlled prompt-set containing benign, dual-use, and malicious variants of an identical underlying task. This paired design enables measuring intent-calibrated behavior — i.e., whether a model appropriately modulates assistance across intent shifts. They evaluate a broad suite of models, analyzing consistency across variants, sensitivity to paraphrasing, and the effect of reframing strategies.
AI.result: Prompt-level safety averages hide critical failures: models frequently fail to remain safe across matched intent variants; dual-use behavior proves brittle under paraphrase; high-level answers on risky topics are not reliably safe; and responses that proactively reframe ambiguous requests into safer tasks substantially reduce the likelihood of crossing the safety boundary.
AI.conclusion: Safe completion should be evaluated as intent-calibrated behavior over controlled task variants rather than as a single safety-helpfulness tradeoff measured on independent prompts. The paired prompt-set methodology provides a more rigorous framework for assessing model safety.

title: UniWind: Toward Unified Day-Ahead Wind Power Forecasting via Physics-Informed State Routing
summary: Day-ahead wind power forecasting is essential for cost-effective power-system operation. It is primarily driven by future meteorological conditions while retaining temporal dependencies in power generation. In practice, observed wind-farm power often entangles physically available power with local environmental effects and latent operational states, such as shutdowns and curtailment. Existing physical models provide useful constraints but adapt poorly across wind farms, whereas data-driven models can capture rich correlations but often conflate meteorological effects with state-induced deviations. In this study, we propose UniWind, a wind power forecasting model based on physics-informed state routing. UniWind first employs a Physical Prior Estimator to construct a site-calibrated physical prior by combining site-conditioned monotonic warping with a shared physical power curve. It further applies a physical upper-bound constraint to shape this prior as a soft envelope of available wind power generation. UniWind then proposes a Latent State Encoder to model operating-state embeddings and transforms the physical prior into final power forecasts through a State-aware Power Corrector, which uses knowledge-guided supervised state routing and bounded, state-specific expert correction. Full-shot and cross-farm zero-shot experiments on more than 20 real-world datasets demonstrate the accuracy and robustness of UniWind.

AI.tldr: UniWind is a wind power forecasting model that combines a site-calibrated physical prior (monotonic warping + physical power curve + upper-bound constraint) with a latent state encoder and state-aware power corrector. The corrector uses supervised state routing and state-specific expert correction to transform the physical prior into final forecasts, demonstrating strong accuracy and zero-shot cross-farm generalization across 20+ real-world datasets.
AI.motivation: Day-ahead wind power forecasting is critical for power system operation. Observed wind-farm power data entangles physically available power with local environmental effects and latent operational states (e.g., shutdowns, curtailment). Existing physical models adapt poorly across farms, while data-driven models conflate meteorological effects with state-induced deviations. A method is needed that leverages physical constraints while disentangling meteorological and operational-state effects.
AI.method: UniWind consists of three components: (1) A Physical Prior Estimator that constructs a site-calibrated physical prior via site-conditioned monotonic warping combined with a shared physical power curve, then applies a physical upper-bound constraint to form a soft envelope of available power; (2) A Latent State Encoder that learns operating-state embeddings; (3) A State-aware Power Corrector that uses knowledge-guided supervised state routing with bounded, state-specific expert correction to transform the physical prior into final forecasts.
AI.result: Full-shot and cross-farm zero-shot experiments on more than 20 real-world datasets demonstrate that UniWind achieves strong accuracy and robustness, outperforming baselines in both in-domain and transfer settings.
AI.conclusion: UniWind effectively bridges physical modeling and data-driven learning by incorporating a physics-informed prior with latent operating-state modeling, enabling accurate day-ahead wind power forecasting that generalizes well across wind farms, even in zero-shot scenarios.

title: Subliminal Clocks: Latent Time Modelling in Diffusion Language Models
comment: Equal contribution: Thomas Fontanari and Simone Petruzzi
summary: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) have recently emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive models. Unlike standard diffusion-based approaches, DLMs are not explicitly conditioned on a timestep, raising a natural question: do these models internally represent denoising progress, and how is such information used downstream? In this work, we show that DLMs do in fact encode a latent representation related to the diffusion timestep within their residual streams. We find that this signal can be reliably extracted using probes across layers, indicating that denoising progress is decodable from internal activations. We further demonstrate that steering the model along a low-dimensional subspace associated with the inferred timestep allows us to systematically modulate its notion of denoising progress, leading to predictable changes in model confidence and entropy. Finally, we analyse the geometry of the identified representation, showing that it exhibits structured and interpretable properties in activation space, and shedding light on how such a signal is processed by these models.

AI.tldr: Diffusion Language Models internally encode a latent timestep signal in their residual streams, which can be probed and steered to modulate model confidence and entropy, revealing structured geometric properties of denoising progress.
AI.motivation: Unlike standard diffusion models, DLMs are not explicitly conditioned on timesteps. This raises the question of whether and how they internally represent denoising progress.
AI.method: Probing classifiers are trained to extract timestep information from internal activations across layers; low-dimensional subspace steering is applied to manipulate the inferred timestep; geometric analysis of the identified representation in activation space is conducted.
AI.result: Timestep information is reliably decodable from residual streams across layers. Steering along the timestep subspace systematically alters model confidence and entropy. The representation exhibits structured, interpretable geometric properties.
AI.conclusion: DLMs do internally represent denoising progress in a structured, manipulable manner, offering insights into their internal mechanisms and potential for controlled generation.

title: SPLIT: Cross-Lingual Empathy and Cultural Grounding in English and Ukrainian LLM Responses
comment: 19 pages, 5 figures, 3 tables. Benchmark paper introducing SPLIT for evaluating empathy, linguistic naturalness, and cultural grounding in English and Ukrainian LLM responses
summary: Large Language Models are increasingly deployed in emotional-support contexts and crisis-related situations. Nevertheless, their cross-lingual abilities in these circumstances remain underexplored. Existing benchmarks emphasize multilingual performance but rarely examine crisis-related empathy and cultural grounding in low-to-mid-resource languages. We introduce SPLIT, a 500-prompt benchmark designed to evaluate LLM consistency in generating emotionally grounded responses across five categories: Stress, Panic, Loneliness, Internal Displacement, and Tension. We evaluate three technically diverse LLMs across three dimensions: Empathetic Accuracy, Linguistic Naturalness, and Contextual & Cultural Grounding. The framework aims to assess and compare the quality of LLM responses in both English and Ukrainian languages, as well as to explore the reliability of the LLM-as-a-jury paradigm. Our findings reveal that Gemini-2.5-Flash and LLaMA-3.3-70B-Instruct degrade when transitioning to Ukrainian, while DeepSeek-V3 remains comparatively stable within our benchmark. We additionally find that human and AI evaluators agree weakly on empathy and naturalness but diverge on cultural grounding. We further argue that producing Ukrainian text is not equivalent to producing Ukrainian emotional support. Our findings may assist in the future development of more culturally tailored benchmark designs, as well as encourage a stronger emphasis on human-centered evaluation.

AI.tldr: SPLIT is a 500-prompt bilingual (English/Ukrainian) benchmark evaluating LLMs on emotionally grounded crisis response across five distress categories. Testing three LLMs reveals performance degradation in Ukrainian for Gemini and LLaMA but not DeepSeek, weak human-AI evaluator agreement especially on cultural grounding, and the finding that producing Ukrainian text ≠ providing Ukrainian emotional support.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used in emotional-support and crisis contexts, yet cross-lingual capabilities for low-to-mid-resource languages remain underexamined. Existing multilingual benchmarks overlook crisis-related empathy and cultural grounding, creating a gap in understanding whether LLMs can provide culturally appropriate emotional support beyond English.
AI.method: The authors introduce SPLIT, a 500-prompt benchmark spanning five emotional categories: Stress, Panic, Loneliness, Internal Displacement, and Tension. Three LLMs (Gemini-2.5-Flash, LLaMA-3.3-70B-Instruct, DeepSeek-V3) are evaluated on English and Ukrainian responses across three dimensions: Empathetic Accuracy, Linguistic Naturalness, and Contextual & Cultural Grounding. Both human evaluators and the LLM-as-a-jury paradigm are employed to assess response quality and evaluator reliability.
AI.result: Gemini-2.5-Flash and LLaMA-3.3-70B-Instruct show performance degradation when switching from English to Ukrainian, while DeepSeek-V3 remains comparatively stable. Human and AI evaluators exhibit weak agreement on empathy and naturalness but diverge significantly on cultural grounding. A key qualitative finding is that generating Ukrainian-language text does not equate to delivering culturally appropriate Ukrainian emotional support.
AI.conclusion: The study highlights a critical gap in cross-lingual emotional-support capabilities of LLMs and questions the reliability of LLM-as-a-jury for culturally nuanced evaluation. The authors advocate for more culturally tailored benchmark designs and stronger emphasis on human-centered evaluation in future work.

title: SCAPE: Accurate and Efficient LLM Training with Extreme Sparse Communication
summary: Communication increasingly dominates the cost of Large Language Model (LLM) pre-training, especially under data-parallel and sharded training schemes, where gradient synchronization and parameter reconstruction overhead increase with model size and system scale. Existing communication-reduction methods either sparsify raw gradients, which can be unstable for modern Adam-style optimizers at high sparsity, or quantize communication, whose savings are fundamentally bounded by bit width and often incur additional runtime overhead. We present SCAPE, a communication-efficient distributed optimizer for LLM training that exploits the stability of AdamS's first-moment to enable aggressive sparsification without loss of LLM quality. Instead of constructing masks from raw gradients, SCAPE derives them from first-moment-based statistics, partitions mask generation across workers to align with optimizer sharding, and delays mask usage by one step so that mask synchronization can overlap with computation. SCAPE also reconstructs the quantities required for second-moment updates from a single synchronized sparse buffer, avoiding an additional collective. We implement SCAPE in Megatron-LM and evaluate its convergence by pre-training GPT-345M on OpenWebText and Llama-500M on SlimPajama-6B using 32 NVIDIA GH200 GPUs on TACC Vista. In both models, SCAPE preserves training stability, validation loss, and downstream task accuracy under 90\% and 99\% sparsity. For Llama-500M, SCAPE reduces end-to-end pre-training wall-clock time by up to 43.3\% while maintaining model quality comparable to dense AdamW and AdamS. For Llama-1.8B, SCAPE achieves up to 3.26$\times$ speedup per step compared to dense AdamS.

AI.tldr: SCAPE is a communication-efficient distributed optimizer for LLM pre-training that leverages AdamS's stable first-moment statistics to enable aggressive gradient sparsification (90-99%), achieving up to 43.3% wall-clock time reduction and 3.26× per-step speedup without degrading model quality.
AI.motivation: Communication dominates LLM pre-training costs under data-parallel and sharded training. Existing methods either sparsify raw gradients (unstable with Adam-style optimizers at high sparsity) or quantize communication (savings bounded by bit width, runtime overhead). A new approach is needed that achieves aggressive communication reduction without compromising training stability or model quality.
AI.method: SCAPE exploits AdamS's stable first-moment to derive sparsification masks instead of using raw gradients. Key techniques: (1) mask generation from first-moment statistics, partitioned across workers to align with optimizer sharding; (2) one-step delayed mask usage so mask synchronization overlaps with computation; (3) reconstruction of second-moment update quantities from a single synchronized sparse buffer, eliminating an extra collective. Implemented in Megatron-LM.
AI.result: Evaluated on GPT-345M (OpenWebText) and Llama-500M (SlimPajama-6B) using 32 NVIDIA GH200 GPUs. SCAPE preserves training stability, validation loss, and downstream accuracy under 90% and 99% sparsity. For Llama-500M, end-to-end wall-clock time reduced by up to 43.3% vs. dense AdamW/AdamS. For Llama-1.8B, achieves up to 3.26× per-step speedup compared to dense AdamS.
AI.conclusion: SCAPE demonstrates that first-moment-based sparsification is a viable and highly effective strategy for communication reduction in LLM pre-training, enabling aggressive sparsity (up to 99%) with maintained model quality and significant practical speedups on real hardware.

title: Safety Testing LLM Agents at Scale: From Risk Discovery to Evidence-Grounded Verification
summary: LLM agents increasingly perform autonomous actions through external tools, leading to complex and evolving safety risks. However, existing safety testing targets expert-designed safety violations, and the corresponding outcomes are evaluated by hard-coded rules, making them costly to extend as agents evolve. To this end, we present Vera, an end-to-end automated safety testing framework that instantiates software engineering testing principles for non-deterministic agents through a three-stage, self-reinforcing pipeline. First, a literature-driven exploration continuously discovers and structures emerging risks into taxonomies of safety risks, attack methods, and tool execution environments. Second, combinatorial composition across taxonomy dimensions produces executable safety cases, each specifying a concrete safety goal, a programmatically constructed initial state, and a deterministic verification predicate grounded in observable artifacts. Third, adaptive execution runs heterogeneous agents in isolated sandboxes where a control agent steers multi-turn interaction based on runtime observations, while evidence-grounded verifiers judge outcomes from environment state and tool-call evidence rather than model self-report. We evaluate Vera on four production agent frameworks (OpenClaw, Hermes, Codex, Claude Code), revealing substantial safety weaknesses, with average attack success rates reaching 93.9\% under multi-channel attacks; we also release Vera-Bench, comprising 1600 executable safety cases spanning 124 risk categories across three execution settings. These results indicate that modular, executable testing infrastructure is essential for rigorous and maintainable safety evaluation of rapidly evolving agentic systems at scale. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/Yunhao-Feng/Vera.

AI.tldr: Vera is an automated safety testing framework for LLM agents that uses a three-stage pipeline (literature-driven risk exploration, combinatorial case composition, and adaptive sandbox execution) to discover vulnerabilities. Tested on four production agent frameworks, it achieved 93.9% average attack success rates under multi-channel attacks and released Vera-Bench (1600 executable safety cases across 124 risk categories).
AI.motivation: Current LLM agent safety testing relies on expert-designed violations evaluated by hard-coded rules, which are costly to extend as agents evolve. The increasing autonomous use of external tools by agents introduces complex and dynamic safety risks that existing approaches cannot systematically address at scale.
AI.method: Vera employs a three-stage self-reinforcing pipeline: (1) Literature-driven exploration that continuously discovers emerging risks and structures them into taxonomies of safety risks, attack methods, and tool execution environments; (2) Combinatorial composition across taxonomy dimensions to generate executable safety cases, each with a concrete safety goal, a programmatically constructed initial state, and a deterministic verification predicate grounded in observable artifacts; (3) Adaptive execution where heterogeneous agents run in isolated sandboxes, with a control agent steering multi-turn interactions based on runtime observations and evidence-grounded verifiers judging outcomes from environment state and tool-call evidence rather than model self-report.
AI.result: Evaluation on four production agent frameworks (OpenClaw, Hermes, Codex, Claude Code) revealed substantial safety weaknesses, with average attack success rates reaching 93.9% under multi-channel attacks. Vera-Bench was released, comprising 1,600 executable safety cases spanning 124 risk categories across three execution settings.
AI.conclusion: Modular, executable testing infrastructure is essential for rigorous and maintainable safety evaluation of rapidly evolving agentic systems at scale. The high attack success rates demonstrate that current production agent frameworks have significant safety vulnerabilities requiring systematic, automated testing approaches like Vera.

title: WARP: Weight-Space Analysis for Recovering Training Data Portfolios
comment: This work appears in the ICML 2026 Workshop on Weight-Space Symmetries (WSS): from Foundations to Practical Applications. Our source code is available at github.com/SprocketLab/WARP
summary: Foundation models are routinely released to the public, yet the data recipes used to train them -- such as domain mixture weights that determine how different sources are sampled -- are rarely disclosed. This creates an access asymmetry: researchers study the resulting models but lack visibility into the training distribution that produces them. Prior works for inferring training data, such as membership inference, detect at the level of individual samples and thus cannot characterize the global composition of the training corpus. We introduce WARP, a framework that recovers a fine-tuned model's training mixtures directly from its released weights. WARP interpolates between the base and fine-tuned models using model merging, generating pseudo-checkpoints that approximate the missing training trajectory and expose a geometric footprint of the training data in the weight space. From these simulated footprints, WARP extracts geometric features and maps them to domain proportions using either a parameter-free softmax readout or an MLP projector trained on synthetic mixtures. In controlled experiments with BERT and GPT-2, WARP recovers domain mixtures with an average MAE as low as 0.046 and 0.104 respectively, outperforming membership inference and a variant with access to the true training trajectory.

AI.tldr: WARP recovers the domain mixture weights of a fine-tuned model's training data directly from weight-space geometry by merging base and fine-tuned models to simulate training trajectories, outperforming membership inference baselines.
AI.motivation: Foundation model training data recipes (e.g., domain mixture weights) are rarely disclosed, creating an information asymmetry where researchers can study models but not the distributions that produced them. Existing methods like membership inference operate at the individual sample level and cannot recover global corpus composition.
AI.method: WARP interpolates between base and fine-tuned model weights via model merging to generate pseudo-checkpoints approximating the training trajectory. Geometric features are extracted from these simulated weight-space footprints and mapped to domain proportions using either a parameter-free softmax readout or an MLP projector trained on synthetic mixtures.
AI.result: On controlled experiments with BERT and GPT-2, WARP recovers domain mixtures with an average MAE as low as 0.046 and 0.104 respectively, outperforming both membership inference baselines and a variant with access to the true training trajectory.
AI.conclusion: Training data composition leaves a recoverable geometric signature in model weights, and model merging between base and fine-tuned checkpoints can effectively surface this signal without requiring access to the original training pipeline.

title: MMIR-TCM: Memory-Integrated Multimodal Inference and Retrieval for TCM Clinical Decision Support
summary: Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) diagnosis, particularly through tongue inspection, faces persistent challenges in subjectivity and reproducibility. The application of multimodal artificial intelligence to TCM clinical tasks, such as syndrome differentiation and prescription generation, is significantly hampered by the semantic gap between visual tongue features and textual reasoning, as well as the lack of large-scale, standardized datasets. To address these challenges, we introduce MMIR-TCM, a novel framework that emulates the diagnostic process of TCM experts by integrating multimodal large language model(MLLM) with memory-augmented segmentation and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Employing a three-stage architecture, MMIR-TCM integrates a training-free Memory-SAM module for robust tongue extraction, a fine-tuned Qwen3-VL model for structured tongue diagnosis generation, and a Qwen3-based RAG component for evidence-grounded clinical decision support generation. The framework was developed and validated using MedTCM, a new large-scale multimodal dataset that we introduce specifically for advanced TCM research. To properly evaluate our framework's clinical accuracy, which existing metrics fail to capture, we also developed TDEU, a domain-specific evaluation metric incorporating semantic understanding and diagnostic importance. Our comprehensive experiments demonstrate that MMIR-TCM significantly outperforms leading models, including GPT-4o and Gemini 2.5 Flash.

AI.tldr: MMIR-TCM is a multimodal AI framework for TCM tongue diagnosis that combines a memory-augmented segmentation module, a fine-tuned MLLM (Qwen3-VL), and a RAG component, trained on a new large-scale dataset (MedTCM) and evaluated with a novel domain-specific metric (TDEU), outperforming GPT-4o and Gemini 2.5 Flash.
AI.motivation: TCM tongue diagnosis suffers from subjectivity and poor reproducibility. The semantic gap between visual tongue features and textual clinical reasoning, coupled with a lack of large-scale standardized multimodal datasets, severely limits the application of multimodal AI to TCM tasks such as syndrome differentiation and prescription generation.
AI.method: The authors propose MMIR-TCM, a three-stage framework: (1) a training-free Memory-SAM module for robust tongue image segmentation; (2) a fine-tuned Qwen3-VL MLLM for generating structured tongue diagnoses from images; (3) a Qwen3-based retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) component for evidence-grounded clinical decision support. They also introduce MedTCM, a new large-scale multimodal dataset, and TDEU, a custom evaluation metric that incorporates semantic understanding and diagnostic importance weighting.
AI.result: Comprehensive experiments show that MMIR-TCM significantly outperforms leading proprietary models, including GPT-4o and Gemini 2.5 Flash, on TCM clinical tasks when assessed using the proposed TDEU metric.
AI.conclusion: The MMIR-TCM framework effectively bridges the semantic gap between visual tongue features and textual TCM reasoning by emulating expert diagnostic workflows through memory-augmented segmentation, MLLM-based diagnosis, and RAG-based decision support. The accompanying MedTCM dataset and TDEU metric provide valuable resources for advancing multimodal AI research in Traditional Chinese Medicine.

title: Rethinking Complexity Metrics for LLM-Integrated Applications: Beyond Source Code
summary: LLM-integrated applications blend natural language prompts with program code, and much of their runtime behavior originates in the prompt layer rather than in the code itself. Existing complexity metrics, however, operate solely at the code level and therefore overlook this behavioral logic entirely. We present HECATE, the first tool designed to assess complexity in both the prompt and code layers of such applications. Central to HECATE is Prompt-as-Specification, a Hoare-logic-inspired formalism that interprets every prompt as a specification of intended behavior. Grounded in 25 complexity dimensions identified across published taxonomies, the tool generates 52 candidate metrics. We assess each metric against 118 components collected from 18 open-source repositories, relying on maintenance activity derived from version history as an empirical proxy for complexity, and discard any metric that loses significance once code size is accounted for. Only ten metrics withstand this test. Seven belong to our newly introduced set; rather than measuring sheer volume, each tallies structurally distinct elements, such as LLM call sites, memory attributes, and prompt templates, an attribute we call structural breadth. Of the three surviving conventional metrics, RFC exhibits a similar breadth-oriented character, while Halstead N and V survive only as a residual effect of size; our top-performing metrics exceed all three. Crucially, the prompt-layer metrics retain significance even when the strongest code-level metric is added as a covariate, establishing prompt complexity as a dimension in its own right. A final validation on 20 components spanning six held-out repositories shows that the two best-performing metrics continue to predict maintenance effort, supporting their generalizability beyond the training set.

AI.tldr: HECATE is a tool that measures complexity in LLM-integrated applications across both code and prompt layers. Using a Hoare-logic-inspired "Prompt-as-Specification" formalism, it generates 52 candidate metrics from 25 complexity dimensions, validates them against maintenance activity in 18 open-source repositories, and identifies 10 significant metrics — 7 of which are novel "structural breadth" measures that count distinct elements rather than volume. Prompt-layer metrics remain significant even when controlling for code-level metrics, establishing prompt complexity as an independent dimension.
AI.motivation: LLM-integrated applications embed substantial behavioral logic in natural language prompts, yet existing complexity metrics operate exclusively at the code level, rendering them blind to an entire layer of system behavior. There is no established method to quantify or assess complexity arising from prompt design, nor any empirical validation of whether prompt-layer complexity independently contributes to maintenance burden.
AI.method: The authors introduce Prompt-as-Specification, a Hoare-logic-inspired formalism treating each prompt as a behavioral specification. From 25 complexity dimensions in published taxonomies, they derive 52 candidate metrics spanning both prompt and code layers. These metrics are evaluated against 118 components from 18 open-source repositories, using version-history maintenance activity as an empirical proxy for complexity. Metrics losing significance after controlling for code size are discarded. Surviving metrics undergo further validation on a held-out set of 20 components from 6 repositories.
AI.result: Only 10 of 52 candidate metrics survive size-controlled significance testing. Seven are newly introduced metrics measuring "structural breadth" — counts of distinct elements like LLM call sites, memory attributes, and prompt templates rather than volume. Three are conventional metrics (RFC, Halstead N, Halstead V), with RFC also exhibiting breadth-oriented character. Prompt-layer metrics retain significance even with the strongest code-level metric as a covariate. The two best-performing metrics generalize successfully to the held-out validation set.
AI.conclusion: Prompt complexity constitutes an independent dimension of software complexity in LLM-integrated applications, distinct from and additive to code-level complexity. Structural breadth — counting distinct elements rather than sheer volume — is a more robust predictor of maintenance effort than traditional size-based metrics. HECATE provides the first validated framework for assessing this dual-layer complexity.

title: Unlocking Speech-Text Compositional Powers: Instruction-Following Speech Language Models without Instruction Tuning
summary: Instruction tuning for speech language models (SLMs) is substantially more challenging than for text-based large language models (LLMs), as it requires learning a new modality and a wide range of speech-specific instructions in addition to those supported by text LLMs. Existing SLM training approaches largely replicate the text LLM training paradigm by synthesizing large-scale speech pre-training and instruction-tuning datasets. However, this strategy is difficult to scale, since speech sequences are significantly longer than text sequences. In this paper, we propose SpeechCombine, an instruction-following speech language model trained without any instruction tuning, using only a single round of speech pre-training on 30k hours of data. Starting from a text LLM base model, we perform continuous pre-training on speech utterances to obtain a speech-adapted model, and then directly combine its weights with the weight difference between the instruction-tuned and base versions of the text LLM. Our results show that this simple combination strategy not only preserves the knowledge and capabilities of the original text LLM, but also effectively transfers them to the speech domain. These findings suggest a new direction for SLM training that avoids reliance on massive speech data.

AI.tldr: SpeechCombine proposes a method to train speech language models without explicit instruction tuning. It starts with a text LLM, performs continuous pre-training on 30k hours of speech, then combines the resulting speech-adapted weights with the weight delta between the instruction-tuned and base text LLM. This preserves textual capabilities while transferring them to speech, avoiding massive speech instruction-tuning datasets.
AI.motivation: Instruction tuning for speech language models (SLMs) is significantly harder than for text LLMs because it demands learning a new modality alongside diverse speech-specific instructions. Current approaches replicate text LLM training by synthesizing large speech pre-training and instruction-tuning datasets, but this is hard to scale since speech sequences are much longer than text. A more efficient paradigm is needed.
AI.method: SpeechCombine uses a single round of speech pre-training on 30k hours of data, starting from a text LLM base model. The speech-adapted model's weights are then combined with the weight difference (delta) computed between the instruction-tuned text LLM and the original base text LLM. No dedicated speech instruction tuning is performed.
AI.result: The weight combination strategy successfully preserves the knowledge and capabilities of the original text LLM while effectively transferring them to the speech domain, without requiring any speech-specific instruction tuning or large-scale speech datasets.
AI.conclusion: SpeechCombine suggests a new direction for SLM training that avoids reliance on massive speech instruction-tuning data, potentially making speech language model development more scalable and accessible.

title: Model Merging as Probabilistic Inference in Fine-Tuning Parameter Space
comment: Accepted for Publication at the 42nd Conference on Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence (UAI), 2026
summary: Model merging aims to combine existing single-task solutions into a multi-task solution without additional data-driven fine-tuning.~Most existing approaches achieve this using geometric properties of local solution spaces. However, such geometric views provide limited guidance for scoring how statistically useful each task-specific update direction is across tasks during merging. To address this, we formulate model merging from a new perspective of probabilistic inference under a product-of-experts (PoE) scenario where each single-task solution defines an energy-based expert model (EBM) over the merged parameters. We show that several existing model merging methods arise as special cases of our framework under energy designs that impose implicit Gaussian assumptions on directional residuals between merged and task-specific models. Empirically, we find that these residuals are often heavy-tailed which exposes a mismatch with the imposed light-tailed Gaussian structures. We address this with a heavy-tailed PoE design based on Cauchy experts, which better captures the observed residual behavior while admitting a provably convergent inference procedure. Experiments across multiple tasks and architectures show significant improvements over state-of-the-arts baselines. Our code is available at https://github.com/MinhLong210/PoE-EBM-Merging.git.

AI.tldr: This paper reformulates model merging as probabilistic inference under a Product-of-Experts (PoE) framework, where each single-task model defines an energy-based expert over merged parameters. It shows that standard merging methods implicitly assume Gaussian residuals, which mismatches the observed heavy-tailed behavior. The authors propose using Cauchy experts for heavy-tailed PoE merging, achieving superior performance.
AI.motivation: Existing model merging methods rely on geometric properties of local solution spaces but offer limited statistical guidance on the usefulness of task-specific update directions across tasks. The observed mismatch between implicit Gaussian assumptions (light-tailed) and actual heavy-tailed residuals in practice motivates a more principled, probabilistically grounded merging framework.
AI.method: The authors formulate model merging as probabilistic inference under a Product-of-Experts (PoE) model, where each single-task solution is an energy-based expert (EBM) over merged parameters. They reveal that existing methods (e.g., Task Arithmetic, TIES, Fisher merging) are special cases with implicit Gaussian energy designs. To address the heavy-tailed residual mismatch, they propose a Cauchy-based heavy-tailed PoE design with a provably convergent inference procedure.
AI.result: Experiments across multiple tasks and architectures demonstrate significant improvements over state-of-the-art merging baselines, validating that the heavy-tailed Cauchy PoE better captures empirical residual distributions than Gaussian-based alternatives.
AI.conclusion: Formulating model merging as PoE inference provides a unifying statistical framework. The heavy-tailed Cauchy design corrects a key mismatch in prior methods, yielding practical performance gains and a provably convergent algorithm for multi-task model merging without fine-tuning.

title: Pre-Flight: A Benchmark for Evaluating Large Language Models on Aviation Operational Knowledge
comment: 9 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables. Benchmark available in inspect_evals (UKGovernmentBEIS/inspect_evals)
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for aviation business operations, from documentation and training generation to customer facing assistants. General purpose benchmarks do not measure whether a model reasons safely and correctly about aviation specific operational knowledge, and the high stakes, regulated nature of the domain makes that gap consequential. We present Pre-Flight, an open source benchmark of 300 multiple choice questions drawn from international standards and airport ground operations material, covering international airport ground operations, ICAO and US FAA regulations, aviation general knowledge and complex operational scenarios. Questions were authored and reviewed by practitioners with experience in air traffic management, ground operations and commercial flying. We evaluate a range of contemporary commercial and open weight models using the Inspect evaluation framework, scoring by accuracy under a standard multiple choice protocol, and we maintain the leaderboard on a rolling basis as new models are released. Against an informal expert reference of around 95%, obtained from a low sample quiz of aviation professionals at a conference, even the strongest model evaluated (released in 2026) reaches 82.7%, having improved only gradually from roughly 75% in early 2025. A substantial and persistent gap below expert level reliability therefore remains. We release the dataset, the evaluation harness and the results, and the benchmark is available within the community evaluations package distributed with inspect_evals. We argue that domain specific evaluation of this kind is a necessary precondition for responsible deployment of generative AI in non safety critical aviation operations.

AI.tldr: Pre-Flight is an open-source benchmark of 300 multiple-choice questions on aviation ground operations, ICAO/FAA regulations, and operational scenarios. Evaluating contemporary LLMs, the best model achieves only 82.7% accuracy against a ~95% expert baseline, revealing a persistent reliability gap that underscores the need for domain-specific evaluation before deploying LLMs in aviation.
AI.motivation: General-purpose LLM benchmarks fail to assess safety-critical, domain-specific aviation knowledge. Given the high-stakes, regulated nature of aviation, this gap is consequential; domain-specific evaluation is a necessary precondition for responsible deployment of generative AI in even non-safety-critical aviation operations.
AI.method: The authors constructed Pre-Flight, a 300-question multiple-choice benchmark sourced from international standards and ground operations material, authored and reviewed by aviation practitioners (air traffic management, ground operations, commercial pilots). They evaluated commercial and open-weight LLMs using the Inspect evaluation framework under a standard multiple-choice protocol, maintaining a rolling leaderboard. An informal expert baseline (~95%) was established via a quiz of aviation professionals at a conference.
AI.result: The strongest model (released 2026) scored 82.7%, improving only gradually from ~75% in early 2025. A substantial gap (~12 percentage points) persists below the ~95% expert reference, indicating that no current LLM approaches expert-level reliability in aviation-specific operational reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Domain-specific benchmarks like Pre-Flight are essential for assessing LLM readiness in aviation. The persistent expert-level gap counsels caution and supports the argument that responsible deployment requires rigorous, domain-tailored evaluation before integrating LLMs into aviation business operations.

title: Challenges and Recommendations for LLMs-as-a-Judge in Multilingual Settings and Low-Resource Languages
summary: LLM-as-a-Judge has become the dominant evaluation paradigm for many natural language generation tasks, due to shortcomings of conventional metrics and high correlations with human judgment, albeit mostly in English. There are now attempts to extend LLM-as-a-Judge to multilingual settings including low-resource languages. However, LLMs have limited proficiency in low-resource languages, and there is often no adequate human validation in these settings. To highlight the scope of the problem and current practices, we explore the use of LLM-as-a-Judge evaluators in ACL Anthology papers focusing on multilingual settings and low-resource languages across a diverse set of tasks. Out of 650 papers mentioning LLM-as-a-judge, only 33 of them focus on low-resource or multilingual settings. Our in-depth analysis of these papers indicates inconsistent evaluation outcomes, a tendency to overtrust LLM judgments in multilingual settings, and the widespread reliance on a single judge model per study. To help the NLP community further, we conclude with recommendations about how to use LLM-as-a-Judge in multilingual and low-resource settings.

AI.tldr: A systematic review of 650 ACL Anthology papers reveals that only 33 address LLM-as-a-Judge in multilingual/low-resource settings, exposing widespread overtrust in LLM judgments, inconsistent evaluation practices, and over-reliance on single judge models—concluding with actionable recommendations.
AI.motivation: LLM-as-a-Judge is widely adopted for NLG evaluation due to high human correlation in English, but its extension to multilingual and low-resource settings lacks adequate validation. LLMs have limited proficiency in low-resource languages, yet no systematic understanding exists of how the NLP community applies this paradigm in such contexts, raising concerns about evaluation validity.
AI.method: The authors conduct a systematic literature review of ACL Anthology papers mentioning LLM-as-a-Judge. From 650 candidate papers, they identify 33 that focus on multilingual or low-resource settings. They then perform an in-depth qualitative and quantitative analysis of these papers, examining evaluation outcomes, judge model selection, validation practices, and reporting consistency across diverse tasks.
AI.result: Only 33 out of 650 papers (≈5%) address multilingual/low-resource settings. Analysis reveals three key findings: (1) inconsistent evaluation outcomes across studies, (2) a systematic tendency to overtrust LLM judgments without sufficient human validation in multilingual contexts, and (3) widespread reliance on a single judge model per study rather than ensemble or comparative approaches.
AI.conclusion: The current application of LLM-as-a-Judge in multilingual and low-resource settings is methodologically underdeveloped and poorly validated. The authors provide concrete recommendations to improve rigor, including the use of multiple judge models, mandatory human correlation studies, and greater transparency in reporting evaluation methodology for low-resource languages.

title: A Mathematical Introduction to Diffusion Models
comment: Lecture notes for the John Tukey Summer Graduate School on Mathematics of Generative Models at SLMath (June 22nd, 2026 -- July 2nd, 2026)
summary: These notes give a proof-oriented introduction to diffusion models from the viewpoint of sampling, tracing a single arc from classical sampling dynamics to modern diffusion samplers, their error analysis, and inference-time control. Throughout, the material is layered into core definitions and identities proved in full, representative estimates proved under simplifying assumptions, and research-level theorems stated with a proof roadmap. The intended audience is beginning graduate students with a background in probability but no prior exposure to stochastic differential equations, stochastic numerics, or diffusion models.

AI.tldr: These notes provide a proof-oriented introduction to diffusion models through the lens of sampling theory, bridging classical sampling dynamics to modern diffusion samplers, with coverage of error analysis and inference-time control, structured across three levels of mathematical depth.
AI.motivation: To fill an educational gap by presenting diffusion models from a unified sampling perspective, making the topic accessible to beginning graduate students with probability background but no prior knowledge of SDEs, stochastic numerics, or diffusion models.
AI.method: The exposition is organized along a single conceptual arc from classical Langevin and overdamped Langevin sampling dynamics to modern diffusion-based generative samplers. The material is layered into three tiers: (1) core definitions and fully proved identities, (2) representative estimates proved under simplifying assumptions, and (3) research-level theorems stated with proof roadmaps.
AI.result: The notes synthesize and present foundational results connecting classical sampling methods to diffusion models, including error analysis bounds and inference-time control techniques, in a pedagogically graduated format.
AI.conclusion: This is a pedagogical manuscript rather than original research; its contribution lies in the structured, proof-oriented exposition that makes the sampling-to-diffusion trajectory accessible to newcomers while providing rigorous depth for more advanced readers.

title: Actual causality in fault trees
summary: Fault trees are a widely used as effective risk models for complex systems, answering the question "what can go wrong?", especially through minimal cut set analysis. We study fault trees from the perspective of Halpern & Pearl's theory of actual causality. This allows us to use fault trees to answer the question "why has it gone wrong?", which is fundamental to failure diagnostics. We give a complete classification of each of the different notions of actual causality in terms of the fault tree's graph structure and logical structure, and show how minimal cut sets give rise to actual causes.

AI.tldr: This paper bridges fault tree analysis with Halpern & Pearl's theory of actual causality, providing a complete classification of actual causality notions in terms of fault tree graph and logical structures, and demonstrating how minimal cut sets correspond to actual causes.
AI.motivation: Fault trees are traditionally used for prospective risk analysis ("what can go wrong?"), but lack a formal framework for retrospective failure diagnostics ("why has it gone wrong?"). The authors aim to fill this gap by connecting fault trees to a rigorous theory of actual causality.
AI.method: The authors apply Halpern & Pearl's formal definitions of actual causality (including the modified HP definition) to fault tree structures. They analyze both the graph-theoretic structure (gates, events, edges) and the logical/probabilistic structure of fault trees, mapping causal notions—actual cause, sufficient cause, necessary cause, etc.—onto minimal cut sets and the Boolean algebra of basic events.
AI.result: A complete classification is given: each variant of actual causality (weak/strong, sufficient/necessary, direct/indirect) is characterized in terms of the fault tree's structural properties. Minimal cut sets are shown to naturally correspond to actual causes, providing a concrete operationalization of Halpern & Pearl's framework in an engineering context.
AI.conclusion: Fault trees, when interpreted through the lens of actual causality, become a dual-purpose tool—usable both for predictive risk assessment and for retrospective failure diagnostics, with minimal cut sets serving as the formal bridge between the two paradigms.

title: BamiBERT: A New BERT-based Language Model for Vietnamese
summary: In this paper, we introduce BamiBERT, a new BERT-based pre-trained language model for Vietnamese that addresses key limitations of PhoBERT -- the current de facto Vietnamese text encoder. Trained from scratch on a 129GB corpus of general-domain Vietnamese text for 20 epochs, BamiBERT supports an extended context length of up to 2048 tokens and operates directly on raw input, eliminating the need for external word segmentation. Across 8 Vietnamese benchmarks, it achieves the best score on 11 of 15 metrics and the second-best on 3 others, setting a new state of the art among "base"-sized Vietnamese encoders and demonstrating strong cross-domain generalization. We release BamiBERT at: https://huggingface.co/Qualcomm-AI-Research/BamiBERT

AI.tldr: BamiBERT is a new BERT-based Vietnamese language model trained from scratch on 129GB of general-domain text. It extends context length to 2048 tokens, eliminates the need for word segmentation, and achieves state-of-the-art results among base-sized Vietnamese encoders across 8 benchmarks.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to address key limitations of PhoBERT, the de facto Vietnamese text encoder, particularly its reliance on external word segmentation and limited context length, by introducing a stronger, more flexible pre-trained model for Vietnamese.
AI.method: BamiBERT is a BERT-based model trained from scratch on a 129GB general-domain Vietnamese corpus for 20 epochs. It operates directly on raw input without requiring external word segmentation and supports an extended context length of up to 2048 tokens.
AI.result: Across 8 Vietnamese NLP benchmarks, BamiBERT achieved the best score on 11 out of 15 metrics and the second-best on 3 others, establishing a new state of the art for base-sized Vietnamese encoders with strong cross-domain generalization.
AI.conclusion: BamiBERT successfully surpasses PhoBERT as a Vietnamese text encoder, demonstrating that raw-input processing, longer context, and large-scale training from scratch yield superior performance. The model is publicly released on HuggingFace.

title: Frequency Shift Physics-Informed Extreme Learning Machine for Solving High-Frequency Partial Differential Equations
summary: Solving partial differential equations (PDEs) with high-frequency solutions remains a central challenge in physics-informed machine learning due to spectral bias -- the tendency of neural networks to learn low-frequency components preferentially. This paper proposes a Frequency Shift Physics-Informed Extreme Learning Machine (FS-PIELM) framework that addresses this limitation through an additive mechanism for weight initialization. Rather than multiplying random weights by a scaling factor, the method translates the mean of the Gaussian weight distribution while keeping the variance fixed at unity, thereby avoiding the variance amplification inherent in scaling-based methods. Two variants are developed: FS-PIELM-L assigns independent frequency magnitudes to individual neurons, while FS-PIELM-G groups neurons for improved robustness. Theoretical analysis shows that the frequency variance under the proposed framework remains bounded and approaches unity regardless of target frequency, in contrast to the quadratic growth of conventional approaches. The method preserves the computational efficiency of extreme learning machines, requiring only a single linear solve. Experiments on seven benchmark problems spanning six equation types -- Helmholtz, wave, Poisson, Klein-Gordon, heat, and advection-diffusion -- on both regular and complex geometries show that the linear variant achieves the best accuracy in six of seven cases, with improvements of one to nearly five orders of magnitude over existing PIELM variants. The code and data accompanying this manuscript will be made publicly available at https://github.com/xgxgnpu/Physics-informed-vibe-coding/tree/main/FS-PIELM.

AI.tldr: FS-PIELM addresses spectral bias in physics-informed extreme learning machines by shifting (rather than scaling) the mean of Gaussian weight initialization, achieving 1–5 orders of magnitude accuracy improvement on high-frequency PDE benchmarks while maintaining single linear-solve efficiency.
AI.motivation: Physics-informed neural networks suffer from spectral bias — preferentially learning low-frequency components — which severely limits their ability to solve PDEs with high-frequency solutions. Existing PIELM variants that multiply random weights by a scaling factor introduce variance amplification, degrading performance.
AI.method: The authors propose a Frequency Shift mechanism: instead of scaling random weights (which amplifies variance quadratically), they translate the mean of the Gaussian weight distribution while keeping variance fixed at unity.
