Two variants are introduced: FS-PIELM-L assigns independent frequency magnitudes per neuron, and FS-PIELM-G groups neurons for robustness. The method requires only a single linear solve, preserving the computational efficiency of extreme learning machines.
AI.result: Theoretical analysis proves the frequency variance remains bounded and approaches unity under the proposed framework, unlike the quadratic growth in scaling-based methods. Experiments across seven benchmarks (Helmholtz, wave, Poisson, Klein-Gordon, heat, advection-diffusion equations) on regular and complex geometries show FS-PIELM-L achieves best accuracy in six of seven cases, with improvements of one to nearly five orders of magnitude over existing PIELM variants.
AI.conclusion: The frequency-shift approach effectively mitigates spectral bias without the variance amplification of scaling-based methods, enabling accurate high-frequency PDE solutions with the computational efficiency of extreme learning machines. Code and data will be publicly released.

title: CLAP: Closed-Loop Training, Evaluation, and Release Control for Domain Agent Post-training
comment: 6 pages, 1 figure. Accepted to CRAE 2026; to appear in SPIE Proceedings. Best Poster Award
summary: Domain agents often face noisy business data, uncertain post-training gains, offline/application mismatch, and adapter-release risk. This paper presents CLAP (Closed-Loop Agent Post-training), a closed-loop method that converts business data into structured SFT samples, decision-preference samples, holdout sets, risk diagnostics, and release-gate records. CLAP combines data validation, target/evidence normalization, reward/KL diagnosis, offline gates, and application-chain replay to decide whether an adapter is suitable for the target application chain. On five anonymized manufacturing-scenario batches, QLoRA-style LoRA-SFT yields modest average gains: overall score increases by 0.0098, pass rate by 0.0240, and evidence accuracy by 0.0280, while hallucination and wrong facts decrease. Yet only 3 of 5 batches improve, some batches regress, and GRPO exposes high KL risks. Application-chain replay further shows that RAG is necessary for factual extraction; under the same 3B backbone and 100 replay cases, an application-RAG-oriented LoRA-SFT adapter improves value, core fields, and answer-evidence doc/page matching over base+RAG, but increases latency. These results support managing domain-agent post-training through an integrated data-training-evaluation-release loop rather than relying on training completion or a single offline score.

AI.tldr: CLAP is a closed-loop method for domain agent post-training that converts business data into structured training/evaluation samples with release-gate diagnostics. Experiments on manufacturing scenarios show modest LoRA-SFT gains (0.01–0.03 improvement across metrics), but only 3/5 batches improve and GRPO reveals high KL risks. Application-chain replay confirms RAG necessity, with RAG-oriented LoRA-SFT improving factual matching at the cost of latency. Results argue for integrated data-training-evaluation-release loops over single offline scores.
AI.motivation: Domain agents face multiple practical challenges: noisy business data, uncertain post-training gains, mismatch between offline evaluation and real applications, and risks associated with releasing adapters. Existing approaches lack an integrated methodology to systematically convert raw business data into training signals, diagnose training quality, and gate adapter releases for target application chains.
AI.method: CLAP (Closed-Loop Agent Post-training) consists of: (1) converting business data into structured SFT samples, decision-preference samples, holdout sets, risk diagnostics, and release-gate records; (2) data validation and target/evidence normalization; (3) reward/KL diagnosis; (4) offline gates; and (5) application-chain replay to determine adapter suitability. The method employs QLoRA-style LoRA-SFT and GRPO training, with a 3B backbone model. Application-chain replay evaluates adapters under realistic RAG conditions using 100 replay cases, measuring value, core fields, answer-evidence doc/page matching, and latency.
AI.result: Across five anonymized manufacturing-scenario batches, LoRA-SFT yields: overall score +0.0098, pass rate +0.0240, evidence accuracy +0.0280, with reduced hallucination and wrong facts. However, only 3 of 5 batches show improvement, with regression in the remainder. GRPO exposes high KL divergence risks. Application-chain replay demonstrates that RAG is essential for factual extraction; an application-RAG-oriented LoRA-SFT adapter outperforms base+RAG on value, core fields, and answer-evidence doc/page matching, but increases latency.
AI.conclusion: Domain-agent post-training should be managed through an integrated closed-loop system spanning data preparation, training, evaluation, and release gating, rather than relying solely on training completion metrics or a single offline score. The modest and inconsistent gains, combined with KL risks and latency trade-offs, underscore the need for continuous diagnosis and application-aware release decisions.

title: CheckRLM: Effective Knowledge-Thought Coherence Checking in Retrieval-Augmented Reasoning
summary: Reasoning Language Models (RLMs) have significantly improved performance on complex tasks by extending the reasoning chain. However, these chains are prone to containing factual errors, particularly in knowledge-intensive tasks. To address this issue, we propose CheckRLM, a framework that improves the reliability of the reasoning process through Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) by timely checking and correcting factual errors. Specifically, CheckRLM extracts factual claims from the reasoning chain to identify and localize subtle knowledge inconsistencies during inference. Upon detection of errors, a refinement mechanism performs minimal-cost yet precise corrections by leveraging external knowledge, ensuring coherence between the reasoning chain and correct knowledge. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CheckRLM substantially outperforms existing baselines, exhibiting a strong capability to mitigate error accumulation in long-horizon reasoning with lower costs. The code and data are available at https://github.com/AI9Stars/CheckRLM.

AI.tldr: CheckRLM proposes a framework that combines Retrieval-Augmented Generation with factual claim extraction to detect and correct knowledge errors in reasoning chains, improving reliability of Reasoning Language Models with lower cost.
AI.motivation: Reasoning Language Models (RLMs) produce long reasoning chains that are prone to factual errors, especially in knowledge-intensive tasks, leading to error accumulation in long-horizon reasoning. Existing approaches lack timely, cost-effective mechanisms to check and correct these errors during inference.
AI.method: CheckRLM extracts factual claims from the reasoning chain during inference to identify and localize subtle knowledge inconsistencies. When errors are detected, a refinement mechanism performs minimal-cost, precise corrections by leveraging external knowledge via Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), ensuring coherence between the reasoning chain and correct knowledge.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show that CheckRLM substantially outperforms existing baselines, demonstrating strong capability to mitigate error accumulation in long-horizon reasoning while incurring lower costs compared to alternative approaches.
AI.conclusion: CheckRLM effectively improves the reliability of RLMs by timely fact-checking and correcting reasoning chains with external knowledge, offering a cost-efficient solution to factual error propagation in complex reasoning tasks.

title: Predicting Closed-Loop Performance of Latent World Models: Offline Checkpoint Selection for MPC and Model-Based RL Under Non-Markovian Rewards in LunarLander
comment: Preprint, 19 pages (16 main text + 3 pages appendix), 7 figures, 4 tables. Video: https://youtu.be/4PxHFW_TYUw , Code: https://github.com/nsmoly/LunarLander_RSSM
summary: We study how to predict the downstream closed-loop performance of a learned latent world model from validation-time diagnostics alone. Choosing the right checkpoint from a world-model training run is difficult: validation loss and multi-step prediction RMSE keep improving long after closed-loop performance has collapsed. We present a suite of structural validation-time diagnostics drawn from optimal-control theory and apply them to Gymnasium's LunarLander v3, which features shaped rewards. We train an RSSM [5, 4] world model on it and treat per checkpoint CEM-MPC return as the oracle for closed-loop quality. By evaluating 40 metrics against this oracle, we find that the strongest single predictor is the Reward Observability Fraction (ROF), which measures the reward predictor's dependence on the observable subspace. We combine ROF with three structural regularizers into a single-number offline checkpoint selection score, the Composite Reward Observability Fraction (CROF). The CROF-selected world model trains a model-based A2C policy that beats a fairly evaluated model-free A2C baseline by ~24.5 return points while using ~65x fewer real-environment interactions, and the same world model also drives a strong zero-shot CEM-MPC policy. Code and data: https://github.com/nsmoly/LunarLander_RSSM.

AI.tldr: World model checkpoint selection is challenging because validation loss and prediction RMSE continue improving even after closed-loop performance degrades. The authors propose Reward Observability Fraction (ROF) — a metric measuring how much the reward predictor depends on the observable subspace — as the best single predictor of downstream performance, and combine it into a composite score (CROF) for offline checkpoint selection, yielding strong model-based policies with far fewer environment interactions.
AI.motivation: During world model training, standard validation metrics (loss, multi-step prediction error) fail to detect when closed-loop control performance collapses, making it difficult to select checkpoints without expensive online evaluation. The authors seek an offline, structural diagnostic that reliably predicts downstream closed-loop quality.
AI.method: An RSSM world model is trained on LunarLander-v3 with shaped rewards. At each checkpoint, CEM-MPC closed-loop return serves as the oracle. The authors evaluate 40 validation-time metrics against this oracle. The key proposed metric, ROF, quantifies how much of the reward predictor's output is explained by the model's observable (as opposed to stochastic/latent) subspace. ROF is combined with three structural regularizers into the Composite Reward Observability Fraction (CROF) for offline checkpoint selection. Selected checkpoints are used for model-based A2C and zero-shot CEM-MPC.
AI.result: ROF is the strongest single predictor of closed-loop return among 40 metrics tested. The CROF-selected world model trains a model-based A2C policy that outperforms a model-free A2C baseline by ~24.5 return points while using ~65× fewer real-environment interactions. The same world model also yields a strong zero-shot CEM-MPC policy.
AI.conclusion: Structural diagnostics from optimal control theory, particularly ROF and its composite extension CROF, enable reliable offline checkpoint selection for world models, bypassing the misleading signals from standard loss curves and dramatically improving sample efficiency in model-based RL.

title: Safety Targeted Embedding Exploit via Refinement
summary: Safety training for large language models (LLMs) is conducted predominantly in English, leaving uncertain how well safety mechanisms generalize to low-resource languages and mixed-language code-switching. We show that this creates an epistemic gap in which models confidently generate harmful responses for inputs that fall outside the distribution of their safety training. To study this phenomenon, we introduce STEER (Safety Targeted Embedding Exploit via Refinement), a gradient-guided attack that identifies words contributing most strongly to the model's refusal behavior and iteratively translates them into low-resource languages to suppress refusal while preserving harmful intent. Across six open-source 8B-parameter models, STEER achieves attack success rates of up to 93.0% on JailbreakBench and 96.7% on AdvBench, outperforming random code-switching and Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG). The resulting prompts also transfer to GPT-4o-mini, achieving a 35.5% attack success rate without requiring access to the target model, suggesting that the underlying weakness is not specific to a single architecture. These findings demonstrate that safety mechanisms aligned primarily on English cannot be assumed to generalize across multilingual inputs. We argue that improving multilingual safety requires broader coverage during alignment and mechanisms that explicitly detect and abstain on out-of-distribution inputs.

AI.tldr: STEER is a gradient-guided attack that iteratively translates refusal-triggering words into low-resource languages, exposing a critical safety generalization gap in LLMs — achieving up to 96.7% attack success rate on open-source models and transferring even to GPT-4o-mini.
AI.motivation: LLM safety training is overwhelmingly English-centric, creating an epistemic gap where models confidently produce harmful outputs when faced with low-resource languages or code-switched inputs. The authors aim to systematically characterize and exploit this vulnerability to demonstrate that multilingual safety alignment cannot be assumed to generalize from English-only training.
AI.method: STEER (Safety Targeted Embedding Exploit via Refinement) is a gradient-guided attack that: (1) identifies tokens/words in a harmful prompt that contribute most strongly to the model's refusal behavior via gradient-based attribution, (2) iteratively translates those high-impact words into low-resource languages using a refinement loop, and (3) preserves harmful intent while suppressing the refusal signal. Evaluated across six 8B-parameter open-source models on JailbreakBench and AdvBench, with transfer testing on GPT-4o-mini.
AI.result: STEER achieves up to 93.0% attack success rate on JailbreakBench and 96.7% on AdvBench, outperforming both random code-switching and the Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG) attack. The generated multilingual adversarial prompts transfer to GPT-4o-mini with 35.5% ASR without white-box access, indicating the vulnerability is architecture-agnostic and stems from a fundamental alignment coverage gap.
AI.conclusion: English-centric safety alignment produces a false sense of security; safety mechanisms do not reliably generalize across languages. The authors argue for broader multilingual coverage during alignment and explicit out-of-distribution detection with abstention mechanisms to mitigate this class of attacks.

title: On the Role of Directionality in Structural Generalization
summary: Several SLOG test categories explicitly involve directional distinctions (modifier position shifts, argument extraction positions), yet AM-Parser, the previous SOTA, uses an AM algebra whose operations do not encode direction. We redesign the symbolic backend around CCG directed types (deterministic CKY + single linear decoder, 30K learnable parameters). Under the same BERT-base encoder, the system achieves 75.9$\pm$6.4% LF exact match, surpassing AM-Parser (70.8$\pm$4.3%). Per SLOG's own category groupings, gains are highly directional: the CCG system outperforms AM-Parser on all 5 position-shift categories (+29.9pp), while AM-Parser outperforms on all 6 recursive-depth categories. Replacing the encoder with DeBERTa-v3-large yields 90.7$\pm$4.9%, with the largest encoder gains in recursive-depth categories, complementary to directionality's gains. Directional representations shift the bottleneck from the symbolic layer (AM-Parser's 0% category ceiling) to the neural layer, which improves with encoder upgrades.

AI.tldr: A CCG-based symbolic backend with directional operations outperforms AM-Parser on position-shift categories in SLOG, shifting the bottleneck from symbolic to neural layers, with further gains from stronger encoders.
AI.motivation: AM-Parser's algebra lacks directional encoding, yet SLOG test categories explicitly require directional distinctions (e.g., modifier position shifts, argument extraction). The authors hypothesize that incorporating directional representations into the symbolic backend will improve performance on these directionally-sensitive tasks.
AI.method: The authors redesign the symbolic backend using CCG directed types with deterministic CKY parsing and a single linear decoder (~30K learnable parameters), paired with a BERT-base encoder. They also experiment with DeBERTa-v3-large to assess encoder scaling effects.
AI.result: Under BERT-base, the CCG system achieves 75.9±6.4% LF exact match vs. AM-Parser's 70.8±4.3%. The CCG system outperforms AM-Parser on all 5 position-shift categories (+29.9pp), while AM-Parser wins on all 6 recursive-depth categories. DeBERTa-v3-large yields 90.7±4.9%, with gains concentrated in recursive-depth categories, complementing the directional gains from the symbolic redesign.
AI.conclusion: Directional symbolic representations shift the performance bottleneck from the symbolic layer (where AM-Parser had a 0% ceiling on certain categories) to the neural encoder, enabling further improvements through encoder upgrades alone.

title: Finite-Lag Operator Geometry of Recurrent Representations
summary: Recurrent representations are trajectories, but representation geometry is often measured from static snapshots. We develop finite-lag operator geometry for recurrent hidden states from observed source-successor pairs $(X_t,X_{t+Δ})$. The primitive is the conditional transport law $Q_Δ(dy\mid x)$, estimated by a dense Gaussian source-smoothing operator. From this directed finite-lag law we derive a source-centered transport tensor $G_Δ$, which decomposes exactly into conditional spread and coherent displacement, and an antisymmetric coordinate circulation $W_Δ^ρ$, which summarizes directed lagged flow. We prove affine covariance with explicit metric dependence of scalar summaries, dense estimator stability on bounded trajectory clouds, and a finite-lag separation result showing that source-centered transport detects deterministic recurrent motion not recorded by infinitesimal carre-du-champ geometry. A linear-Gaussian closed form calibrates the quantities in terms of the update $A_Δ$, source covariance, and innovation covariance. Controlled experiments validate the decomposition, circulation, covariance, and stability predictions. In performance matched repeat-copy networks, the framework reveals architecture dependent differences in total transport scale and coherent displacement trace, while coherent displacement fraction is metric and resolution dependent.

AI.tldr: Develops finite-lag operator geometry for recurrent neural representations, decomposing conditional transport into coherent displacement, spread, and circulation. Reveals architecture-dependent transport properties in matched RNNs.
AI.motivation: Recurrent neural representations evolve as trajectories, yet standard representation geometry relies on static snapshots, missing directed temporal structure. Existing infinitesimal generators (carré-du-champ) fail to capture deterministic recurrent motion at finite lags.
AI.method: Introduces the finite-lag conditional transport law Q_Δ(dy|x) estimated via dense Gaussian source-smoothing. From this, derives a source-centered transport tensor G_Δ decomposing into conditional spread and coherent displacement, plus an antisymmetric coordinate circulation W_Δ^ρ. Proves affine covariance, estimator stability on bounded trajectory clouds, and a finite-lag separation result. Validates via controlled experiments and applies to performance-matched repeat-copy RNNs.
AI.result: The transport tensor decomposition exactly separates coherent displacement from conditional spread. Circulation captures directed lagged flow. Linear-Gaussian closed form connects quantities to update matrix A_Δ, source covariance, and innovation covariance. In matched repeat-copy networks, total transport scale and coherent displacement trace differ by architecture, while coherent displacement fraction depends on metric and resolution.
AI.conclusion: Finite-lag source-centered transport geometry captures directed recurrent dynamics invisible to static or infinitesimal methods, providing a principled tool for comparing recurrent architectures and understanding temporal representation structure.

title: CamoNAS: Neural Architecture Search for Enhanced Camouflaged Object Detection
comment: Published in The Visual Computer. Author manuscript version
summary: Camouflaged Object Detection (COD) aims to locate and segment objects that blend into their surroundings, presenting challenges due to weak edge cues and ill-defined boundaries. Traditional COD models rely on hand-designed architectures and multi-scale feature fusion, which are often guided by intuition rather than systematic search. This paper introduces CamoNAS, a frequency-aware multi-resolution Neural Architecture Search (NAS) framework for COD. CamoNAS automatically searches both cell-level operations and network-level downsampling paths, forming a hierarchical search space tailored to detect camouflaged objects. Additionally, it adopts an RGB frequency dual-stream architecture, where a learnable wavelet transform complements the RGB spatial stream. CamoNAS achieves state-of-the-art performance on four COD benchmarks (CAMO, COD10K, NC4K, CHAMELEON), highlighting the effectiveness of NAS for COD. Our code is available at https://github.com/rendaweiSIMIT/CamoNAS.

AI.tldr: CamoNAS is a neural architecture search framework for camouflaged object detection that automatically searches cell-level operations and network-level downsampling paths, using a frequency-aware RGB dual-stream design with learnable wavelet transforms, achieving SOTA on four COD benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Traditional COD models rely on hand-designed, intuition-guided architectures and multi-scale feature fusion, lacking systematic architectural optimization tailored to the unique challenges of camouflaged objects (weak edges, ill-defined boundaries).
AI.method: CamoNAS introduces a hierarchical NAS search space covering both cell-level operations and network-level downsampling paths. It employs an RGB frequency dual-stream architecture where a learnable wavelet transform complements the RGB spatial stream, enabling frequency-aware feature learning.
AI.result: CamoNAS achieves state-of-the-art performance on four COD benchmarks: CAMO, COD10K, NC4K, and CHAMELEON.
AI.conclusion: NAS is an effective and promising approach for COD, outperforming hand-crafted architectures by systematically discovering architectures optimized for camouflaged object detection.

title: World Wide Models: Literary Tools for Cultural AI
summary: LLMs stage a new form of cultural encounter that is massive, automated, and monolingual. Literary disciplines have always negotiated cultural struggles with comparative reading of literature, narratological and poetic analysis, critical theory, world literature, and translation. These tools have now become indispensable for building culturally literate AI. The essay develops a layered framework toward more nuanced textual models and pluralistic interpretations of AI, emphasizing the natural intersections of literature and AI development, connecting current debates in critical theory with structural monolingualism, and suggesting a new application of world literature approaches to address global AI textuality through macrostructure, circulation, and untranslatability.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that literary disciplines offer essential tools—comparative reading, narratology, critical theory, world literature—for building culturally literate AI, and proposes a layered framework to address the structural monolingualism and cultural homogenization inherent in large language models.
AI.motivation: LLMs represent a massive, automated, and monolingual form of cultural encounter that risks flattening cultural diversity. Literary studies have long developed sophisticated methods for negotiating cultural struggles across texts and traditions. The author contends these disciplinary tools are now indispensable for creating AI systems that are genuinely culturally literate rather than structurally monolingual.
AI.method: The essay develops a layered framework that connects three domains: (1) current debates in critical theory with the problem of structural monolingualism in AI, (2) literary analysis techniques (narratology, poetics, comparative reading) as methods for building nuanced textual models, and (3) world literature approaches—specifically macrostructure, circulation, and untranslatability—as a novel lens for addressing global AI textuality and enabling pluralistic interpretation.
AI.result: The proposed framework demonstrates that literary disciplines can productively intervene in AI development by revealing the natural intersections between literature and AI, offering concrete analytical tools for more nuanced textual models, and reframing global AI textuality through the conceptual vocabulary of world literature studies.
AI.conclusion: Building culturally literate AI requires integrating the interpretive and comparative traditions of literary scholarship. The world literature paradigm—with its attention to macrostructure, circulation, and untranslatability—provides a particularly apt model for developing AI systems capable of pluralistic, culturally aware textual engagement rather than monolingual homogenization.

title: Efficient Temporal Point Processes via Monotone Alternating Splines
summary: Temporal point processes (TPPs) have widespread applications across various domains. Compared to modeling the conditional intensity of a TPP, modeling its cumulative conditional intensity function (CCIF) improves computational efficiency and eliminates numerical approximation errors. However, current CCIF parameterizations uniformly rely on Monotone Neural Networks (MNNs), which we identify as suffering from three structural deadlocks--convexity restrictions, saturation limits, and violations of CCIF modeling requirements--that fundamentally restrict their representational capacity for complex temporal dynamics. To resolve these bottlenecks, this paper proposes a novel framework called Monotone Alternating Splines (MAS). By leveraging distinct interpolation and extrapolation components, MAS provides a flexible and efficient framework for modeling CCIFs. Theoretically, MAS's interpolation provides strong fitting accuracy, while its extrapolation supports robust generalization, reducing the irreducible approximation gaps of MNNs. Extensive experiments show that MAS achieves superior performance on both synthetic and real-world datasets.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies critical limitations (convexity, saturation, CCIF violation) in existing Monotone Neural Network-based CCIF parameterizations for temporal point processes and proposes Monotone Alternating Splines (MAS), which use separate interpolation and extrapolation components to achieve better fitting accuracy and generalization.
AI.motivation: Existing cumulative conditional intensity function (CCIF) parameterizations for TPPs uniformly rely on Monotone Neural Networks (MNNs), which suffer from three structural deadlocks: convexity restrictions limiting shape flexibility, saturation limits at extreme values, and inherent violations of CCIF modeling requirements. These bottlenecks fundamentally restrict representational capacity for complex temporal dynamics.
AI.method: The authors propose Monotone Alternating Splines (MAS), a novel framework that decomposes CCIF modeling into distinct interpolation and extrapolation components. The interpolation component provides high fitting accuracy within the observed data range, while the extrapolation component ensures robust generalization beyond observed data, together reducing the irreducible approximation gaps inherent in MNNs.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that MAS achieves superior performance compared to existing MNN-based approaches.
AI.conclusion: MAS effectively resolves the structural deadlocks of MNNs for CCIF modeling in TPPs, offering a more flexible, efficient, and theoretically grounded framework with strong empirical performance.

title: SkillCoach: Self-Evolving Rubrics for Evaluating and Enhancing Agentic Skill-Use
summary: Skills are becoming a reusable operational layer for LLM agents, encoding SOPs, domain rules, tool workflows, scripts, and validation routines. In realistic skill repositories, overlapping skills make reliable skill-use difficult. Final verifier success is too coarse for both evaluation and training, since an agent may pass through trial and error while selecting distractor skills, skipping required steps, composing workflows incorrectly or omitting final checks. We introduce SkillCoach, a self-evolving rubric framework for evaluating and enhancing agentic skill-use. SkillCoach derives skill-grounded process rubrics from real rollouts and evaluates trajectories along four dimensions: skill selection, skill following, skill composition, and skill-grounded reflection. It keeps the external verifier as a separate outcome signal, allowing process quality to be distinguished from accidental task success. The evolved rubrics further serve as process supervision for selecting high-quality training trajectories. Experiments show that evolved rubrics substantially improve evaluation quality, expose failures hidden by final accuracy, and provide stronger supervision signals than outcome-only filtering for enhancing agentic skill-use.

AI.tldr: SkillCoach introduces self-evolving rubrics that evaluate LLM agent skill-use along four process dimensions (selection, following, composition, reflection), distinguishing process quality from accidental task success, and using these rubrics as supervision for training data selection.
AI.motivation: In realistic skill repositories with overlapping skills, final verifier success is too coarse a signal—agents can succeed accidentally despite selecting wrong skills, skipping steps, composing workflows incorrectly, or omitting final checks. Process-quality evaluation is needed to identify these hidden failures.
AI.method: SkillCoach derives skill-grounded process rubrics from real agent rollouts and evaluates trajectories along four dimensions: skill selection, skill following, skill composition, and skill-grounded reflection. The external verifier is kept as a separate outcome signal. Evolved rubrics are used for process supervision to select high-quality training trajectories.
AI.result: Evolved rubrics substantially improve evaluation quality, expose failures hidden by final accuracy, and provide stronger supervision signals than outcome-only filtering for enhancing agentic skill-use.
AI.conclusion: SkillCoach demonstrates that process-oriented rubric evaluation is a more effective and diagnostic approach than outcome-only signals for both assessing and improving LLM agent skill-use in environments with overlapping skill repositories.

title: HULAT2 at MER-TRANS 2026: Governed Multi-Agent Simplification for Spanish Easy-to-Read Generation
summary: This paper describes the participation of HULAT2-UC3M in the Spanish track of MER-TRANS 2026, a shared task on multilingual Easy-to-Read translation. Three fully automatic Spanish runs were submitted. RUN1 and RUN2 used a LangGraph-based multi-agent workflow combining Gemini 2.5 Flash and RigoChat-7B-v2, parallel generation strategies, internal quality signals, Event-Condition-Action routing, controlled editing and traceable decisions. RUN1 used the base workflow, while RUN2 activated an additional lexical-support layer based on a glossary and lexical resources. RUN3 was a RigoChat-based generate-evaluate-regenerate baseline with prompt engineering and LoRA-based adaptation. The official leaderboard reports BLEU-Orig, BLEU-Gold, SARI and BERTScore. During development, additional internal signals were also inspected, including semantic fidelity, readability, lexical simplicity, syntactic clarity and factual consistency. According to official SARI, RUN1 was the best HULAT2 run, with 44.0543 points, followed by RUN2 with 43.1049 and RUN3 with 38.5136. These results indicate that, in this task setting, signal-guided multi-agent routing outperformed the linear regeneration baseline. They also show that adding lexical support did not automatically improve reference-based scores. Further segment-level and document-level analysis are required to assess readability, factual consistency and user-oriented adequacy.

AI.tldr: HULAT2-UC3M participated in the MER-TRANS 2026 Spanish Easy-to-Read translation task with three runs. A LangGraph multi-agent workflow (RUN1/RUN2) using signal-guided routing outperformed a LoRA-adapted baseline (RUN3), with RUN1 achieving the best SARI score of 44.05.
AI.motivation: The goal is to advance multilingual Easy-to-Read (E2R) translation — simplifying complex texts for readers with cognitive or literacy challenges. The team aimed to compare a sophisticated multi-agent workflow with signal-guided routing against a simpler regeneration baseline, and to assess whether lexical support layers improve automatic metrics.
AI.method: Three fully automatic Spanish runs were submitted. RUN1 and RUN2 employed a LangGraph-based multi-agent architecture integrating Gemini 2.5 Flash and RigoChat-7B-v2, with parallel generation strategies, internal quality signals, Event-Condition-Action (ECA) routing, controlled editing, and traceable decisions. RUN2 added a lexical-support layer using glossaries and lexical resources. RUN3 served as a RigoChat-based generate-evaluate-regenerate baseline with prompt engineering and LoRA adaptation. Evaluation used BLEU-Orig, BLEU-Gold, SARI, and BERTScore, supplemented by internal signals: semantic fidelity, readability, lexical simplicity, syntactic clarity, and factual consistency.
AI.result: Official SARI scores: RUN1 = 44.0543, RUN2 = 43.1049, RUN3 = 38.5136. The multi-agent routing approach (RUN1/RUN2) significantly outperformed the linear regeneration baseline (RUN3). Adding lexical support (RUN2) did not improve reference-based scores and slightly degraded SARI relative to RUN1.
AI.conclusion: Signal-guided multi-agent routing with ECA-based control is more effective than linear generate-evaluate-regenerate pipelines for E2R translation under these metrics. Lexical support layers do not automatically yield better reference-based scores and may require more nuanced integration. Further segment-level and document-level analysis is needed to evaluate readability, factual consistency, and user-oriented adequacy beyond automatic metrics.

title: Role-Aware Neural Convex Divergence Heads for Asymmetric Representation Learning
summary: Many representation learning problems involve directed relations, such as lexical entailment, sentence entailment, ontology hierarchy, and citation links. Standard Euclidean, cosine, and Mahalanobis heads are symmetric, while generic neural scorers can model directionality but provide limited geometric structure. This paper proposes a role-aware neural convex divergence head for asymmetric representation learning. The head applies source- and target-role projections before evaluating an input-convex neural Bregman divergence, yielding a nonnegative structured score in the role-projected space. We characterize its projected-space identity, source-role convexity, directional-gap decomposition, and Hessian-based local curvature. Experiments on lexical, sentence, ontology, and directed graph benchmarks compare symmetric distances, unstructured asymmetric scorers, order/hyperbolic baselines, plain ICNN-Bregman heads, and the proposed role-aware variant. Across ten random seeds on the main semantic and ontology benchmarks, role-aware projections consistently improve directional accuracy over plain ICNN-Bregman heads while preserving zero observed negative divergence rate. The results also identify a boundary case: on large fixed-feature citation prediction, specialized symmetric or hyperbolic baselines remain stronger in ranking accuracy. Overall, the proposed head is best understood as a structured and interpretable plug-in distance module for tasks where directional relations matter.

AI.tldr: Proposes a role-aware neural convex divergence head for asymmetric representation learning that applies source/target-role projections before computing an input-convex neural Bregman divergence, yielding structured nonnegative scores. Experiments show consistent directional accuracy gains on semantic and ontology benchmarks over plain ICNN-Bregman heads, though specialized symmetric/hyperbolic baselines remain stronger on large citation prediction tasks.
AI.motivation: Standard distance/similarity heads (Euclidean, cosine, Mahalanobis) are symmetric and cannot capture directed relations like entailment, hierarchy, or citation links. Generic neural scorers can model directionality but lack geometric interpretability. There is a need for a structured, interpretable scoring module that naturally handles asymmetry while preserving geometric properties.
AI.method: Proposes a role-aware neural convex divergence head built on input-convex neural networks (ICNNs). The head first applies distinct source-role and target-role linear projections to the input representations, then evaluates a Bregman divergence parameterized by an ICNN in the role-projected space. The authors characterize theoretical properties including projected-space identity, source-role convexity, a directional-gap decomposition, and Hessian-based local curvature analysis.
AI.result: Across ten random seeds on semantic and ontology benchmarks, role-aware projections consistently improve directional accuracy over plain ICNN-Bregman heads while maintaining zero observed negative divergence rate. However, on large fixed-feature citation prediction tasks, specialized symmetric or hyperbolic baselines outperform in ranking accuracy, identifying a boundary case where the proposed method is less suited.
AI.conclusion: The role-aware neural convex divergence head is best understood as a structured, interpretable plug-in distance module for tasks where directional relations matter. It offers a principled middle ground between symmetric distances and unstructured asymmetric scorers, though it may not replace specialized baselines in all settings.

title: Spec-AUF: Accept-Until-Fail Training under Train-Inference Misalignment for Masked Block Drafters
summary: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive generation by drafting a block of tokens that the target model verifies left-to-right, committing only the longest accepted prefix. Block (DLM-style) drafters predict the whole block in parallel, which is fast but trained with a full-block cross-entropy that supervises every position against the gold continuation -- even though inference discards every token after the first rejection. Recent acceptance-aware objectives patch this by reweighting the full-block loss; we instead use teacher-forced learning as a motivation for how supervision should concentrate on the accepted prefix. A mask-only block drafter has no input-side channel for gold-prefix conditioning, so AUF approximates that prefix-sensitive supervision on the loss side by keeping the cross-entropy support only through the drafter's first predicted failure. AUF is a single, detached change to the CE support -- no auxiliary objective, no verifier rollouts, and no change to the inference pipeline or the exactness contract. Within fixed drafter backbones and serving settings on Qwen3-8B, AUF raises the DFlash drafter's average emitted length $τ$, averaged over six benchmarks, from 2.40 to 2.61, with a gain on every benchmark, and transfers to Domino's two-branch head (2.56 to 2.68). Two findings sharpen the picture: the decay-only baseline reaches higher token accuracy on the shared block mask yet decodes worse, and on DFlash, once AUF truncates the support, the standard exponential position-decay weighting becomes empirically inert.

AI.tldr: AUF (Accepted Until Failure) improves block speculative decoding by truncating the cross-entropy loss to only supervise draft tokens up to the first predicted rejection, yielding higher average accepted lengths (+0.21 on DFlash, +0.12 on Domino) across six benchmarks with Qwen3-8B, without modifying inference.
AI.motivation: Standard block drafters (DLM-style) are trained with full-block cross-entropy that supervises every position, but at inference, all tokens after the first rejection are discarded. Existing acceptance-aware objectives reweight the full-block loss; the authors instead argue supervision should concentrate on the accepted prefix, inspired by teacher-forced learning. Current mask-only drafters lack an input-side channel for gold-prefix conditioning, necessitating a loss-side approximation.
AI.method: AUF modifies the cross-entropy support to terminate at the drafter's first predicted failure — i.e., the first position where the drafter's own greedy prediction diverges from the gold token. This is a single, detached change: no auxiliary objective, no verifier rollouts, no inference pipeline changes, and the exactness contract (speculative decoding guarantee) is preserved.
AI.result: On Qwen3-8B across six benchmarks, AUF improves DFlash's average emitted length τ from 2.40 to 2.61 (gain on every benchmark) and transfers to Domino's two-branch head (2.56 → 2.68). Two counterintuitive findings: (1) a decay-only baseline achieves higher token accuracy on the shared block mask yet decodes worse; (2) once AUF truncates the support, standard exponential position-decay weighting becomes empirically inert.
AI.conclusion: Concentrating supervision on the accepted prefix via AUF is both simpler and more effective than full-block reweighting schemes. The decay-weighting nullification suggests that loss support truncation, not positional reweighting, is the critical mechanism for acceptance-aware training of block drafters.

title: Know Your Source: A Public Knowledge Store for Media Background Checks
summary: LLM-based retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is increasingly used for automated fact-checking (AFC) and related tasks. By grounding LLM outputs in retrieved evidence, RAG-based systems provide transparent justifications while allowing external information to be updated independently of the underlying model. However, existing approaches often assume retrieved evidence is reliable, although real-world information may be conflicting, outdated, and can originate from unreliable or biased sources. Recent work on *source-critical reasoning* addresses this challenge through media background checks (MBCs) (Schlichtkrull, 2024), which assess the credibility of evidence sources to support downstream fact verification. However, generating MBCs relies on costly proprietary search APIs, limiting reproducibility. To mitigate this issue, we introduce MEDIAREF, a publicly available knowledge store of web-sourced documents that enables reproducible, low-cost evaluation of MBC generation across 200 media sources. We describe a reproducible methodology for constructing and updating the collection, assess widely used LLMs on the MBC generation task, and demonstrate that MEDIAREF supports higher-quality MBC generation through both automatic and qualitative evaluation.

AI.tldr: MEDIAREF is a publicly available knowledge store of web-sourced documents covering 200 media sources, designed to enable reproducible, low-cost evaluation of media background check (MBC) generation for source-critical reasoning in RAG-based automated fact-checking, offering an alternative to costly proprietary search APIs.
AI.motivation: RAG-based automated fact-checking systems naively assume retrieved evidence is reliable, ignoring that real-world information can be conflicting, outdated, or biased. Source-critical reasoning via media background checks (MBCs) addresses this but currently relies on expensive proprietary search APIs, limiting reproducibility and accessibility. A publicly available, reproducible alternative is needed.
AI.method: The authors introduce MEDIAREF, a curated knowledge store of web-sourced documents spanning 200 media sources. They describe a reproducible methodology for constructing and updating this collection. They then evaluate widely used LLMs on the MBC generation task using MEDIAREF, conducting both automatic and qualitative assessments.
AI.result: MEDIAREF supports higher-quality MBC generation compared to existing approaches, as demonstrated through both automatic metrics and qualitative evaluation. The resource enables reproducible, low-cost benchmarking of LLMs for source-critical reasoning.
AI.conclusion: MEDIAREF provides a reproducible, cost-effective foundation for advancing source-critical reasoning in RAG-based fact-checking, removing dependency on proprietary search APIs and enabling broader research on media source credibility assessment.

title: Denser $\neq$ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training
summary: Continual post-training enables foundation models to acquire new knowledge while preserving existing capabilities. Recent work suggests that on-policy learning can mitigate forgetting, with on-policy self-distillation emerging as a particularly attractive approach. In this work, we revisit this optimistic view through self-distillation policy optimization (SDPO). Our experiments show that SDPO can accelerate in-domain specialization when teacher signals are stable and well aligned, but it struggles to generalize to out-of-distribution scenarios. In continual post-training, SDPO exhibits stronger forgetting and can even collapse, whereas on-policy reinforcement learning methods such as GRPO adapt more conservatively and better preserve prior capabilities. Further analyses reveal that denser self-distillation induces larger drift in both parameter space and response space, and can amplify high-frequency formatting artifacts through a self-reinforcing teacher--student loop. These findings suggest that on-policy data alone is insufficient for continual learning. Dense self-distillation can accelerate specialization when teacher targets are stable and token-level supervision is reliable, but it should not be treated as a default stabilizer for continual post-training. Our code is available at https://github.com/Moenupa/SDPO-CL.

AI.tldr: This paper challenges the optimistic view of on-policy self-distillation for continual post-training. Through SDPO experiments, the authors show that while self-distillation accelerates in-domain specialization under stable teacher signals, it causes stronger forgetting, potential collapse, and amplified formatting artifacts in continual learning settings. On-policy RL methods like GRPO better preserve prior capabilities.
AI.motivation: Recent work has suggested that on-policy learning, particularly on-policy self-distillation, can mitigate catastrophic forgetting during continual post-training of foundation models. The authors aim to critically re-examine this optimistic claim and understand when self-distillation helps versus harms in continual learning scenarios.
AI.method: The authors propose and analyze Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (SDPO), conducting experiments that compare SDPO against on-policy reinforcement learning methods (specifically GRPO) in continual post-training settings. They measure in-domain specialization, out-of-distribution generalization, forgetting, and parameter/response-space drift. They also analyze the self-reinforcing teacher-student loop and its effect on formatting artifacts.
AI.result: SDPO accelerates in-domain specialization when teacher signals are stable and well-aligned, but struggles with out-of-distribution generalization. In continual post-training, SDPO exhibits stronger forgetting and can collapse, while GRPO adapts more conservatively. Denser self-distillation induces larger drift in both parameter space and response space, and amplifies high-frequency formatting artifacts through the self-reinforcing loop.
AI.conclusion: On-policy data alone is insufficient for continual learning. Dense self-distillation can accelerate specialization with stable teachers and reliable token-level supervision, but it should not be treated as a default stabilizer for continual post-training. More conservative on-policy RL methods like GRPO are better at preserving prior capabilities.

title: The Future of NLP may not be at NLP Conferences: Scholarly Migration Patterns in Natural Language Processing
summary: Natural Language Processing (NLP) has traditionally been published in its core disciplinary venues like ACL. However, advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) has led to a blurring of the disciplinary lines between NLP and general Machine Learning (ML), with authors regularly publishing in venues from both fields. Here, we ask whether the disciplinary center of gravity is shifting. Using NLP research published from 2010 to 2026 and studies of both established and new authors, we find that a migration is taking place. First, comparing the pre- and post-LLM eras, established authors lost 19.2pp of share at flagship *ACL main-conference tracks while gaining 14.8pp in the newer Findings tracks, and general ML venues rose 8.6pp, even when adjusting for parallel growth in the fields. Second, among newer authors who debut with at least three first-author NLP-topic papers, the share whose work appears mostly at *ACL venues fell from 84% (2019) to 74% (2024), while the share appearing mostly at general ML venues rose from 5% to 21%. Using causal inference techniques, we estimate that these general ML venues confer a significant citation premium, which influences venue selection. Together, these results point to a significant shift in where NLP research is published.

AI.tldr: NLP research is migrating away from traditional *ACL venues toward general ML venues, driven in part by a citation premium at ML venues, with established authors shifting to Findings tracks and new authors increasingly publishing in ML venues post-LLM.
AI.motivation: The advent of LLMs has blurred disciplinary boundaries between NLP and general ML. The authors investigate whether this has caused a measurable shift in where NLP research is published — i.e., whether the "disciplinary center of gravity" is moving from traditional ACL venues to general ML venues.
AI.method: The study analyzes NLP publications from 2010–2026 across two dimensions: (1) established authors, comparing publication venue distributions pre- and post-LLM (flagship *ACL tracks, Findings tracks, and general ML venues), adjusting for parallel field growth; (2) new authors who debut with ≥3 first-author NLP papers, tracking the proportion publishing primarily in *ACL vs. general ML venues (2019 vs. 2024). Causal inference techniques are applied to estimate the citation premium of general ML venues and its influence on venue choice.
AI.result: Established authors lost 19.2 percentage points of share at flagship *ACL main-conference tracks, gained 14.8pp in Findings tracks, and shifted 8.6pp toward general ML venues. Among new authors, the share publishing mostly at *ACL venues dropped from 84% (2019) to 74% (2024), while those publishing mostly at ML venues rose from 5% to 21%. General ML venues confer a significant citation premium, which causally influences venue selection.
AI.conclusion: A significant and quantifiable migration of NLP research from traditional *ACL venues to general ML venues is underway, with both established and new authors participating. The Findings tracks partially absorb internal displacement, but general ML venues are gaining share, incentivized by citation advantages.

title: Set Diffusion: Interpolating Token Orderings Between Autoregression and Diffusion for Fast and Flexible Decoding
comment: ICML 2026. We provide the code at https://github.com/kuleshov-group/setdlms
summary: Discrete diffusion models have steadily improved in quality relative to autoregressive (AR) models. However, these models are normally constrained to fixed-length generation and do not support key-value (KV) caching. Block diffusion partially bridges diffusion and AR by generating token blocks left-to-right, but its fixed-size sequential blocks limit decoding flexibility and parallelism. Here, we present a new class of language models, set diffusion, comprised of (i) a likelihood parameterization that factorizes over flexible-position, flexible-length token sets and (ii) a set-causal diffusion architecture that supports KV cache updates after every inference step. By factorizing over token sets instead of fixed-size blocks, tokens can be decoded in arbitrarily-ordered sets, including sliding-window sets, enabling faster inference and support for any-order decoding. Set diffusion achieves better speed-quality tradeoffs on mathematical reasoning, summarization, and unconditional generation compared to prior diffusion language models while offering stronger infilling performance than block diffusion. We provide the code, along with the model weights and blog post on the project page: https://m-arriola.com/setdlms/

AI.tldr: Set diffusion introduces a new language model class that factorizes over flexible-position, flexible-length token sets with a set-causal diffusion architecture supporting KV caching, enabling arbitrarily-ordered decoding, faster inference, and superior speed-quality tradeoffs compared to prior diffusion language models.
AI.motivation: Discrete diffusion models are constrained by fixed-length generation and lack KV caching support. Block diffusion offers partial improvements but is limited by fixed-size sequential blocks that restrict decoding flexibility and parallelism. The authors aim to overcome these limitations with a more flexible generation framework.
AI.method: The method consists of two components: (1) a likelihood parameterization that factorizes over flexible-position, flexible-length token sets rather than fixed blocks, and (2) a set-causal diffusion architecture that enables KV cache updates after every inference step, supporting arbitrarily-ordered decoding schemes such as sliding-window sets.
AI.result: Set diffusion achieves better speed-quality tradeoffs on mathematical reasoning, summarization, and unconditional generation compared to prior diffusion language models, and demonstrates stronger infilling performance than block diffusion.
AI.conclusion: By moving from fixed-block factorization to flexible token sets with KV caching, set diffusion unlocks faster, more flexible any-order decoding, establishing a new Pareto frontier for diffusion-based language modeling.

title: ContextSniper: AntTrail's Token-Efficient Code Memory for Repository-Level Program Repair
summary: Large language model agents can repair real repository issues, but they often spend large context budgets on whole-file reads, broad searches, and long terminal outputs where useful evidence is mixed with irrelevant code and logs. This paper presents ContextSniper, AntTrail's token-efficient code memory layer for repository-level program repair. As the coding specialization of AntTrail's broader agent memory engine, ContextSniper implements the Sniper feature for precision evidence selection: it retrieves candidate code and runtime evidence, ranks it with hybrid retrieval signals, filters long outputs through an intention-aware context gate, and returns compact evidence packets while preserving recoverable source context outside the prompt. We evaluate ContextSniper on SWE-bench Lite with OpenClaw and Claude Code, using 50 task runs per host-agent condition. ContextSniper reduces total token use by 51.5% and logged cost by 36.4% for OpenClaw, and reduces total token use by 38.9% and estimated cost by 27.3% for Claude Code. Submitted-resolution rates decrease slightly, from 26.0% to 24.0% for OpenClaw and from 32.0% to 30.0% for Claude Code. ContextSniper's pilot testing scripts are open-sourced at https://github.com/Calluking/ContextSniper

AI.tldr: ContextSniper is a token-efficient code memory layer that reduces LLM token consumption during repository-level program repair by up to 51.5%, with only minor resolution rate trade-offs (2% drop), by implementing precision evidence selection with hybrid retrieval and intention-aware context gating.
AI.motivation: LLM-based agents for program repair waste large context budgets on whole-file reads, over-broad searches, and verbose terminal outputs where useful evidence is buried in irrelevant code and logs. This motivates a memory layer that selectively retrieves only the most relevant evidence to reduce token usage and cost.
AI.method: ContextSniper implements the Sniper feature with four components: (1) retrieval of candidate code and runtime evidence, (2) ranking via hybrid retrieval signals, (3) filtering long outputs through an intention-aware context gate, and (4) returning compact evidence packets while preserving recoverable source context outside the prompt. It is integrated as AntTrail's code memory layer and evaluated on SWE-bench Lite with OpenClaw and Claude Code (50 runs per condition).
AI.result: OpenClaw: 51.5% token reduction, 36.4% cost reduction, resolution rate dropped from 26.0% to 24.0%. Claude Code: 38.9% token reduction, 27.3% cost reduction, resolution rate dropped from 32.0% to 30.0%.
AI.conclusion: ContextSniper achieves substantial token and cost savings with only a marginal degradation in repair accuracy (~2 percentage points), demonstrating that precision evidence selection is a viable strategy for making LLM-based program repair more economical without severely compromising effectiveness.

title: Language Models as Measurement Apparatus for Culture
comment: Accepted to the Big Picture workshop co-located with ACL 2026. This version expands the camera-ready (adding Fig. 3 and section 6.3, as well as correcting minor typos) in Proceedings of The Big Picture v2: Crafting a Research Narrative, pp. 131--143, San Diego, CA, USA. Association for Computational Linguistics
summary: Language models are increasingly used to quantify cultural phenomena, but what makes such measurement distinctively cultural? This paper argues that NLP work on culture is a material-discursive practice: the apparatus -- model, data, annotation, evaluation -- participates in constituting the cultural reality it measures, rather than passively recording it. Drawing on Karen Barad's concept of the agential cut -- the contingent boundary between phenomenon and instrument -- I show that the apparatus's substantive design choices draw such boundaries, and that the boundary is entangled from the start because language models have already internalized much of the cultural material they measure. I illustrate this through three case studies on television and film dialogue (measuring structure, interaction, and deviation) and three examinations of the apparatus itself (erasure of cultural markers, attunement to historical material, and agency in an agentic workflow). This big picture analysis proposes a research program that is theory-driven, empirically rigorous, and culturally contingent, treating each agential cut as a conscious commitment, at once methodological and ethical.

AI.tldr: This paper argues that NLP-based cultural measurement is not neutral observation but a material-discursive practice where the apparatus (model, data, annotation) actively constitutes cultural reality. Drawing on Barad's "agential cut," it demonstrates through case studies on media dialogue that design choices create contingent boundaries entangled with culture, proposing a theory-driven, ethically conscious research program.
AI.motivation: To critically examine what makes NLP-based cultural measurement distinctively cultural, challenging the assumption that language models passively record cultural phenomena. The author argues that the apparatus itself participates in constructing the cultural reality it purports to measure, requiring deeper theoretical and ethical reflection.
AI.method: The paper employs a theoretical-philosophical framework grounded in Karen Barad's agential realism, specifically the concept of the "agential cut." It applies this lens through three case studies on television/film dialogue (measuring structure, interaction, and deviation) and three examinations of the apparatus (erasure of cultural markers, attunement to historical material, and agency in agentic workflows).
AI.result: The analysis reveals that every substantive design choice in the NLP apparatus draws a contingent boundary between phenomenon and instrument, and that this boundary is always already entangled because language models have internalized cultural material. The case studies illustrate how cultural markers can be erased, historical attunement shapes outputs, and agency is distributed in unexpected ways.
AI.conclusion: The author proposes a research program for cultural NLP that is theory-driven, empirically rigorous, and culturally contingent, where each agential cut is treated as a conscious commitment that is simultaneously methodological and ethical.

title: EHHN: An Event-driven Heterogeneous Hypergraph Network for Object-Centric Next Activity Prediction
summary: Next activity prediction helps service-oriented processes anticipate upcoming steps before delays, exceptions, or service-level risks occur. Most existing methods assume classical single-case event logs, whereas real service processes often involve events shared by multiple typed business objects. Object-centric event logs (OCELs) capture such interactions, but current predictors remain limited. Flattening-based approaches lose cross-object context, and native OCEL graph-based approaches encode multi-object events through pairwise relations. Existing models also do not jointly capture event-driven object state changes, inter-event timing, and global execution patterns. We propose EHHN, an Event-driven Heterogeneous Hypergraph Network for object-centric next activity prediction. EHHN represents each prediction prefix as a heterogeneous hypergraph, where event--object hyperedges bind retained co-participating objects and a lifecycle hyperedge groups the primary object's observed lifecycle events. Based on this representation, EHHN uses a dual-stream architecture in which a micro-spatial stream models event-driven object-state evolution and a macro-evolution stream captures temporal dynamics using retrieved global prototypes. The two streams are fused to predict the next activity. Experiments on four public OCEL benchmarks against nine baselines show that EHHN achieves the best accuracy and macro F1-score on all datasets, with improvements of up to 8.1 and 12.4 percentage points over the strongest baselines. Compared with the strongest OCEL-native graph baseline, EHHN also reduces peak GPU memory by up to 24 times. Code is available at https://github.com/chenkaitao1112/EHHN.

AI.tldr: EHHN proposes a heterogeneous hypergraph network for next activity prediction in object-centric event logs, using a dual-stream architecture to model event-driven object state changes and temporal dynamics. It significantly outperforms nine baselines on four public benchmarks while reducing GPU memory by up to 24×.
AI.motivation: Existing next activity prediction methods either flatten object-centric event logs (losing cross-object context) or use graph-based approaches limited to pairwise relations. They also fail to jointly model event-driven object state changes, inter-event timing, and global execution patterns. A unified representation and architecture are needed.
AI.method: EHHN represents each prediction prefix as a heterogeneous hypergraph with two hyperedge types: event–object hyperedges (binding co-participating objects) and lifecycle hyperedges (grouping a primary object's lifecycle events). A dual-stream architecture follows: (1) a micro-spatial stream models event-driven object-state evolution, and (2) a macro-evolution stream captures temporal dynamics via retrieved global prototypes. The two streams are fused for prediction.
AI.result: On four public OCEL benchmarks against nine baselines, EHHN achieves the best accuracy and macro F1-score on all datasets, with improvements up to 8.1 and 12.4 percentage points over the strongest baselines. It also reduces peak GPU memory up to 24× compared to the strongest OCEL-native graph baseline.
AI.conclusion: EHHN demonstrates that heterogeneous hypergraph modeling with dual-stream spatial-temporal fusion is highly effective for object-centric next activity prediction, offering both superior predictive performance and memory efficiency.

title: Will Scaling Improve Social Simulation with LLMs?
summary: Large Language Model (LLM) social simulations are a promising research method, but they are not yet faithful enough to be adopted widely. In this work, we investigate whether the current scaling paradigm in language modeling is likely to close these gaps, or whether simulation fidelity is orthogonal to general capabilities and therefore deserving of more research attention. We use scaling laws to study the relationship between LLMs' compute scale, general capability benchmarks, and the fidelity of social simulation in three representative sub-domains: opinion modeling, behavioral simulation, and longitudinal forecasting. Surprisingly, we discover strong compute scaling in all three settings, using a suite of 85 transformer LLMs with the Qwen3 architecture pre-trained on the DCLM web text corpus under fixed-compute budgets from $10^{18}$ to $10^{20}$ FLOPs. Then we evaluate 35 larger and more capable open-weight models up to 70B parameters, allowing us to predict downstream accuracy from loss. This reveals that the majority of behavioral and opinion simulation tasks will rapidly improve with scale, particularly when they involve populations that are well-represented in English web corpora. Longitudinal forecasting and underrepresented opinions scale more slowly, especially when they are less correlated with general knowledge and reasoning benchmarks like MMLU. In behavior simulation, scaling fails to improve model calibration with human cognitive biases like risk aversion, as well as human heuristics like learning correlated rewards from related tasks. On these tasks, even fine-tuned models fail to noticeably scale up performance from 0.5B to 8B parameters. Taken together, we conclude that scale will improve social simulations in most settings, but outliers exist, and improvements will be less reliable in low-resource domains.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether scaling LLMs improves the fidelity of social simulations. Using 85 Qwen3-based models (10^18–10^20 FLOPs) and 35 open-weight models (up to 70B), the authors find strong scaling trends for opinion modeling and behavioral simulation, but weaker scaling for longitudinal forecasting and underrepresented opinions. Notably, scaling fails to improve calibration with human cognitive biases and heuristics, highlighting that some aspects of simulation fidelity are orthogonal to general capability gains.
AI.motivation: LLM-based social simulations show promise but lack sufficient fidelity for widespread adoption. The authors aim to determine whether scaling models (the dominant paradigm) will naturally close fidelity gaps, or whether simulation fidelity is orthogonal to general capabilities and thus requires dedicated research attention beyond scaling.
AI.method: The authors employ scaling laws methodology: they train a suite of 85 transformer LLMs based on the Qwen3 architecture on the DCLM web text corpus under fixed compute budgets from 10^18 to 10^20 FLOPs. They then evaluate 35 larger open-weight models (up to 70B parameters) to predict downstream accuracy from loss. Evaluation spans three social simulation sub-domains: opinion modeling, behavioral simulation, and longitudinal forecasting.
AI.result: Strong compute scaling is observed across all three sub-domains. Behavioral and opinion simulation tasks improve rapidly with scale, especially for populations well-represented in English web corpora. However, longitudinal forecasting and underrepresented opinions scale more slowly, particularly when uncorrelated with MMLU-style benchmarks. Critically, scaling fails to improve model calibration with human cognitive biases (e.g., risk aversion) and heuristics (e.g., learning correlated rewards); fine-tuning from 0.5B to 8B parameters yields negligible gains on these tasks.
AI.conclusion: Scale will improve social simulation fidelity in most settings, but notable outliers persist. Improvements are less reliable in low-resource domains, and some aspects of human-like behavior (cognitive biases, heuristics) appear orthogonal to scaling. Dedicated research beyond scaling is warranted for these fidelity gaps.

title: EPnG: Adaptive Expert Prune-and-Grow for Parameter-Efficient MoE Fine-tuning
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models scale efficiently but remain costly to adapt due to redundant experts and uniform parameter allocation. Existing parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods such as LoRA ignore MoE routing dynamics, leading to suboptimal resource use. We propose EPnG, an adaptive prune-and-grow framework that reallocates LoRA capacity based on expert importance derived from router gate probabilities. EPnG prunes under-utilized experts and expands high-importance experts via rank growth with orthogonal initialization, while maintaining a fixed parameter budget. Across OLMoE and Qwen1.5-MoE, EPnG consistently outperforms LoRA under the same budget and achieves performance comparable to full fine-tuning while updating only 0.55%-0.72% of parameters (up to 140x-180x fewer). These results demonstrate that aligning PEFT with MoE routing yields a more effective and scalable fine-tuning strategy.

AI.tldr: EPnG is an adaptive prune-and-grow framework for fine-tuning Mixture-of-Experts models that reallocates LoRA capacity based on expert importance from router gate probabilities, achieving full fine-tuning performance while updating only 0.55%–0.72% of parameters.
AI.motivation: MoE models face inefficient adaptation due to (1) redundant experts that contribute little to downstream tasks, (2) uniform parameter allocation across experts regardless of their importance, and (3) existing PEFT methods like LoRA ignoring MoE routing dynamics, resulting in suboptimal resource utilization.
AI.method: EPnG is an adaptive prune-and-grow framework that: (1) computes expert importance scores from router gate probabilities, (2) prunes LoRA adapters from under-utilized experts, (3) reallocates the freed parameter budget to high-importance experts via rank growth with orthogonal initialization, all while maintaining a fixed total parameter budget.
AI.result: On OLMoE and Qwen1.5-MoE models, EPnG consistently outperforms standard LoRA under identical parameter budgets and achieves performance comparable to full fine-tuning while updating only 0.55%–0.72% of parameters (up to 140x–180x fewer parameters).
AI.conclusion: Aligning parameter-efficient fine-tuning with MoE routing dynamics—by adaptively reallocating capacity from pruned to important experts—yields a more effective and scalable fine-tuning strategy than uniform LoRA allocation.

title: A-TMA: Decoupling State-Aware Memory Failures in Long-Term Agent Memory
summary: Long term memory lets LLM agents act as persistent assistants, but user facts change. A useful memory system must know what is true now, what used to be true, and what changed. We study \emph{ghost memory}, a state coordination failure in which old, current, and transition facts coexist in the memory bank, remain mixed during retrieval, and mislead the answer model. We argue that memory systems should be understood and optimized from three levels: bank maintenance, retrieval, and answer time resolution. We propose ATMA, a state aware overlay for existing memory systems. ATMA keeps superseded and transition records in the bank, builds evidence packets for the query's requested state view, and exposes current, historical, and transition labels to QA. We further call for decoupled evaluation of bank, retrieval, and answer level failures, since final QA accuracy can hide where ghost memory occurs. To make this failure measurable, we build LTP (LoCoMo Temporal Plus), a conflict heavy benchmark for ghost memory, and evaluate on LoCoMo for long conversation generalization. On LTP, Graphiti+ATMA improves conflict accuracy by 0.240 absolute over Graphiti. On LoCoMo, Graphiti+ATMA raises temporal F1 from 0.0295 to 0.1705. The gains are host dependent, but they indicate that explicit state roles can reduce memory failures hidden by final QA accuracy.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "ghost memory" — a failure mode in LLM agent memory systems where outdated, current, and transitional facts coexist and mislead answers. It proposes ATMA, a state-aware overlay that annotates memory records with temporal roles (current/historical/transition) and structures retrieval accordingly. A new benchmark, LTP, quantifies ghost memory failures, and experiments show ATMA significantly improves conflict accuracy and temporal F1 over baseline memory systems.
AI.motivation: LLM-based agents with persistent memory must track evolving user facts over time. Existing memory systems suffer from "ghost memory": a state coordination failure where superseded, current, and transitional facts become mixed during retrieval, causing the answer model to produce incorrect or temporally inconsistent responses. Current systems lack mechanisms to explicitly label and resolve these temporal states, and standard QA accuracy metrics obscure where such failures occur.
AI.method: The authors propose ATMA (A Temporal Memory Architecture), a state-aware overlay for existing memory systems operating at three levels: (1) bank maintenance — retaining superseded and transition records with explicit state labels rather than deleting them; (2) retrieval — building evidence packets keyed to the query's requested state view (current, historical, or transitional); (3) answer-time resolution — exposing state labels to the QA model. They also construct LTP (LoCoMo Temporal Plus), a conflict-heavy benchmark designed to isolate and measure ghost memory failures, and introduce decoupled evaluation across bank, retrieval, and answer levels.
AI.result: On the LTP benchmark, Graphiti+ATMA improves conflict accuracy by 0.240 absolute over standalone Graphiti. On the LoCoMo dataset (testing long-conversation generalization), Graphiti+ATMA raises temporal F1 from 0.0295 to 0.1705. Gains are host-system dependent, but the results demonstrate that explicit state-role annotations reduce memory failures that final QA accuracy alone would conceal.
AI.conclusion: Memory systems for LLM agents should be understood and optimized across three distinct levels — bank maintenance, retrieval, and answer-time resolution — rather than evaluated solely on end-to-end QA accuracy. Explicitly modeling temporal state roles (current, historical, transition) via an overlay like ATMA meaningfully reduces ghost memory failures, and decoupled evaluation using conflict-heavy benchmarks like LTP is essential for diagnosing where these failures originate.

title: Audio-Based Understanding of Audiobook Narration Appeal
summary: Narration is central to the audiobook listening experience, shaping how listeners engage with and understand the content. This work explores how narration qualities shape an audiobook's appeal, noting that their effects can vary by genre, title, and audience. We extract vocal and acoustic features (e.g., tone, pace, loudness) from LibriVox using pre-trained audio models and analyse their relationship with consumption data (specifically, view-rate) and their interplay with genre and title. Despite limited consumption data, we find that acoustic information alone has a robust association with appeal, even after accounting for title effects. We further validate these findings using more nuanced proprietary engagement metrics. To our knowledge, this is the first systematic computational study linking narration qualities, genre, title, and audiobook consumption, highlighting the potential of data-driven insights to improve audiobook personalisation and narrator casting.

AI.tldr: This study computationally analyzes how audiobook narration qualities (tone, pace, loudness) extracted via pre-trained audio models relate to listener appeal, finding that acoustic features robustly predict consumption even after controlling for title effects, with validation from proprietary engagement metrics.
AI.motivation: Narration is central to audiobook appeal, yet no prior systematic computational study has examined how quantifiable vocal and acoustic features relate to actual consumption data across different genres, titles, and audiences. The authors aim to fill this gap to enable data-driven improvements in audiobook personalization and narrator casting.
AI.method: The authors extract vocal and acoustic features (tone, pace, loudness) from LibriVox audiobooks using pre-trained audio models. They then analyze the statistical relationship between these features and consumption data (view-rate), examining interactions with genre and title, while controlling for title-level fixed effects. Findings are further validated using proprietary engagement metrics.
AI.result: Acoustic information alone exhibits a robust association with audiobook appeal (view-rate), and this relationship persists even after accounting for title effects. The findings are corroborated by more nuanced proprietary engagement metrics.
AI.conclusion: This is the first systematic computational study to link narration qualities, genre, title, and audiobook consumption, demonstrating that data-driven acoustic analysis holds significant potential for enhancing audiobook personalization and informing narrator casting decisions.

title: Single-Channel EEG-Based Cognitive Load Assessment in Online Learning: A Hybrid Deep Learning Approach
summary: Monitoring cognitive load during online learning could help instructors identify content that learners find difficult, but remote settings remove the visual cues that support this judgement in a classroom. We study whether a single-channel, consumer-grade EEG device (the NeuroSky MindWave Mobile 2) can distinguish easy from difficult educational-video content, using the publicly available dataset of Wang et al. [24] (ten learners, one excluded for excessive noise, leaving nine). We implement a hybrid CNN+LSTM+Attention model that combines the raw waveform with band-power features. In a within-subject setting, the model reaches up to 78.5% accuracy, compared with 55% for conventional feature-based classifiers; regularization (dropout and L2) closes the large gap between training and validation accuracy that we observe without it, keeping validation accuracy stable at roughly 68-73%.
