Experiments on video prediction tasks in 2D and 3D environments demonstrate that SUNTA outperforms baselines, uniquely maintaining accurate predictions over 250 timesteps, whereas all baselines degrade within the first 10 timesteps.

AI.tldr: SUNTA introduces surprise-driven chunking in hierarchical state-space models for long-horizon prediction, using decoupled training and internal inconsistency metrics to determine chunk boundaries, achieving accurate predictions over 250+ timesteps where baselines fail within 10.
AI.motivation: Existing HSSMs rely on fixed-length or similarity-based chunking that misaligns with intrinsic temporal structure. The authors argue that prediction errors (surprise) are a more direct signal for determining when longer-range context is needed, but integrating surprise-based chunking into HSSMs is challenging due to hierarchical collapse during end-to-end training and the absence of surprise signals during open-loop prediction.
AI.method: SUNTA (Surprise-based Nested Temporal Abstraction) uses two key innovations: (1) a decoupled training strategy that preserves surprise signals by preventing hierarchical collapse during training, and (2) an internal inconsistency metric that serves as a top-down surprise signal to determine chunk boundaries during imagined rollouts when ground-truth surprise is unavailable.
AI.result: On video prediction tasks in both 2D and 3D environments, SUNTA outperforms all baselines. Crucially, SUNTA uniquely maintains accurate predictions over 250 timesteps, while all baseline methods degrade within the first 10 timesteps.
AI.conclusion: Surprise-driven chunking, when properly integrated via decoupled training and internal inconsistency metrics, enables HSSMs to achieve substantially longer-horizon prediction than prior approaches. SUNTA demonstrates that aligning chunk boundaries with prediction errors is key to maintaining temporal coherence over extended rollouts.

title: Population-Based Multi-Objective Training of Discriminators for Semi-Supervised GANs
comment: The 2nd International Conference on Federated Learning and Intelligent Computing Systems (FLICS2026)
summary: Semi-supervised generative adversarial networks (SSL-GANs) can exploit large unlabeled datasets while retaining a classifier in the discriminator, but their training is often unstable. This paper proposes a population-based evolutionary training strategy in which discriminator learning is formulated as a multi-objective optimization problem. Instead of aggregating the supervised and unsupervised components of the SSL objective into a single scalar loss, the method maintains a population of discriminators ranked by Pareto dominance, enabling the exploration of different trade-offs between classification accuracy and real/fake discrimination. This formulation aims to improve both roles of SSL-GANs: learning accurate classifiers and training generators capable of producing realistic samples. We analyze several variants, including an elitist strategy and a mono-objective ablation, to assess the role of multi-objective selection. Experiments on MNIST with limited labels show improved training robustness compared to SSL-GAN and CE-SSL-GAN state-of-the-art baselines, while the elitist variant consistently achieves the highest classification accuracy.

AI.tldr: Proposes training SSL-GANs via multi-objective evolutionary optimization, maintaining a Pareto-ranked population of discriminators to balance classification accuracy and real/fake discrimination, improving training robustness and accuracy over baselines.
AI.motivation: SSL-GANs suffer from training instability caused by aggregating supervised and unsupervised losses into a single scalar objective, which forces the discriminator to compromise between classification and adversarial discrimination without exploring trade-offs.
AI.method: A population-based evolutionary strategy where discriminator learning is cast as multi-objective optimization. A population of discriminators is maintained and ranked by Pareto dominance across two objectives: (1) supervised classification accuracy and (2) unsupervised real/fake discrimination. Variants include an elitist strategy and a mono-objective ablation for comparison.
AI.result: The approach demonstrates improved training robustness on MNIST with limited labels compared to SSL-GAN and CE-SSL-GAN baselines. The elitist variant consistently achieves the highest classification accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Multi-objective evolutionary training effectively decouples the competing objectives in SSL-GAN discriminators, yielding more robust training and better classifiers, particularly with the elitist selection strategy.

title: ContextNest: Verifiable Context Governance for Autonomous AI Agent
summary:
Autonomous AI agents increasingly depend on external knowledge stores, yet most retrieval pipelines provide relevance without durable guarantees of provenance, version identity, integrity, traceability, or point-in-time reconstruction. We formalize this as context governance and present ContextNext, an open specification and reference implementation for governed AI-consumable knowledge vaults. ContextNext does not replace Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG); it supplies the governance layer beneath retrieval, determining which artifacts are approved, current, attributable, and integrity-verified before retrieval systems operate over them.
  The specification combines typed Markdown documents with metadata, deterministic set-algebraic selectors, contextnest:// URI references, SHA-256 hash-chained version histories, graph-level checkpoints, source nodes for live data through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), and audit traces of agent context consumption. These mechanisms let organizations reconstruct which knowledge versions informed an agent output and whether those versions were AI-eligible when consumed.
  We report first empirical results from two controlled experiments. In a stale-version attack isolating the governance-versus-retrieval failure mode, governed selection strictly Pareto-dominates BM25 sparse retrieval, with higher answer-quality pass rate (97% versus 93-90%) at about one-third the input-token cost. In a retrieval-determinism experiment over a 1,060-document corpus, deterministic selectors and BM25 return stable document sets across repeated identical queries (Jaccard 1.0), while a dense+HNSW baseline is non-deterministic on 80% of queries (mean Jaccard 0.611, worst case 0.210). These results suggest that context governance addresses failure modes retrieval quality alone is not designed to resolve. We release a core engine, CLI, and MCP server under open licenses.

AI.tldr: ContextNext introduces a governance layer beneath RAG systems that ensures provenance, versioning, integrity, and traceability of knowledge artifacts. Experiments show governed selection outperforms BM25 on answer quality at lower token cost (97% vs 93-90%) and provides deterministic retrieval where dense+HNSW methods are non-deterministic on 80% of queries.
AI.motivation: Autonomous AI agents increasingly rely on external knowledge retrieval, but existing retrieval pipelines lack durable guarantees of provenance, version identity, integrity, traceability, and point-in-time reconstruction. This gap creates risks around stale knowledge, unverifiable outputs, and inability to audit which knowledge versions informed an agent's decisions.
AI.method: ContextNext is an open specification and reference implementation for governed knowledge vaults. It combines typed Markdown documents with metadata, deterministic set-algebraic selectors, contextnest:// URI references, SHA-256 hash-chained version histories, graph-level checkpoints, MCP source nodes for live data, and audit traces. It sits as a governance layer beneath RAG, determining artifact eligibility (approval, currency, attribution, integrity) before retrieval operates. Two experiments evaluate: (1) a stale-version attack scenario comparing governed selection against BM25, and (2) a retrieval-determinism test on 1,060 documents comparing deterministic selectors, BM25, and dense+HNSW retrieval.
AI.result: In the stale-version attack experiment, governed selection strictly Pareto-dominates BM25 sparse retrieval with higher answer-quality pass rate (97% vs 93-90%) at approximately one-third the input-token cost. In the determinism experiment, deterministic selectors and BM25 achieved Jaccard similarity of 1.0 on repeated identical queries, while the dense+HNSW baseline was non-deterministic on 80% of queries (mean Jaccard 0.611, worst case 0.210).
AI.conclusion: Context governance addresses failure modes that retrieval quality alone cannot resolve. By adding provenance, version control, and deterministic selection beneath RAG, systems gain auditability and reliability without sacrificing answer quality. The authors release the core engine, CLI, and MCP server under open licenses.

title: Zeus: Towards Tuning-Free Foundation Model for Time Series Analysis
summary: We present Zeus, a unified tuning-free Time Series Foundation Model (TSFM) that delivers superior performance across diverse analysis tasks without any task-specific fine-tuning. Unlike prior studies that primarily focus on zero-shot forecasting but require task-specific tuning for other tasks, Zeus bridges this gap by addressing two fundamental challenges in multi-task generalization. First, to reconcile point-level granularity with long-sequence scalability, Zeus incorporates a multi-scale Transformer featuring point-wise tokenization and a U-shaped hierarchy, effectively balancing fine-grained fidelity with computational efficiency. Second, to accommodate varying inductive biases across different tasks, Zeus introduces Multi-Objective Temporal Masking (MOTM), a unified strategy that supports heterogeneous tasks (e.g., extrapolation, interpolation, and global abstraction) within a single framework. Extensive experiments across five representative tasks demonstrate that Zeus consistently achieves competitive results in tuning-free settings, underscoring its potential as a general-purpose TSFM.

AI.tldr: Zeus is a tuning-free Time Series Foundation Model that uses a multi-scale Transformer with U-shaped hierarchy and Multi-Objective Temporal Masking (MOTM) to achieve competitive zero-shot performance across five diverse time series tasks without any task-specific fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Existing Time Series Foundation Models primarily excel at zero-shot forecasting but require task-specific tuning for other tasks (e.g., interpolation, global abstraction). There is a need for a unified model that generalizes across heterogeneous time series tasks without fine-tuning, bridging the gap between point-level granularity and long-sequence scalability while accommodating diverse inductive biases.
AI.method: Zeus employs two key innovations: (1) a multi-scale Transformer architecture with point-wise tokenization and a U-shaped hierarchy to balance fine-grained fidelity with computational efficiency for long sequences; and (2) Multi-Objective Temporal Masking (MOTM), a unified self-supervised pretraining strategy that handles extrapolation (forecasting), interpolation (imputation), and global abstraction (classification, anomaly detection) within a single framework by applying diverse masking objectives.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across five representative time series tasks demonstrate that Zeus consistently achieves competitive results in tuning-free (zero-shot) settings, validating its capability as a general-purpose Time Series Foundation Model.
AI.conclusion: Zeus demonstrates that a single, tuning-free foundation model can effectively handle multiple heterogeneous time series tasks by reconciling granularity–scalability trade-offs and unifying diverse inductive biases via multi-objective pretraining, underscoring its potential as a general-purpose TSFM.

title: Enhancing Fitness Intelligence through Domain-Specific LLM Post-Training
comment: 8 pages, 6 tables, 2 figures. Accepted by the 12th International Conference on Big Data Computing and Communications (BigCom 2026)
summary: Scientific Fitness Coaching (SFC) is typically delivered by human professionals, making it costly and inaccessible to many. While recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) show considerable promise for more inclusive fitness coaching, directly deploying prevailing general-purpose LLMs in SFC reveals critical limitations. These models often lack sufficient domain-specific knowledge integration, leading to weak performance on complex SFC scenarios. In this paper, we introduce FitOne, a series of fitness LLMs (with 8B and 32B parameters) designed to improve reliability and domain specialization for SFC applications. Built upon the Qwen3 foundation models, FitOne is developed through a three-stage post-training pipeline consisting of continual pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning, using large-scale, high-quality datasets derived from rigorous knowledge engineering. We conduct comprehensive evaluations of FitOne on professional fitness certification exams, including ACSM-EP and NSCA-CSCS, as well as general capabilities such as knowledge reasoning and instruction following. Experimental results show that, while retaining strong general capabilities, FitOne-8B/32B achieves average improvements of up to 10.09%/9.29% and 12.73%/7.01% on the ACSM-EP and NSCA-CSCS exams, respectively, compared with the Qwen3 base models. Furthermore, in-depth ablation studies confirm the necessity of each training stage, highlighting the pipeline's effectiveness in balancing domain expertise enhancement with general ability retention. We believe this research advances LLM systems toward more reliable fitness intelligence and will inspire future research on developing domain-specific LLMs.

AI.tldr: FitOne is a series of domain-specific LLMs (8B/32B) fine-tuned on Qwen3 for scientific fitness coaching, using a three-stage pipeline (continual pre-training, SFT, RL). It achieves 7–12% improvements on professional fitness exams while retaining general capabilities.
AI.motivation: Human-delivered scientific fitness coaching is costly and inaccessible. General-purpose LLMs lack sufficient domain-specific knowledge, resulting in weak performance on complex SFC scenarios. There is a need for specialized LLMs that reliably integrate fitness domain expertise without sacrificing general reasoning abilities.
AI.method: FitOne is built on Qwen3 foundation models via a three-stage post-training pipeline: (1) continual pre-training on large-scale fitness-domain corpora, (2) supervised fine-tuning on high-quality, curated fitness datasets, and (3) reinforcement learning to further align and refine outputs. All datasets are constructed through rigorous knowledge engineering. Two model scales (8B and 32B) are produced.
AI.result: On ACSM-EP and NSCA-CSCS professional fitness certification exams, FitOne-8B gains 10.09%/12.73% and FitOne-32B gains 9.29%/7.01% over Qwen3 base models. Both models retain strong general capabilities (knowledge reasoning, instruction following). Ablation studies validate the necessity of each training stage.
AI.conclusion: The three-stage post-training pipeline effectively balances domain expertise enhancement with general ability retention. FitOne advances LLM systems toward more reliable fitness intelligence and provides a blueprint for developing domain-specific LLMs in other fields.

title: Conditional Co-Ablation: Recovering Self-Repair Backups in Transformer Circuits
summary: Mechanistic interpretability often relies on component-level interventions to discover how a model produces a behavior. This guides attribution, capability knockout, and model pruning downstream to operate by scoring each unit by the effect of ablation in isolation. Such first-order scoring is natural when component importance is additive, but becomes misleading when a transformer self-repairs: after a primary component is removed, a dormant backup can take over, muting the primary's measured effect while the backup itself appears irrelevant on the intact model. We recast this failure as a recovery task, conditional circuit completion, and introduce Conditional Co-Ablation (CoAx), a label-free, output-grounded score that asks how much each remaining unit's ablation effect grows once a primary set has been removed. This conditional growth exposes the second-order interaction that single-unit scores discard. On the GPT-2-small IOI circuit, CoAx raises backup-head recovery from 0.33 to 0.91 ROC-AUC, outperforming all baselines, including self-repair-aware gradient scores (best 0.82); counterfactual patching verifies that the recovered heads causally carry the repair. The same label-free procedure transfers to induction across eight models. Beyond discovery, the recovered backups correct self-repair-masked attribution, identify the components required for capability knockout, and yield repair-aware structured pruning scaling from 124M to 7B. Component importance is therefore not merely an isolated-unit property: in robust circuits, the components that matter can become visible only under the interventions that make them necessary.

AI.tldr: Standard component ablation scores miss "backup" units in transformers because self-repair masks their importance; the paper introduces Conditional Co-Ablation (CoAx), a second-order scoring method that identifies dormant backup components by measuring how their ablation effect grows after primary components are removed, achieving superior recovery on GPT-2 and across eight models, with applications to attribution, knockout, and structured pruning.
AI.motivation: First-order ablation scoring (measuring the effect of removing a single component in isolation) assumes additive component importance. However, transformers exhibit self-repair: when a primary component is ablated, a previously dormant backup component can take over its function. This causes two failures — the primary's measured importance is muted (since the backup compensates), and the backup appears irrelevant on the intact model. The authors frame this as a conditional circuit completion problem requiring second-order interaction scoring.
AI.method: The authors introduce Conditional Co-Ablation (CoAx), a label-free, output-grounded score. Given a primary set of components already removed, CoAx measures how much each remaining unit's ablation effect *grows* relative to its effect on the intact model. Formally, this captures the conditional interaction: the difference between a unit's ablation impact with vs. without the primary set present. This exposes second-order dependencies that single-unit scores discard. The method is evaluated on GPT-2-small's IOI circuit for backup-head recovery and transfers to induction tasks across eight models (124M–7B).
AI.result: On the GPT-2-small IOI circuit, CoAx raises backup-head recovery from 0.33 to 0.91 ROC-AUC, outperforming all baselines including self-repair-aware gradient scores (best 0.82). Counterfactual patching verifies that recovered heads causally carry the repair. The method transfers to induction across eight models (124M to 7B). Downstream, CoAx corrects self-repair-masked attribution, identifies components needed for capability knockout, and enables repair-aware structured pruning that scales across model sizes.
AI.conclusion: Component importance is not merely an isolated-unit property; in robust circuits, the components that matter may become visible only under interventions that make them necessary. CoAx provides a principled, second-order approach to discovering these conditionally important backup components, with broad applicability to interpretability, model editing, and pruning.

title: Coding-agents can replicate scientific machine learning papers
summary: Scientific machine learning papers typically make computational claims, e.g., that the relative mean square error is less than 5% or that the 95% predictive credible interval covers the test data. A coding agent can be prompted to replicate those claims from paper materials alone, but the prompt does not by itself reliably preserve progress or check whether generated evidence supports the paper's claims. We introduce Paper-replication, a workflow that makes each selected paper claim a target with recorded evidence, and implement it as a coding-agent skill. The workflow makes the agent record those targets, reconstruct the paper's method, run computational experiments, link generated outputs to provenance and comparisons with the paper's claims, record where matched evidence appears in the replication report, and pass validation checks before completion. We evaluate Paper-replication on twelve independent runs across four scientific machine learning papers. All twelve workspaces pass the completion gate, and all 158 recorded targets are matched with report coverage. Even in this completed workspace state, repeated runs differ in how papers are divided into targets, in numerical fidelity to the source papers, in elapsed replication time, in the number of intermediate executions replaced before final evidence is accepted, and in the rules used to accept evidence. Paper-replication makes completion depend on workspace evidence and validation checks rather than on the agent's final message.

AI.tldr: Paper-replication is a coding-agent workflow that systematically reconstructs scientific ML papers' methods, runs computational experiments, and validates results against original claims by recording targets and evidence in a structured workspace, with completion gated by validation checks rather than agent messages.
AI.motivation: Existing coding agents can attempt to replicate scientific ML papers but lack mechanisms to reliably preserve progress, verify whether generated evidence supports the paper's claims, or ensure completion quality. Prompts alone are insufficient for guaranteeing faithful replication.
AI.method: The authors propose Paper-replication, a structured workflow implemented as a coding-agent skill. It decomposes each paper claim into recorded targets, reconstructs the paper's method, runs computational experiments, links outputs to provenance and claim comparisons, records where matched evidence appears in the replication report, and enforces validation checks before allowing completion.
AI.result: Evaluated across twelve independent runs on four scientific ML papers, all twelve workspaces passed the completion gate, and all 158 recorded targets were matched with report coverage. However, repeated runs exhibited variability in target decomposition, numerical fidelity, elapsed time, number of intermediate executions replaced before final evidence acceptance, and evidence-acceptance rules.
AI.conclusion: Paper-replication shifts completion dependency from the agent's final message to workspace evidence and validation checks, enabling more reliable and auditable computational reproducibility for scientific ML claims.

title: Hybrid quantum-classical neural network for sentiment analysis
summary: Quantum machine learning has recently emerged as a promising paradigm that leverages the expressive power of quantum circuits to address complex learning tasks. In this work, we investigate the applicability of hybrid quantum-classical neural networks to sentiment analysis, a central problem in natural language processing. We focus on a dataset of tweets related to COVID-19, where the textual content is vectorized using TF-IDF and fed into both classical feedforward networks and hybrid architectures incorporating parameterized quantum circuits. Our results show that hybrid models can achieve accuracy comparable to the classical baseline, while exhibiting distinct learning dynamics, especially in terms of validation loss and accuracy, that suggest a richer representational capacity. Moreover, when applying transfer learning to an SMS spam classification task, the hybrid models consistently outperform the classical counterpart, achieving an accuracy increase of 15 percentage points (from 66% to 81%) on the spam class, demonstrating enhanced generalization. These findings highlight the feasibility of employing QML for natural language processing and point toward the potential advantages of hybrid models as quantum hardware continues to advance.

AI.tldr: The paper explores hybrid quantum-classical neural networks for NLP tasks, showing they match classical baselines on COVID-19 tweet sentiment analysis and significantly outperform them in transfer learning to SMS spam classification (achieving 81% vs. 66% accuracy on the spam class).
AI.motivation: To investigate whether hybrid quantum-classical neural networks can offer representational advantages over purely classical models for natural language processing tasks, and to assess the feasibility of quantum machine learning (QML) in this domain as quantum hardware matures.
AI.method: The authors vectorize COVID-19 tweet text using TF-IDF and feed these representations into both classical feedforward networks and hybrid architectures incorporating parameterized quantum circuits. They evaluate on sentiment analysis and further assess generalization via transfer learning to an SMS spam classification task.
AI.result: Hybrid quantum-classical models achieve accuracy comparable to the classical baseline on sentiment analysis, with distinct learning dynamics (validation loss and accuracy curves) suggesting richer representational capacity. In transfer learning, hybrid models consistently outperform the classical counterpart, improving spam-class accuracy by 15 percentage points (66% → 81%).
AI.conclusion: Hybrid QML models are viable for NLP tasks and demonstrate promising generalization advantages, particularly in transfer learning settings, pointing to the potential of hybrid architectures as quantum hardware continues to advance.

title: A$^{2}$utoLPBench: An Auto-Generated, Agent-Friendly LP Benchmark via Inverse-KKT Construction
summary: Most LP-from-text benchmarks are static datasets of word problems written and labeled by hand. Once such a dataset is released, its size is fixed, its difficulty is fixed, and every problem can leak into the training data of future LLMs. We present \textbf{A$^{2}$utoLPBench}, a benchmark for testing LLM-driven agents on linear programming problems written in plain text. We first pick a feasible point and dual, then write down a problem for which that point is optimal and the objective value is known. The answer is known by construction, with no solver call and no human annotator. The evaluation environment bundles a reference solver-critic baseline and a Docker image whose usage instructions are written for an LLM-driven agent to read. With these in place, any agent can run the benchmark and get a calibrated score with one command. Because the benchmark is a generator rather than a fixed dataset, it has properties no fixed dataset can match: an unlimited supply of fresh problems, a difficulty knob set by $(n,m)$, ground-truth answers correct by construction, low LLM-side cost per problem relative to human authoring, repeatable scores across independent batches, and resistance to training-data leakage when fresh post-cutoff seed ranges are used.

AI.tldr: A$^{2}$utoLPBench is a generative benchmark for testing LLM agents on linear programming word problems. Problems are constructed backward from a known optimal point and dual, guaranteeing ground-truth answers without solvers or human annotators. It offers unlimited fresh problems, a tunable difficulty knob (n, m), and resistance to data leakage.
AI.motivation: Existing LP-from-text benchmarks are static, hand-labeled datasets with fixed size, fixed difficulty, and vulnerability to training-data leakage. There is a need for a scalable, repeatable, and leakage-resistant evaluation framework for LLM-driven agents solving linear programming problems.
AI.method: The benchmark generates problems by constructing them backward: first pick a feasible primal point and dual solution, then synthesize a word problem for which that point is provably optimal with a known objective value. The evaluation environment includes a reference solver-critic baseline and a Docker image with usage instructions written for LLM agents. Scores are calibrated and obtained with a single command.
AI.result: The benchmark achieves: unlimited fresh problem generation, difficulty controlled by parameters (n, m), ground-truth answers correct by construction, low per-problem cost vs. human authoring, repeatable scores across independent batches, and leakage resistance when fresh post-cutoff seed ranges are used.
AI.conclusion: A generative benchmark like A$^{2}$utoLPBench overcomes fundamental limitations of static datasets, offering a more robust, scalable, and fair evaluation paradigm for measuring LLM-driven agents' capabilities on linear programming tasks.

title: A More Accurate Algorithm Comparison through A/B Testing using Offline Evaluation Methods
summary: A/B testing is the gold standard for selecting the better algorithm in online services. While offline evaluation has attracted attention as a safer alternative due to the high experimental costs and the potential risk of degrading user experience and revenue in A/B testing, it is widely recognized that the estimation accuracy of offline evaluation is substantially lower. As a result, final selection decisions are typically made through A/B testing. Contrary to this conventional view, we reveal a counterintuitive phenomenon in which A/B testing can produce a higher algorithm selection error rate than offline evaluation. This occurs because the sample mean estimator used in A/B testing does not induce positive correlation, which is crucial for reducing critical selection errors, namely underestimating the truly superior algorithm and overestimating the truly inferior one. In contrast, offline evaluation methods unintentionally generate this beneficial correlation by relying on shared offline data when estimating and comparing the performance of multiple algorithms. Building on this insight, we propose an estimator that intentionally induces positive correlation to improve algorithm selection in A/B testing. The key idea is to introduce a hypothetical middle algorithm and to estimate the performance difference between algorithms A, M, and B in a stepwise manner using shared data at each step. This approach enables the application of offline evaluation techniques in each step, thereby inducing positive correlation and reducing critical selection errors. Furthermore, we derive the optimal middle algorithm regarding the resulting variance and analyze its advantages over existing methods through bias-variance analysis. Experiments on real-world data demonstrate that our estimator achieves the same selection error rate as existing approaches while using only one half of the A/B testing data.

AI.tldr: A/B testing can surprisingly yield higher algorithm selection error than offline evaluation because its sample mean estimator lacks positive correlation; the authors propose a stepwise estimator with a hypothetical middle algorithm that induces this correlation, halving the data needed for equivalent selection accuracy.
AI.motivation: Offline evaluation is considered safer but less accurate than A/B testing for algorithm selection. The authors challenge this orthodoxy by revealing that A/B testing can actually produce higher selection error rates due to the absence of positive correlation in its estimators, which offline methods inadvertently provide through shared data.
AI.method: The authors introduce a stepwise estimator for A/B testing that induces positive correlation by positing a hypothetical middle algorithm M. Performance differences between algorithms A, M, and B are estimated sequentially using overlapping/shared data at each step, enabling offline evaluation techniques to be embedded within the A/B testing framework. The optimal middle algorithm is derived analytically based on variance minimization, and bias-variance analysis is used to characterize advantages over standard methods.
AI.result: Experiments on real-world data show the proposed estimator achieves the same algorithm selection error rate as existing A/B testing approaches while requiring only half the data.
AI.conclusion: Intentionally inducing positive correlation via a stepwise estimation procedure with a middle algorithm significantly improves the data efficiency of A/B testing for algorithm selection, matching conventional performance at half the sample size.

title: A rubric-based controlled comparison of frontier language models on expert-authored clinical reasoning tasks
summary: Multiple-choice medical benchmarks are increasingly saturated, and recent rubric-based evaluations such as HealthBench have shown that open-ended clinical performance is far from solved - its "Hard" subset top score remains 32%. We present a small, deliberately difficult evaluation dataset of five clinician-authored clinical scenarios spanning four specialties (anaesthesia, internal/family medicine, emergency medicine, and obstetrics), each accompanied by an atomic, weighted, MECE rubric (25-62 criteria per task; 184 criteria total) authored from a clinician-drafted golden answer. We evaluate three frontier models: GPT 5.4, Claude Opus 4.7, and Gemini 3.1 Pro. Mean rubric pass rates were 0.47 (Claude), 0.39 (GPT), and 0.37 (Gemini). The central finding is an inversion of clinical priority: the highest-weighted (weight-5, critical) criteria passed at only 32.4-41.7%, while low-stakes weight-1 criteria passed at 80-90%. 56 of 108 critical (weight-5) criteria (52%) were satisfied by no model. Three LLM autoraters reproduced expert met/not-met labels on 92.8-94.7% of 552 graded criteria. We position this as a methods-and-preliminary-findings contribution: the five tasks demonstrate a scalable, defensible pipeline ready to develop into a large-scale benchmark.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a small, clinician-authored evaluation dataset of five open-ended clinical scenarios with weighted MECE rubrics (184 criteria total). Evaluating three frontier models (GPT, Claude, Gemini), mean rubric pass rates were 0.37–0.47, with a critical inversion: high-weight (critical) criteria passed at only 32–42%, while low-stakes criteria passed at 80–90%. Over half of critical criteria were satisfied by no model. LLM autoraters reproduced expert labels at 93–95%.
AI.motivation: Multiple-choice medical benchmarks are saturated and fail to capture real clinical reasoning. Recent rubric-based evaluations show open-ended clinical performance remains poor (HealthBench Hard top score: 32%). The authors aim to construct a deliberately difficult, defensible, scalable evaluation framework that reveals where frontier models fail on clinically critical tasks.
AI.method: Five clinician-authored clinical scenarios across four specialties (anaesthesia, internal/family medicine, emergency medicine, obstetrics). Each scenario includes a clinician-drafted golden answer and an atomic, weighted, MECE (Mutually Exclusive, Collectively Exhaustive) rubric of 25–62 criteria (184 total), weighted from 1 (low-stakes) to 5 (critical). Three frontier models (GPT 5.4, Claude Opus 4.7, Gemini 3.1 Pro) evaluated. Three LLM autoraters validated against expert met/not-met labels on 552 graded criteria.
AI.result: Mean rubric pass rates: Claude 0.47, GPT 0.39, Gemini 0.37. Critical inversion: weight-5 criteria passed at 32.4–41.7% vs. weight-1 criteria at 80–90%. 56 of 108 critical criteria (52%) passed by no model. LLM autoraters achieved 92.8–94.7% agreement with expert labels.
AI.conclusion: Frontier models exhibit a dangerous inversion of clinical priority, performing worst on the most critical clinical criteria. The five-task dataset demonstrates a scalable, defensible pipeline suitable for expansion into a large-scale benchmark for open-ended clinical reasoning.

title: Probabilistic Low-Voltage Peak Load Forecasting with Time Series Foundation Models Evaluated on Application-Oriented Metrics
comment: A poster abstract of this publication will be available at the 15th DACH+ Conference on Energy Informatics (2026 in Linz, Austria)
summary: Low-voltage load forecasting is an important component in current and future energy systems with a high degree of electrification and decentralized generation. However, current forecasting methods require significant manual effort, often lack uncertainty estimation and proper peak prediction, and they are often not adequately evaluated in terms of grid requirements. In the present study, we provide an extensive evaluation of short-term net load forecasts of 200 real-world low-voltage feeders with a focus on the rapidly evolving time series foundation models. Our study compares Chronos-Bolt, Chronos-2 and TabPFN-TS to six baseline models and demonstrates superior performance, in particular for Chronos-2. An ablation study, in which weather covariates are omitted, shows that time series foundation models adapt to increased uncertainty, despite the importance of weather information. A novel application-oriented metric links the model's forecasting capabilities in peak prediction to the trade-off in grid asset planning and operation between cost reduction and minimizing the risk of failure.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates short-term net load forecasting across 200 real-world low-voltage feeders, comparing time series foundation models (Chronos-Bolt, Chronos-2, TabPFN-TS) against six baselines. Chronos-2 achieves superior performance. A novel metric links peak prediction quality to grid asset planning trade-offs between cost and failure risk.
AI.motivation: Current low-voltage load forecasting methods suffer from three key deficiencies: (1) they demand substantial manual effort, (2) they frequently lack uncertainty quantification and reliable peak prediction, and (3) they are rarely evaluated against actual grid-level requirements. With increasing electrification and decentralized generation, robust forecasting becomes critical for grid operation and planning.
AI.method: The authors conduct an extensive empirical evaluation of three time series foundation models — Chronos-Bolt, Chronos-2, and TabPFN-TS — benchmarked against six conventional baseline models. The evaluation spans 200 real-world low-voltage feeders. An ablation study removes weather covariates to assess model robustness under increased uncertainty. Additionally, a novel application-oriented metric is introduced that explicitly connects peak forecasting accuracy to the economic trade-off in grid asset planning between cost reduction and failure risk minimization.
AI.result: Time series foundation models, particularly Chronos-2, consistently outperform all six baseline models on net load forecasting across 200 LV feeders. The ablation study reveals that these foundation models adapt effectively to heightened uncertainty when weather covariates are removed, despite weather information being demonstrably important. The proposed application-oriented metric successfully captures the operational tension between cost savings and reliability risk in grid planning.
AI.conclusion: Time series foundation models represent a compelling, low-effort solution for short-term low-voltage net load forecasting, with Chronos-2 delivering best-in-class performance. Their robustness under missing weather data and the practical relevance of peak-prediction evaluation via the new metric underscore their suitability for real-world grid applications.

title: UA-ChatDev: Uncertainty-Aware Multi-Agent Collaboration for Reliable Software Development
summary: Software development is a complex task that demands cooperation among agents with diverse roles. Large language models (LLMs) have enabled autonomous multi-agent software development frameworks that leverage role-based collaboration to automate requirements analysis, coding, testing, and refinement. However, existing approaches typically assume that intermediate agent outputs are equally reliable, leaving them vulnerable to hallucination propagation, where incorrect decisions generated in early development phases are transferred to downstream agents and negatively impact final software quality. To address this challenge, we propose UA-ChatDev, an uncertainty-aware multi-agent software development framework that integrates uncertainty quantification into agent interactions. It introduces a lightweight uncertainty estimation mechanism based on token-level log probabilities to assess the confidence of agent responses and employs phase-aware threshold calibration to selectively trigger retrieval-based verification when uncertainty exceeds acceptable levels. Extensive experiments on the SRDD benchmark demonstrate that UA-ChatDev consistently outperforms existing single-agent and multi-agent software development frameworks across completeness, executability, consistency, and overall quality metrics. Further ablation studies and communication analyses verify that uncertainty-aware interactions enhance code execution reliability.

AI.tldr: UA-ChatDev is an uncertainty-aware multi-agent software development framework that uses token-level log probabilities to quantify confidence in agent outputs and selectively triggers retrieval-based verification when uncertainty exceeds calibrated thresholds, thereby preventing hallucination propagation across development phases.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-agent LLM-based software development frameworks treat all intermediate agent outputs as equally reliable, which allows hallucinations generated in early phases (requirements, design) to propagate to downstream agents (coding, testing), degrading final software quality.
AI.method: UA-ChatDev introduces (1) a lightweight uncertainty estimation mechanism using token-level log probabilities to assess response confidence, and (2) phase-aware threshold calibration that selectively invokes retrieval-based verification when uncertainty surpasses acceptable levels for a given development phase.
AI.result: Experiments on the SRDD benchmark show UA-ChatDev consistently outperforms existing single-agent and multi-agent frameworks on completeness, executability, consistency, and overall quality. Ablation studies and communication analyses confirm that uncertainty-aware interactions improve code execution reliability.
AI.conclusion: Integrating uncertainty quantification into multi-agent software development effectively mitigates hallucination propagation, leading to more reliable and higher-quality software outputs.

title: Do Newer Lightweight CNNs Perform Better Under Resource Constraints? A Controlled Multigenerational Study of Architecture, Initialization, Training Budget, and Efficiency
summary: Newer lightweight convolutional neural networks are often presented as improving predictive performance and deployment efficiency, but such claims require controlled evaluation. This study compares nine lightweight CNN model packages across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet under a shared downstream protocol. We report top-1 accuracy, macro F1, top-5 accuracy, parameter count, FP32 storage, GMACs, batch-size-1 latency on an NVIDIA L4 and AMD Ryzen 5 5500U CPU, peak PyTorch CUDA allocated tensor memory, and point estimate Pareto frontiers. EfficientNetV2-S achieves the highest observed top-1 accuracy on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 at 97.57% and 86.98%, while RepViT-M1.0 leads Tiny ImageNet at 79.87%. EfficientNet-B0 remains within 0.22, 0.85, and 1.79 percentage points of the best result on the three datasets while using approximately 79% fewer parameters and 86% fewer GMACs than EfficientNetV2-S. It also appears on every evaluated accuracy and resource Pareto frontier, making it the most consistently competitive intermediate-budget option. MobileNetV3-Small has the lowest GMAC count, is the fastest model under both CPU thread settings, and records higher observed accuracy than MobileNetV4-Conv-S on all three datasets. Under random initialization, it leads MobileNetV4-Conv-S by 2.55, 1.76, and 0.99 points, with paired test-set intervals excluding zero for the fixed trained models. EfficientNet-B0 remains 3.29, 10.10, and 17.54 points below its pretrained counterpart after 100 epochs of scratch training, despite requiring about five times the recorded training time. SqueezeNet1.1 has the fewest parameters and lowest peak CUDA allocation, but substantially weaker accuracy. Latency rankings differ sharply between the L4 and CPU environments, showing that GMACs alone do not predict measured inference performance. Overall, newer designs provide selective rather than universal gains

AI.tldr: A controlled comparison of nine lightweight CNNs across three datasets reveals that newer models offer selective rather than universal gains. EfficientNet-B0 emerges as the most consistently competitive intermediate-budget option, appearing on every accuracy-resource Pareto frontier, while EfficientNetV2-S achieves highest accuracy on CIFAR-10/100 and RepViT-M1.0 leads on Tiny ImageNet.
AI.motivation: Newer lightweight CNNs are frequently claimed to improve both predictive performance and deployment efficiency, but these claims lack rigorous controlled evaluation across consistent downstream protocols. The authors aim to provide a standardized, multi-metric comparison to determine whether newer designs genuinely outperform established baselines across the accuracy-efficiency spectrum.
AI.method: Nine lightweight CNN model packages (including EfficientNet variants, MobileNet variants, RepViT, and SqueezeNet) are evaluated under a shared downstream protocol on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet. Metrics include top-1 accuracy, macro F1, top-5 accuracy, parameter count, FP32 storage, GMACs, batch-size-1 latency on NVIDIA L4 GPU and AMD Ryzen 5 5500U CPU, peak PyTorch CUDA allocated tensor memory, and point estimate Pareto frontiers. Both pretrained and random-initialization (scratch training) settings are assessed.
AI.result: EfficientNetV2-S achieves highest top-1 accuracy on CIFAR-10 (97.57%) and CIFAR-100 (86.98%); RepViT-M1.0 leads Tiny ImageNet (79.87%). EfficientNet-B0 trails the best results by only 0.22–1.79 points while using ~79% fewer parameters and 86% fewer GMACs than EfficientNetV2-S, appearing on every Pareto frontier. MobileNetV3-Small has the lowest GMACs, is fastest on CPU, and outperforms MobileNetV4-Conv-S across all datasets. Under scratch training, EfficientNet-B0 falls 3.29–17.54 points below its pretrained counterpart despite ~5× longer training time. SqueezeNet1.1 has fewest parameters and lowest peak CUDA memory but weakest accuracy. Latency rankings differ sharply between L4 GPU and CPU, demonstrating that GMACs alone do not predict measured inference speed.
AI.conclusion: Newer lightweight CNN designs provide selective rather than universal improvements. EfficientNet-B0 remains the most consistently competitive intermediate-budget model, while MobileNetV3-Small offers the best efficiency for extremely resource-constrained deployment. The divergence between GMACs and measured latency underscores the need for hardware-specific benchmarking rather than relying solely on theoretical FLOPs.

title: Criticality-Based Guard Rail Validation for AI Agent Decisions in Autonomous Telecom Networks
summary: The evolution toward fully autonomous telecommunications networks (Autonomous Network Levels 4-5) requires AI/ML agents to make real-time network decisions without human intervention. However, no standardized runtime mechanism exists to intercept and validate individual inference outputs before they trigger live network state changes, creating risks of erroneous autonomous decisions. This paper proposes the Guard Rail Validation (GRV) framework, a standardizable runtime architecture for intercepting and validating AI-driven decisions before execution. The framework evaluates decisions across multiple weighted dimensions -- including action scope, action type, service criticality, agent autonomy level, reversibility, and temporal behavioural patterns -- to determine a criticality level. Based on this level, graduated validation mechanisms are applied: execute-with-logging, bounds checking, independent agent validation, or multi-agent consensus. The framework additionally provides cross-agent conflict detection with criticality-weighted priority resolution and runtime conformance logging for regulatory compliance (e.g., EU AI Act Article 14). We present the architecture, algorithmic procedures, O-RAN deployment model, and evaluate threat coverage against known AI/ML attacks in telecommunications.

AI.tldr: Proposes GRV, a runtime framework that intercepts AI/ML inference outputs in autonomous networks, evaluates their criticality across multiple weighted dimensions, and applies graduated validation mechanisms (logging, bounds checking, independent validation, multi-agent consensus) before decisions trigger live network changes, with cross-agent conflict resolution and regulatory compliance logging.
AI.motivation: Autonomous Networks Levels 4–5 require fully automated AI/ML decision-making, yet no standardized runtime mechanism exists to validate individual inference outputs before they cause live network state changes, creating significant risk of erroneous autonomous actions.
AI.method: The GRV framework intercepts AI inference outputs and computes a criticality score using six weighted dimensions: action scope, action type, service criticality, agent autonomy level, reversibility, and temporal behavioral patterns. Based on this score, it applies one of four graduated validation mechanisms: execute-with-logging, bounds checking, independent agent validation, or multi-agent consensus. It also features cross-agent conflict detection with criticality-weighted priority resolution and runtime conformance logging mapped to EU AI Act Article 14. Deployment is demonstrated in an O-RAN architecture model.
AI.result: The paper presents the architecture and algorithmic procedures, demonstrates an O-RAN deployment model, and evaluates threat coverage against known AI/ML attacks in telecommunications contexts.
AI.conclusion: A standardizable runtime guardrail architecture like GRV is essential for safe, compliant transition to fully autonomous networks, providing graduated, criticality-aware validation without blocking legitimate autonomous decisions.

title: Liquid Latent State Dynamics for Interpretable Turbofan Degradation Modeling
summary: Multivariate time-series models for prognostics are often evaluated by point prediction accuracy, yet their internal states rarely expose a coherent degradation process. We study liquid neural networks as latent dynamics models for aircraft engine health monitoring on the C-MAPSS benchmark. The proposed model encodes a history window into a latent state, evolves that state with a liquid transition model, and decodes future sensor observations. To separate health evolution from operating-condition variation, the latent state is factorized into degradation and condition components. Remaining useful life, monotonic risk, and latent-consistency losses supervise the degradation component, while condition prediction and decorrelation losses discourage operating-condition leakage. Across FD001--FD004, the full disentangled model improves overall sensor forecasting RMSE from 0.2438 for a GRU baseline to 0.2266, with the largest gains on the multi-condition subsets FD002 and FD004. The learned degradation state also forms a clearer temporal degradation axis, reaching an average state-speed Spearman correlation of 0.5960. Direct remaining-useful-life regression remains stronger for the GRU baseline, indicating that the proposed representation is currently more effective as an interpretable world model for degradation dynamics than as a calibrated lifetime regressor. These results suggest that liquid latent dynamics can bridge predictive maintenance forecasting and inspectable health-state modeling.

AI.tldr: A liquid neural network with a factorized latent space (degradation vs. operating condition) is proposed for aircraft engine prognostics. It improves sensor forecasting over GRU baselines and yields a more interpretable degradation trajectory, though direct RUL regression still favors the GRU baseline.
AI.motivation: Prognostics models are typically judged by point-prediction accuracy, but their internal states rarely reflect a physically meaningful degradation process. There is a need for latent dynamics models that not only forecast well but also learn coherent, inspectable health-state representations, especially under varying operating conditions.
AI.method: The authors propose a liquid neural network that encodes a history window of sensor data into a latent state, evolves it via a liquid time-constant transition, and decodes future observations. The latent state is explicitly factorized into a degradation component and a condition component. The degradation component is supervised by remaining-useful-life labels, monotonic risk, and latent-consistency losses; the condition component is guided by condition-prediction and decorrelation losses to prevent operating-condition information from leaking into the health representation.
AI.result: Across C-MAPSS subsets FD001–FD004, the disentangled model reduces overall sensor forecasting RMSE from 0.2438 (GRU baseline) to 0.2266, with largest gains on multi-condition subsets FD002 and FD004. The degradation state yields a clearer temporal degradation axis, achieving an average state-speed Spearman correlation of 0.5960. However, direct RUL regression remains stronger for the GRU baseline.
AI.conclusion: Liquid latent dynamics can bridge predictive maintenance forecasting and interpretable health-state modeling, but the current representation functions better as an inspectable world model for degradation dynamics than as a calibrated lifetime regressor.

title: Purified OPSD: On-Policy Self-Distillation Without Losing How to Think
summary: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) has emerged as a promising paradigm for improving LLM reasoning, where a privileged teacher with access to reference solutions provides token-level supervision on the student's own generated trajectories. However, we find that OPSD consistently fails on long chain-of-thought (long-CoT) reasoning models, yielding at best marginal gains while destabilizing the reflective reasoning capability these models depend on. Through a novel decomposition of the teacher's supervision signal, we identify the root cause: the teacher's supervision is dominated by a reference-induced component that drives rote memorization of reference-specific shortcuts, while the question-conditioned, inference-transferable component is ignored or actively opposed. Based on this diagnosis, we propose a two-step solution. First, we construct a reference-only teacher (the same model conditioned on the reference without the question) to isolate the non-transferable component of the supervision signal; the residual after subtracting this component captures the question-conditioned, inference-transferable correction. Second, we use pointwise mutual information (PMI) as the mechanism to transform this residual into a well-formed PMI target distribution that the student can directly distill from, filtering out the reference-induced shortcut. Experiments on four long-CoT models across two datasets demonstrate consistent improvements over both the base model and standard OPSD, while preserving the models' natural epistemic behavior throughout training.

AI.tldr: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) fails on long chain-of-thought reasoning models because the teacher's supervision is dominated by reference-induced shortcuts that promote rote memorization rather than transferable reasoning. The authors propose isolating and subtracting this non-transferable component, then using pointwise mutual information (PMI) to construct a clean distillation target, yielding consistent improvements across multiple long-CoT models.
AI.motivation: OPSD shows promise for improving LLM reasoning but consistently fails on long chain-of-thought models—yielding marginal gains and destabilizing the reflective reasoning these models rely on. The paper seeks to diagnose why this failure occurs and develop a remedy that preserves reasoning capabilities.
AI.method: The authors first decompose the teacher's supervision signal into a reference-induced (rote memorization) component and a question-conditioned (inference-transferable) component. They then propose: (1) constructing a reference-only teacher to isolate the non-transferable component, and subtracting it to obtain the question-conditioned residual; (2) applying pointwise mutual information (PMI) to transform this residual into a well-formed target distribution for student distillation, effectively filtering out reference-induced shortcuts.
AI.result: Experiments on four long-CoT models across two datasets show consistent improvements over both the base model and standard OPSD, while preserving the models' natural epistemic behavior (e.g., reflective reasoning) throughout training.
AI.conclusion: Standard OPSD fails on long-CoT models because reference-induced shortcuts dominate the supervision signal. The proposed two-step solution—reference-only teacher subtraction plus PMI-based distillation—effectively recovers the transferable reasoning signal and yields robust improvements without destabilizing reflective reasoning capabilities.

title: Fast and Accurate Anomaly Detection in Time Series
summary: Anomaly detection is a critical and evolving field in Machine Learning, with applications targeting different domains such as cybersecurity, finance, healthcare, manufacturing and IoT (Internet of Things) systems. Traditionally, anomaly detection algorithms have been designed using both supervised and unsupervised learning paradigms. The fundamental challenge in real-world anomaly detection scenarios is related to the inherent class imbalance (anomalies are typically rare) and, for supervised methods, to the scarcity of labelled anomalous data. Indeed, labelling is both expensive and time-consuming. Conversely unsupervised methods do not require labelling, but may suffer from high false positive rates when deployed in safety-critical applications. In this work we introduce a novel unsupervised algorithm for anomaly detection in time series based on the Haar discrete wavelet and a suitably designed $t$-test. We establish the theoretical foundation of the proposed $t$-test and, through extensive experimentation across 343 datasets, demonstrate that our algorithm outperforms state-of-the-art unsupervised and self-supervised benchmarks.

AI.tldr: A novel unsupervised anomaly detection algorithm for time series is proposed, combining Haar discrete wavelet decomposition with a specially designed t-test. Tested across 343 datasets, it outperforms existing unsupervised and self-supervised methods.
AI.motivation: Real-world anomaly detection suffers from severe class imbalance (rare anomalies) and, in supervised settings, from scarce labeled anomalous data due to costly and time-consuming labeling. Unsupervised methods avoid labeling but often yield high false positive rates in safety-critical applications, motivating a more robust unsupervised approach.
AI.method: The authors propose an unsupervised anomaly detection algorithm for time series that integrates the Haar discrete wavelet transform with a purpose-designed t-test, supported by a formal theoretical foundation for the test.
AI.result: Extensive experimentation on 343 datasets shows the proposed algorithm outperforms state-of-the-art unsupervised and self-supervised benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The Haar wavelet-based t-test method provides a theoretically grounded, highly effective unsupervised anomaly detection solution for time series, surpassing current benchmarks across a large-scale empirical evaluation.

title: A Memory Efficient Unified Algorithm for Online Learning of Linear Dynamical Systems
summary: Motivated by the challenge of stabilizing a general unknown linear dynamical system (LDS) from observations, we study the natural prerequisite of online prediction. Our goal is to achieve sublinear regret with a memory footprint that adapts to the intrinsic complexity of the dynamics rather than the full hidden -- state dimension. We focus on the practically central regime of systems with low instability complexity -- eigenvalues outside the real stable interval that do not decay rapidly, together with non-semisimple modes-potentially embedded in an otherwise stable real spectrum of much higher dimension; we write $k$ for this count. This regime is the primary setting in which stabilization is plausible: we show that many systems with high instability complexity cannot be stabilized without exponentially large controls. Thus, prediction is meaningful for stabilization precisely when the instability complexity is small. Within this regime, we introduce a unified online algorithm that handles every LDS (including non-diagonalizable systems with complex or exploding modes) with a learnable parameter count of $\widetilde{O}(k)$. Finally, we prove a lower bound showing that $k$ is a valid complexity measure: any filter-based predictor needs at least $k$ filters. Experiments corroborate our theory: on a high-dimensional system, our predictor sharply outperforms prior methods at an equal parameter budget.

AI.tldr: For stabilizing unknown linear dynamical systems, this paper shows that online prediction is feasible with memory scaling in the system's "instability complexity" k (number of problematic eigenvalues/modes) rather than the full state dimension, and provides a matching algorithm and lower bound.
AI.motivation: Stabilizing unknown LDS from observations requires online prediction as a prerequisite. Existing methods have memory requirements scaling with the full hidden-state dimension, which is prohibitive for high-dimensional systems. The paper asks: can prediction memory instead scale with the intrinsic "instability complexity" — the number of eigenvalues outside the stable interval plus non-semisimple modes — which is often much smaller?
AI.method: The authors introduce a unified online prediction algorithm for general LDS (including non-diagonalizable systems with complex or exploding modes) whose learnable parameter count is Õ(k), where k is the instability complexity. They also prove a lower bound showing any filter-based predictor requires at least k filters. The analysis connects prediction feasibility to stabilization: systems with high instability complexity are shown to require exponentially large controls for stabilization.
AI.result: An algorithm achieving sublinear regret with Õ(k) parameters for online LDS prediction. A lower bound proving k filters are necessary for any filter-based predictor. A separation result: high instability complexity prevents stabilization without exponential control cost. Experiments on high-dimensional systems show the method sharply outperforms prior approaches at equal parameter budgets.
AI.conclusion: Instability complexity k is both a sufficient and necessary complexity measure for online LDS prediction. By designing algorithms that scale with k rather than the full state dimension, efficient prediction (and thus stabilization) becomes possible for high-dimensional systems with only a small number of unstable or problematic modes.

title: AgenticSTS: A Bounded-Memory Testbed for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
summary: Memory for a long-horizon LLM agent is a contract about what each future decision is allowed to see. The simplest contract appends past observations, tool calls, and reflections to every prompt, which makes prior context easy to access but also turns it into a jumbled mixture in which the effect of any single memory component is hard to isolate. We introduce and instrument an alternative bounded contract: every decision is made from a fresh user message assembled by typed retrieval, with no raw cross-decision transcript appended. The prompt thus stays bounded across runs of any length, and any single layer can be ablated in isolation. We instantiate the contract in Slay the Spire 2, a closed-rule stochastic deck-building game whose runs require hundreds of tactical and strategic decisions. A public online benchmark of frontier LLMs on the same game reports zero wins at the lowest difficulty across five configurations, and the developer-reported human win rate at the same difficulty is 16%; the task is hard but not saturated. Within our harness, a fixed-A0 ablation shows the largest observed difference when triggered strategic skills are enabled: the no-store baseline wins 3/10 games and adding the skill layer 6/10. At this sample size the comparison is directional rather than statistically decisive (Fisher exact p\approx0.37); a cross-backbone probe and public accumulating-context baselines are reported as operational comparisons rather than controlled tests of the contract variable itself. We release a reproducible testbed: 298 completed trajectories with condition tags, frozen memory/skill snapshots, prompt records, and analysis scripts -- an agent design and a validated, reusable methodology for studying how explicit memory layers shape long-horizon LLM-agent decisions.

AI.tldr: Proposes a "bounded contract" for LLM agent memory where each decision uses typed retrieval into a fresh prompt instead of appending full history, tested on Slay the Spire 2 with a reproducible testbed of 298 trajectories.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon LLM agents suffer from unbounded prompt growth when appending full history, making it impossible to isolate the effect of individual memory components. A structured, bounded approach is needed for both practical scaling and scientific ablation.
AI.method: Introduces a bounded memory contract where each decision prompt is assembled fresh via typed retrieval (no raw cross-decision transcript). Tested in a Slay the Spire 2 harness with ablatable memory/skill layers. Evaluated via win-rate comparisons (no-store baseline vs. skill-enabled), cross-backbone probes, and public accumulating-context baselines.
AI.result: The no-store baseline wins 3/10 games; adding triggered strategic skills achieves 6/10 wins. Directional but not statistically decisive (Fisher exact p≈0.37). Frontier LLMs on public benchmark score 0 wins at lowest difficulty; human win rate is 16%.
AI.conclusion: A bounded, retrieval-based memory contract enables modular ablation and shows promising directional gains from strategic skill layers. The authors release a reproducible testbed with 298 trajectories, frozen snapshots, and analysis tools as a methodology for studying explicit memory in LLM agents.

title: Bayesian Sparse Low-Rank Adaptation for Large Language Model Uncertainty Estimation
summary: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable reasoning capabilities, but their task-specific fine-tuning is notoriously plagued by overconfidence, severely hindering trustworthy deployment. We propose Data-Adaptive Lower-Rank Adaptation (DALorRA), a simple and effective variational Bayesian sparse framework that shifts the paradigm of uncertainty quantification from the dense parameter space to the lightweight rank level of low-rank adaptation (LoRA). With the insight that LoRA essentially aggregates multiple rank-one components that may provide superfluous model capacity, DALorRA imposes stochastic masking on rank dimensions, enabling Bayesian regularization of model capacity during training and ensemble-like calibration during inference. Extensive experiments demonstrate DALorRA's excellent calibration of LLMs without compromising reasoning accuracy.

AI.tldr: DALorRA introduces a variational Bayesian sparse framework that applies stochastic masking on LoRA rank dimensions, achieving excellent uncertainty calibration in fine-tuned LLMs without sacrificing reasoning accuracy.
AI.motivation: Task-specific fine-tuning of LLMs suffers from overconfidence, undermining trustworthy deployment. Existing LoRA methods provide superfluous model capacity through aggregated rank-one components, motivating a need for principled uncertainty quantification at the rank level.
AI.method: DALorRA is a variational Bayesian framework that operates on LoRA's low-rank adaptation structure. It imposes stochastic binary masking on rank dimensions during training, enabling Bayesian regularization of model capacity. During inference, the stochastic masks produce ensemble-like calibration through Monte Carlo sampling of the learned variational posterior over rank structures.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show DALorRA achieves excellent calibration of LLMs while maintaining reasoning accuracy comparable to or surpassing deterministic fine-tuned baselines.
AI.conclusion: Shifting uncertainty quantification from dense parameters to the lightweight rank level of LoRA provides an effective and practical solution for calibrating fine-tuned LLMs, enabling more trustworthy deployment.

title: Beyond the Performance Illusion: Structure-Aware Stratified Partitioning and Curriculum Distributionally Robust Optimization for Spatially Correlated Domains
summary: Performance evaluation in AI systems commonly assumes that random dataset splits produce independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) subsets. We show that this assumption often breaks down in spatiotemporally correlated domains such as aerial surveillance, precision agriculture, and medical imaging, leading to two systematic failures: data leakage, where correlated samples span training and validation splits and inflate performance estimates, and hidden stratification, where errors on minority subpopulations are obscured by aggregate metrics. To address these issues, we propose a unified evaluation and training framework for spatially correlated data. We introduce Structure-Aware Stratified Partitioning (SASP), which constructs validation splits that reduce spatiotemporal leakage while preserving meaningful class balance, and Curriculum Distributionally Robust Optimization (CDRO), a curriculum-based relaxation of distributionally robust training that stabilizes optimization under these stricter splits. Across multiple benchmarks, this combination yields consistently improved generalization, more reliable confidence calibration, and exposes failure modes that remain hidden under conventional random-split evaluation.

AI.tldr: Random dataset splits fail in spatiotemporally correlated domains, causing data leakage and hidden stratification. The authors propose SASP for better validation splits and CDRO for robust training, yielding improved generalization, calibration, and exposed failure modes.
AI.motivation: Standard i.i.d. random splitting assumptions break down in spatiotemporally correlated domains (aerial surveillance, precision agriculture, medical imaging), causing two critical failures: (1) data leakage inflating performance estimates, and (2) hidden stratification obscuring minority subpopulation errors. Current evaluation and training paradigms lack mechanisms to address these spatial dependencies.
AI.method: Two complementary components: (1) Structure-Aware Stratified Partitioning (SASP), which constructs validation splits that explicitly reduce spatiotemporal leakage by accounting for spatial autocorrelation while preserving class balance; and (2) Curriculum Distributionally Robust Optimization (CDRO), a curriculum-based relaxation of distributionally robust training that stabilizes optimization under the stricter, non-i.i.d. splits produced by SASP.
AI.result: Across multiple benchmarks, the SASP + CDRO combination consistently yields: improved generalization performance, more reliable confidence calibration, and successful exposure of failure modes that remain hidden under conventional random-split evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Spatiotemporally correlated domains require structure-aware evaluation and training paradigms. SASP and CDRO together form a unified framework that provides more honest performance estimates, better-calibrated models, and actionable insights into previously hidden failure modes.

title: A Hippocampus for Linear Attention: An Exact Memory for What the Recurrent State Forgets
summary: Linear-attention and state-space language models compress the prefix into a fixed-size recurrent state, yielding O(1) memory at the cost of a lossy exact memory: when many key--value associations compete, earlier facts are overwritten and needle recall degrades. Inspired by Complementary Learning Systems, we give linear attention a hippocampal complement. HOLA (Hippocampal Linear Attention) keeps the usual delta-rule state as a compressive memory and adds a bounded exact KV cache, forming a semiparametric test-time memory: the state models linearly compressible structure, while the cache stores associations that should not be forced through that state. The cache writes without a learned eviction module, keeping tokens with large beta * ||e||, the prediction residual actually committed to the state; a decoupled RMSNorm-gamma cache read then turns these exact KV pairs into sharp retrieval rather than soft averaging. At 340M parameters trained on 15B SlimPajama tokens, HOLA lowers Wikitext perplexity from 27.32 to 22.92 (-16.1%), below a full-attention Transformer++ (26.88), and improves LAMBADA perplexity from 30.95 to 30.26. It also achieves the best linear in-context retrieval and remains much more robust than GDN or a matched HOLA+recency cache on RULER needle-in-a-haystack recall out to 32k tokens (16x its training length).

AI.tldr: HOLA augments linear attention with a bounded exact KV cache (hippocampal complement), using prediction residuals to decide what to cache and a decoupled norm-gamma readout for sharp retrieval, achieving better perplexity than full Transformers and robust needle recall up to 32k tokens.
AI.motivation: Linear attention and state-space models compress the prefix into a fixed recurrent state (O(1) memory), but this lossy compression causes earlier facts to be overwritten under competition, degrading needle recall. Inspired by Complementary Learning Systems theory, the authors aim to give linear attention a "hippocampal" exact memory to preserve associations that don't fit the compressive state.
AI.method: HOLA keeps the standard delta-rule linear attention state as compressive memory and adds a bounded exact KV cache, forming a semiparametric test-time memory. The cache uses a write rule based on large beta * ||e|| — the prediction residual committed to the state — without a learned eviction module. A decoupled RMSNorm-gamma cache read turns exact KV pairs into sharp retrieval rather than soft averaging over the state.
AI.result: At 340M params / 15B SlimPajama tokens: Wikitext perplexity drops from 27.32 to 22.92 (-16.1%), beating full-attention Transformer++ (26.88); LAMBADA perplexity improves from 30.95 to 30.26. HOLA achieves best linear in-context retrieval and remains far more robust than GDN or a recency-cache baseline on RULER needle-in-a-haystack out to 32k tokens (16× training length).
AI.conclusion: A hippocampal exact KV cache complementing compressive linear attention yields substantial perplexity gains, surpasses full-attention baselines, and dramatically improves long-context needle recall without learned eviction, validating the CLS-inspired semiparametric memory design.

title: SA-HGNN: Sample-Adaptive Hyperbolic Graph Neural Network for EEG-Based Depression Recognition
summary: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have been widely used to capture spatial functional connectivity patterns to improve electroencephalography (EEG)-based depression recognition performance. However, the functional connectivity of brain networks in patients with depression exhibits an inherent hierarchical structure, making it difficult to capture accurate connection patterns. To address these issues, this paper proposes a novel model named Sample-Adaptive Hyperbolic Graph Neural Network (SA-HGNN), which aims to accurately extract the authentic hierarchical structure of depression-affected brain networks. Specifically, the proposed model comprises three core modules. First, a Sample-Adaptive Graph Construction module dynamically constructs personalized brain network topologies to capture more complex spatial relationships within the brain network. Second, hyperbolic graph convolution is employed to overcome the representation bottlenecks of Euclidean space, leveraging hyperbolic geometry to precisely capture latent hierarchical relationships within the brain network. Finally, an Attention Pooling module adaptively filters out highly redundant noise channels in EEG signals, effectively mitigating the interference of inherent noise on the authentic hierarchical topology. Extensive experiments on public EEG datasets demonstrate the superior performance of our method across resting-state and task-related paradigms, validating its robustness to noise and efficacy in capturing abnormal functional connectivity patterns in brain networks of patients with depression.

AI.tldr: SA-HGNN introduces a sample-adaptive hyperbolic graph neural network for EEG-based depression recognition, combining personalized graph construction, hyperbolic geometry for hierarchical brain network modeling, and attention-based noise filtering to outperform existing methods on public datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing GNN-based EEG depression recognition methods fail to adequately capture the inherent hierarchical structure of functional connectivity in depressed brain networks, and suffer from representational bottlenecks in Euclidean space.
AI.method: SA-HGNN proposes three core modules: (1) Sample-Adaptive Graph Construction that dynamically builds personalized brain network topologies; (2) Hyperbolic Graph Convolution that leverages hyperbolic geometry to capture latent hierarchical relationships; (3) Attention Pooling that adaptively filters redundant noise channels in EEG signals.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on public EEG datasets demonstrate superior performance across both resting-state and task-related paradigms, with validated robustness to noise and efficacy in capturing abnormal functional connectivity patterns in depression.
AI.conclusion: SA-HGNN effectively addresses the hierarchical structure modeling challenge in depression-affected brain networks by combining personalized graph construction, hyperbolic representations, and attention-based denoising, achieving state-of-the-art depression recognition from EEG signals.

title: Grounded autonomous research: a fault-tolerant LLM pipeline from corpus to manuscript in frontier computational physics
comment: 39 pages, 5 figures. Accepted at the ICML 2026 AI for Science Workshop (https://openreview.net/forum?id=R5YXaPgUAx). Includes the pipeline-generated companion physics manuscript as an appendix. Data and scaffolding archive: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21126996
summary: Autonomous-research agents have demonstrated end-to-end LLM automation in machine-learning sandboxes where execution provides calibration. Frontier physical science differs categorically: physical reasoning underlies every methodology choice, toolchains are often underdocumented, and calibration must come from external literature anchors - which unscaffolded agents cite but do not confront, hallucinating plausible, unverifiable results from internal priors.
