We present a pipeline that runs end-to-end from a corpus of 11,083 recent condensed-matter physics arXiv papers to a publication-grade manuscript with three substantive physics findings (here on altermagnetic piezomagnetism): the agent autonomously conceives a research direction by mapping the corpus, calibrates methodology by reproducing published references, conducts novel first-principles computations, and writes the manuscript - grounded in literature throughout, across 47 fresh-context sessions in six phases sharing only on-disk state, with 2,162 literature-consultation events. Fault tolerance emerges from redundancy: fresh-context isolation, distributed grounding, and adversarial review catch what any single session misses; pre- and post-pilot stages are fully autonomous, and pilot requires bounded human intervention only at reproduction failures - operational knowledge curation, not scientific direction. Two paired failure modes - a pre-architecture baseline and a no-pilot ablation - isolate structurally enforced numerical confrontation at calibration checkpoints as the operative grounding mechanism. The primitives, characterized failure modes, and quantified intervention pattern lay a foundation for autonomous research in high-stakes scientific domains beyond computational physics.

AI.tldr: A pipeline is presented that autonomously conducts end-to-end scientific research in condensed-matter physics, moving from a corpus of 11,083 arXiv papers to a publication-grade manuscript with three substantive findings on altermagnetic piezomagnetism. The system operates across 47 sessions and 2,162 literature-consultation events, with grounding enforced through numerical confrontation at calibration checkpoints and fault tolerance achieved via redundancy and adversarial review. Minimal human intervention is required only at reproduction failures.
AI.motivation: Existing autonomous-research agents succeed in ML sandboxes where execution provides calibration, but frontier physical science demands physical reasoning for methodology choices, involves underdocumented toolchains, and requires calibration from external literature rather than internal priors. Unscaffolded agents hallucinate plausible but unverifiable results because they fail to genuinely confront literature. The work aims to bridge this gap by introducing structural grounding mechanisms that enforce numerical confrontation with published references.
AI.method: The pipeline operates in six phases across 47 fresh-context sessions sharing only on-disk state: (1) corpus mapping to conceive a research direction, (2) methodology calibration via reproduction of published references, (3) novel first-principles computations, and (4) manuscript writing. Grounding is structurally enforced through calibration checkpoints requiring numerical confrontation with literature. Fault tolerance emerges from fresh-context isolation, distributed grounding, and adversarial review. Two paired failure modes — a pre-architecture baseline and a no-pilot ablation — are used to isolate the operative grounding mechanism. Pilot phase requires bounded human intervention only at reproduction failures (operational knowledge curation, not scientific direction).
AI.result: The system produced a publication-grade manuscript with three substantive physics findings on altermagnetic piezomagnetism, autonomously processing 11,083 recent condensed-matter physics arXiv papers, with 2,162 literature-consultation events across 47 sessions. The pre- and post-pilot stages ran fully autonomously. The ablation studies demonstrated that structurally enforced numerical confrontation at calibration checkpoints is the operative grounding mechanism, and that removing it leads to hallucinated, unverifiable results.
AI.conclusion: The primitives, characterized failure modes, and quantified intervention pattern provide a foundation for deploying autonomous research agents in high-stakes scientific domains beyond computational physics, where grounding against external literature is essential for reliability.

title: HERMES: A Multi-Granularity Labeling Substrate for Pre-training Data Mixtures
summary: Most data-mixing methods assume the corpus has already been partitioned into groups, and the choice of those groups determines what a mixer can express. Existing labels, including provenance, topic or format taxonomies, and flat embedding clusters, commit to one semantic axis at one granularity; changing the resolution rebuilds the labels. We argue the bottleneck is the label system, not the mixer, and provide a hierarchical one. HERMES is a data-derived labeling substrate: a Learned Semantic Transform followed by 3-stage residual vector quantization annotates each document once into a coarse-to-fine code whose prefix length controls granularity up to approximately 130k cells. At coarse granularity HERMES sits at a plateau with KMeans-family methods on standard clustering metrics, so the contribution is the substrate, not the clusterer. On 1B-parameter, 25B-token pre-training, the hierarchy exposes an interaction fixed-granularity pipelines cannot test: at one prefix length, a combined Stage-2 rule contrast, equal-subbucket coverage versus size-proportional within-bucket quality top-30%, lifts a 16-task capability macro-average by +0.0253; at the next finer level, the same rule loses its measurable edge as candidate pools contract approximately 5x. HERMES reframes data mixture design from choosing among fixed label sets to navigating a reusable, data-derived granularity hierarchy.

AI.tldr: HERMES introduces a hierarchical, data-derived labeling substrate using Learned Semantic Transform and residual vector quantization to annotate documents at multiple granularities, enabling dynamic data mixture design that outperforms fixed-granularity pipelines in pre-training experiments.
AI.motivation: Existing data-mixing methods rely on pre-partitioned corpora with fixed semantic axes and granularities (provenance, topic taxonomies, embedding clusters). Changing resolution requires rebuilding labels entirely. The authors identify the label system—not the mixer—as the bottleneck and propose a hierarchical alternative that supports navigating multiple granularities without re-labeling.
AI.method: HERMES uses a Learned Semantic Transform followed by 3-stage residual vector quantization to produce a coarse-to-fine code per document. Prefix length controls granularity, yielding up to ~130k cells. This creates a single, reusable labeling substrate where granularity can be adjusted dynamically without re-annotation.
AI.result: At coarse granularity, HERMES matches KMeans-family methods on standard clustering metrics. In 1B-parameter, 25B-token pre-training, the hierarchy reveals granularity-dependent interactions: a Stage-2 contrastive mixing rule (equal-subbucket coverage vs. size-proportional within-bucket quality top-30%) lifts a 16-task macro-average by +0.0253 at one prefix length, but loses its edge at the next finer level (~5× candidate pool contraction).
AI.conclusion: HERMES reframes data mixture design from selecting among fixed label sets to navigating a reusable, data-derived granularity hierarchy, demonstrating that mixing strategy effectiveness is granularity-dependent—an insight inaccessible to fixed-granularity pipelines.

title: DRIFTLENS: Measuring Memory-Induced Reasoning Drift in Personalized Language Models
summary: Personalization changes what a model says to a user; we show that it can also change the reasoning trajectory used to justify the response. Modern LLMs personalize interactions by storing user attributes, preferences, and prior context, then injecting this information into future prompts. We study whether such memory reshapes reasoning on open-ended questions where no single ground-truth answer exists. To quantify this effect, we introduce DRIFTLENS, a ground-truth-free framework that maps each expressed reasoning step to a value category and measures divergence between a question's no-memory trajectory and its trajectory under injected user-attribute memory. We first validate that DRIFTLENS distinguishes content-free pragmatic noise from substantive reasoning changes. Across four LLMs and 10 user-attribute categories, including age, occupation, and disability, user-attribute memory induces medium-to-large reasoning drift above each model's pragmatic-noise floor, even when final answers remain fluent, on-topic, and plausible. We then evaluate GRPO- and DPO-based post-training methods for reducing drift. Both reduce drift, but neither uniformly dominates; effects on downstream capability, helpfulness, and instruction following are model-and reward-dependent. These results suggest that memory-induced reasoning drift is a measurable and only partly mitigated failure mode of personalized language models.

AI.tldr: User-attribute memory in LLMs causes measurable shifts in reasoning trajectories (not just final answers), a phenomenon termed "reasoning drift." The DRIFTLENS framework quantifies this without ground-truth, revealing medium-to-large drift across models and attributes. Post-training mitigation (GRPO/DPO) reduces but does not fully eliminate drift.
AI.motivation: Personalization in LLMs—injecting user attributes and context into prompts—is increasingly common, but its impact on the model's underlying reasoning process (not just output text) is poorly understood. The authors aim to investigate whether memory injection reshapes how models justify their responses on open-ended questions lacking a single correct answer.
AI.method: The authors propose DRIFTLENS, a ground-truth-free framework that: (1) maps each expressed reasoning step to a value category, and (2) measures divergence between reasoning trajectories with and without injected user-attribute memory. They validate DRIFTLENS against pragmatic noise, then test across four LLMs and 10 user-attribute categories (age, occupation, disability, etc.). They further evaluate GRPO- and DPO-based post-training as mitigation strategies, assessing downstream effects on helpfulness, capability, and instruction following.
AI.result: User-attribute memory consistently induces medium-to-large reasoning drift above each model's pragmatic-noise floor, even when final answers remain fluent, on-topic, and plausible. Both GRPO and DPO post-training reduce drift, but neither method uniformly dominates; their effectiveness is model- and reward-dependent, and downstream capabilities can be affected.
AI.conclusion: Memory-induced reasoning drift is a measurable and only partially mitigated failure mode in personalized LLMs. This highlights a subtle but important risk: personalization can alter not just what models say, but how they reason to arrive at those responses.

title: Fourier Neural Operators for Rayleigh-Bénard Convection
summary: We propose an improved Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) for modeling two-dimensional Rayleigh-Bénard convection by predicting time increments instead of full solutions, achieving higher accuracy than a standard FNO baseline. The resulting model is compact (314k parameters, 1.26 MB) and fast (7 ms inference), while maintaining similar accuracy as demonstrated in previous benchmarks. We show that although FNOs generalize to finer meshes, accuracy remains limited by the resolution of the training data.

AI.tldr: An improved Fourier Neural Operator predicts time increments for 2D Rayleigh-Bénard convection, achieving compact size, fast inference, and superior accuracy over a standard FNO baseline, though accuracy is bounded by training data resolution.
AI.motivation: To develop an accurate, compact, and fast surrogate model for two-dimensional Rayleigh-Bénard convection that outperforms the standard Fourier Neural Operator by reformulating the learning objective from predicting full solutions to predicting time increments.
AI.method: An improved Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) that predicts time increments (i.e., the difference between successive time steps) rather than directly predicting full solution fields. The model is trained on 2D Rayleigh-Bénard convection data and compared against a standard FNO baseline in terms of accuracy, parameter count, model size, and inference speed. Generalization to finer meshes is also evaluated, with analysis of the effect of training data resolution.
AI.result: The proposed time-increment FNO achieves higher accuracy than the standard FNO baseline while being compact (314k parameters, 1.26 MB) and fast (7 ms inference time). It generalizes to finer meshes, but accuracy remains fundamentally limited by the resolution of the training data.
AI.conclusion: Predicting time increments rather than full solutions is an effective strategy for improving FNO accuracy in modeling Rayleigh-Bénard convection. The resulting model is both lightweight and fast, making it practical for surrogate modeling, but training data resolution remains a critical bottleneck for mesh generalization.

title: Automated grading of Linux/bash examinations using large language models: a four-level cognitive taxonomy approach
summary: Scalable and reliable grading of command-line examinations remains a challenge in computing education, where rising enrolments make manual marking difficult and rule-based autograders cannot handle partial credit, equivalent solutions, or syntactic variation. This paper evaluates whether four frontier Large Language Models (GPT, Claude Opus, Gemini, and GLM) can approximate expert judgment when grading short Linux/bash command responses. The study adopts a four-level cognitive taxonomy that combines cognitive complexity and operational impact, ranging from information retrieval (L1) and basic file manipulation (L2) to structural operations (L3) and advanced system management (L4). The models were tested with two prompt variants, a minimal baseline and a rubric-enhanced version, on 1200 real responses from second-year Computer Engineering students independently graded by three expert instructors. Gemini~3.0 Pro with rubric-guided prompting achieved the highest human-AI agreement (ICC(3,1) = 0.888, MAE = 0.10, Bland-Altman bias = -0.014). Agreement declined consistently as taxonomy level increased, with the largest discrepancies at higher levels. Across all models, rubric quality had a larger effect than provider choice, with structured prompts consistently improving agreement. These results show that question complexity is a reliable predictor of the difficulty LLMs face in grading accurately, and they establish a principled, taxonomy-based framework for determining which questions are suitable for AI-assisted grading and which require human review, while also providing a transferable evaluation protocol and prompt templates.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates four frontier LLMs (GPT, Claude Opus, Gemini, GLM) for grading Linux/bash command-line exam responses using a four-level cognitive taxonomy. Gemini 3.0 Pro with rubric-enhanced prompting achieved the highest agreement with human experts (ICC=0.888, MAE=0.10). Rubric quality mattered more than model choice, and agreement declined as question complexity increased, establishing a principled framework for determining which questions are suitable for AI-assisted grading.
AI.motivation: Rising enrollments in computing education make manual grading of command-line examinations increasingly burdensome. Existing rule-based autograders are brittle—they cannot handle partial credit, semantically equivalent solutions, or syntactic variations. The authors seek to determine whether LLMs can serve as scalable, reliable graders that approximate expert human judgment for short-answer Linux/bash responses.
AI.method: Four frontier LLMs (GPT, Claude Opus, Gemini, GLM) were tested on 1,200 real student responses from second-year Computer Engineering students. Responses were independently graded by three expert instructors to establish ground truth. Two prompt variants were evaluated: a minimal baseline prompt and a rubric-enhanced prompt. Grading was assessed across a four-level cognitive taxonomy (L1: information retrieval, L2: basic file manipulation, L3: structural operations, L4: advanced system management). Agreement was measured using ICC(3,1), MAE, and Bland-Altman analysis.
AI.result: Gemini 3.0 Pro with rubric-guided prompting achieved the best performance (ICC(3,1) = 0.888, MAE = 0.10, Bland-Altman bias = -0.014). Agreement between LLMs and human experts consistently declined as taxonomy level increased, with L4 tasks showing the largest discrepancies. Across all models, structured rubric prompts had a larger positive effect on agreement than the choice of model provider.
AI.conclusion: Question complexity, as captured by the taxonomy, is a reliable predictor of grading difficulty for LLMs. The taxonomy-based framework provides a principled method for triaging questions: lower-level questions are suitable for AI-assisted grading, while higher-level questions warrant human review. The study also contributes transferable evaluation protocols and prompt templates for broader adoption.

title: Ask the Right Comparison:Bias-Aware Bayesian Active Top-$k$ Ranking with LLM Judges
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as cheap, scalable judges that compare candidate outputs pairwise -- to rank responses, select models, or triage papers. Yet LLM judges are both noisy and systematically biased: they favor verbose or well-formatted answers and exhibit position effects, so simply aggregating their votes recovers a ranking of presentation, not of true quality. We study the practical goal of identifying the \topk{} items under a fixed comparison budget, and make two contributions. First, we cast judging as Bayesian inference over latent quality with explicit, judge-specific bias covariates (verbosity, position), regularized by a shrinkage prior so that the data decide which biases a given judge actually exhibits. Second, we introduce a \topk-aware active acquisition rule that chooses the next comparison to maximally reduce uncertainty about \topk{} \emph{membership}, rather than about the full ranking. On a controlled benchmark with known ground-truth quality, judged by sixteen real LLMs spanning open and proprietary families (Llama, Qwen, Phi-4, GPT-4o-mini/5.1/5.5, Gemini, DeepSeek, and Claude Haiku/Sonnet/Opus), naive aggregation plateaus at a wrong \topk{} on biased judges regardless of budget, while our bias-aware model recovers it; \topk-aware acquisition reaches this ceiling with far fewer comparisons than round-robin or a global-uncertainty (D-optimal) rule. Bias is real but heterogeneous and capability-dependent: cheap and mid-tier judges carry a strong verbosity bias that our model corrects (lifting recall from $\sim$$0.5$--$0.6$ to $0.84$--$1.0$), whereas the frontier judges we tested show little bias and already rank accurately, so bias-aware modeling changes little there.

AI.tldr: LLM judges exhibit systematic biases (verbosity, position) that distort pairwise rankings. This paper proposes a Bayesian inference framework with judge-specific bias covariates and a top-k-aware active acquisition strategy, achieving accurate top-k recovery with fewer comparisons, especially for biased mid-tier judges.
AI.motivation: LLM judges are increasingly used for scalable pairwise evaluation, but they are noisy and systematically biased (favoring verbose/well-formatted responses, position effects). Simply aggregating biased votes recovers a ranking of presentation style rather than true quality. The authors aim to reliably identify the top-k items under a fixed comparison budget, correcting for these biases.
AI.method: Two contributions: (1) A Bayesian inference framework that models latent quality with explicit, judge-specific bias covariates (verbosity, position), regularized by a shrinkage prior so the data determines which biases each judge exhibits. (2) A top-k-aware active acquisition rule that selects the next comparison to maximally reduce uncertainty about top-k membership, rather than about the full ranking. Evaluated on a controlled benchmark with ground-truth quality using 16 real LLM judges (Llama, Qwen, Phi-4, GPT-4o-mini/5.1/5.5, Gemini, DeepSeek, Claude Haiku/Sonnet/Opus).
AI.result: Naive aggregation plateaus at an incorrect top-k on biased judges regardless of budget, while the bias-aware model recovers the true top-k. The top-k-aware acquisition rule reaches this ceiling with far fewer comparisons than round-robin or D-optimal rules. Bias is heterogeneous and capability-dependent: cheap/mid-tier judges show strong verbosity bias (corrected by the model, lifting recall from ~0.5-0.6 to 0.84-1.0), while frontier judges exhibit little bias and already rank accurately.
AI.conclusion: Bias in LLM judges is real but heterogeneous. The proposed bias-aware Bayesian model with top-k-aware active acquisition effectively corrects systematic biases in mid-tier judges, substantially improving top-k recall. Frontier judges already rank well, so bias correction provides marginal benefit there. The approach enables reliable, budget-efficient top-k identification using imperfect LLM judges.

title: EvoPolicyGym: Evaluating Autonomous Policy Evolution in Interactive Environments
summary: Autonomous agents are increasingly expected to improve executable policies through feedback, yet existing evaluations often collapse this process into a final score or confound it with open-ended software-engineering progress. We introduce Autonomous Policy Evolution, a controlled evaluation setting in which a harness-model agent repeatedly edits an executable policy system under a fixed interaction budget. We instantiate this setting in EvoPolicyGym, a benchmark built from compact interactive RL environments that evaluates how agents iteratively improve explored policies. On the EvoPolicyGym suite, GPT-5.5 achieves the strongest aggregate rank score and top-two performance on all 16 environments. Beyond leaderboard results, EvoPolicyGym also provides trajectory-level diagnostics that distinguish how agents allocate budget, convert feedback into parametric tuning. These analyses show that strong autonomous policy evolution depends not only on isolated task wins, but on discovering task-appropriate mechanisms and refining policies under bounded feedback.

AI.tldr: Introduces Autonomous Policy Evolution, a controlled benchmark (EvoPolicyGym) where agents iteratively refine executable policies under a fixed budget. GPT-5.5 ranks best across all 16 environments. The benchmark provides trajectory-level diagnostics revealing that strong performance depends on discovering task-appropriate mechanisms and efficient use of bounded feedback, not just isolated task wins.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of autonomous agents' ability to improve from feedback either collapse the process into a single final score or conflate it with open-ended software engineering progress. The authors argue for a controlled, isolated setting that specifically measures iterative policy refinement under constraints.
AI.method: Proposes the Autonomous Policy Evolution framework: a harness-model agent repeatedly edits an executable policy system with a fixed interaction budget. Instantiates this via EvoPolicyGym, a benchmark built from compact interactive RL environments, evaluating how agents iteratively improve explored policies. Provides trajectory-level diagnostics tracking budget allocation and feedback-to-parameter conversion.
AI.result: GPT-5.5 achieves the strongest aggregate rank score and top-two performance across all 16 EvoPolicyGym environments. Trajectory-level analysis reveals that strong autonomous policy evolution depends on discovering task-appropriate mechanisms and refining policies under bounded feedback, rather than merely winning isolated tasks.
AI.conclusion: Autonomous policy evolution is a distinct capability from raw task performance. Effective agents must discover suitable mechanisms and efficiently convert limited feedback into parametric improvements. EvoPolicyGym enables fine-grained, trajectory-level evaluation of this capability.

title: Predictive Conformal Slip Monitoring: An Empirical Evaluation of Rolling Split Conformal Prediction for Pre-Incident Traction Loss Detection
comment: 10 pages, 4 tables. codes and data available at:https://github.com/nearpot/predictive-conformal-slip-monitoring
summary: Conventional traction control architectures intervene only after the adhesion limit of a tire has already been breached. This paper investigates whether Rolling Split Conformal Prediction , monitoring the volatility of non-conformity residuals from a per-driver Random Forest model of expected slip behavior , can serve as a statistically grounded pre-incident warning signal, ahead of gross traction loss. Unlike an earlier internal draft of this work, the evaluation reported here corrects a confound in the slip proxy (vehicle speed is included as an explicit model feature, not left implicit in the target's denominator), uses every racing lap for each driver rather than only the fastest lap, and is scored against real, timestamped incident labels extracted from FIA Race Control Messages and track-limits lap deletions rather than narrated post-hoc. The result is negative: across 19 drivers and 55,563 test-phase telemetry samples, the rolling-volatility detector achieves a mean precision of essentially 0.0 and mean recall of 0.0 against 14 ground-truth incidents, while flagging on average 15.3% of all samples as anomalous , too high a false-alarm rate for any early-warning use. A static 95th-percentile threshold baseline performs no better in any way that would justify the added complexity of the conformal-volatility formulation. Residual autocorrelation diagnostics show the split-conformal exchangeability assumption is violated for every driver (Ljung-Box p < 0.001, n = 19/19), which is one plausible driver of the high false-alarm rate. We report this as a methodologically rigorous negative finding, diagnose its likely causes, and outline what a genuinely predictive version of this approach would require.

AI.tldr: A statistically grounded early-warning system for traction loss using Rolling Split Conformal Prediction on Random Forest slip models fails completely, achieving near-zero precision and recall with a ~15% false-alarm rate across 55,563 telemetry samples from 19 drivers, likely due to violated exchangeability assumptions.
AI.motivation: Conventional traction control systems are reactive, intervening only after a tire's adhesion limit is exceeded. The authors investigate whether a predictive, statistically principled early-warning signal — based on conformal prediction monitoring of per-driver slip models — can anticipate traction loss before it occurs, enabling pre-incident intervention.
AI.method: The paper applies Rolling Split Conformal Prediction (RSCP) to monitor volatility of non-conformity residuals from per-driver Random Forest models predicting expected slip behavior. Key methodological corrections from prior work include: (1) making vehicle speed an explicit model feature rather than leaving it implicit in the slip target's denominator, (2) using all racing laps per driver rather than only the fastest lap, and (3) scoring against real, timestamped incident labels from FIA Race Control Messages and track-limits lap deletions. A static 95th-percentile threshold baseline is also evaluated.
AI.result: Strictly negative: across 19 drivers and 55,563 test-phase telemetry samples, the rolling-volatility RSCP detector achieves mean precision ≈ 0.0 and mean recall = 0.0 against 14 ground-truth incidents, while flagging ~15.3% of all samples as anomalous — an unacceptably high false-alarm rate. The static baseline performs no better. Ljung-Box diagnostics reveal that the split-conformal exchangeability assumption is violated for every driver (p < 0.001, n = 19/19), likely driving the high false-alarm rate.
AI.conclusion: This is reported as a methodologically rigorous negative finding. The conformal-volatility approach fails as a pre-incident warning system. The authors diagnose violated exchangeability as a plausible root cause and outline requirements for a genuinely predictive future version of this approach.

title: Fast Multi-dimensional Refusal Subspaces via RFM-AGOP
comment: Accepted to the Mechanistic Interpretability Workshop at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, Seoul, South Korea, 2026
summary: Steering and monitoring activations in Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used for both safety and interpretability. Early work assumed behaviours are encoded along single linear directions, but recent findings suggest complex behaviours, such as the refusal to answer harmful queries, live in multi-dimensional subspaces. However, existing methods for extracting these subspaces are computationally expensive, which becomes prohibitive on reasoning models who produce long reasoning traces. By adapting the Recursive Feature Machine (RFM) algorithm -- which can be computed efficiently -- with a probe-informed initialization, we are able to identify the multi-dimensional refusal subspace in seconds, on reasoning (Qwen 3) and non-reasoning (Qwen 2.5) models. While RFM allows for faster subspace identification, it also showed better performances on the ablation task than its alternatives. More work is planned to better understand the relations between subspaces found by different methods. If confirmed, RFM could be a cheap and scalable complement to existing subspace-extraction methods in LLMs.

AI.tldr: The paper adapts the Recursive Feature Machine (RFM) algorithm with probe-informed initialization to efficiently identify multi-dimensional refusal subspaces in LLMs, achieving extraction in seconds on both reasoning and non-reasoning models, with superior ablation performance compared to alternatives.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for extracting multi-dimensional behavioural subspaces (e.g., refusal) in LLMs are computationally expensive, which becomes prohibitive for reasoning models that produce long reasoning traces. A faster, scalable approach is needed.
AI.method: Adaptation of the Recursive Feature Machine (RFM) algorithm with a probe-informed initialization to identify refusal subspaces. Evaluated on reasoning models (Qwen 3) and non-reasoning models (Qwen 2.5).
AI.result: RFM identifies the multi-dimensional refusal subspace in seconds and demonstrates better performance on the ablation task compared to alternative methods.
AI.conclusion: If confirmed by further work investigating relationships between subspaces found by different methods, RFM could serve as a cheap and scalable complement to existing subspace-extraction methods in LLMs.

title: ART for Diffusion Sampling: Continuous-Time Control and Actor-Critic Learning
summary: We study timestep allocation for score-based diffusion sampling, where a learned reverse-time dynamics is discretized on a finite grid. Uniform and hand-crafted schedules are standard choices, but they rely on fixed prescriptions and can therefore be suboptimal. To address this limitation, we propose Adaptive Reparameterized Time (ART), a continuous-time control formulation that learns a time change by treating the speed of the sampling clock as the control, so that a uniform grid on the learned clock induces adaptive timesteps in the original diffusion time. Based on a leading-order Euler error surrogate, ART provides a principled objective for allocating timesteps along the sampling trajectory. To solve this deterministic control problem, we introduce ART-RL, an auxiliary randomized formulation with Gaussian policies that turns schedule learning into a continuous-time reinforcement learning problem. We prove that the randomized ART-RL formulation is equivalent to ART at the optimizer level, in the sense that its optimal Gaussian policy recovers the optimal ART time-warping rate through its mean. We further establish policy evaluation and policy improvement characterizations and derive trajectory-based moment identities that yield implementable actor--critic updates for learning the schedule. Across experiments ranging from controlled low-dimensional settings to image generation, ART-RL can be plugged into existing diffusion samplers by changing only the timestep grid, consistently improving sample quality over strong baseline schedules at matched budgets while leaving the rest of the sampling pipeline unchanged. The learned schedules also exhibit broad generalization, transferring without retraining across sampling budgets, datasets, solvers, pipelines, and representation spaces.

AI.tldr: ART-RL formulates diffusion sampling timestep allocation as a continuous-time control problem, learning an adaptive time-warping schedule via an equivalent reinforcement learning formulation that improves sample quality while generalizing across budgets, solvers, and datasets.
AI.motivation: Standard uniform or hand-crafted timestep schedules for score-based diffusion sampling are fixed and suboptimal. No principled, learnable method exists for allocating a finite number of discretization steps adaptively along the sampling trajectory to minimize discretization error.
AI.method: The authors propose Adaptive Reparameterized Time (ART), a deterministic continuous-time control formulation where the clock speed is the control variable, making a uniform grid on the learned clock correspond to adaptive timesteps. A leading-order Euler error surrogate serves as the objective. ART-RL converts this into an equivalent continuous-time RL problem using Gaussian policies, with the optimal policy's mean recovering the optimal time-warping rate. Policy evaluation/improvement characterizations and trajectory-based moment identities yield implementable actor-critic updates.
AI.result: ART-RL consistently improves sample quality over strong baseline schedules (uniform, hand-crafted) at matched computational budgets across low-dimensional controlled settings and image generation tasks. Learned schedules generalize without retraining across different sampling budgets, datasets, solvers, pipelines, and representation spaces.
AI.conclusion: Casting timestep allocation as a continuous-time control/RL problem provides a principled, plug-and-play method for improving diffusion samplers without modifying the underlying model or sampling pipeline, with strong empirical performance and broad generalizability.

title: Text-Driven 3D Indoor Scene Synthesis in Non-Manhattan Environments
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in 3D indoor synthesis for Manhattan environments. However, existing methods often fail to capture plausible object layout patterns in non-Manhattan settings, primarily because they struggle to model non-orthogonal spatial relationships, leading to high geometric violations and low physical fidelity. To address this challenge, we propose SPG-Layout, a novel text-driven framework designed to generate physically plausible indoor scenes within complex non-Manhattan environments. Specifically, we first utilize statistical priors of object distributions to guide the training process, enhancing environmental understanding and fidelity. Furthermore, mirroring human design workflows, we adopt a hierarchical layout strategy that prioritizes the placement of large objects, thereby substantially minimizing layout violations. By synergizing these components, SPG-Layout achieves a balanced optimization of semantic realism and physical plausibility. To evaluate performance in these complex settings, we constructed a new benchmark comprising 500 diverse non-Manhattan environments. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SPG-Layout consistently and significantly outperforms existing methods across both Manhattan and non-Manhattan environments. The code will be publicly released.

AI.tldr: SPG-Layout is a text-driven framework that generates physically plausible 3D indoor scenes in non-Manhattan environments by leveraging statistical object priors and a hierarchical large-object-first layout strategy, outperforming existing methods on a new 500-scene benchmark.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based 3D indoor synthesis methods are limited to Manhattan (orthogonal) layouts and fail in non-Manhattan settings due to their inability to model non-orthogonal spatial relationships, resulting in high geometric violations and poor physical fidelity.
AI.method: SPG-Layout employs two key components: (1) statistical priors of object distributions to guide training for better environmental understanding, and (2) a hierarchical layout strategy that places large objects first, mirroring human design workflows. These synergize to balance semantic realism with physical plausibility.
AI.result: A new benchmark of 500 diverse non-Manhattan environments was constructed. Extensive experiments show SPG-Layout consistently and significantly outperforms existing methods in both Manhattan and non-Manhattan settings.
AI.conclusion: SPG-Layout effectively addresses the challenge of non-Manhattan indoor scene synthesis by combining statistical priors with hierarchical layout planning, achieving state-of-the-art physical plausibility and semantic realism. Code will be publicly released.

title: Probing Chemical Language Models: Effects of Pre-training and Fine-tuning
summary: Chemical language models (CLMs) are trained with linearized representations such as SMILES, yet it remains unclear which chemically meaningful substructures they encode. To foster a better understanding of CLMs, we conduct a systematic study and probe for 78 molecular substructures across eight pre-trained and six randomly initialized models. We furthermore study how fine-tuning on chemical downstream tasks affects the learned representations of molecular substructures. Our results show that pre-training generally improves molecular structure awareness of CLMs, particularly in the upper layers. Moreover, randomly initialized models already encode ring structures well in the first layer. Our analysis on two chemical downstream tasks further reveals that, interestingly, fine-tuning affects task-relevant molecular substructures more than others, indicating that the changes in the representations follow chemical theory.

AI.tldr: A systematic probing study across 78 molecular substructures in 8 pre-trained and 6 randomly initialized chemical language models reveals that pre-training improves molecular structure awareness (especially in upper layers), randomly initialized models already encode rings in the first layer, and fine-tuning affects task-relevant substructures more than others, following chemical theory.
AI.motivation: It remains unclear which chemically meaningful substructures chemical language models (CLMs) trained on linearized representations like SMILES actually encode. Understanding this is critical for interpreting model behavior and improving model design.
AI.method: The authors conduct a systematic probing study: they probe for 78 molecular substructures across eight pre-trained CLMs and six randomly initialized (untrained) models. They also analyze how fine-tuning on two chemical downstream tasks alters the learned substructure representations, comparing changes across layers and substructure types.
AI.result: Pre-training generally improves molecular structure awareness, particularly in upper layers. Randomly initialized models already encode ring structures well in the first layer. Fine-tuning disproportionately affects task-relevant molecular substructures compared to irrelevant ones, suggesting that representational changes align with chemical theory.
AI.conclusion: CLMs encode chemically meaningful substructures in a hierarchical, task-sensitive manner. Pre-training enhances this capacity, but some structural priors (e.g., rings) exist even without training. Fine-tuning induces chemically plausible representational shifts, reinforcing the interpretability and chemical validity of CLM representations.

title: Online Safety Monitoring for LLMs
summary: Despite alignment training, LLMs remain prone to generating unsafe outputs at deployment time. Monitoring outputs online and raising an alarm when safety can no longer be assumed is therefore critical. We study a simple real-time monitor that turns a verifier signal from an external model into an alarm decision by thresholding, with the threshold calibrated via risk control. In experiments on mathematical reasoning and red teaming datasets, we show that this simple design is competitive with more advanced monitors based on sequential hypothesis testing.

AI.tldr: A simple real-time safety monitor for LLMs that thresholds an external verifier signal with risk-controlled calibration is competitive with more complex sequential hypothesis testing methods.
AI.motivation: LLMs remain vulnerable to generating unsafe outputs even after alignment training, necessitating online output monitoring with reliable alarm mechanisms at deployment time.
AI.method: A real-time monitor that converts a verifier signal from an external model into a binary alarm decision via thresholding, where the threshold is calibrated using risk control techniques.
AI.result: On mathematical reasoning and red teaming benchmarks, the simple thresholding monitor performs competitively with more sophisticated monitors based on sequential hypothesis testing.
AI.conclusion: Simplicity suffices: a straightforward risk-controlled thresholding approach to online safety monitoring matches the performance of more complex sequential testing methods, offering a practical deployment solution.

title: Predicting Early Stages Of Alzheimer's Disease And Identifying Key Biomarkers Using Deep Artificial Neural Network And Ensemble Of Machine Learning Methodologies
summary: Alzheimers disease (AD) is a brain disorder that develops slowly and mainly affects memory, thinking, language, and daily activities. It is one of the most common causes of dementia and creates many difficulties for patients as well as their families. In the early stage, the symptoms are often mild and may look like normal ageing. For this reason, many people are diagnosed late, when the disease has already progressed. At present, there is no complete cure for AD. Still, early detection can help doctors manage the condition better and take suitable steps at the right time. In this study, a machine learning model is proposed to detect the early stages of Alzheimers disease using clinical details, neuropsychological test scores, and neuroimaging-related measures. The data used in this work is collected from the Alzheimers Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI). As the dataset has missing values, iterative imputation is applied to fill them. The dataset also has class imbalance, which is handled using Borderline SVM-SMOTE. After that, feature selection is carried out using wrapper-based and embedded methods so that only important features are used for training. The selected features are divided into training and testing sets, and feature scaling is applied. A stacking ensemble model is developed using Logistic Regression, Extra Trees, Bagging KNN, and LightGBM as base classifiers. Along with this, an artificial neural network is also trained on the same dataset. The performance of these models is compared using precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC-ROC. This study aims to find the best classifier and also identify important biomarkers that may help in the early diagnosis of Alzheimers disease.

AI.tldr: A stacking ensemble model combining Logistic Regression, Extra Trees, Bagging KNN, and LightGBM, alongside an ANN, is proposed for early-stage Alzheimer's disease detection using ADNI clinical, neuropsychological, and neuroimaging data. The pipeline employs iterative imputation, Borderline SVM-SMOTE for class imbalance, and wrapper/embedded feature selection, with models compared via precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC-ROC.
AI.motivation: Alzheimer's disease is often diagnosed late because early symptoms resemble normal aging, and no complete cure exists. Early detection is critical for better disease management and timely intervention, motivating the development of accurate, biomarker-driven machine learning diagnostic tools.
AI.method: Data from ADNI is preprocessed with iterative imputation for missing values and Borderline SVM-SMOTE for class imbalance. Feature selection uses wrapper-based and embedded methods. A stacking ensemble is built with Logistic Regression, Extra Trees, Bagging KNN, and LightGBM as base classifiers; an ANN is also trained for comparison. Models are evaluated on precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC-ROC.
AI.result: The abstract does not report specific quantitative results; it only states that model performance will be compared to identify the best classifier and important biomarkers for early AD diagnosis.
AI.conclusion: The study aims to determine the best-performing classifier and pinpoint key biomarkers that facilitate early diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease, though final conclusions are not presented in the abstract.

title: Program-as-Weights: A Programming Paradigm for Fuzzy Functions
summary: Many everyday programming tasks resist clean rule-based implementation, such as alerting on important log lines, repairing malformed JSON, or ranking search results by intent, and are increasingly outsourced to large language model APIs at the cost of locality, reproducibility, and price. We propose fuzzy-function programming: compiling such a function from a natural-language specification into a compact, locally-executable neural artifact. We instantiate this paradigm with Program-as-Weights (PAW), in which a 4B compiler trained on FuzzyBench, a 10M-example dataset we release, emits parameter-efficient adapters for a frozen, lightweight interpreter. A 0.6B Qwen3 interpreter executing PAW programs matches the performance of direct prompting of Qwen3-32B, while using roughly one fiftieth of the inference memory and running at 30 tokens/s on a MacBook M3. PAW reframes the foundation model from a per-input problem solver into a tool builder: invoked once per function definition, it produces a small reusable artifact whose subsequent calls per function application are cheap and offline.

AI.tldr: PAW introduces "fuzzy-function programming," where natural-language task specifications are compiled into compact neural adapters (PAW programs) for a frozen lightweight interpreter. A 4B compiler trained on the 10M-example FuzzyBench dataset produces these adapters, enabling a 0.6B Qwen3 interpreter to match Qwen3-32B direct prompting performance at ~1/50th the memory and 30 tokens/s on a MacBook M3.
AI.motivation: Many everyday programming tasks (log alerting, JSON repair, search ranking) resist rule-based solutions and are increasingly delegated to large language model APIs. This outsourcing incurs costs in locality (cloud dependency), reproducibility (non-deterministic outputs), and price (per-query API fees). The authors seek to retain LLM-quality results while eliminating these drawbacks by shifting from per-input model invocation to a compile-once, run-locally paradigm.
AI.method: The approach, called Program-as-Weights (PAW), frames a frozen 0.6B Qwen3 model as a lightweight interpreter. A separate 4B compiler model is trained on FuzzyBench (a 10M-example dataset of natural-language function specifications paired with input-output examples) to emit parameter-efficient adapters (e.g., LoRA weights) that specialize the interpreter for a given task. Function definition invokes the compiler once to produce a reusable PAW program; subsequent function applications run cheaply and locally by loading that adapter into the frozen interpreter.
AI.result: A 0.6B Qwen3 interpreter executing PAW programs matches the performance of directly prompting Qwen3-32B, while using approximately 1/50th of the inference memory and achieving 30 tokens/s on a MacBook M3. PAW reframes foundation models from per-input problem solvers into tool builders.
AI.conclusion: Fuzzy-function programming via PAW demonstrates that compiling natural-language specifications into compact, locally-executable neural artifacts is viable, enabling high-quality task performance at a fraction of the computational cost. This paradigm decouples function definition (one-time compiler invocation) from function application (cheap, local, reusable inference), addressing locality, reproducibility, and cost concerns of LLM API outsourcing.

title: Dynamic Neural Graph Encoding of Inference Processes in Deep Weight Space
comment: Published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR), 2026. 28 pages, 5 figures
summary: The rapid advancements in using neural networks as implicit data representations have attracted significant interest in developing machine learning methods that analyze and process the weight spaces of other neural networks. However, efficiently handling these highdimensional weight spaces remains challenging. Existing methods often overlook the sequential nature of layer-by-layer processing in neural network inference. In this work, we propose a novel approach using dynamic graphs to represent neural network parameters, capturing the temporal dynamics of inference. Our Dynamic Neural Graph Encoder (DNG-Encoder) processes these graphs, preserving the sequential nature of neural processing. Additionally, we also leverage DNG-Encoder to develop INR2JLS (Implicit Neural Representation to Joint Latent Space) for facilitate downstream applications, such as classifying Implicit Neural Representations (INRs). Our approach demonstrates significant improvements across multiple tasks, surpassing the state-of-the-art INR classification accuracy by approximately 10% on the CIFAR-100-INR.

AI.tldr: Proposes DNG-Encoder, a dynamic graph approach to represent and encode neural network weight spaces while preserving sequential inference dynamics. Achieves ~10% improvement on INR classification (CIFAR-100-INR). Also introduces INR2JLS for downstream INR applications.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for analyzing neural network weight spaces treat weights as static, high-dimensional vectors, ignoring the inherently sequential, layer-by-layer nature of neural network inference. Efficiently handling these high-dimensional weight spaces for downstream tasks remains an open challenge.
AI.method: The authors propose (1) representing neural network parameters as dynamic graphs that capture temporal dynamics of inference, (2) a Dynamic Neural Graph Encoder (DNG-Encoder) that processes these graphs while preserving sequential processing order, and (3) INR2JLS (Implicit Neural Representation to Joint Latent Space), built on DNG-Encoder, to map INRs into a shared latent space for downstream tasks such as classification.
AI.result: The approach surpasses state-of-the-art INR classification accuracy by approximately 10% on the CIFAR-100-INR benchmark, with significant improvements across multiple tasks.
AI.conclusion: Modeling neural network weight spaces as dynamic graphs with explicit sequential structure yields substantial performance gains for tasks involving the analysis and processing of implicit neural representations.

title: G-RRM: Guiding Symbolic Solvers with Recurrent Reasoning Models
summary:
In this work, we focus on SE-RRMs, a symbol-equivariant instantiation of RRMs that exhibits improved extrapolation to larger problem sizes. We propose a neuro-symbolic approach, ``Guiding with Recurrent Reasoning Models'' (G-RRM), which integrates SE-RRMs with symbolic solvers for constraint satisfaction problems. SE-RRMs act as neural solvers that generate full solution proposals and guide classical symbolic solvers, such as backtracking or SAT-based methods like Glucose 4.1 and CaDiCaL 3.0.0, that produce globally correct solutions. Centrally, we investigate when neural guidance with G-RRM improves the search efficiency of symbolic solvers. %
Our experiments show that the efficacy of G-RRM depends on two conditions: first, the problem instances must have an expansive combinatorial search space to expose potential gains, and second, the solver architecture must be capable of dynamically overwriting its branching choices to recover when neural hints are imperfect. When these conditions hold, guidance drives median conflict counts to zero and yields significant wall-clock speedups: on $9\times9$ Sudoku, where the SE-RRM correctly solves $91.1\%$ of instances, backtracking accelerates by $33.3\times$ and Glucose 4.1 by $1.70\times$ (median, $p<0.001$), with Glucose 4.1 retaining a $1.17\times$ speedup on perfect-hint $25\times25$ grids. In contrast, CaDiCaL 3.0.0, whose runtime is overhead-dominated and which always respects the injected branching hints rather than overwriting them, shows no significant speedup (median $1.02\times$, n.s.) and even a small significant mean slowdown ($0.90\times$) on $9\times9$. These results delineate the regimes in which neural guidance translates into practical speedups.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes G-RRM, a neuro-symbolic approach that integrates symbol-equivariant recurrent reasoning models (SE-RRMs) with classical symbolic solvers. Neural guidance improves solver efficiency only when the problem has a large combinatorial search space and the solver can dynamically overwrite imperfect neural hints. Under these conditions, significant speedups are observed (e.g., 33.3× for backtracking on 9×9 Sudoku), while solvers that rigidly respect injected hints show no benefit.
AI.motivation: Investigate the conditions under which neural guidance from SE-RRMs can improve the search efficiency of classical symbolic solvers (backtracking, SAT solvers) on constraint satisfaction problems, particularly as problem sizes scale.
AI.method: G-RRM framework: SE-RRMs generate full solution proposals that serve as branching hints for symbolic solvers (backtracking, Glucose 4.1, CaDiCaL 3.0.0). The study systematically tests guidance efficacy across Sudoku grid sizes (9×9, 25×25) and analyzes two critical conditions: expansive combinatorial search space and the solver's ability to dynamically overwrite incorrect neural hints.
AI.result: On 9×9 Sudoku (91.1% SE-RRM accuracy): backtracking gains 33.3× speedup, Glucose 4.1 gains 1.70× (median, p<0.001). Glucose retains 1.17× speedup on perfect-hint 25×25 grids. CaDiCaL 3.0.0 shows no significant speedup (1.02×, n.s.) and a small significant mean slowdown (0.90×) because it respects injected hints rather than overwriting them. Median conflict counts drop to zero under effective guidance.
AI.conclusion: Neural guidance translates into practical speedups only when two conditions are met: (1) large combinatorial search spaces that expose potential gains, and (2) solver architectures capable of dynamically overwriting imperfect branching choices. The results delineate the effective operational regimes for neuro-symbolic integration in constraint solving.

title: ReContext: Recursive Evidence Replay as LLM Harness for Long-Context Reasoning
summary: Understanding and reasoning over long contexts has become a key requirement for deploying large language models (LLMs) in realistic applications. Although recent LLMs support increasingly long context windows, they often fail to use relevant evidence that is already present in the input, revealing a gap between context access and effective context utilization. In this work, we propose Recursive Evidence Replay as LLM Harness for Long-Context Reasoning (RECONTEXT), a training-free inference method for improving long-context reasoning. RECONTEXT uses model-internal relevance signals to construct a query-conditioned evidence pool and replays it before final generation while preserving the full original context. This recursive selection process separates evidence organization from answer generation without training, external memory, or context pruning. We also provide a theoretical analysis based on associative memory, which characterizes the context as a memory store, the question as a retrieval cue, attention as cue-trace association, and replay as trace reactivation. Experiments on eight long-context datasets with 128K context length show that RECONTEXT consistently improves evidence utilization across Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, and Llama3-8B, achieving the best average rank on all three backbones. Code is available at https://github.com/Yanjun-Zhao/ReContext.

AI.tldr: RECONTEXT is a training-free inference method that recursively selects and replays query-relevant evidence from long contexts before final generation, improving long-context reasoning in LLMs without training, external memory, or pruning.
AI.motivation: LLMs with long context windows still struggle to effectively utilize relevant evidence already present in the input, revealing a gap between context access and context utilization. This work aims to bridge that gap.
AI.method: RECONTEXT uses model-internal relevance signals (attention-based) to recursively construct a query-conditioned evidence pool. Before final generation, it replays this selected evidence while preserving the full original context. The method separates evidence organization from answer generation, requiring no training, external memory, or context pruning. A theoretical analysis frames the process using associative memory concepts: context as memory store, question as retrieval cue, attention as cue-trace association, and replay as trace reactivation.
AI.result: Experiments on eight long-context datasets with 128K context length demonstrate consistent improvements in evidence utilization across three backbones: Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, and Llama3-8B. RECONTEXT achieves the best average rank on all three backbones.
AI.conclusion: RECONTEXT effectively improves long-context reasoning in LLMs through recursive evidence replay, validated both empirically and theoretically, without requiring any model training or architectural changes.

title: An Optimisation Framework for the Well-Conditioned Training of Physics-Informed Neural Networks
summary:
Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have emerged as a promising route to solve partial differential equations, yet they have struggled to reach the precision of classical solvers. The obstacle is increasingly understood to be one of optimisation, owing to the severely ill-conditioned loss landscape. We present $\textbf{DSGNAR}$: Doubly-Sketched Gauss-Newton with Adaptive Ratio, a scalable second-order optimisation framework that confronts this ill-conditioning and, in doing so, obtains unprecedented accuracy and speed. $\textbf{DSGNAR}$ couples a doubly-sketched Gauss-Newton model with a novel strategy that carefully controls both regularisation and step length. Across a suite of problems spanning nonlinear, chaotic, multi-scale, high-dimensional, and Navier-Stokes, the framework greatly improves on the state of the art: able to attain relative $\ell_2$ errors as low as $3\times10^{-16}$ in double precision, improve contemporary results by five orders of magnitude on the canonical Burgers' equation, and as much as eight orders on a high-dimensional Poisson problem, while remaining markedly faster. We further show that, in single precision, solutions at the limit of round-off error can be obtained very quickly: Burgers' equation to $\ell_2^{\text{rel}} = 4.75 \times 10^{-7}$ in under ten seconds. The framework is also robust to the choice of architecture, arithmetic precision, and initial hyperparameters.
  The code is available at https://www.github.com/wephy/physics-informed-neural-networks

AI.tldr: DSGNAR is a scalable second-order optimization framework for PINNs that uses a doubly-sketched Gauss-Newton method with adaptive regularization and step-length control, achieving unprecedented accuracy (down to 3×10⁻¹⁶ relative ℓ₂ error) and speed across diverse PDE benchmarks.
AI.motivation: PINNs have struggled to match the precision of classical PDE solvers due to severely ill-conditioned loss landscapes that hamper first-order optimizers like Adam. A second-order method capable of navigating this ill-conditioning is needed to close the accuracy gap while remaining computationally feasible.
AI.method: The authors propose DSGNAR, which combines: (1) a doubly-sketched Gauss-Newton (GN) approximation — sketching both the Jacobian and the GN matrix to reduce memory and computational cost; and (2) an adaptive ratio strategy that jointly tunes regularization (damping) and step length per iteration. This enables scalable, numerically stable second-order updates tailored to PINN training dynamics.
AI.result: Across nonlinear, chaotic, multi-scale, high-dimensional, and Navier-Stokes problems, DSGNAR achieves relative ℓ₂ errors as low as 3×10⁻¹⁶ (double precision), improves prior art by 5 orders of magnitude on Burgers' equation and 8 orders on a high-dimensional Poisson problem, and reaches 4.75×10⁻⁷ on Burgers' in under 10 seconds (single precision). It is robust to architecture choice, precision, and initial hyperparameters.
AI.conclusion: DSGNAR demonstrates that properly designed second-order optimization can overcome the ill-conditioning bottleneck in PINN training, delivering solver-class precision while retaining the flexibility of neural networks. This significantly narrows the gap between PINNs and classical numerical methods.

title: Online Resource Allocation with Continuous Random Consumption: Regret under Degeneracy
summary:
We study online resource allocation when both rewards and consumption sizes may be continuously distributed. Requests arrive sequentially and must be accepted or rejected irrevocably under fixed resource capacities. Each request belongs to one of finitely many observable types; conditional on an observable request type, both the reward and the scalar size are random, and the realized size scales a fixed type-specific resource-consumption vector. The model allows the deterministic fluid relaxation to be degenerate.
  We show that additive regret is governed by the size-weighted mass of requests whose value-to-size ratios lie near the active acceptance cutoffs. We formalize this quantity through an active weighted-mass exponent p. When p > 1, this cutoff mass is thin, and the problem is genuinely hard: every online policy must incur regret of order at least $T^{1/2 - 1/(2p)}$, and this holds for every p > 1. A sample-path marginal policy matches this lower bound up to polylogarithmic factors; and when p = 1, so that the mass grows linearly near the cutoff, it attains $O((\log T)^2)$ regret. For example, if the size and the value-to-size ratio are independent and uniformly distributed, then p = 1; if instead the size and the reward are independent and uniformly distributed, then p = 2. Thus the policy achieves $o(\sqrt{T})$ regret throughout this regularity class without any fluid non-degeneracy assumption, allowing both primal degeneracy and dual non-uniqueness.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes online resource allocation with continuous reward and consumption size distributions, establishing that regret is governed by an "active weighted-mass exponent" p. It proves a lower bound of Ω(T^{1/2 - 1/(2p)}) for p > 1, and provides a sample-path marginal policy that matches this bound while achieving O((log T)²) regret when p = 1, all without requiring fluid non-degeneracy assumptions.
AI.motivation: Prior work on online resource allocation typically assumes either discrete rewards/sizes or requires non-degenerate fluid relaxations. The authors aim to characterize regret in a general continuous setting where the deterministic fluid relaxation may be degenerate (allowing both primal degeneracy and dual non-uniqueness), and to understand what structural properties of the distribution govern the difficulty of the problem.
AI.method: The framework models requests arriving sequentially with finitely many observable types. Conditional on type, reward and scalar size are random; realized size scales a type-specific resource-consumption vector. The authors introduce the active weighted-mass exponent p, which quantifies the density of requests whose value-to-size ratios lie near the optimal acceptance cutoffs. They derive a lower bound via information-theoretic arguments and construct a sample-path marginal policy that makes acceptance decisions based on tracking the empirical distribution of arrivals against fluid-based thresholds.
AI.result: For p > 1, every online policy incurs regret at least Ω(T^{1/2 - 1/(2p)}). The proposed sample-path marginal policy matches this lower bound up to polylogarithmic factors. When p = 1 (mass grows linearly near the cutoff), regret improves to O((log T)²). Two illustrative cases: independent uniform size and value-to-size ratio yield p = 1; independent uniform size and reward yield p = 2. The policy achieves o(√T) regret throughout without fluid non-degeneracy.
AI.conclusion: The active weighted-mass exponent p cleanly characterizes the hardness of online resource allocation with continuous randomness. The sample-path marginal policy is near-optimal across the entire regularity class, and the results hold even with degenerate fluid relaxations — significantly broadening the applicability of regret bounds in this domain.

title: Distributed Attacks in Persistent-State AI Control
summary: As AI coding agents become more autonomous, they increasingly ship code iteratively, with the codebase persisting across sessions. This persistence creates a new attack surface: a misaligned or prompt-injected agent can distribute attacks across pull requests (PRs) and time its payload for the PR with the best natural cover. To study the resulting dynamics, we introduce Iterative VibeCoding, a setting for AI control, the study of safely deploying capable but potentially untrusted AI. In Iterative VibeCoding, a coding agent builds software over a sequence of PRs in a persistent codebase while pursuing a covert side task. Our benchmark includes two task families: CLI tools and Flask web services, across 20 total task variations. We use Claude Sonnet 4.5 as the attack agent and GPT-4o as the monitor. We compare gradual attacks, which distribute the side task across PRs, against non-gradual attacks concentrated in a single PR. No single monitor is robust to both: which strategy evades best (success while evading the monitor) depends on the monitor type, so a defender cannot close off both gradual and non-gradual attacks with any one monitor. High evasion (>= 65%) generalizes across model attack agent backends (Sonnet 4.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Kimi K2.5), confirming this is a property of the persistent-state attack surface rather than a single model's capability. Evasion also remains high across state-of-the-art monitor models and the gap between gradual and non-gradual evasion widens for more capable models. We introduce a stateful link-tracker monitor that tracks suspicious buildup across PRs. On both task families, it detects gradual attacks substantially better than diff monitors that merely see more accumulated history. Combining this stronger monitor with trajectory monitors in a four-monitor ensemble reduces gradual-attack evasion from 93% under the weakest standard diff monitor to 47%.

AI.tldr: Autonomous AI coding agents that persist code across sessions create a new attack surface where malicious agents can distribute covert side tasks gradually across multiple pull requests. The paper introduces Iterative VibeCoding, a benchmark showing that gradual and non-gradual attacks evade different monitors, forcing a trade-off. A novel stateful link-tracker monitor significantly reduces gradual-attack evasion when combined with trajectory monitors.
AI.motivation: As AI coding agents operate autonomously across multiple sessions with persistent codebases, they gain a new capability: distributing malicious payloads across several pull requests, timing insertion for the PR with best natural cover. This creates a fundamental control challenge — a single monitor cannot simultaneously defend against both gradual and concentrated attacks, necessitating new monitoring paradigms.
AI.method: The authors propose Iterative VibeCoding, a benchmark where Claude Sonnet 4.5 acts as an attack agent building software over sequential PRs while pursuing a covert side task. Two task families (CLI tools and Flask web services) span 20 variations. GPT-4o serves as the monitor. Gradual attacks (distributing the side task across PRs) are compared against non-gradual attacks (concentrated in one PR). A novel stateful link-tracker monitor is introduced to track suspicious buildup across PRs, and is evaluated in a four-monitor ensemble alongside trajectory monitors.
AI.result: No single monitor is robust to both gradual and non-gradual attacks — evasion strategy effectiveness depends on monitor type. High evasion (≥65%) generalizes across attack agent backends (Sonnet 4.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Kimi K2.5), confirming this is a property of the persistent-state attack surface. The evasion gap between gradual and non-gradual attacks widens for more capable models. The stateful link-tracker monitor detects gradual attacks substantially better than diff monitors with accumulated history. A four-monitor ensemble reduces gradual-attack evasion from 93% (weakest standard diff monitor) to 47%.
AI.conclusion: The persistent-state attack surface is a robust property, not model-specific. Defenders cannot rely on a single monitor type and must deploy ensembles including stateful monitors that track cross-PR buildup. The link-tracker monitor combined with trajectory monitors offers substantial improvement, but evasion remains non-trivial, indicating this is an open problem for AI control.

title: Self-explainable Operator Learning for Discovering Spatial Patterns in Functional Data
summary: Operator learning has emerged as a powerful tool for modeling complex physical systems in functional spaces. However, their neural network-based architectures make them opaque models, obscuring the reasoning behind their predictions. In this work, we introduce a self-explainable operator learning framework that overcomes this challenge by reformulating operator learning as a linear combination of generalized functional linear models expressed through integral equations. Exploiting the additive decomposability of these integral equations, we divide the input domain into subdomains and compute localized integrals to evaluate the contribution of each region to the final prediction. This decomposition enables direct interpretability where the model explains both inputs and outputs by linking specific input regions to corresponding output patterns, thereby revealing which spatial features drive predictions. We demonstrate the framework on function-to-scalar and function-to-function mappings in fluid flow problems involving blood flow and unsteady aerodynamics. The results show that the operator most often prioritizes regions with strong feature gradients, providing physically meaningful insight into the model's decision-making process. Comparisons with established post-hoc explainability methods demonstrate qualitative agreement while highlighting the key advantage of the proposed approach: explainability is embedded directly within the operator structure itself and does not require an external tool. Therefore, our framework provides a mathematically transparent and physically interpretable approach to uncover relationships within data, fostering trust in machine learning for scientific applications by enabling more informed data-driven analysis of physical systems.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a self-explainable operator learning framework that reformulates operator learning as linear combinations of generalized functional linear models via integral equations. By decomposing the input domain into subdomains and computing localized integrals, the model directly links specific input regions to output patterns, providing built-in interpretability without external post-hoc tools. Demonstrated on fluid flow problems, it reveals that the operator prioritizes regions with strong feature gradients, yielding physically meaningful insights.
AI.motivation: Neural network-based operator learning models are opaque black boxes, making it difficult to understand the reasoning behind their predictions. Existing interpretability methods rely on post-hoc external tools rather than being intrinsic to the model. There is a need for mathematically transparent operator learning that embeds explainability directly within the model structure to foster trust in scientific and engineering applications.
AI.method: The authors reformulate operator learning as a linear combination of generalized functional linear models expressed through integral equations. They exploit the additive decomposability of these integrals by partitioning the input domain into subdomains and computing localized integral contributions. The contribution of each region to the final prediction is evaluated directly, enabling inherent attribution of outputs to specific input regions without needing any post-hoc explainability technique.
AI.result: The framework was demonstrated on function-to-scalar and function-to-function mappings in blood flow and unsteady aerodynamics problems. Results show the operator consistently prioritizes spatial regions with strong feature gradients. Comparisons with established post-hoc explainability methods showed qualitative agreement, while the proposed approach's key advantage is that explainability is embedded directly in the operator structure.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework offers a mathematically transparent and physically interpretable approach to operator learning. By embedding explainability natively within the model, it reveals spatial relationships in data, builds trust in ML for scientific applications, and enables more informed data-driven analysis of physical systems without reliance on external interpretability tools.

title: Generalization in offline RL: The structure is more important than the amount of pessimism
summary: While pessimism counteracts overestimation bias in offline reinforcement learning (RL), being overly conservative has been associated with hindering certain forms of generalization. However, in this paper we demonstrate that being overly pessimistic does not inherently prevent optimal generalization in contextual MDPs (CMDPs). Instead, we argue successful generalization depends not on the amount of pessimism, but whether the pessimistic structure respects the underlying symmetries of the optimal solution. We prove that a mildly pessimistic, non-symmetric value function can generalize worse than an overly pessimistic, symmetric one. In offline RL, the structure of the pessimism is determined by the structure of the dataset coverage. As such, enforcing a symmetric value function can be non-trivial, and might require techniques such as data augmentation (DA). Inspired by our theoretical results, we argue that DA can best be applied through a consistency loss during policy extraction, rather than the common practice of (regular) offline training on an augmented dataset. This is empirically validated using IQL and CQL on a rotationally symmetric reacher environment.

AI.tldr: In contextual MDPs, generalization quality in offline RL depends not on the degree of pessimism but on whether the pessimistic structure respects the symmetries of the optimal solution. A symmetric over-pessimistic value function can outperform a mildly pessimistic asymmetric one. The authors advocate applying data augmentation via a consistency loss during policy extraction rather than during offline training on augmented data.
AI.motivation: Prior work suggests that overly conservative pessimism in offline RL hinders generalization. This paper challenges that view, arguing that the key factor is not pessimism magnitude but alignment of the pessimistic structure with underlying symmetries of the optimal policy/value function. The goal is to clarify when and why pessimism helps or hurts generalization in CMDPs.
AI.method: The authors provide a theoretical analysis in contextual MDPs, proving that a mildly pessimistic but non-symmetric value function can generalize worse than an overly pessimistic symmetric one. They show that dataset coverage structure determines pessimism structure, and that enforcing symmetry may require data augmentation. They propose applying DA through a consistency loss during policy extraction rather than standard offline training on augmented data, and validate empirically using IQL and CQL on a rotationally symmetric reacher task.
AI.result: Theoretically, symmetric pessimism outperforms asymmetric pessimism for generalization even when the former is more conservative. Empirically, applying data augmentation via consistency loss during policy extraction proves more effective than the common practice of training on an augmented dataset, as demonstrated with IQL and CQL on a rotationally symmetric reacher environment.
AI.conclusion: Over-pessimism is not inherently detrimental to generalization in offline RL; rather, the alignment of the pessimistic structure with problem symmetries is critical. Data augmentation should be applied through consistency regularization during policy extraction, not by augmenting the training dataset, to better enforce symmetric value functions.

title: Optimizing Visual Generative Models via Distribution-wise Rewards
summary: Conventional reinforcement learning strategies for visual generation typically employ sample-wise reward functions, yet this practice frequently results in reward hacking that degrades image diversity and introduces visual anomalies. To address these limitations, we present a novel framework that finetunes generative models using distribution-wise rewards, ensuring better alignment with real-world data distributions. Unlike rewards that evaluate samples individually, distribution-wise reward accounts for the data distribution of the samples, mitigating the mode collapse problem that occurs when all samples optimize towards the same direction independently. To overcome the prohibitive computational cost of estimating these rewards, we introduce a subset-replace strategy that efficiently provides reward signals by updating only a small subset of a generated reference set. Additionally, we apply RL to optimize post-hoc model merging coefficients, potentially mitigating the train-inference inconsistency caused by introducing stochastic differential equation (SDE) in regular RL practices. Extensive experiments show our approach significantly improves FID-50K across various base models, from 8.30 to 5.77 for SiT and from 3.74 to 3.52 for EDM2. Qualitative evaluation also confirms that our method enhances perceptual quality while preserving sample diversity.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a reinforcement learning framework for visual generation that uses distribution-wise rewards instead of sample-wise rewards to mitigate reward hacking, mode collapse, and diversity loss. A subset-replace strategy enables efficient reward estimation, and RL-optimized post-hoc model merging addresses train-inference inconsistency from SDE usage.
AI.motivation: Conventional RL for visual generation relies on sample-wise reward functions, which leads to reward hacking — degrading image diversity and introducing visual anomalies. The authors identify that independent per-sample optimization causes mode collapse, where all samples converge toward the same direction, misaligning with real-world data distributions.
